These people, when a long time passed over them and no warner came to them, became heedless, as though they had not been created to worship Allah. They made idols for themselves to worship besides Allah, bowing to them, prostrating to them, making vows to them and fulfilling them.

﴿So they are heedless﴾ [Yasin 6] due to the absence of anyone to awaken them. But among these people are some who had knowledge of the message. Among those who lived in the period of fatrah, there were those who had knowledge of the message yet were stubborn and remained upon what their fathers were upon, like those whom the Prophet ﷺ testified would be in the Fire. For we know with certainty that those whom the Messenger ﷺ testified would be in the Fire had the proof established against them, and were it not so, they would not be among the people of the Fire. So the people of fatrah are of two kinds: one kind, whose situation we know through the Prophet's ﷺ testimony that the message reached them, so the Messenger ﷺ ruled that they are among the people of the Fire; and others about whom we know nothing. It is obligatory upon us to withhold judgment about them and to say: "Allah knows best what they used to do." The soundest of the opinions about them is that they will be tested on the Day of Resurrection with obligations which Allah knows best. Whoever obeys among them enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys enters the Fire.

* There are benefits in the noble verse. First: it shows that this Qur'an, which defeated human beings, was not something new in their language, and that it is made of the letters from which they compose their speech. Allah's saying ﴿Yā-Sīn﴾ points to this. For this reason, whenever these alphabetic letters occur at the beginning of a surah, you will generally find after them a mention of the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the greatness of the Mighty Qur'an, because Allah swore by it, and one swears only by something great. Something may be great in its essence, or it may be honored because of the one sworn by. Those who swear by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā swear by something honored, not by something great, because it is honored in their eyes, but it is not great in itself. Those who swear by Allah and His signs swear by something great and honored in their hearts, and it is great in itself. The noble Qur'an is great in itself, isn't it?

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of the Qur'an as wise, in the three respects we mentioned, by His saying: ﴿And the wise Qur'an﴾ [Yasin 2].

* Among its benefits: the emphasis on establishing the Prophet's ﷺ messengership, because Allah swore to it and emphasized it beyond the oath with inna and the lam. Among its benefits is the affirmation of the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood, and whoever denies it is a disbeliever, because he denies Allah and His Messenger, and the consensus (ijmaʿ) of the Muslims.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of messengers, and that there were messengers other than Muhammad ﷺ, by His saying: ﴿among the messengers﴾ [Yasin 3]. For this reason Allah said in another verse: ﴿Say: "I am not an innovation among the messengers"﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 9], meaning: "I am not the first messenger, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, was preceded by messengers before him."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that what the Prophet ﷺ brought of the law is the straight path, by His saying: ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Yasin 4].

It contains as much crookedness and evil as it deviates from the law of the Prophet ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. The noble verses are many verses; by His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5].

* Among the benefits of the verses: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. How is that?

* A student: His saying ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5].

* The Shaykh: What is its aspect?

* The student: (...) it was sent down (...), subsisting in itself or subsisting in another.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and speech?

* The student: Subsisting in another.

* The Shaykh: Subsisting in another, so it follows?

* The student: Uncreated.

* The Shaykh: Uncreated. So the speech of Allah is uncreated.

* Therefore it is derived from it: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, uncreated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 1–6 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of these verses is the affirmation of Allah's highness (ʿuluw), based on His saying: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾. Descent (nuzul) only comes from above. The highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah). All five types of evidence point to the highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the affirmation of al-ʿAziz (the All-Mighty) and al-Rahim (the Most Merciful) as two of Allah's names, the affirmation of the attributes they contain, and the effect contained in al-Rahim, which is judgment (al-hukm).
* Among the benefits of these verses: al-ʿAziz in one of its meanings, which is the Victorious (al-Ghalib).
* Among the benefits of these verses: the warning to those who oppose this Quran. This is through the attribution of ﴿revelation﴾ to ﴿the All-Mighty﴾, because if it is said, for example, "This came from a mighty one (ʿaziz)," what does that indicate? It indicates a warning to, and caution against, whoever opposes it. So in this warning and caution there is a caution against opposing this revealed text, because it was sent down from the All-Mighty.
* Among the benefits of these verses: that the Quran, and indeed the whole Shariʿah, is one of the effects of Allah's mercy, based on His saying: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 5].
If you say: Where is the mercy in cutting off the hand of the thief, in stoning the married adulterer, in executing the murderer, and similar things?
The answer: The mercy in these is very clear. Cutting off the hand of the thief contains mercy toward the thief and toward others: mercy toward the thief, to deter him from stealing again, and to be an expiation (kaffarah) for his sin, because the prescribed penalties (hudud) are an expiation through which the one who commits them is forgiven. It also contains the reform of society and its protection from chaos. Is this mercy or not? There is no doubt that this is mercy. Likewise we say regarding the rest of the hudud and retaliation (qisas): it is from the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the Prophet ﷺ is a warner (mundhir), that is, one who informs in a way that includes intimidation. If you say: Is he also a bringer of good news (mubashshir)? The answer: Yes, a bringer of good news. But here the warning is mentioned without the good news. The answer to this may be given in one of two ways: either because the context requires it, since he is addressing a people who are rebellious (taghun), so warning and intimidation are most fitting for them, because they are opposers and rebellious; or it may be said that this is from the category of mentioning one of two correlatives or opposites, being sufficed by its mention from mentioning the other, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ was sent specifically to the Arabs. From those whose forefathers were not warned?
* Students: The Arabs.
* The Shaykh: The Arabs. Therefore the Jews and Christians were not sent to, since their forefathers were warned.
* A student: In other verses...
* Another student: "A people" is indefinite.
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾ is an indefinite qualified noun. So we say: the other verses indicate the generality of his message, such as His saying: ﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-A'raf 158], and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan 1], and the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "I was sent to mankind in general" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, and the wording is his (438), and Muslim with similar wording (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both]. The texts on this are many and abundant, and whoever denies them has also denied his message to the Arabs, because the category is one. But it may be asked: why did He single out the Arabs?
It is said: He singled them out for two reasons. First: he is one of them, as the Almighty said: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. Second: he personally undertook their call, and Allah guided the Arabs through his hands before his death, after which his message spread throughout the horizons.
Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned here a principle we pointed out earlier, namely that mentioning some individuals of a general ruling with a ruling that agrees with it does not require specification, as the scholars of legal theory (usul) mentioned, such as al-Shinqiti in his tafsir and others. This is the view of the majority, and it is the truth: that mentioning some individuals of a general category in a ruling does not require restricting it when it matches the ruling of the general category. So if you say, for example: "Honour the students," and then you say: "Honour Zayd, who is among them," this does not require restricting the honouring to him, because the ruling here agrees with the general ruling. Mentioning some individuals of the general category with a ruling that agrees with the general one is not a specification of it. Is this clear? In what context did we mention this?
* A student: In the chapter on tayammum.
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: In the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me a purifier" [narrated by al-Bukhari (438) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Muslim (521/3), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. In some narrations it came that it is the dust (turbah).
* The Shaykh: Its dust?
* The student: A purifier.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: So the Prophet ﷺ mentioning the dust does not suffice to mean that tayammum is not valid with anything else.
* The Shaykh: Correct, right. And likewise?
* The student: In prayer (...) between the two prostrations, in moving the finger. Here the Prophet's saying in the tashahhud does not require (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, in prayer. We also mentioned it regarding jewelry, at his saying concerning silver: "for every two hundred dirhams, one fortieth." We said: this does not require that jewelry is not subject to zakat, because mentioning some individuals of a general ruling with a ruling that agrees with the general one does not require specification.
* Among the benefits of these verses: the rebuke of those who were heedless of the messages, as in His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ [Ya-Sin 6], and that heedlessness in seeking out the message is considered blameworthy. Likewise we say of one who is heedless of researching the details of the Shariʿah. For example, whoever is heedless of researching the rulings of prayer is blameworthy, and whoever is heedless of researching the rulings of zakat while needing them, we say he is blameworthy. For this reason we say: seeking Islamic knowledge is a communal obligation (fard kifayah), and whoever wishes to perform a act of worship, learning its rulings is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) upon him.
Based on this, we say: all students of knowledge everywhere are performing a communal obligation. Therefore it is good that we keep this in mind: that in these gatherings of ours we are performing a communal obligation for which we are rewarded with the reward of an obligatory act. Allah the Almighty said: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him" [al-Bukhari (6502) with his chain from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "And My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him..." the hadith].
This is a matter that many students overlook, both in gatherings of remembrance and knowledge and in other gatherings of review. You find a person, for example, reviewing a book, but not keeping in mind that he is at that moment performing a communal obligation. This causes us to miss much good. Therefore we ask Allah to help us remember this meaning, so that we gain good from what we read and what we review (...)
* * *
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful. (5) That you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾ [Ya-Sin 5-6]. As for His saying ﴿tanzil (revelation)﴾, there are two readings in it, brother? (...)
I think what you mentioned (...).
For Allah, Mighty and Majestic; because the lam is for causation (ta'lil). So add them to it, because I think the last of the benefits we took is this verse, meaning we took nothing other than it.
* So add to the benefits: the affirmation of wisdom for Allah, derived from His saying: ﴿that you may warn﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 3):

The noble verse establishes the Last Day and recompense in it, based on His saying: ﴿He defers them until a specified term; but when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants﴾ [Fatir 45].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the Divine name "the All-Seeing" (al-Basir) for Allah, and of the attribute it contains, which is sight. Is the sight here the sight of insight or the sight of the eye? It includes both.

* Can we derive from this that a person may be punished by the loss of wealth? Yes. His saying: ﴿He leaves not on its back a single creature﴾ [Fatir 45] includes even animals. So if a person's property is destroyed, this is among the punishments for sins, whether the property is of living beings, such as animals, or of non-living things. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. All of these occur as a trial from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they also occur as a punishment, based on His saying: ﴿And whatever disaster strikes you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura 30].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom in His decree of things, a decree that is precisely firm, neither advanced nor delayed, based on His saying: ﴿But when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants﴾ [Fatir 45].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2].

The author said: "Surat Ya-Sin is Meccan." The Meccan (makki) is what was revealed before the Hijrah, not what was revealed in Mecca, since something may be revealed in Mecca after the Hijrah and be Medinan (madani). Whatever was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and whatever was revealed after it is Medinan. This is the most sound of the opinions of the scholars.

He said: "Except His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, 'Spend'…﴾ [Ya-Sin 47] etc., or it is Medinan." So the opinions on it are three: either it is entirely Meccan, or entirely Medinan, or Meccan except for His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend"﴾ [Ya-Sin 47]. What appears to be the case is that it is Meccan, because its style is the style of the Meccan surahs. Meccan surahs are distinguished from Medinan surahs by the strength of their style and the grandeur of their wording, whereas the style of the Medinan surahs is softer and gentler, because it addresses a people who had believed, and also addresses people among whom were People of the Book, who did not possess the eloquence in the Arabic language that the Arabs had.

So, Allah knows best, it is apparently Meccan. And if we hold it to be Meccan, we do not say that any part of it is excepted, because the principle is that the entire Meccan surah is Meccan and the entire Medinan surah is Medinan. Whoever claims that one verse, or two, or more is excepted must provide evidence. Merely that the meaning suits the people of Medina, for example, is not sufficient grounds for an exception, because Allah the Exalted may mention a meaning suited to the people of Medina as a preparation and a groundwork so that people may be upon insight. For this reason, Allah the Exalted mentions in the Meccan verses the stories of Musa, peace be upon him, even though attention to the story of Musa would be more fitting in Medina, because the Jews were there, whereas there were no Jews in Mecca.

The point is that some scholars, when they consider that the meaning suits a Medinan surah or Medinan rulings, go on to make exceptions and say: "Except verse so-and-so, except verse so-and-so." This is not a consistent method.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. The basmalah is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is not part of al-Fatihah, nor of any other surah. This is the most sound view. As for the one who says it is part of al-Fatihah and not of any other surah, his view is weak. Firstly, because it makes a distinction without evidence. Secondly, the authentic hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Sahih, which is: "Allah the Exalted said: 'I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves'" [[Recorded by Muslim (395/38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. This shows that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah, because it is not mentioned in this hadith. Also, the Prophet, peace be upon him, did not pronounce the basmalah aloud in his prayer. He did not pronounce the basmalah audibly. This indicates that it is not part of al-Fatihah, for otherwise he would have recited it aloud as he recited the other verses audibly.

As for its grammatical analysis (i'rab), we have mentioned it many times before: it is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) functioning as a descriptive phrase (sifah) and a described noun (mawsuf), and this prepositional phrase is dependent on an omitted element. That omitted element should be a specific verb placed later. Why is it a verb? Because the principle regarding governing words (al-'awamil) is verbs; therefore verbs govern without condition, whereas nouns that function as verbs require conditions. This is one reason. It is specific, because it is more indicative of the specific intended meaning. It is placed later for two benefits: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and conveying restriction (hasr).

When you say the basmalah for ablution, what do you estimate? "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." If you said "In the name of Allah, my beginning (ibtida'i)?" It is valid, but "beginning" is general, whereas "I perform ablution" is more specific, and bringing the more specific is more indicative of the intended meaning.

If you said: "My beginning is in the name of Allah"? It is valid, but you miss the postponement, the specification, and the verbal form. If you say "my beginning," [and not "I begin"], you miss... If you say "I begin in the name of Allah," you miss the postponement and the specification. If you say "I perform ablution in the name of Allah," you miss only the postponement.

So we estimate the element governed by the basmalah as a specific verb placed later. It is a verb because verbs are the basis of governing. It is specific because it is more indicative of the specific. It is placed later for two reasons: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, and conveying restriction, meaning: I begin with nothing except the name of Allah.

Someone may say: Can we derive evidence for this view from the text?

We say: Yes. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said while addressing the people on the day of Eid al-Adha: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah," or: "let him slaughter upon the name of Allah" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7400) and Muslim (1960/1 and 2) from the hadith of Jundab ibn Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Both wordings. This indicates that estimating the more specific is preferable to estimating the more general (...). Then, regarding its recitation in the Quran, we have mentioned that the basmalah is a prepositional phrase dependent on an omitted element (...)

[Allah is] the most knowing of the knowers, knowing even more than the pronoun, because it is a name that belongs exclusively to Allah, and no one can share it with Him. For this reason they said: the most definite of definites absolutely is the name Allah, because no one shares it with Him. A pronoun, when you say "I stood," is correct that no one else shares it with me, but it is suitable for others to use it. As for Allah, sharing in it is not valid.

As for "Ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim" (the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful), they are two attributes of Allah. Both al-Rahman and al-Rahim mean "possessor of mercy." But al-Rahman is considered as an attribute of Allah, while al-Rahim is considered as an action of His. For this reason al-Rahman is general and al-Rahim is specific. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He was ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43]. So in al-Rahman the attribute is considered, and in al-Rahim the act is considered. Therefore, since the attribute is considered in al-Rahman, it came in the patterns that indicate fullness and expansiveness, so it became in the form fa'lan.

Mercy is one of the true attributes of Allah the Glorified and Exalted, established for Him in its real sense, not figuratively. The people of ta'til (denial of attributes), among them the Ash'arites, denied it and said: Allah has no attribute called mercy, because mercy is tenderness and softness, and this is not fitting for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They interpreted it either as will, because they affirm the will, or as an act, because an act is separate from the agent, meaning the object is separate from the doer. So they interpret it either as benevolence, which is a separate created thing, or as the will to benevolence, since they affirm the will.

There is no doubt that their view is false, and that it is a denial of one of the greatest attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and one of its most prominent. Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath" [[Recorded by al-Bukhari (7422) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. And it is most astonishing that they say: the will is indicated by reason, but mercy, reason indicates its negation. How? They said: because specification indicates will. Specification means, for example, that this is a sky and that is an earth, this is a sun and that is a moon, and so on, which indicates will, because there is no specifier except by will.

As for mercy, they say: reason does not indicate it, rather it indicates its negation. We say: How strange you are! Reason's indication of mercy is more eloquent, clearer and more evident than its indication of will. Therefore you made reason's indication of will to be through specification, and this is not understood except by the elite of people. A student of knowledge, if you asked him without his having studied the matter, may not derive will from specification even though he is a student of knowledge. But mercy, everyone knows that Allah the Exalted has mercy, and proves it by reason. You can ask a common person in the market: "By Allah, rain has fallen, the land has turned green, the crops have been watered, and similar things." Where is this from? What does he tell you? "From the mercy of Allah," immediately. So he takes the blessings, which are effects of mercy, as proof of mercy. But we ask Allah for guidance for us and for you, [for He is the one] "to whom Allah has not given light, for him there is no light."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2]. The author said: "﴿Ya-Sin﴾: Allah knows best its meaning." There is no doubt that Allah knows His own meaning and the meaning of others, and He knows everything. But what is meant by these letters, or by these two letters of the alphabet? The author says: "Allah knows best," and we do not know what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intended.

Some say that the meaning of ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is "O man," so that "Ya" is a vocative particle according to their claim, and "Sin" is a word by which a human being is referred to. Others have offered other interpretations that have no basis and no evidence. But the question remains: shall we say, as the author said, "Allah knows best what He meant," regarding all the disjointed letters with which surahs begin, or shall we say that they have no meaning, in accordance with His saying: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in clear Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193–195]? The requirement of "clear Arabic speech" is that these letters have no meaning. If we judge by this general principle, "in clear Arabic speech," concerning every word or letter in the noble Quran, then we know that ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ has no meaning according to the requirement of clear Arabic speech: "Ya" has no meaning as a particle, it is a letter of the alphabet; "Sin" likewise has no meaning, it is a letter of the alphabet. This view was mentioned by Ibn Kathir from Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is a strong view, and the verse I cited bears witness to it.

So we say: these letters have no meaning. Then an objection arises if we say they have no meaning: how would Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, bring into His great Book speech that is void and meaningless?

The answer to this is that it has a great purpose. This purpose is that you, O Arabs, who were unable to oppose the Quran and produce its like, were unable to do so not because this Quran brought new letters or new words, but because it is made of the words from which you compose your speech: letters of the alphabet. For this reason you will rarely find a surah beginning with these letters that is not followed by mention of the Quran, which indicates that this is what is meant by them. This is the view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and before him al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir, and other scholars, that these are letters of the alphabet brought to demonstrate the inability of the Arabs to oppose this Quran, even though it brought nothing new in their speech.

He said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2]. The "wa" here is for an oath (qasam). It has meaning and it has a grammatical effect: its effect is to govern in the genitive (jarr), and its meaning is emphasis. An oath is the affirmation of a thing by mentioning an exalted thing in a particular form. This is an oath. It is necessary that the thing sworn by be exalted, even if only in the mind of the one swearing. It is as if the one swearing by the exalted were saying: "To the degree that I exalt this thing, and confirm it and affirm it for myself, I confirm what I swore to." To the degree of my exaltation of this thing, and my certainty about it, and my affirmation of it, I affirm the matter sworn upon. For this reason, what is sworn by must be exalted, otherwise the oath would have no benefit.

﴿The wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 2]: "Quran" here means this which we recite, the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is derived from qara'a, meaning "to recite," because it is recited; or from qara, meaning "to gather," because it is gathered and gathers. So it is derived from both meanings: from reading in the sense of recitation, and from qara in the sense of gathering, from which comes qarya (town), because it is a gathering place of people. The Quran combines both meanings: it is recited, it gathers, and it is collected. It is words gathered one to another, speech that gathers all that is good and righteous.

His saying: ﴿The wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 2]. "Al-Hakim" (the wise) is an attribute of the Quran, and it may mean muhkim (making firm), or muhkam (made firm), or hakim (judging). All of these are possible. The Quran is judging, because it must be referred to: ﴿If you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59]; ﴿This Book of Ours speaks against you with truth; indeed We were recording what you used to do﴾ [al-Jathiyah 29], if we say it is the Quran. Good, it is muhkam (made firm), because it perfects things, ﴿and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. Likewise it is muhkam, because Allah the Exalted made it firm and perfected it, so there is no contradiction or conflict in it: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa' 82]. So it also includes wisdom, does it not? Yes, it includes wisdom. So it has the meaning of wisdom and of judgment.

If it is wise, we know it is wise in its arrangement: each verse beside the next, even if we think there is no connection between them. That is only because of our deficiency or our negligence. For example, if someone said: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah 238], which came in the context of verses about the waiting period ('iddah). What is the connection? We say: there must be wisdom, but our understanding fell short of it, or we fell short in reflecting to seek it and in referring to the books of the scholars.

So it is wise in its arrangement and wise in its rulings. Its rulings are all just, in accordance with the natural disposition (fitrah) and sound reason. For this reason you will not find anything in the rulings of the Quran contradicting the natural disposition at all; rather it agrees with the natural disposition. And you will not find anything in the Quran that sound reason rejects or deems impossible at all; rather reason, in general, affirms what the Quran brings.

Likewise it is wise in its style: it is firm where firmness is needed and gentle where gentleness is needed, and it employs unusual styles not known in the styles of the Arabs. While a verse's context is declarative, it suddenly shifts to an imperative context, of interrogation, prohibition, command, or the like. All of this is part of wisdom. While the Quran speaks in the third person, it suddenly shifts to the second person. It moves from one style to another, which is called iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and its kinds are many in the Quran.

So the Quran is wise in every sense of wisdom, and in every sense of making firm, and in every sense of judgment.

The author, limiting himself to one of these meanings, said: "Muhkam in wondrous composition and marvelous meanings." He mentioned one meaning of al-Hakim, while we have mentioned three: possessing wisdom, muhkim, and muhkam. Muhkim, muhkam, and also hakim. We mentioned that it is judging, possessing wisdom, judgment, and making firm. So it includes more than what the author said. This is what is sworn by. Allah the Exalted's swearing by His great Book, or by His wise Book, indicates the greatness of this Quran and the greatness of what it brought of firmness, wisdom and judgment.

Then he mentioned what is sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed you [are]﴾ [Ya-Sin 3], O Muhammad, ﴿among the messengers﴾. So Allah the Exalted swore by His Book that Muhammad (ﷺ) is among the messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 3):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Yasin 3]. This is because the messengers came before him, and he is the Seal of the Messengers and the most complete in law. He came to perfect noble character. The Prophet ﷺ compared his message to "a man who built a palace and perfected it, leaving out the place of one brick. People went around it, marvelling at it, except for the place of that brick. He said: 'I am that brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets.'"[[Al-Bukhari, whose wording this is (3534), and Muslim (2287/23), with their chains, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "My example and the example of the prophets is like a man who built a house, perfected it and beautified it, except for the place of one brick. People enter it and marvel and say: 'If only the place of that brick were filled.'"]]

This sentence, ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾, is emphasized by three emphatics: the oath, inna (indeed), and the lam (the emphatic lam). His saying: ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Yasin 4] is connected to what precedes it, which is ﴿the messengers﴾. Mursal is a passive participle that is able to govern an object. The meaning is: "Indeed, you are among those who were sent upon a straight path," because all the messengers were upon a straight path without doubt. However, there is another possibility that is better than what the author said: that ﴿upon a straight path﴾ is a second predicate of inna. So: "Indeed, you are among the messengers. Indeed, you are upon a straight path." This is more fitting, and what supports it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path (52), the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ash-Shura 52–53].

So we say: the second possibility in the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Yasin 4] is that it is a second predicate of inna. His saying: ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Yasin 4]: he said, meaning: the way of the prophets before you was monotheism and guidance.

﴿A straight path﴾: ﴿ṣirāṭ﴾ is on the pattern fiʿāl in the sense of mafʿūl (passive), because fiʿāl often comes in the sense of mafʿūl, as in their saying: binā' (building), ghirās (planting) and firāsh (bedding) meaning mabnī (built), maghrūs (planted), mafrūsh (spread out). Ṣirāṭ (fiʿāl) means maṣrūṭ (swallowed or traversed), i.e., "that which is passed over quickly." Al-ṣarṭ is passing through quickly, and from it comes their saying: ṣarṭa al-luqmah, meaning he swallowed the morsel quickly. In our colloquial language we say zarṭ, and it is an Arabic usage. Ṣirāṭ also appears as sirāṭ with the letter sīn, and as zirāṭ with the letter zāy, all of which are Arabic.

The ṣirāṭ is not a ṣirāṭ unless it is a wide road that can bear groups crossing over it. They said: among its attributes is that it is level, with no ascent or descent. And ﴿straight﴾ (mustaqīm) is an emphatic descriptor of it, meaning that there is no crookedness in it.

There is no doubt that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is a straight path, because it is a wide road that accommodates the whole Ummah from the time he was sent until the Hour is established. It cannot be lost. It is also a wide path, and it can never be too narrow for the legal rulings. Every event that occurs from the time the Messenger ﷺ was sent until the Day of Resurrection must have a solution to its problem, if it is a problem, within what the Messenger ﷺ brought. For this reason we say that this legislation in the Qur'an and Sunnah is complete and needs no completion, and it is also wide and can never be constricted by any part or detail that occurs until the Day of Resurrection.

So is there anything problematic in the Sharia or not? But the difficulty only comes from people: either from a deficiency in understanding, or from negligence in seeking knowledge and guidance, or from things that have covered their hearts and darkened them so that they cannot see the truth. A person may be neither negligent nor deficient; he may have strong understanding, a strong faculty and knowledge, but there may be sins upon his heart that stand between him and seeing what is correct. For this reason, when a matter becomes unclear to a person after reviewing and tracing the words of the scholars, he should frequently seek forgiveness, because seeking forgiveness is how Allah wipes out sins, so the heart becomes illuminated. This may be deduced from the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you might judge between the people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be a advocate for the treacherous. And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [An-Nisa' 105–106].

It is also supported by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says: "Legends of the former peoples." (13) No! Rather, what they used to earn has covered their hearts﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 13–14]. So sins prevented their hearts from seeing the truth of this Book, until one of them said: "They are the legends of the former peoples."

The summary is that we say: this religion is a straight path, wide, which accommodates all people when they enter it, wide enough to include the rulings for all events and occurrences from the time the Messenger ﷺ was sent until the Hour is established. But the difficulty that arises either comes from our deficiency or our negligence, or from matters that have covered hearts so that they do not see the truth (...)

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Yā-Sīn (1). By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Yasin 1–2]. What is the meaning of His saying "Yā-Sīn"? (...)

By the oath and other emphatics: the oath is emphasis in His saying ﴿By the Qur'an﴾, and other emphatics. That is, inna and the lam are a response to the disbelievers' saying to him: "You are not a messenger," as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "You are not a messenger."﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 43].

So the statement fits the requirement of the situation, because it addresses one who denies. It has already been mentioned in rhetoric (balaghah) that when one who denies is addressed, the statement must be emphasized for him. The rhetoricians say: the addressee has three levels: one who denies, one who is hesitant, and one who has in his mind neither denial nor hesitation. They said: if he denies, emphasis of the statement is required for him; if he is hesitant, emphasis is preferable; and if there is nothing in his mind, the statement is delivered to him without emphasis. This is the basic principle.

If you are addressing a person who has nothing in his mind about the content of the statement, deliver the statement to him without emphasis. You say: "Zayd is standing." If you are addressing one who is hesitant about the truth of the statement, emphasize it for him: is that obligatory or recommended? It is recommended. If you are addressing one who denies, it is obligatory that you emphasize the statement for him. This is the principle.

Emphasis may be omitted where it is called for, and emphasis may come where it is not called for, for reasons known from the context. Here the disbelievers say, "You are not a messenger," so emphasizing the statement about the message was required for them, meaning it is demanded by rhetoric. The obligation here is not the legal obligation whose neglect is sinful, but the obligation from the standpoint of rhetoric.

He said: ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5]. ﴿Revelation﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is "he," meaning the Qur'an: ﴿the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾.

And ﴿tanzīl﴾ is a verbal noun from "nazzala, yunazzilu" (to send down gradually), and the Qur'an is described as munazzal (sent down gradually) and munzal (sent down). Munazzal means that it is sent down bit by bit, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided that you might recite it to the people over time, and We have sent it down in stages﴾ [Al-Isra' 106]. It descends bit by bit. Sometimes the Qur'an is described as having been sent down (unzila) with regard to its completion. In terms of completion, it has been sent down in its entirety, and in terms of its gradual descent, it has been sent down in stages. Likewise, with rain in the Qur'an: sometimes it says ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾ [Qaf 9], and ﴿He sends down from the sky water﴾ [Al-An'am 99]. Because rain descends bit by bit, one says "nazzalna" (We sent down gradually), and with regard to its completion and gathering all together, one says "anzalna" (We sent down).

His saying: ﴿the revelation of the Mighty﴾: the author said, "in His dominion," meaning the Victorious in His dominion, over which none prevails. It has been mentioned to us in the chapter on creed that al-'Azīz is one of Allah's names, and that might (al-'izza) has three meanings: might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr), might of subjugation (ʿizzat al-qahr), and might of invulnerability (ʿizzat al-imtināʿ). Three. What are they?

* A student: Might of rank, might of invulnerability, might of subjugation.

* The Shaykh: Yes. Might of rank, meaning He is of great and lofty rank. Might of subjugation, meaning He is the Subduer, the Victorious. Might of invulnerability, meaning He is strong, and nothing can reach Him. Ibn al-Qayyim said:

"He is the Mighty, so His threshold cannot be approached; / how can the threshold of the possessor of authority be approached?"

So He, may He be exalted, is Mighty, invulnerable to harm. From this comes al-arḍ al-ʿazāz (hard, firm ground) because of its strength and hardness. So the author's statement "the Mighty in His dominion" is deficient.

He said: ﴿the Merciful﴾, "to His creation." Here we say: al-Raḥīm is general, because it is not restricted, so it means general mercy. He, may He be exalted, is merciful to all His creation. There is no creature on earth except that its provision is upon Allah. Even the disbeliever is given by Allah reason, health, children, wealth and spouses. But this is general mercy. As for the mercy specific to the believers, it is in His saying: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 43].

He said: ﴿the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5], "to His creation." Here He attributed the revelation of the Qur'an to these two names, as an indication of the obligation to act upon what came in the Qur'an, and that whoever does not act upon it, before him is the Mighty who will seize him with the seizure of one who is mighty and powerful.

﴿The Merciful﴾ is an indication that this Qur'an's revelation is part of the requirement of His mercy to His creation, because Allah, the Exalted, has shown no mercy to His creation greater than sending down the noble Qur'an, because by it is life: the life of the heart, the body, the individual and the society. So there is in it an indication, as I said, indeed a warning to those who oppose this Qur'an, that it was sent down from the Mighty who takes vengeance on whoever opposes it. "The Merciful" is an indication that this Qur'an is part of the requirement of His mercy, may He be exalted.

He said: "(predicate of an estimated subject)." What is meant by "predicate of an estimated subject"? ﴿Tanzīl﴾ in the nominative means "the Qur'an," meaning the estimate is: the Qur'an is the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful. In a seven-canonical reading: ﴿tanzīla al-ʿazīz al-raḥīm﴾, and on this reading it is in the accusative as a verbal noun whose governing verb is omitted, meaning: "It was sent down, the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful."

He said: ﴿to warn﴾ [Yasin 6] with it ﴿a people﴾ is connected to ﴿tanzīl﴾. The lam in ﴿li-tundhira﴾ is called the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlīl), and the verb after it is in the subjunctive by it. According to the school that says it is governed by the lam, or by "an"?

* A student: By the lam.

* The Shaykh: By the lam. According to the Basran school, it is governed by "an" (that) implied after the lam. In any case, it requires a complement. The lam in ﴿li-tundhira﴾ requires a complement, so where is its complement? It is His saying ﴿tanzīl﴾, meaning the revelation of the Merciful, the Compassionate, ﴿li-tundhira﴾, meaning it was sent down ﴿that you might warn a people, to whom no warner had come before them, that they might be guided﴾ [Yasin 6]. Warn.

The scholars said: warning (inadhār) is notification combined with intimidation, or containing intimidation. For example, a man comes to his people shouting: "The enemy! The enemy!" It is said: "This is a warner (mundhir) and a nadhīr," because the nadhīr is about something that frightens, so it is notification containing intimidation. This Qur'an was sent down by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that the Prophet ﷺ might warn with it a people whose fathers were not warned, meaning they were not warned in a time of fatrah (interval between prophets). On this basis, "mā" is negating, meaning: "so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned," i.e., they were not warned, not frightened, but this was in a period of fatrah. As for before that, they had been warned through Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, for he was sent to the Arabs, to his people. After that, these people were not warned.

Some grammarians who gather all the opinions, whether they are correct or not, said that any possibility may be claimed. They say: it is possible that "mā" is a relative pronoun, meaning "so that you may warn a people, the one whose fathers warned them," making "mā" a relative pronoun and the returning pronoun omitted, with the estimate "those whom their fathers warned," meaning "to warn them, what their fathers were warned of." But although this is possible from the standpoint of wording, it is far-fetched from the standpoint of meaning, because numerous verses show that the Quraysh, to whom the Messenger ﷺ was sent, had not been warned by their fathers. Among them is His saying in Surah (Alif Lam Mim, Tanzil), As-Sajda: ﴿That you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [As-Sajda 3]. This is explicit that "mā" here is purely negating.

﴿So they are heedless﴾ [Yasin 6], meaning the people are heedless of faith and right guidance, because no warner came to them. It is well known that warnings produce life in hearts and awakening. For this reason, you find that when a person is not visited by a preacher, he becomes heedless, and heedlessness increases in him. When a preacher comes to him, it is as if he has awakened him from sleep. These people, when a long time passed over them and no warner came to them, became heedless, as though they had not been created to worship Allah. They made idols for themselves to worship besides Allah, bowing to them, prostrating to them, making vows to them and fulfilling them.

﴿So they are heedless﴾ [Yasin 6] due to the absence of anyone to awaken them. But among these people are some who had knowledge of the message. Among those who lived in the period of fatrah, there were those who had knowledge of the message yet were stubborn and remained upon what their fathers were upon, like those whom the Prophet ﷺ testified would be in the Fire. For we know with certainty that those whom the Messenger ﷺ testified would be in the Fire had the proof established against them, and were it not so, they would not be among the people of the Fire. So the people of fatrah are of two kinds: one kind, whose situation we know through the Prophet's ﷺ testimony that the message reached them, so the Messenger ﷺ ruled that they are among the people of the Fire; and others about whom we know nothing. It is obligatory upon us to withhold judgment about them and to say: "Allah knows best what they used to do." The soundest of the opinions about them is that they will be tested on the Day of Resurrection with obligations which Allah knows best. Whoever obeys among them enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys enters the Fire.

* There are benefits in the noble verse. First: it shows that this Qur'an, which defeated human beings, was not something new in their language, and that it is made of the letters from which they compose their speech. Allah's saying ﴿Yā-Sīn﴾ points to this. For this reason, whenever these alphabetic letters occur at the beginning of a surah, you will generally find after them a mention of the Qur'an.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the greatness of the Mighty Qur'an, because Allah swore by it, and one swears only by something great. Something may be great in its essence, or it may be honored because of the one sworn by. Those who swear by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā swear by something honored, not by something great, because it is honored in their eyes, but it is not great in itself. Those who swear by Allah and His signs swear by something great and honored in their hearts, and it is great in itself. The noble Qur'an is great in itself, isn't it?

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of the Qur'an as wise, in the three respects we mentioned, by His saying: ﴿And the wise Qur'an﴾ [Yasin 2].

* Among its benefits: the emphasis on establishing the Prophet's ﷺ messengership, because Allah swore to it and emphasized it beyond the oath with inna and the lam. Among its benefits is the affirmation of the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood, and whoever denies it is a disbeliever, because he denies Allah and His Messenger, and the consensus (ijmaʿ) of the Muslims.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of messengers, and that there were messengers other than Muhammad ﷺ, by His saying: ﴿among the messengers﴾ [Yasin 3]. For this reason Allah said in another verse: ﴿Say: "I am not an innovation among the messengers"﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 9], meaning: "I am not the first messenger, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, was preceded by messengers before him."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that what the Prophet ﷺ brought of the law is the straight path, by His saying: ﴿upon a straight path﴾ [Yasin 4].

It contains as much crookedness and evil as it deviates from the law of the Prophet ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. The noble verses are many verses; by His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5].

* Among the benefits of the verses: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. How is that?

* A student: His saying ﴿The revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Yasin 5].

* The Shaykh: What is its aspect?

* The student: (...) it was sent down (...), subsisting in itself or subsisting in another.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and speech?

* The student: Subsisting in another.

* The Shaykh: Subsisting in another, so it follows?

* The student: Uncreated.

* The Shaykh: Uncreated. So the speech of Allah is uncreated.

* Therefore it is derived from it: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, uncreated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 1–6 (part 3 of 3):

* Among the benefits of these verses is the affirmation of Allah's highness (ʿuluw), based on His saying: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾. Descent (nuzul) only comes from above. The highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma'), reason, and innate nature (fitrah). All five types of evidence point to the highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the affirmation of al-ʿAziz (the All-Mighty) and al-Rahim (the Most Merciful) as two of Allah's names, the affirmation of the attributes they contain, and the effect contained in al-Rahim, which is judgment (al-hukm).
* Among the benefits of these verses: al-ʿAziz in one of its meanings, which is the Victorious (al-Ghalib).
* Among the benefits of these verses: the warning to those who oppose this Quran. This is through the attribution of ﴿revelation﴾ to ﴿the All-Mighty﴾, because if it is said, for example, "This came from a mighty one (ʿaziz)," what does that indicate? It indicates a warning to, and caution against, whoever opposes it. So in this warning and caution there is a caution against opposing this revealed text, because it was sent down from the All-Mighty.
* Among the benefits of these verses: that the Quran, and indeed the whole Shariʿah, is one of the effects of Allah's mercy, based on His saying: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 5].
If you say: Where is the mercy in cutting off the hand of the thief, in stoning the married adulterer, in executing the murderer, and similar things?
The answer: The mercy in these is very clear. Cutting off the hand of the thief contains mercy toward the thief and toward others: mercy toward the thief, to deter him from stealing again, and to be an expiation (kaffarah) for his sin, because the prescribed penalties (hudud) are an expiation through which the one who commits them is forgiven. It also contains the reform of society and its protection from chaos. Is this mercy or not? There is no doubt that this is mercy. Likewise we say regarding the rest of the hudud and retaliation (qisas): it is from the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the Prophet ﷺ is a warner (mundhir), that is, one who informs in a way that includes intimidation. If you say: Is he also a bringer of good news (mubashshir)? The answer: Yes, a bringer of good news. But here the warning is mentioned without the good news. The answer to this may be given in one of two ways: either because the context requires it, since he is addressing a people who are rebellious (taghun), so warning and intimidation are most fitting for them, because they are opposers and rebellious; or it may be said that this is from the category of mentioning one of two correlatives or opposites, being sufficed by its mention from mentioning the other, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ was sent specifically to the Arabs. From those whose forefathers were not warned?
* Students: The Arabs.
* The Shaykh: The Arabs. Therefore the Jews and Christians were not sent to, since their forefathers were warned.
* A student: In other verses...
* Another student: "A people" is indefinite.
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾ is an indefinite qualified noun. So we say: the other verses indicate the generality of his message, such as His saying: ﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [al-A'raf 158], and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan 1], and the Prophet's saying ﷺ: "I was sent to mankind in general" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari, and the wording is his (438), and Muslim with similar wording (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both]. The texts on this are many and abundant, and whoever denies them has also denied his message to the Arabs, because the category is one. But it may be asked: why did He single out the Arabs?
It is said: He singled them out for two reasons. First: he is one of them, as the Almighty said: ﴿It is He who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. Second: he personally undertook their call, and Allah guided the Arabs through his hands before his death, after which his message spread throughout the horizons.
Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned here a principle we pointed out earlier, namely that mentioning some individuals of a general ruling with a ruling that agrees with it does not require specification, as the scholars of legal theory (usul) mentioned, such as al-Shinqiti in his tafsir and others. This is the view of the majority, and it is the truth: that mentioning some individuals of a general category in a ruling does not require restricting it when it matches the ruling of the general category. So if you say, for example: "Honour the students," and then you say: "Honour Zayd, who is among them," this does not require restricting the honouring to him, because the ruling here agrees with the general ruling. Mentioning some individuals of the general category with a ruling that agrees with the general one is not a specification of it. Is this clear? In what context did we mention this?
* A student: In the chapter on tayammum.
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: In the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The earth has been made for me a purifier" [narrated by al-Bukhari (438) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Muslim (521/3), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. In some narrations it came that it is the dust (turbah).
* The Shaykh: Its dust?
* The student: A purifier.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: So the Prophet ﷺ mentioning the dust does not suffice to mean that tayammum is not valid with anything else.
* The Shaykh: Correct, right. And likewise?
* The student: In prayer (...) between the two prostrations, in moving the finger. Here the Prophet's saying in the tashahhud does not require (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, in prayer. We also mentioned it regarding jewelry, at his saying concerning silver: "for every two hundred dirhams, one fortieth." We said: this does not require that jewelry is not subject to zakat, because mentioning some individuals of a general ruling with a ruling that agrees with the general one does not require specification.
* Among the benefits of these verses: the rebuke of those who were heedless of the messages, as in His saying: ﴿so they are heedless﴾ [Ya-Sin 6], and that heedlessness in seeking out the message is considered blameworthy. Likewise we say of one who is heedless of researching the details of the Shariʿah. For example, whoever is heedless of researching the rulings of prayer is blameworthy, and whoever is heedless of researching the rulings of zakat while needing them, we say he is blameworthy. For this reason we say: seeking Islamic knowledge is a communal obligation (fard kifayah), and whoever wishes to perform a act of worship, learning its rulings is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) upon him.
Based on this, we say: all students of knowledge everywhere are performing a communal obligation. Therefore it is good that we keep this in mind: that in these gatherings of ours we are performing a communal obligation for which we are rewarded with the reward of an obligatory act. Allah the Almighty said: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him" [al-Bukhari (6502) with his chain from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "And My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him..." the hadith].
This is a matter that many students overlook, both in gatherings of remembrance and knowledge and in other gatherings of review. You find a person, for example, reviewing a book, but not keeping in mind that he is at that moment performing a communal obligation. This causes us to miss much good. Therefore we ask Allah to help us remember this meaning, so that we gain good from what we read and what we review (...)
* * *
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿The revelation of the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful. (5) That you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾ [Ya-Sin 5-6]. As for His saying ﴿tanzil (revelation)﴾, there are two readings in it, brother? (...)
I think what you mentioned (...).
For Allah, Mighty and Majestic; because the lam is for causation (ta'lil). So add them to it, because I think the last of the benefits we took is this verse, meaning we took nothing other than it.
* So add to the benefits: the affirmation of wisdom for Allah, derived from His saying: ﴿that you may warn﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 3):

The noble verse establishes the Last Day and recompense in it, based on His saying: ﴿He defers them until a specified term; but when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants﴾ [Fatir 45].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the Divine name "the All-Seeing" (al-Basir) for Allah, and of the attribute it contains, which is sight. Is the sight here the sight of insight or the sight of the eye? It includes both.

* Can we derive from this that a person may be punished by the loss of wealth? Yes. His saying: ﴿He leaves not on its back a single creature﴾ [Fatir 45] includes even animals. So if a person's property is destroyed, this is among the punishments for sins, whether the property is of living beings, such as animals, or of non-living things. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. All of these occur as a trial from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and they also occur as a punishment, based on His saying: ﴿And whatever disaster strikes you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura 30].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom in His decree of things, a decree that is precisely firm, neither advanced nor delayed, based on His saying: ﴿But when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants﴾ [Fatir 45].

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2].

The author said: "Surat Ya-Sin is Meccan." The Meccan (makki) is what was revealed before the Hijrah, not what was revealed in Mecca, since something may be revealed in Mecca after the Hijrah and be Medinan (madani). Whatever was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and whatever was revealed after it is Medinan. This is the most sound of the opinions of the scholars.

He said: "Except His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, 'Spend'…﴾ [Ya-Sin 47] etc., or it is Medinan." So the opinions on it are three: either it is entirely Meccan, or entirely Medinan, or Meccan except for His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend"﴾ [Ya-Sin 47]. What appears to be the case is that it is Meccan, because its style is the style of the Meccan surahs. Meccan surahs are distinguished from Medinan surahs by the strength of their style and the grandeur of their wording, whereas the style of the Medinan surahs is softer and gentler, because it addresses a people who had believed, and also addresses people among whom were People of the Book, who did not possess the eloquence in the Arabic language that the Arabs had.

So, Allah knows best, it is apparently Meccan. And if we hold it to be Meccan, we do not say that any part of it is excepted, because the principle is that the entire Meccan surah is Meccan and the entire Medinan surah is Medinan. Whoever claims that one verse, or two, or more is excepted must provide evidence. Merely that the meaning suits the people of Medina, for example, is not sufficient grounds for an exception, because Allah the Exalted may mention a meaning suited to the people of Medina as a preparation and a groundwork so that people may be upon insight. For this reason, Allah the Exalted mentions in the Meccan verses the stories of Musa, peace be upon him, even though attention to the story of Musa would be more fitting in Medina, because the Jews were there, whereas there were no Jews in Mecca.

The point is that some scholars, when they consider that the meaning suits a Medinan surah or Medinan rulings, go on to make exceptions and say: "Except verse so-and-so, except verse so-and-so." This is not a consistent method.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. The basmalah is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is not part of al-Fatihah, nor of any other surah. This is the most sound view. As for the one who says it is part of al-Fatihah and not of any other surah, his view is weak. Firstly, because it makes a distinction without evidence. Secondly, the authentic hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Sahih, which is: "Allah the Exalted said: 'I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves'" [[Recorded by Muslim (395/38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. This shows that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatihah, because it is not mentioned in this hadith. Also, the Prophet, peace be upon him, did not pronounce the basmalah aloud in his prayer. He did not pronounce the basmalah audibly. This indicates that it is not part of al-Fatihah, for otherwise he would have recited it aloud as he recited the other verses audibly.

As for its grammatical analysis (i'rab), we have mentioned it many times before: it is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) functioning as a descriptive phrase (sifah) and a described noun (mawsuf), and this prepositional phrase is dependent on an omitted element. That omitted element should be a specific verb placed later. Why is it a verb? Because the principle regarding governing words (al-'awamil) is verbs; therefore verbs govern without condition, whereas nouns that function as verbs require conditions. This is one reason. It is specific, because it is more indicative of the specific intended meaning. It is placed later for two benefits: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and conveying restriction (hasr).

When you say the basmalah for ablution, what do you estimate? "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." If you said "In the name of Allah, my beginning (ibtida'i)?" It is valid, but "beginning" is general, whereas "I perform ablution" is more specific, and bringing the more specific is more indicative of the intended meaning.

If you said: "My beginning is in the name of Allah"? It is valid, but you miss the postponement, the specification, and the verbal form. If you say "my beginning," [and not "I begin"], you miss... If you say "I begin in the name of Allah," you miss the postponement and the specification. If you say "I perform ablution in the name of Allah," you miss only the postponement.

So we estimate the element governed by the basmalah as a specific verb placed later. It is a verb because verbs are the basis of governing. It is specific because it is more indicative of the specific. It is placed later for two reasons: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah, and conveying restriction, meaning: I begin with nothing except the name of Allah.

Someone may say: Can we derive evidence for this view from the text?

We say: Yes. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said while addressing the people on the day of Eid al-Adha: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah," or: "let him slaughter upon the name of Allah" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7400) and Muslim (1960/1 and 2) from the hadith of Jundab ibn Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Both wordings. This indicates that estimating the more specific is preferable to estimating the more general (...). Then, regarding its recitation in the Quran, we have mentioned that the basmalah is a prepositional phrase dependent on an omitted element (...)

[Allah is] the most knowing of the knowers, knowing even more than the pronoun, because it is a name that belongs exclusively to Allah, and no one can share it with Him. For this reason they said: the most definite of definites absolutely is the name Allah, because no one shares it with Him. A pronoun, when you say "I stood," is correct that no one else shares it with me, but it is suitable for others to use it. As for Allah, sharing in it is not valid.

As for "Ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim" (the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful), they are two attributes of Allah. Both al-Rahman and al-Rahim mean "possessor of mercy." But al-Rahman is considered as an attribute of Allah, while al-Rahim is considered as an action of His. For this reason al-Rahman is general and al-Rahim is specific. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He was ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab 43]. So in al-Rahman the attribute is considered, and in al-Rahim the act is considered. Therefore, since the attribute is considered in al-Rahman, it came in the patterns that indicate fullness and expansiveness, so it became in the form fa'lan.

Mercy is one of the true attributes of Allah the Glorified and Exalted, established for Him in its real sense, not figuratively. The people of ta'til (denial of attributes), among them the Ash'arites, denied it and said: Allah has no attribute called mercy, because mercy is tenderness and softness, and this is not fitting for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They interpreted it either as will, because they affirm the will, or as an act, because an act is separate from the agent, meaning the object is separate from the doer. So they interpret it either as benevolence, which is a separate created thing, or as the will to benevolence, since they affirm the will.

There is no doubt that their view is false, and that it is a denial of one of the greatest attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and one of its most prominent. Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath" [[Recorded by al-Bukhari (7422) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. And it is most astonishing that they say: the will is indicated by reason, but mercy, reason indicates its negation. How? They said: because specification indicates will. Specification means, for example, that this is a sky and that is an earth, this is a sun and that is a moon, and so on, which indicates will, because there is no specifier except by will.

As for mercy, they say: reason does not indicate it, rather it indicates its negation. We say: How strange you are! Reason's indication of mercy is more eloquent, clearer and more evident than its indication of will. Therefore you made reason's indication of will to be through specification, and this is not understood except by the elite of people. A student of knowledge, if you asked him without his having studied the matter, may not derive will from specification even though he is a student of knowledge. But mercy, everyone knows that Allah the Exalted has mercy, and proves it by reason. You can ask a common person in the market: "By Allah, rain has fallen, the land has turned green, the crops have been watered, and similar things." Where is this from? What does he tell you? "From the mercy of Allah," immediately. So he takes the blessings, which are effects of mercy, as proof of mercy. But we ask Allah for guidance for us and for you, [for He is the one] "to whom Allah has not given light, for him there is no light."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2]. The author said: "﴿Ya-Sin﴾: Allah knows best its meaning." There is no doubt that Allah knows His own meaning and the meaning of others, and He knows everything. But what is meant by these letters, or by these two letters of the alphabet? The author says: "Allah knows best," and we do not know what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intended.

Some say that the meaning of ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ is "O man," so that "Ya" is a vocative particle according to their claim, and "Sin" is a word by which a human being is referred to. Others have offered other interpretations that have no basis and no evidence. But the question remains: shall we say, as the author said, "Allah knows best what He meant," regarding all the disjointed letters with which surahs begin, or shall we say that they have no meaning, in accordance with His saying: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in clear Arabic speech﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193–195]? The requirement of "clear Arabic speech" is that these letters have no meaning. If we judge by this general principle, "in clear Arabic speech," concerning every word or letter in the noble Quran, then we know that ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ has no meaning according to the requirement of clear Arabic speech: "Ya" has no meaning as a particle, it is a letter of the alphabet; "Sin" likewise has no meaning, it is a letter of the alphabet. This view was mentioned by Ibn Kathir from Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is a strong view, and the verse I cited bears witness to it.

So we say: these letters have no meaning. Then an objection arises if we say they have no meaning: how would Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, bring into His great Book speech that is void and meaningless?

The answer to this is that it has a great purpose. This purpose is that you, O Arabs, who were unable to oppose the Quran and produce its like, were unable to do so not because this Quran brought new letters or new words, but because it is made of the words from which you compose your speech: letters of the alphabet. For this reason you will rarely find a surah beginning with these letters that is not followed by mention of the Quran, which indicates that this is what is meant by them. This is the view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and before him al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir, and other scholars, that these are letters of the alphabet brought to demonstrate the inability of the Arabs to oppose this Quran, even though it brought nothing new in their speech.

He said: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 1–2]. The "wa" here is for an oath (qasam). It has meaning and it has a grammatical effect: its effect is to govern in the genitive (jarr), and its meaning is emphasis. An oath is the affirmation of a thing by mentioning an exalted thing in a particular form. This is an oath. It is necessary that the thing sworn by be exalted, even if only in the mind of the one swearing. It is as if the one swearing by the exalted were saying: "To the degree that I exalt this thing, and confirm it and affirm it for myself, I confirm what I swore to." To the degree of my exaltation of this thing, and my certainty about it, and my affirmation of it, I affirm the matter sworn upon. For this reason, what is sworn by must be exalted, otherwise the oath would have no benefit.

﴿The wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 2]: "Quran" here means this which we recite, the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is derived from qara'a, meaning "to recite," because it is recited; or from qara, meaning "to gather," because it is gathered and gathers. So it is derived from both meanings: from reading in the sense of recitation, and from qara in the sense of gathering, from which comes qarya (town), because it is a gathering place of people. The Quran combines both meanings: it is recited, it gathers, and it is collected. It is words gathered one to another, speech that gathers all that is good and righteous.

His saying: ﴿The wise Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 2]. "Al-Hakim" (the wise) is an attribute of the Quran, and it may mean muhkim (making firm), or muhkam (made firm), or hakim (judging). All of these are possible. The Quran is judging, because it must be referred to: ﴿If you disagree about anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59]; ﴿This Book of Ours speaks against you with truth; indeed We were recording what you used to do﴾ [al-Jathiyah 29], if we say it is the Quran. Good, it is muhkam (made firm), because it perfects things, ﴿and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. Likewise it is muhkam, because Allah the Exalted made it firm and perfected it, so there is no contradiction or conflict in it: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa' 82]. So it also includes wisdom, does it not? Yes, it includes wisdom. So it has the meaning of wisdom and of judgment.

If it is wise, we know it is wise in its arrangement: each verse beside the next, even if we think there is no connection between them. That is only because of our deficiency or our negligence. For example, if someone said: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah 238], which came in the context of verses about the waiting period ('iddah). What is the connection? We say: there must be wisdom, but our understanding fell short of it, or we fell short in reflecting to seek it and in referring to the books of the scholars.

So it is wise in its arrangement and wise in its rulings. Its rulings are all just, in accordance with the natural disposition (fitrah) and sound reason. For this reason you will not find anything in the rulings of the Quran contradicting the natural disposition at all; rather it agrees with the natural disposition. And you will not find anything in the Quran that sound reason rejects or deems impossible at all; rather reason, in general, affirms what the Quran brings.

Likewise it is wise in its style: it is firm where firmness is needed and gentle where gentleness is needed, and it employs unusual styles not known in the styles of the Arabs. While a verse's context is declarative, it suddenly shifts to an imperative context, of interrogation, prohibition, command, or the like. All of this is part of wisdom. While the Quran speaks in the third person, it suddenly shifts to the second person. It moves from one style to another, which is called iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and its kinds are many in the Quran.

So the Quran is wise in every sense of wisdom, and in every sense of making firm, and in every sense of judgment.

The author, limiting himself to one of these meanings, said: "Muhkam in wondrous composition and marvelous meanings." He mentioned one meaning of al-Hakim, while we have mentioned three: possessing wisdom, muhkim, and muhkam. Muhkim, muhkam, and also hakim. We mentioned that it is judging, possessing wisdom, judgment, and making firm. So it includes more than what the author said. This is what is sworn by. Allah the Exalted's swearing by His great Book, or by His wise Book, indicates the greatness of this Quran and the greatness of what it brought of firmness, wisdom and judgment.

Then he mentioned what is sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed you [are]﴾ [Ya-Sin 3], O Muhammad, ﴿among the messengers﴾. So Allah the Exalted swore by His Book that Muhammad (ﷺ) is among the messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 1–6 (part 2 of 3):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾ [Yasin 3]. This is because the messengers came before him, and he is the Seal of the Messengers and the most complete in law. He came to perfect noble character. The Prophet ﷺ compared his message to "a man who built a palace and perfected it, leaving out the place of one brick. People went around it, marvelling at it, except for the place of that brick. He said: 'I am that brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets.'"[[Al-Bukhari, whose wording this is (3534), and Muslim (2287/23), with their chains, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "My example and the example of the prophets is like a man who built a house, perfected it and beautified it, except for the place of one brick. People enter it and marvel and say: 'If only the place of that brick were filled.'"]]

This sentence, ﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers﴾, is emphasized by three emphatics: the oath, inna (indeed), and the lam (the emphatic lam).
