﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. He said: Would that my people knew﴾: in it is the affirmation of the comfort of the grave, from His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise,﴾ even though the Hour has not yet risen and people have not yet entered Paradise.

* Among its lessons: this man was sincere during his life and after his death. During his life he called his people to affirm the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as has been mentioned to us. After his death he wished that his people would know of Allah's forgiveness toward him, for what reason? So that they would believe and follow the messengers. This is evidence that the believer is only met as a sincere advisor, and even after his death he remains a sincere advisor. This man wished that his people would know of what Allah had forgiven him, perhaps they would return and believe as he believed.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the existence of Paradise (al-Jannah). This is established by many verses and hadiths, such as His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Ali 'Imran 133]. The word "u'iddat" (prepared) means made ready, and the texts on this are numerous. Paradise and Hell were displayed to the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying the eclipse prayer (salat al-kusuf)[[Muslim (904/9) related with its chain from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The sun eclipsed during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a very hot day. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led his companions in prayer and prolonged the standing until they began to fall down. Then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he prostrated twice, then he stood and did something similar, so there were four bowings and four prostrations. Then he said: "There was displayed to me everything you are promised, and Paradise was displayed to me, so that if I had reached out for a cluster of it, I would have taken it, or he said: I reached out for a cluster of it, but my hand fell short of it. And the Fire was displayed to me..." The hadith.]].

So, will Paradise last forever? The answer is yes, and this is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. The Fire exists now, and this too is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. Will it perish? The correct and definitive position is that it does not perish, because the verses are explicit on this. Allah the Exalted has mentioned the eternity of abiding therein in three verses of His Book. What are they? Has Allah mentioned the eternal abiding in the Fire in three verses of the Quran?

* The Shaykh: No, it does not indicate it, as long as they remain therein. The important point is the explicit statement of eternity. Nevertheless, despite the explicit statement of eternity, it has been reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they used to say that it perishes. But there is no doubt that this view, whoever states it, is rejected.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the favor of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon the one who believed, through forgiveness and honor. From this benefit it follows that faith is a cause of forgiveness and a cause of Allah the Exalted honoring the servant.

Among its benefits: perfect bliss is not complete except with the removal of what is disliked. This is derived from His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾.

Also among them: what some men of letters pointed out, that clearing away (at-takhliyah) precedes adornment (at-tahliyah). How so? Because of His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾, which is clearing and removal, and ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, which is adornment. Hence, if you wish to adorn a woman, you first clean her, then you dress her in jewelry. If you dressed her in jewelry while she was not clean, it would not be fitting, and you would find no beauty in her. Yes indeed.

So it is derived from it that forgiveness precedes honor and mercy. The induction (at-tatabbu') supports this rule, for generally when Allah the Mighty and Majestic joins the two names, al-Ghafur and ar-Rahim, He mentions al-Ghafur before ar-Rahim.

Also among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the special lordship (ar-rububiyyah al-khassah), from His saying: ﴿my Lord﴾. This is of the special lordship.

Also among its benefits: the honor from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is not restricted to this man. Rather, there is a whole category whom Allah honors, from His saying: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾. In it is an exhortation that a person do as he did in order to attain what he attained. He did not say "with what my Lord forgave me and honored me," but said: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, to show that honor is not specific to him, but honor exists for everyone who performs a deed like his.

(...) Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ [Ya-Sin 24, 25]

﴿Indeed, I would then be﴾: This sentence is emphasized with (inna), because the context calls for emphasis.

His saying ﴿then﴾ means: if I worshipped other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾ It is also permissible to estimate it as: if I took other deities besides Him, as in His saying: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾

﴿Then﴾ (idhan) here is an adverb indicating the present. (Idha) is an adverb indicating the future, and (idh) is an adverb indicating the past. These three divide up time: (idhan) is for the present, (idha) for the future, and (idh) for the past. (Idh) also comes for other purposes, such as causation. For example: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾ The lam here is for emphasis, so the sentence is emphasized by two emphatics. That is: if I took gods along with Him, or worshipped other than Him, ﴿I would be in manifest error.﴾

The author said: (manifest). Error (dalal) is when a person wanders away from the right path. If it is deliberate, his path is the path of those who earned anger. If it is out of ignorance, his path is the path of those who are astray. Allah mentioned this in Surah al-Fatihah, saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked [Your] anger or of those who are astray.﴾ [al-Fatihah 6, 7] So those who have evoked anger are those who deviated from what is right knowingly, and those who are astray are those who deviated from it without knowledge, while the guided, upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, are those who acted rightly with knowledge.

The reason it is manifest error, that is, taking deities besides Allah, is that it is a deviation from what is obligatory, both by revelation and by reason. What is obligatory by revelation is that we not take any deity alongside Allah, as all the messengers came with this. What is obligatory by reason is that we not take deities alongside Allah, because Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who created man and originated him, and He is the One in whose hand is benefit and harm. So how can we take alongside Him deities that create nothing and neither benefit nor harm?!

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ May Allah have mercy on him, he declared that he believed in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and said: ﴿I have believed in your Lord﴾. Earlier he had said: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾, which points to the fact that He is not only his Lord, but the Lord of all. ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord.﴾ Belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, includes belief in four matters: belief in His existence; belief in His lordship (rububiyyah), which he stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿I have believed in your Lord,﴾ since affirming lordship is affirming existence; the third is belief in His divinity (uluhiyyah); and the fourth is belief in His names and attributes. That is, He alone is the Lord, the God, and possesses the names and attributes.

As for His saying: ﴿I have believed﴾: it has been mentioned to us many times that belief (iman) linguistically means affirmation (tasdiq), according to many exegetes who explain the meaning of belief. It has also been said that its meaning is acknowledgment and confession, so it is more specific than affirmation.

He said: ﴿So listen to me.﴾ This fa' (so) is conjunctive, linking to His saying: ﴿I have believed in your Lord,﴾ or to the entire sentence. His saying: ﴿listen to me﴾ means: listen to my words. This is a public declaration from him, may Allah have mercy on him, of his faith, defying his people and establishing the proof against them. For this reason, when he made this declaration, they killed him.

The author said: (They stoned him and he died. It was said to him at his death: Enter Paradise. And it was said: He entered it while alive.) When he made this declaration and defied them, not caring about them and not being concerned by them, and apparently, and Allah knows best, they threatened him. Then they stoned him and killed him. It was said to him after his death: Enter Paradise. The command here is one of honor. Paradise is the abode that Allah, glorified and exalted, prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

His saying: ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ was after his death, because a person is punished in his grave or granted comfort there. If he was one of the people of good, he is granted comfort, and if he was one of the people of evil, he is punished.

He said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. When it was said to him: Enter Paradise, and this command, as you have said, is a command of honor, he said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. The exegete says: the particle (ya) is a particle of alerting, meaning ﴿ya﴾, and is not a particle of calling, because it entered upon a particle, and the (ya) of calling only enters upon a noun. When it enters upon something it cannot validly precede, it is not a particle of calling. We have already learned in the signs of the noun that one of its signs is what? Calling, the entry of the particle (ya) of calling upon it. So when the particle (ya) of calling enters upon something other than a noun, it is for alerting, whether it enters upon a particle, such as ﴿Would that my people knew﴾, or upon a verb, and most often it enters upon imperative verbs, in which case it is for alerting. It is also permissible that it be a particle of calling with an omitted vocative, estimated according to the context. So in this verse we estimate it and say: O Lord, would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me. So its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has two possibilities: one, that it is for alerting, and the second, that it is for calling, with an omitted vocative estimated according to what the context requires.

His saying: ﴿Would that my people knew, [of] how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: ﴿Would that﴾ (layta) here is for wishing (tamanni), and (la'alla) is for hoping (tarajji). The difference between them is that wishing is for what is difficult to attain, and hoping is for what is close to being attained. What lies between these is sometimes expressed with (layta) and sometimes with (la'alla). So there are three states: what is close to attainment is expressed with (la'alla), what is impossible is expressed with (layta), and what lies between is sometimes (la'alla) and sometimes (layta), according to how close it is to being unattainable or to being attainable.

﴿He said: Would that my people knew﴾: they would know what had happened to him. For this reason he said: (﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾ by His forgiveness ﴿and made me among the honored﴾). ﴿How my Lord has forgiven me﴾: the (ba') here is connected to ﴿knew﴾, and knowledge here means recognition, so it transitively takes only one object. And (ma) is a verbal-masdar particle, as the exegete explained it, converting it into a verbal noun, saying: by His forgiveness. Here we should recall the meanings of (ma). Who will mention them to us?

Student: Yes, the poet said:
The carryings of (ma) are ten, if you wish to count them,
so guard against a sound verse free from poetic faults.
You will understand the condition of connection; so marvel at its denial,
with a palm, and a negation, and an augmentation, and the glorification of the verbal noun.

Shaykh: "The glorification of the verbal noun," good, complete. The meanings have become ten. ( Satafham) means for interrogation. (Shart) (al-wasl) [conditional, relative]. (Fa-'jab) is exclamatory. (Li-nukrihā) is indefinite. (Bi-kaff) [interrogative/prohibitive]. (Wa-nafy) is negative. (Zid) is a superfluous particle. (Ta'zim) is for glorification. (Masdar) is verbal-masdar.

So here it is in the last category, or the last meaning: verbal-masdar. The sign of verbal-masdar is that it converts what follows it, or what follows it is made into a verbal noun, into a verbal noun that is converted. His saying: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: it has already been explained to us that forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of a sin and overlooking it, because it is derived from (al-mighfar), and (al-mighfar) has two meanings or two things: one, covering, because it covers the head; and the second, protection, because a person puts a helmet on his head in battle to protect himself from arrows. Forgiveness is not merely the meaning of covering.

Then he said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾, attributing lordship to Him. This is particular lordship, because lordship is of two kinds: general lordship and particular lordship. General lordship is that which encompasses all creation, whose requirement is management and disposal of creation as His wisdom requires. Particular lordship is that in which there is special care for the one who is nurtured, such as the lordship of Allah, glorified and exalted, toward His messengers and His friends. Both kinds were combined in the saying of the magicians: ﴿They said: We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122] The first is general, and the second is particular. The opposite of this is servitude, which is also general and particular. General servitude is like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿There is none in the heavens and earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. Particular servitude is like His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63]. Within particular servitude there is something more particular, which is the servitude of Allah toward the messengers, like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

He said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾. Here, is the lordship particular or not? Particular. ﴿And made me among the honored﴾, yes, ﴿and made me among the honored﴾: because of his entry into Paradise, since entering Paradise is an honor for a person, an honor from Allah and an honor from the angels. The angels will enter upon them from every gate: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home.﴾ [al-Ra'd 24] It is an honor from the young boys who are immortal and who serve the people of Paradise. It is an honor from the wives who are restrained of gaze, whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them. It is an honor from some of them toward others, for they are brothers upon couches facing each other, and Allah has removed from their breasts any resentment. Such honor must involve honor from some of them toward others. So the people of Paradise are honored, and among them is this faithful, sincere, and devoted man, for he is honored by entering Paradise.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He mentioned those who maintain their prayer, concluded these attributes with His saying: ﴿Those will be in gardens, honored﴾ [al-Ma'arij 35]. For this reason He said here: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾.

Let us take the lessons from these verses, for I think we agreed to take a lesson from each verse.

Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error﴾ [Ya-Sin 24].

* In this noble verse: a clarification that among the most manifest and severe forms of error is that a person takes deities alongside Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾

* Among its lessons: emphasis is appropriate when the addressee is a denier, or his state is that of a denier. For he is addressing whom? He is addressing his people, who took deities alongside Allah, saying: If I took deities alongside Allah, I would be in manifest error. For this reason he emphasized the sentence with how many? With two emphatics: (inna) and the lam.

* It may be derived from the noble verse that everyone who strays from the truth, or everyone who opposes the truth, will suffer error in proportion to his opposition to the truth. His saying: ﴿in manifest error﴾ indicates that error may be hidden and may be clear and evident.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfect sincerity of this man, for he affirmed the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through several matters. Among them is what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾ Among them is a warning against associating partners with Him, by describing the associator as being in manifest error. Likewise, the one calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, should, when calling to the truth, mention the virtues of adhering to it and mention the error and evil in opposing it, so that he combines encouragement and warning.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the opposite of one who took deities alongside Allah and was in manifest error is that one who affirmed the oneness of Allah is upon clear and evident guidance, because he has hit upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and what the messengers brought.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ * From this verse is derived: the virtue of this man in declaring his faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Every person who declares his faith in Allah has a distinction and virtue in that. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says: Indeed, I am of the Muslims?﴾ [Fussilat 33] He declared that he was among the Muslims, and he feared no one but Allah.

* Among them: the strength of this man's character, for he declared before these people that he had believed, and believed in their Lord, which entails that they should be sincere to Him in worship if He is their Lord. It is as if he established the proof against them by this. If Allah is your Lord, then it is obligatory that you affirm His oneness and not take deities alongside Him. This shows the strength of his character. Furthermore, he challenged them, saying: ﴿so listen to me﴾, meaning: I do not care about you, I am not concerned with you. Listen: I have believed in your Lord, whom you must affirm as one, because He is your Lord.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's general lordship, for He said: ﴿your Lord﴾, even though they were polytheists and disbelievers. This is from general lordship.

Then He said: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. * The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever, they will find no protector or helper﴾. The third verse, in Surat al-Jinn?
* Student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. These are three verses explicit in the eternity of the people of the Fire therein.
* Student: (...) Does it indicate that? (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it does not indicate it, as long as they remain therein. The important point is the explicit statement of eternity. Nevertheless, despite the explicit statement of eternity, it has been reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they used to say that it perishes. But there is no doubt that this view, whoever states it, is rejected.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the favor of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon the one who believed, through forgiveness and honor. From this benefit it follows that faith is a cause of forgiveness and a cause of Allah the Exalted honoring the servant.

Among its benefits: perfect bliss is not complete except with the removal of what is disliked. This is derived from His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾.

Also among them: what some men of letters pointed out, that clearing away (at-takhliyah) precedes adornment (at-tahliyah). How so? Because of His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾, which is clearing and removal, and ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, which is adornment. Hence, if you wish to adorn a woman, you first clean her, then you dress her in jewelry. If you dressed her in jewelry while she was not clean, it would not be fitting, and you would find no beauty in her. Yes indeed.

So it is derived from it that forgiveness precedes honor and mercy. The induction (at-tatabbu') supports this rule, for generally when Allah the Mighty and Majestic joins the two names, al-Ghafur and ar-Rahim, He mentions al-Ghafur before ar-Rahim.

Also among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the special lordship (ar-rububiyyah al-khassah), from His saying: ﴿my Lord﴾. This is of the special lordship.

Also among its benefits: the honor from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is not restricted to this man. Rather, there is a whole category whom Allah honors, from His saying: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾. In it is an exhortation that a person do as he did in order to attain what he attained. He did not say "with what my Lord forgave me and honored me," but said: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, to show that honor is not specific to him, but honor exists for everyone who performs a deed like his.

(...) Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ [Ya-Sin 24, 25]

﴿Indeed, I would then be﴾: This sentence is emphasized with (inna), because the context calls for emphasis.

His saying ﴿then﴾ means: if I worshipped other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾ It is also permissible to estimate it as: if I took other deities besides Him, as in His saying: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾

﴿Then﴾ (idhan) here is an adverb indicating the present. (Idha) is an adverb indicating the future, and (idh) is an adverb indicating the past. These three divide up time: (idhan) is for the present, (idha) for the future, and (idh) for the past. (Idh) also comes for other purposes, such as causation. For example: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾ The lam here is for emphasis, so the sentence is emphasized by two emphatics. That is: if I took gods along with Him, or worshipped other than Him, ﴿I would be in manifest error.﴾

The author said: (manifest). Error (dalal) is when a person wanders away from the right path. If it is deliberate, his path is the path of those who earned anger. If it is out of ignorance, his path is the path of those who are astray. Allah mentioned this in Surah al-Fatihah, saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked [Your] anger or of those who are astray.﴾ [al-Fatihah 6, 7] So those who have evoked anger are those who deviated from what is right knowingly, and those who are astray are those who deviated from it without knowledge, while the guided, upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, are those who acted rightly with knowledge.

The reason it is manifest error, that is, taking deities besides Allah, is that it is a deviation from what is obligatory, both by revelation and by reason. What is obligatory by revelation is that we not take any deity alongside Allah, as all the messengers came with this. What is obligatory by reason is that we not take deities alongside Allah, because Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who created man and originated him, and He is the One in whose hand is benefit and harm. So how can we take alongside Him deities that create nothing and neither benefit nor harm?!

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ May Allah have mercy on him, he declared that he believed in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and said: ﴿I have believed in your Lord﴾. Earlier he had said: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾, which points to the fact that He is not only his Lord, but the Lord of all. ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord.﴾ Belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, includes belief in four matters: belief in His existence; belief in His lordship (rububiyyah), which he stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿I have believed in your Lord,﴾ since affirming lordship is affirming existence; the third is belief in His divinity (uluhiyyah); and the fourth is belief in His names and attributes. That is, He alone is the Lord, the God, and possesses the names and attributes.

As for His saying: ﴿I have believed﴾: it has been mentioned to us many times that belief (iman) linguistically means affirmation (tasdiq), according to many exegetes who explain the meaning of belief. It has also been said that its meaning is acknowledgment and confession, so it is more specific than affirmation.

He said: ﴿So listen to me.﴾ This fa' (so) is conjunctive, linking to His saying: ﴿I have believed in your Lord,﴾ or to the entire sentence. His saying: ﴿listen to me﴾ means: listen to my words. This is a public declaration from him, may Allah have mercy on him, of his faith, defying his people and establishing the proof against them. For this reason, when he made this declaration, they killed him.

The author said: (They stoned him and he died. It was said to him at his death: Enter Paradise. And it was said: He entered it while alive.) When he made this declaration and defied them, not caring about them and not being concerned by them, and apparently, and Allah knows best, they threatened him. Then they stoned him and killed him. It was said to him after his death: Enter Paradise. The command here is one of honor. Paradise is the abode that Allah, glorified and exalted, prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

His saying: ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ was after his death, because a person is punished in his grave or granted comfort there. If he was one of the people of good, he is granted comfort, and if he was one of the people of evil, he is punished.

He said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. When it was said to him: Enter Paradise, and this command, as you have said, is a command of honor, he said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. The exegete says: the particle (ya) is a particle of alerting, meaning ﴿ya﴾, and is not a particle of calling, because it entered upon a particle, and the (ya) of calling only enters upon a noun. When it enters upon something it cannot validly precede, it is not a particle of calling. We have already learned in the signs of the noun that one of its signs is what? Calling, the entry of the particle (ya) of calling upon it. So when the particle (ya) of calling enters upon something other than a noun, it is for alerting, whether it enters upon a particle, such as ﴿Would that my people knew﴾, or upon a verb, and most often it enters upon imperative verbs, in which case it is for alerting. It is also permissible that it be a particle of calling with an omitted vocative, estimated according to the context. So in this verse we estimate it and say: O Lord, would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me. So its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has two possibilities: one, that it is for alerting, and the second, that it is for calling, with an omitted vocative estimated according to what the context requires.

His saying: ﴿Would that my people knew, [of] how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: ﴿Would that﴾ (layta) here is for wishing (tamanni), and (la'alla) is for hoping (tarajji). The difference between them is that wishing is for what is difficult to attain, and hoping is for what is close to being attained. What lies between these is sometimes expressed with (layta) and sometimes with (la'alla). So there are three states: what is close to attainment is expressed with (la'alla), what is impossible is expressed with (layta), and what lies between is sometimes (la'alla) and sometimes (layta), according to how close it is to being unattainable or to being attainable.

﴿He said: Would that my people knew﴾: they would know what had happened to him. For this reason he said: (﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾ by His forgiveness ﴿and made me among the honored﴾). ﴿How my Lord has forgiven me﴾: the (ba') here is connected to ﴿knew﴾, and knowledge here means recognition, so it transitively takes only one object. And (ma) is a verbal-masdar particle, as the exegete explained it, converting it into a verbal noun, saying: by His forgiveness. Here we should recall the meanings of (ma). Who will mention them to us?

Student: Yes, the poet said:
The carryings of (ma) are ten, if you wish to count them,
so guard against a sound verse free from poetic faults.
You will understand the condition of connection; so marvel at its denial,
with a palm, and a negation, and an augmentation, and the glorification of the verbal noun.

Shaykh: "The glorification of the verbal noun," good, complete. The meanings have become ten. ( Satafham) means for interrogation. (Shart) (al-wasl) [conditional, relative]. (Fa-'jab) is exclamatory. (Li-nukrihā) is indefinite. (Bi-kaff) [interrogative/prohibitive]. (Wa-nafy) is negative. (Zid) is a superfluous particle. (Ta'zim) is for glorification. (Masdar) is verbal-masdar.

So here it is in the last category, or the last meaning: verbal-masdar. The sign of verbal-masdar is that it converts what follows it, or what follows it is made into a verbal noun, into a verbal noun that is converted. His saying: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: it has already been explained to us that forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of a sin and overlooking it, because it is derived from (al-mighfar), and (al-mighfar) has two meanings or two things: one, covering, because it covers the head; and the second, protection, because a person puts a helmet on his head in battle to protect himself from arrows. Forgiveness is not merely the meaning of covering.

Then he said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾, attributing lordship to Him. This is particular lordship, because lordship is of two kinds: general lordship and particular lordship. General lordship is that which encompasses all creation, whose requirement is management and disposal of creation as His wisdom requires. Particular lordship is that in which there is special care for the one who is nurtured, such as the lordship of Allah, glorified and exalted, toward His messengers and His friends. Both kinds were combined in the saying of the magicians: ﴿They said: We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122] The first is general, and the second is particular. The opposite of this is servitude, which is also general and particular. General servitude is like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿There is none in the heavens and earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. Particular servitude is like His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63]. Within particular servitude there is something more particular, which is the servitude of Allah toward the messengers, like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

He said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾. Here, is the lordship particular or not? Particular. ﴿And made me among the honored﴾, yes, ﴿and made me among the honored﴾: because of his entry into Paradise, since entering Paradise is an honor for a person, an honor from Allah and an honor from the angels. The angels will enter upon them from every gate: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home.﴾ [al-Ra'd 24] It is an honor from the young boys who are immortal and who serve the people of Paradise. It is an honor from the wives who are restrained of gaze, whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them. It is an honor from some of them toward others, for they are brothers upon couches facing each other, and Allah has removed from their breasts any resentment. Such honor must involve honor from some of them toward others. So the people of Paradise are honored, and among them is this faithful, sincere, and devoted man, for he is honored by entering Paradise.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He mentioned those who maintain their prayer, concluded these attributes with His saying: ﴿Those will be in gardens, honored﴾ [al-Ma'arij 35]. For this reason He said here: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾.

Let us take the lessons from these verses, for I think we agreed to take a lesson from each verse.

Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error﴾ [Ya-Sin 24].

* In this noble verse: a clarification that among the most manifest and severe forms of error is that a person takes deities alongside Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾

* Among its lessons: emphasis is appropriate when the addressee is a denier, or his state is that of a denier. For he is addressing whom? He is addressing his people, who took deities alongside Allah, saying: If I took deities alongside Allah, I would be in manifest error. For this reason he emphasized the sentence with how many? With two emphatics: (inna) and the lam.

* It may be derived from the noble verse that everyone who strays from the truth, or everyone who opposes the truth, will suffer error in proportion to his opposition to the truth. His saying: ﴿in manifest error﴾ indicates that error may be hidden and may be clear and evident.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfect sincerity of this man, for he affirmed the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through several matters. Among them is what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾ Among them is a warning against associating partners with Him, by describing the associator as being in manifest error. Likewise, the one calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, should, when calling to the truth, mention the virtues of adhering to it and mention the error and evil in opposing it, so that he combines encouragement and warning.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the opposite of one who took deities alongside Allah and was in manifest error is that one who affirmed the oneness of Allah is upon clear and evident guidance, because he has hit upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and what the messengers brought.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ * From this verse is derived: the virtue of this man in declaring his faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Every person who declares his faith in Allah has a distinction and virtue in that. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says: Indeed, I am of the Muslims?﴾ [Fussilat 33] He declared that he was among the Muslims, and he feared no one but Allah.

* Among them: the strength of this man's character, for he declared before these people that he had believed, and believed in their Lord, which entails that they should be sincere to Him in worship if He is their Lord. It is as if he established the proof against them by this. If Allah is your Lord, then it is obligatory that you affirm His oneness and not take deities alongside Him. This shows the strength of his character. Furthermore, he challenged them, saying: ﴿so listen to me﴾, meaning: I do not care about you, I am not concerned with you. Listen: I have believed in your Lord, whom you must affirm as one, because He is your Lord.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's general lordship, for He said: ﴿your Lord﴾, even though they were polytheists and disbelievers. This is from general lordship.

Then He said: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. He said: Would that my people knew﴾ [Ya-Sin 26]. * From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of the comfort of the grave, from His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise.﴾ Verses from the Qur'an support this, such as His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying: Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 32]. ﴿Whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾: ﴿good﴾ is a circumstantial state of the pronoun (hu), and ﴿saying﴾ is a circumstantial state of the angels, meaning: the angels say at the time of their taking, when they are in this state: Enter Paradise. * From this verse is derived: the affirmation of the comfort of the grave. There is another verse for it... what is it? The affirmation of the comfort of the grave.

* Student: From where, I mean?

* Shaykh: The Qur'an, from ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 1, 2], from al-Fatihah, to ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas 1].

* Student: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Ibrahim 27].

* Shaykh: That is not the proof.

* Student: The implication of the opposite, like the people of Pharaoh.

* Shaykh: No. ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see? ... As for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–89]. Here He said: ﴿Then why, when it reaches﴾ at the time of death, then He said: ﴿As for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure.﴾ Among them is this verse: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise.﴾ Because ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾ and the Hour has not yet come now, it is evidence that the deceased is granted comfort in his grave as if he had entered Paradise, because he is clothed from Paradise, spread with Paradise, a door to Paradise is opened for him, and its breeze and its pleasure reach him, so it is as if he had entered it.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, because ﴿As for if he was of those brought near﴾ refers to the time when the soul reaches the throat.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Now, I mean.

﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. He said: Would that my people knew﴾: in it is the affirmation of the comfort of the grave, from His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise,﴾ even though the Hour has not yet risen and people have not yet entered Paradise.

* Among its lessons: this man was sincere during his life and after his death. During his life he called his people to affirm the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as has been mentioned to us. After his death he wished that his people would know of Allah's forgiveness toward him, for what reason? So that they would believe and follow the messengers. This is evidence that the believer is only met as a sincere advisor, and even after his death he remains a sincere advisor. This man wished that his people would know of what Allah had forgiven him, perhaps they would return and believe as he believed.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the existence of Paradise (al-Jannah). This is established by many verses and hadiths, such as His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Ali 'Imran 133]. The word "u'iddat" (prepared) means made ready, and the texts on this are numerous. Paradise and Hell were displayed to the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying the eclipse prayer (salat al-kusuf)[[Muslim (904/9) related with its chain from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The sun eclipsed during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a very hot day. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led his companions in prayer and prolonged the standing until they began to fall down. Then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he prostrated twice, then he stood and did something similar, so there were four bowings and four prostrations. Then he said: "There was displayed to me everything you are promised, and Paradise was displayed to me, so that if I had reached out for a cluster of it, I would have taken it, or he said: I reached out for a cluster of it, but my hand fell short of it. And the Fire was displayed to me..." The hadith.]].

So, will Paradise last forever? The answer is yes, and this is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. The Fire exists now, and this too is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. Will it perish? The correct and definitive position is that it does not perish, because the verses are explicit on this. Allah the Exalted has mentioned the eternity of abiding therein in three verses of His Book. What are they? Has Allah mentioned the eternal abiding in the Fire in three verses of the Quran?

* The Shaykh: You don't mention it?

* The Shaykh: Good.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged, Allah will not forgive them, nor guide them to any path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. Good. In Surat al-Ahzab?

* The Shaykh: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. These are three verses explicit in the eternity of the people of the Fire therein.

But there is no doubt that this view, whoever states it, is rejected.

This is a public declaration from him, may Allah have mercy on him, of his faith, defying his people and establishing the proof against them. For this reason, when he made this declaration, they killed him.

The author said: (They stoned him and he died. It was said to him at his death: Enter Paradise. And it was said: He entered it while alive.) When he made this declaration and defied them, not caring about them and not being concerned by them, and apparently, and Allah knows best, they threatened him. Then they stoned him and killed him. It was said to him after his death: Enter Paradise. The command here is one of honor. Paradise is the abode that Allah, glorified and exalted, prepared for His friends, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

His saying: ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ was after his death, because a person is punished in his grave or granted comfort there. If he was one of the people of good, he is granted comfort, and if he was one of the people of evil, he is punished.

He said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. When it was said to him: Enter Paradise, and this command, as you have said, is a command of honor, he said: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. The exegete says: the particle (ya) is a particle of alerting, meaning ﴿ya﴾, and is not a particle of calling, because it entered upon a particle, and the (ya) of calling only enters upon a noun. When it enters upon something it cannot validly precede, it is not a particle of calling. We have already learned in the signs of the noun that one of its signs is what? Calling, the entry of the particle (ya) of calling upon it. So when the particle (ya) of calling enters upon something other than a noun, it is for alerting, whether it enters upon a particle, such as ﴿Would that my people knew﴾, or upon a verb, and most often it enters upon imperative verbs, in which case it is for alerting. It is also permissible that it be a particle of calling with an omitted vocative, estimated according to the context. So in this verse we estimate it and say: O Lord, would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me. So its grammatical analysis (i'rab) has two possibilities: one, that it is for alerting, and the second, that it is for calling, with an omitted vocative estimated according to what the context requires.

His saying: ﴿Would that my people knew, [of] how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: ﴿Would that﴾ (layta) here is for wishing (tamanni), and (la'alla) is for hoping (tarajji). The difference between them is that wishing is for what is difficult to attain, and hoping is for what is close to being attained. What lies between these is sometimes expressed with (layta) and sometimes with (la'alla). So there are three states: what is close to attainment is expressed with (la'alla), what is impossible is expressed with (layta), and what lies between is sometimes (la'alla) and sometimes (layta), according to how close it is to being unattainable or to being attainable.

﴿He said: Would that my people knew﴾: they would know what had happened to him. For this reason he said: (﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾ by His forgiveness ﴿and made me among the honored﴾). ﴿How my Lord has forgiven me﴾: the (ba') here is connected to ﴿knew﴾, and knowledge here means recognition, so it transitively takes only one object. And (ma) is a verbal-masdar particle, as the exegete explained it, converting it into a verbal noun, saying: by His forgiveness. Here we should recall the meanings of (ma). Who will mention them to us?

Student: Yes, the poet said:
The carryings of (ma) are ten, if you wish to count them,
so guard against a sound verse free from poetic faults.
You will understand the condition of connection; so marvel at its denial,
with a palm, and a negation, and an augmentation, and the glorification of the verbal noun.

Shaykh: "The glorification of the verbal noun," good, complete. The meanings have become ten. ( Satafham) means for interrogation. (Shart) (al-wasl) [conditional, relative]. (Fa-'jab) is exclamatory. (Li-nukrihā) is indefinite. (Bi-kaff) [interrogative/prohibitive]. (Wa-nafy) is negative. (Zid) is a superfluous particle. (Ta'zim) is for glorification. (Masdar) is verbal-masdar.

So here it is in the last category, or the last meaning: verbal-masdar. The sign of verbal-masdar is that it converts what follows it, or what follows it is made into a verbal noun, into a verbal noun that is converted. His saying: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾: it has already been explained to us that forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of a sin and overlooking it, because it is derived from (al-mighfar), and (al-mighfar) has two meanings or two things: one, covering, because it covers the head; and the second, protection, because a person puts a helmet on his head in battle to protect himself from arrows. Forgiveness is not merely the meaning of covering.

Then he said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾, attributing lordship to Him. This is particular lordship, because lordship is of two kinds: general lordship and particular lordship. General lordship is that which encompasses all creation, whose requirement is management and disposal of creation as His wisdom requires. Particular lordship is that in which there is special care for the one who is nurtured, such as the lordship of Allah, glorified and exalted, toward His messengers and His friends. Both kinds were combined in the saying of the magicians: ﴿They said: We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾ [al-A'raf 121, 122] The first is general, and the second is particular. The opposite of this is servitude, which is also general and particular. General servitude is like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿There is none in the heavens and earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. Particular servitude is like His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63]. Within particular servitude there is something more particular, which is the servitude of Allah toward the messengers, like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1].

He said: ﴿how my Lord has forgiven me﴾. Here, is the lordship particular or not? Particular. ﴿And made me among the honored﴾, yes, ﴿and made me among the honored﴾: because of his entry into Paradise, since entering Paradise is an honor for a person, an honor from Allah and an honor from the angels. The angels will enter upon them from every gate: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home.﴾ [al-Ra'd 24] It is an honor from the young boys who are immortal and who serve the people of Paradise. It is an honor from the wives who are restrained of gaze, whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them. It is an honor from some of them toward others, for they are brothers upon couches facing each other, and Allah has removed from their breasts any resentment. Such honor must involve honor from some of them toward others. So the people of Paradise are honored, and among them is this faithful, sincere, and devoted man, for he is honored by entering Paradise.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when He mentioned those who maintain their prayer, concluded these attributes with His saying: ﴿Those will be in gardens, honored﴾ [al-Ma'arij 35]. For this reason He said here: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾.

Let us take the lessons from these verses, for I think we agreed to take a lesson from each verse.

Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error﴾ [Ya-Sin 24].

* In this noble verse: a clarification that among the most manifest and severe forms of error is that a person takes deities alongside Allah, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I would then be in manifest error.﴾

* Among its lessons: emphasis is appropriate when the addressee is a denier, or his state is that of a denier. For he is addressing whom? He is addressing his people, who took deities alongside Allah, saying: If I took deities alongside Allah, I would be in manifest error. For this reason he emphasized the sentence with how many? With two emphatics: (inna) and the lam.

* It may be derived from the noble verse that everyone who strays from the truth, or everyone who opposes the truth, will suffer error in proportion to his opposition to the truth. His saying: ﴿in manifest error﴾ indicates that error may be hidden and may be clear and evident.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfect sincerity of this man, for he affirmed the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through several matters. Among them is what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me?﴾ Among them is a warning against associating partners with Him, by describing the associator as being in manifest error. Likewise, the one calling to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, should, when calling to the truth, mention the virtues of adhering to it and mention the error and evil in opposing it, so that he combines encouragement and warning.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the opposite of one who took deities alongside Allah and was in manifest error is that one who affirmed the oneness of Allah is upon clear and evident guidance, because he has hit upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and what the messengers brought.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.﴾ * From this verse is derived: the virtue of this man in declaring his faith in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Every person who declares his faith in Allah has a distinction and virtue in that. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says: Indeed, I am of the Muslims?﴾ [Fussilat 33] He declared that he was among the Muslims, and he feared no one but Allah.

* Among them: the strength of this man's character, for he declared before these people that he had believed, and believed in their Lord, which entails that they should be sincere to Him in worship if He is their Lord. It is as if he established the proof against them by this. If Allah is your Lord, then it is obligatory that you affirm His oneness and not take deities alongside Him. This shows the strength of his character. Furthermore, he challenged them, saying: ﴿so listen to me﴾, meaning: I do not care about you, I am not concerned with you. Listen: I have believed in your Lord, whom you must affirm as one, because He is your Lord.

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's general lordship, for He said: ﴿your Lord﴾, even though they were polytheists and disbelievers. This is from general lordship.

Then He said: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. He said: Would that my people knew﴾ [Ya-Sin 26]. * From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of the comfort of the grave, from His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise.﴾ Verses from the Qur'an support this, such as His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying: Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 32]. ﴿Whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾: ﴿good﴾ is a circumstantial state of the pronoun (hu), and ﴿saying﴾ is a circumstantial state of the angels, meaning: the angels say at the time of their taking, when they are in this state: Enter Paradise. * From this verse is derived: the affirmation of the comfort of the grave. There is another verse for it... what is it? The affirmation of the comfort of the grave.

* Student: From where, I mean?

* Shaykh: The Qur'an, from ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 1, 2], from al-Fatihah, to ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas 1].

* Student: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Ibrahim 27].

* Shaykh: That is not the proof.

* Student: The implication of the opposite, like the people of Pharaoh.

* Shaykh: No. ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see? ... As for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–89]. Here He said: ﴿Then why, when it reaches﴾ at the time of death, then He said: ﴿As for if he was of those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure.﴾ Among them is this verse: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise.﴾ Because ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise﴾ and the Hour has not yet come now, it is evidence that the deceased is granted comfort in his grave as if he had entered Paradise, because he is clothed from Paradise, spread with Paradise, a door to Paradise is opened for him, and its breeze and its pleasure reach him, so it is as if he had entered it.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, because ﴿As for if he was of those brought near﴾ refers to the time when the soul reaches the throat.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Now, I mean.

﴿It was said: Enter Paradise. He said: Would that my people knew﴾: in it is the affirmation of the comfort of the grave, from His saying: ﴿It was said: Enter Paradise,﴾ even though the Hour has not yet risen and people have not yet entered Paradise.

* Among its lessons: this man was sincere during his life and after his death. During his life he called his people to affirm the oneness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as has been mentioned to us. After his death he wished that his people would know of Allah's forgiveness toward him, for what reason? So that they would believe and follow the messengers. This is evidence that the believer is only met as a sincere advisor, and even after his death he remains a sincere advisor. This man wished that his people would know of what Allah had forgiven him, perhaps they would return and believe as he believed.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the existence of Paradise (al-Jannah). This is established by many verses and hadiths, such as His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Ali 'Imran 133]. The word "u'iddat" (prepared) means made ready, and the texts on this are numerous. Paradise and Hell were displayed to the Prophet ﷺ while he was praying the eclipse prayer (salat al-kusuf)[[Muslim (904/9) related with its chain from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The sun eclipsed during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a very hot day. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led his companions in prayer and prolonged the standing until they began to fall down. Then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he bowed and prolonged it, then he rose and prolonged it, then he prostrated twice, then he stood and did something similar, so there were four bowings and four prostrations. Then he said: "There was displayed to me everything you are promised, and Paradise was displayed to me, so that if I had reached out for a cluster of it, I would have taken it, or he said: I reached out for a cluster of it, but my hand fell short of it. And the Fire was displayed to me..." The hadith.]].

So, will Paradise last forever? The answer is yes, and this is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. The Fire exists now, and this too is agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah. Will it perish? The correct and definitive position is that it does not perish, because the verses are explicit on this. Allah the Exalted has mentioned the eternity of abiding therein in three verses of His Book. What are they? Has Allah mentioned the eternal abiding in the Fire in three verses of the Quran?

* Student: In Surat an-Nisa', al-Ahzab and al-Jinn.
* The Shaykh: In Surat an-Nisa', al-Ahzab and al-Jinn. Good. In Surat an-Nisa'?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: You don't mention it?
* Student: It doesn't come to mind.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged, Allah will not forgive them, nor guide them to any path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [an-Nisa' 168, 169].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged, Allah will not forgive them, nor guide them to any path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. Good. In Surat al-Ahzab?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is in al-Baqarah, and not there either.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Ahzab 64, 65].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever, they will find no protector or helper﴾. The third verse, in Surat al-Jinn?
* Student: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. These are three verses explicit in the eternity of the people of the Fire therein.
* Student: (...) Does it indicate that? (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it does not indicate it, as long as they remain therein. The important point is the explicit statement of eternity. Nevertheless, despite the explicit statement of eternity, it has been reported from some of the early scholars (salaf) that they used to say that it perishes. But there is no doubt that this view, whoever states it, is rejected.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the favor of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon the one who believed, through forgiveness and honor. From this benefit it follows that faith is a cause of forgiveness and a cause of Allah the Exalted honoring the servant.

Among its benefits: perfect bliss is not complete except with the removal of what is disliked. This is derived from His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾.

Also among them: what some men of letters pointed out, that clearing away (at-takhliyah) precedes adornment (at-tahliyah). How so? Because of His saying: ﴿with what my Lord has forgiven me﴾, which is clearing and removal, and ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, which is adornment. Hence, if you wish to adorn a woman, you first clean her, then you dress her in jewelry. If you dressed her in jewelry while she was not clean, it would not be fitting, and you would find no beauty in her. Yes indeed.

So it is derived from it that forgiveness precedes honor and mercy. The induction (at-tatabbu') supports this rule, for generally when Allah the Mighty and Majestic joins the two names, al-Ghafur and ar-Rahim, He mentions al-Ghafur before ar-Rahim.

Also among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the special lordship (ar-rububiyyah al-khassah), from His saying: ﴿my Lord﴾. This is of the special lordship.

Also among its benefits: the honor from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is not restricted to this man. Rather, there is a whole category whom Allah honors, from His saying: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾. In it is an exhortation that a person do as he did in order to attain what he attained. He did not say "with what my Lord forgave me and honored me," but said: ﴿and made me among the honored﴾, to show that honor is not specific to him, but honor exists for everyone who performs a deed like his.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down [one]﴾ [Yasin 28].

﴿And We did not send down﴾ — ﴿mā﴾ is negating. His saying ﴿upon his people﴾: the author said, "i.e., Habib," based on the premise that his name is Habib. It has already been mentioned that his name is not of concern to us; what matters is the story.

﴿upon his people after him﴾ — i.e., after he had been destroyed and had died at their hands. ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ — the ﴿min﴾ here is extra (ziyadah), because if it were removed the sentence would stand without it: if he had said, "And We did not send down upon his people an army from the heaven," the sentence would still be correct. His saying ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ means angels, for the angels are the armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none knows the armies of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 31], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed Our army, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat 173]. So the "jund" (army) are the angels. But [the author] said: "(for their destruction)" — ﴿and We were not ever going to send down﴾ angels to destroy anyone. So no angels were sent down to destroy anyone. It has also been said: "We were not going to send down [angels] to destroy these people, because they were too few and too insignificant for Allah to send angels from the heaven to destroy them." This is the closer view. So the negation here is specific to whom? To these people, because Allah sent down angels at Badr, and sent down angels at the battle of Hunayn, and Allah, the Exalted, sent down armies; likewise also at the battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see﴾ [al-Ahzab 9]. But ﴿and We were not going to send down armies﴾ against these people, out of contempt for them. And this which the author followed is the correct view.

Some scholars said: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾ means: any revelation or messengers, because revelation is brought down by the angels. But what the author followed is more correct, by the evidence that comes afterward. And Allah knows best.

(...) He said: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾. The author said: ﴿in﴾ here means ﴿mā﴾, and on this basis it is negating. ﴿In﴾ here is negating. We should keep in mind the meanings of ﴿in﴾: it comes as a negation, as here; and what else? And conditional, as when you say, "If Zayd stands, 'Amr stands." That is two.

* A student: And a lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah).

* The Shaykh: And a lightened form of the heavy, like:
"And if Malik was, noble of origins..." [poetic line incomplete in the source]
What else?

* A student: Interrogative.

* The Shaykh: No, it does not come as interrogative. ("In") does not come as interrogative.

* The student: Verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah).

* The Shaykh: No, that is ("ka'anna"). It also comes as extra (za'idah), as in his saying:
"Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, nor silver, but you are the potsherd."
It comes in four aspects: negating, conditional, lightened form of the heavy, and extra. When ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating; it may also be negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in Allah's saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], meaning, "You do not have." But the rule is that when ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating. Does it necessarily follow that it only comes as negating together with ﴿illa﴾? No, that is not necessary. It may come negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, meaning: "You do not have."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It was not﴾. The commentator said: "(their punishment)," meaning: their punishment with which Allah punished them for their disbelief was not ﴿but one shout﴾ — Jibril cried out at them, ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ — meaning: they did not need toil or armies; it was only a shout. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not specify who cried out. The author said it was Jibril, but we should not assert this without evidence, because it is obligatory upon us to leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified, unless its specification is reported by sound evidence; no sound evidence has come for specifying it. So we say: they were cried at, and we do not assert who this crier was. The point is that it was one shout; they were cried at and so they perished to the last of them. For this reason He said: ﴿then they were extinguished﴾. ﴿Idhā﴾ here is "fujā'iyyah" (sudden), indicating that what follows occurred immediately after what preceded it; that is, what follows happened directly after what came before. That is why it is called fujā'iyyah, because it comes suddenly and immediately: from the moment they were cried at, they were extinguished to the last of them.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿then they were extinguished﴾ — then they were silent and dead). From this we know that these people all died, because ﴿hum﴾ is a pronoun indicating plurality and comprehensiveness.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Oh, what regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 30] — these people and those like them who denied the messengers were destroyed, and it (i.e., regret, ḥasrah) is intense pain — intense pain and remorse is called ḥasrah — and calling to it is metaphorical, meaning: "This is your time, so come."

His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: ḥasrah is intense remorse, pain, grief, and sorrow over what has passed. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their means are cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and ﴿those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167] — meaning: remorse and pains — ﴿and they will not be removed from the Fire﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: regret upon the servants — from whom? It has been said that the speakers are the deniers, who lament over themselves and say, "Oh, regret upon the servants!", then state the reason as will come. It has also been said that the regret belongs to the followers of the messengers; that is, this man and others like him lament over these servants. It has also been said that the lamentation is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but this does not mean He is characterized by it; rather, the meaning is that He describes the servants' regret over themselves, saying: "Oh, regret that befalls the servants," falling upon them, so that ﴿upon﴾ comes close in meaning to ﴿from﴾; that is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these servants...

That is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these denying servants will lament over their denial. This is closer to the context of His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished. Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 29–30]. The speech is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but since lamentation is remorse and pain, Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from it, so it must be said that the meaning is: "Oh, regret befalling upon them," i.e., how intense is the servants' lamentation over what they did of denying the messengers, as its last part of the verse clarifies.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿upon the servants﴾ — the servants here refers to general servitude, not special servitude, because special servitude does not lead to lamentation for its people. We have already learned that servitude is general and special. The general is, as an example... we said "general servitude," because it includes only the deniers. Nevertheless, we say: it is general servitude, but a general term by which the specific is intended — who are they? The deniers of the messengers.

He said: (and calling to it is metaphorical), meaning not literal, because calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands. As for one who does not understand, calling to him is not literal. For this reason they said regarding the poet's verse:
"Oh you long night, will you not clear away / with dawn? And the morning is not the best of tidings."
This is meant as wishing, not a call in the sense of demanding, a demand for presence, because the night does not understand. Calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands; if it is directed to one who does not understand, it takes on another meaning by way of figurative usage (tajawwuz). The meaning is that the non-understanding is treated as if it understood, as though regret were a thing that comes and goes: you say, "Oh regret upon the servants, come!" ﴿What does not come to them﴾ [Yasin 30] — this explains its cause, the cause of the regret: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin 30]. ﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is extra, because it occurs within a negated context. It is extra — extra in wording, adding to the meaning. This is the meaning of our saying "extra, extra": there is not a single letter in the Qur'an that conveys no meaning at all; everything in the Qur'an contains meanings, but it may be extra only in terms of grammatical parsing. For this reason we parse ﴿messenger﴾ in this verse as a subject (fā'il), and say: a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed ḍammah at its end, its appearance prevented by the occupation of the position by the movement of the extra letter.

﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾ — its benefit is to make the generality explicit, because ﴿messenger﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negated context and so generalizes. When ﴿min﴾ comes, it becomes more explicit and more indicative of generality than if it were omitted. For this reason they said that its benefit in such a context is: making the generality explicit.

His saying: ﴿from a messenger﴾ — the messenger, according to the general scholars, is a human being to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it. The term "messenger" is also applied to an angelic messenger, for Allah named Jibril a messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure﴾ [al-Takwir 19–20], to the end.

His saying: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ means: except that they used to mock him — but the object was placed first, namely ﴿him﴾ (bihi), to convey restriction (ḥaṣr) and to match the rhythm of the verse-endings. It was placed first for two benefits: a verbal benefit, which is observing the verse-endings (fawāṣil), and a semantic benefit, which is restriction. It is as if He said: when the messenger comes to them, they mock no one except this messenger.

﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — that is, not someone else; they do mock others, but since these people had gone to excess in mocking the messengers, they became as though they mocked only the messengers. ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — and mockery is ridicule and derision.

* Benefits derived from these verses, from His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: first, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may send down angels to destroy the deniers. Its basis: the negation of sending down angels upon these people indicates that it is possible with others; otherwise the negation would not be valid.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the angels are armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿army﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the angels' place is the heavens, by His saying: ﴿from the heaven﴾, and this is the original state; but they may descend to earth, as in His saying concerning the Night of Decree: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4], and like the angels who guard the children of Adam, and who record their deeds, and similar things, and those who record those who arrive early for Friday prayer at the doors of the mosques.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the contemptibility of these people who denied the three messengers, by His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾, up to His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through mentioning Him in the plural form: ﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾. It should not be said that this indicates plurality, as the Christians argue, saying that the gods are many because Allah says ﴿We﴾ and similar verses. It is said to them: this plurality is for magnification (ta'ẓīm). How can you take proof from this ambiguous verse while being blind to clear verses such as: ﴿Indeed your God is one God﴾ [al-Saffat 4], ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171], ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73]? But the Christians, like other people of deviation, follow what is ambiguous in the Qur'an seeking discord and seeking its interpretation.

Whoever observes the following of doubts by the Christians and others in the texts of the Book and the Sunnah will be amazed at astonishing things, and it is obligatory upon us, with strong obligation, to seek knowledge to repel the doubts of these people; for these people, as you know, have spread among us now, and have multiplied in these lands of which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Expel the Jews and the Christians from the Arabian Peninsula" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Ma'rifat al-Sunan wa al-Athar (5538) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him]. These people spread poison among our youth and elders as well. Indeed they now—as we have heard—send pamphlets calling to Christianity, and send tapes calling to Christianity, because they have begun to know the addresses and know the locations, and then send to them. We have a number of these here: pamphlets and recorded tapes come to us calling to Christianity. If these fall into the hands of people who are ignorant, at least, their souls incline toward them. And although I think it very unlikely that any Muslim would become Christian, since the entire religion of the Christians as they are now is misguidance, nevertheless there is no doubt that it casts doubt, and produces inclination and reassurance toward these people. Therefore I see that today it is obligatory upon the youth of the Muslims to arm themselves with the weapon of knowledge: knowledge founded on transmitted text (athar) and reasoning (nazar); for those people are a people who make things resemble what they claim to be reason. It is no longer sufficient for us merely to learn transmitted text; there must be both transmitted text and reasoning. Transmitted text alone suffices for whom? For the believer about whom Allah said: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. But for the denier, transmitted text does not suffice, because he does not believe in transmitted text at all; he needs reasoning and intellect by which his argument may be refuted.

The point is that such a noble verse—﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾—is used as a comparison by the Christians to claim that Allah, glorified and exalted, is plural, more than one. We have already mentioned that they have been heedless, indeed blind, to the clear, explicit verses that Allah is one God, and that Allah declared disbelievers those who claim that Allah is plural: ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. In this verse is evidence that Allah destroyed these people with one shout, which was not repeated a second time: they were destroyed by one shout. But if someone asks: what kind of shout was it? Was it said, "Perish!"? We say: What? Allah knows this shout, may Allah protect us; it may be a cry, and it may be that they were commanded to perish. The point is that it was one shout, and they perished to the last of them. I said: there is in it a clarification.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Clarification of what? That they were destroyed. Good: by one shout.

Second: * Among its benefits: the explanation of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that whoever opposes Allah or wars against Allah, however great he may be, his destruction is easy for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything happens with one word: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar 49], ﴿And Our command is but one [word]﴾ [al-Qamar 50], and at this one command ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50]—it is neither delayed nor postponed; a glance of the eye is the swiftest thing there is. When Allah wills something He says to it, "Be," and it is—like a glance of the eye. Glory be to Allah! This indicates the greatness and power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these people who denied the three messengers were all destroyed, by His saying: ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. This indicates that whoever claims that this town to which the three were sent is Antioch, his claim is false; for the messengers of Jesus who were sent to Antioch came after Moses, and Allah, the Exalted, did not destroy a nation in a general manner after the Torah had been revealed. So said many scholars, based on His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43]. They said: this verse shows that Allah did not destroy any nation in a general manner after the revelation of the Torah. And this verse, as you know, in Surah Yasin—﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]—indicates that they were destroyed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 28–30 (part 2 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!
