No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This is evidence of the intense regret of the servants who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾. For this reason the address came in indefinite form (tankir), to indicate that it is a great regret, since indefiniteness sometimes conveys magnitude and severity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, namely that He does not punish anyone except for his sin. From His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ So Allah, exalted is He, punishes no one except for a sin. Rather, He, the Mighty and Majestic, may pardon a sin if it is less than shirk.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of prophethood, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾, and that the message is general to every nation, because He said: ﴿to the servants﴾, then said: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾. So all the servants have had the proof established against them: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ [Fatir 24]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief that entails punishment. The context here concerns a people who denied the messengers and were all destroyed, then it was said: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This indicates that mocking the prophets or the messengers is disbelief. This is supported by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Was it Allah and His signs and His messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief."﴾ [At-Tawbah 65–66]

Is mocking the Books disbelief? Yes, from His saying: ﴿and His signs﴾. Mocking any single part of the Sharia, even one ritual (sha'irah), is disbelief, because mocking a single ritual is mocking the entire Sharia, just as disbelief in a single ritual is disbelief in the whole Sharia. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 85] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and wish to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers, truly.﴾ [An-Nisa 150–151] So whoever believes in the message but disbelieves in one ritual of it has fully disbelieved in all of it. Whoever mocks anything of the laws of the messengers, even something that is not obligatory, has disbelieved; even a recommended matter, if he mocks it, he has disbelieved, because it is not possible to believe in some and not others. Rather, whoever hates what Allah has sent down has disbelieved. What is the evidence? ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah revealed, so He made their deeds fruitless.﴾ [Muhammad 9] Deeds are rendered void only by disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 217] So this is a great matter, not a trivial one. For this reason, a person must be content with everything that Allah has legislated: he is content, for example, with the obligation of prayer, the prohibition of wine, the obligation of zakat, the prohibition of usury, and so on by analogy. That is, you must be content with and accept everything. Then, if you act upon it, you are rewarded; if you do not act upon it, you are punished if it is obligatory, or you deserve punishment, unless leaving that obligation is itself disbelief, in which case you have disbelieved by abandoning it. For example, a person must believe in the prohibition of usury. If he denies its prohibition, he disbelieves; or if he does not accept its prohibition, he disbelieves. If he believes in its prohibition, accepts it, and is content with the prohibition, but commits usury, does he disbelieve or not? He does not disbelieve; his ruling is the ruling of sinners.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, the scholars have derived this, and it appears that they derived it from this and from reality.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, before the Torah? The Torah was not revealed until after Allah had saved the Children of Israel.
* Student: The ruling on mocking the righteous (...)?
* Shaykh: Mocking the righteous is either directed at their persons or at their deeds. If it is at their deeds, it is mocking the Sharia. If it is at their persons, it is not disbelief, but it is a dangerous matter, except for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, for whoever mocks him, even only his person, is a disbeliever.
* Student: What indicates that this warner who...?
* Shaykh: Cried out to them.
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ when 'Abdullah ibn Salam came to him and asked him about things, and he answered him, and he asked him about the messenger who comes to him. Jibril said: "That is the enemy of (...) the angels." Also, when (...) Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, said: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [Al-Baqarah 98]", that these people said: "This is an enemy of the angels," when the Messenger ﷺ told them that he comes to him. [[Al-Bukhari (4480) narrated with his chain from Anas, who said: 'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in his orchard picking dates. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I will ask you about three things that none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And what causes a child to resemble its father or its mother?" He said: "Jibril informed me of them just now." He said: "Jibril?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels," and he recited this verse: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril — indeed, he has sent it down upon your heart by permission of Allah﴾"... the hadith.]]
* Shaykh: This would be if it were supposed that the Children of Israel were his enemies, because he brings punishment to them; it does not necessarily follow that these people are like him.
* Student: That is, what is derived from the verse is that he is the one who descends with punishment upon the Children of Israel.
* Shaykh: I say it does not follow, because are these people from the Children of Israel? We do not know; for we have preferred the view that they are not messengers of 'Isa, they are not messengers from the side of 'Isa.
* Student: The Children of Israel from when? From after...
* Shaykh: From after Ya'qub, because Israel is Ya'qub.

﴿All of them will be brought before Us.﴾ (Inna) here. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished.﴾

* Among the benefits of this verse: showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is able to destroy creation with a single shout alone, without any other act, a disturbing sound that tears hearts apart. From His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.
* And among them: showing the submission of everything to His greatness, such that He does not repeat or reiterate what He wills. From His saying: ﴿but one shout﴾. For this reason He emphasized it with "one", to show that they did not need the shout to be repeated a second time. Likewise, all that Allah commands in the cosmic order does not need repetition, as He said in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾ [Al-Qamar 50]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this shout destroyed them all, and none of them was spared, from His saying: ﴿and immediately they were extinguished﴾ [Ya-Sin 29]. Upon this there follows another benefit: that the seizing of human souls by the Angel of Death is greater than we imagine. One might say: how can he seize these souls while they die in a single instant? We say: the question "how" is not raised regarding unseen matters, for these are matters we do not perceive with our senses. So for every unseen matter, do not say "how." For this reason, when Imam Malik was asked, "How did He establish Himself?", he said: "The 'how' is unintelligible," meaning it is not possible for us to grasp it by reason so as to ask about it.

And He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ to the end. In this is evidence of the great regret of those who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾, for this indefinite form indicates magnitude.

* Among its benefits: that these deniers of the messengers will find their deeds to be regrets upon them, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾

* Among its benefits: that no prophet was sent, nor any messenger dispatched, except that he found someone who mocked him. And does he also find someone who believes in him? Yes, and someone who believes in him. But among them is one who finds no one believing in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of the seventy thousand: "And the prophet, with him no one [at all]."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5705) and Muslim (220), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] So mockery occurs for every messenger; every messenger who is sent finds someone who mocks him, and finds someone who believes in him, but not every messenger who is sent finds someone who believes in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "And the prophet, with him no one."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ [Ya-Sin 30]. Likewise, mocking the laws of the messengers is disbelief, and likewise mocking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is disbelief. The scholars differed concerning one who reviles Allah or His Messenger: is his repentance accepted? There are two opinions. Some said his repentance is not accepted, but he is to be killed as an apostate: he is not washed, not shrouded, not prayed over, and not buried with the Muslims; as for his affair in the Hereafter, it is up to Allah, so if Allah knows of his sincere repentance, He will not punish him, and if Allah knows that it is false, he will be punished in the Hereafter. This is the well-known position in the school of Imam Ahmad.

The second opinion: his repentance is valid, meaning the repentance of one who mocks Allah and His Messenger and reviles Allah and His Messenger. But with respect to one who mocks or reviles the Messenger ﷺ, he is killed; as for one who reviles Allah or mocks Him, he is not killed. This is the correct view: that if a person reviles Allah or His Messenger or mocks them, he becomes a disbeliever; if he repents, his repentance is accepted, but he is killed if the reviling or mockery was directed at the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and is not killed if it was directed at Allah. The difference between them is that mocking and reviling the Messenger is a right of a human being, whereas mocking and reviling Allah is a right of Allah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that He accepts repentance from all sins, and when Allah accepts his repentance, its consequence, which is death, is lifted from him. As for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, we do not know that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, pardoned his right, so it is obligatory upon us to apply the ruling.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down [one]﴾ [Yasin 28].

﴿And We did not send down﴾ — ﴿mā﴾ is negating. His saying ﴿upon his people﴾: the author said, "i.e., Habib," based on the premise that his name is Habib. It has already been mentioned that his name is not of concern to us; what matters is the story.

﴿upon his people after him﴾ — i.e., after he had been destroyed and had died at their hands. ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ — the ﴿min﴾ here is extra (ziyadah), because if it were removed the sentence would stand without it: if he had said, "And We did not send down upon his people an army from the heaven," the sentence would still be correct. His saying ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ means angels, for the angels are the armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none knows the armies of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 31], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed Our army, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat 173]. So the "jund" (army) are the angels. But [the author] said: "(for their destruction)" — ﴿and We were not ever going to send down﴾ angels to destroy anyone. So no angels were sent down to destroy anyone. It has also been said: "We were not going to send down [angels] to destroy these people, because they were too few and too insignificant for Allah to send angels from the heaven to destroy them." This is the closer view. So the negation here is specific to whom? To these people, because Allah sent down angels at Badr, and sent down angels at the battle of Hunayn, and Allah, the Exalted, sent down armies; likewise also at the battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see﴾ [al-Ahzab 9]. But ﴿and We were not going to send down armies﴾ against these people, out of contempt for them. And this which the author followed is the correct view.

Some scholars said: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾ means: any revelation or messengers, because revelation is brought down by the angels. But what the author followed is more correct, by the evidence that comes afterward. And Allah knows best.

(...) He said: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾. The author said: ﴿in﴾ here means ﴿mā﴾, and on this basis it is negating. ﴿In﴾ here is negating. We should keep in mind the meanings of ﴿in﴾: it comes as a negation, as here; and what else? And conditional, as when you say, "If Zayd stands, 'Amr stands." That is two.

* A student: And a lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah).

* The Shaykh: And a lightened form of the heavy, like:
"And if Malik was, noble of origins..." [poetic line incomplete in the source]
What else?

* A student: Interrogative.

* The Shaykh: No, it does not come as interrogative. ("In") does not come as interrogative.

* The student: Verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah).

* The Shaykh: No, that is ("ka'anna"). It also comes as extra (za'idah), as in his saying:
"Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, nor silver, but you are the potsherd."
It comes in four aspects: negating, conditional, lightened form of the heavy, and extra. When ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating; it may also be negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in Allah's saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], meaning, "You do not have." But the rule is that when ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating. Does it necessarily follow that it only comes as negating together with ﴿illa﴾? No, that is not necessary. It may come negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, meaning: "You do not have."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It was not﴾. The commentator said: "(their punishment)," meaning: their punishment with which Allah punished them for their disbelief was not ﴿but one shout﴾ — Jibril cried out at them, ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ — meaning: they did not need toil or armies; it was only a shout. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not specify who cried out. The author said it was Jibril, but we should not assert this without evidence, because it is obligatory upon us to leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified, unless its specification is reported by sound evidence; no sound evidence has come for specifying it. So we say: they were cried at, and we do not assert who this crier was. The point is that it was one shout; they were cried at and so they perished to the last of them. For this reason He said: ﴿then they were extinguished﴾. ﴿Idhā﴾ here is "fujā'iyyah" (sudden), indicating that what follows occurred immediately after what preceded it; that is, what follows happened directly after what came before. That is why it is called fujā'iyyah, because it comes suddenly and immediately: from the moment they were cried at, they were extinguished to the last of them.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿then they were extinguished﴾ — then they were silent and dead). From this we know that these people all died, because ﴿hum﴾ is a pronoun indicating plurality and comprehensiveness.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Oh, what regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 30] — these people and those like them who denied the messengers were destroyed, and it (i.e., regret, ḥasrah) is intense pain — intense pain and remorse is called ḥasrah — and calling to it is metaphorical, meaning: "This is your time, so come."

His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: ḥasrah is intense remorse, pain, grief, and sorrow over what has passed. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their means are cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and ﴿those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167] — meaning: remorse and pains — ﴿and they will not be removed from the Fire﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: regret upon the servants — from whom? It has been said that the speakers are the deniers, who lament over themselves and say, "Oh, regret upon the servants!", then state the reason as will come. It has also been said that the regret belongs to the followers of the messengers; that is, this man and others like him lament over these servants. It has also been said that the lamentation is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but this does not mean He is characterized by it; rather, the meaning is that He describes the servants' regret over themselves, saying: "Oh, regret that befalls the servants," falling upon them, so that ﴿upon﴾ comes close in meaning to ﴿from﴾; that is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these servants...

That is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these denying servants will lament over their denial. This is closer to the context of His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished. Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 29–30]. The speech is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but since lamentation is remorse and pain, Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from it, so it must be said that the meaning is: "Oh, regret befalling upon them," i.e., how intense is the servants' lamentation over what they did of denying the messengers, as its last part of the verse clarifies.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿upon the servants﴾ — the servants here refers to general servitude, not special servitude, because special servitude does not lead to lamentation for its people. We have already learned that servitude is general and special. The general is, as an example... we said "general servitude," because it includes only the deniers. Nevertheless, we say: it is general servitude, but a general term by which the specific is intended — who are they? The deniers of the messengers.

He said: (and calling to it is metaphorical), meaning not literal, because calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands. As for one who does not understand, calling to him is not literal. For this reason they said regarding the poet's verse:
"Oh you long night, will you not clear away / with dawn? And the morning is not the best of tidings."
This is meant as wishing, not a call in the sense of demanding, a demand for presence, because the night does not understand. Calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands; if it is directed to one who does not understand, it takes on another meaning by way of figurative usage (tajawwuz). The meaning is that the non-understanding is treated as if it understood, as though regret were a thing that comes and goes: you say, "Oh regret upon the servants, come!" ﴿What does not come to them﴾ [Yasin 30] — this explains its cause, the cause of the regret: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin 30]. ﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is extra, because it occurs within a negated context. It is extra — extra in wording, adding to the meaning. This is the meaning of our saying "extra, extra": there is not a single letter in the Qur'an that conveys no meaning at all; everything in the Qur'an contains meanings, but it may be extra only in terms of grammatical parsing. For this reason we parse ﴿messenger﴾ in this verse as a subject (fā'il), and say: a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed ḍammah at its end, its appearance prevented by the occupation of the position by the movement of the extra letter.

﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾ — its benefit is to make the generality explicit, because ﴿messenger﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negated context and so generalizes. When ﴿min﴾ comes, it becomes more explicit and more indicative of generality than if it were omitted. For this reason they said that its benefit in such a context is: making the generality explicit.

His saying: ﴿from a messenger﴾ — the messenger, according to the general scholars, is a human being to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it. The term "messenger" is also applied to an angelic messenger, for Allah named Jibril a messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure﴾ [al-Takwir 19–20], to the end.

His saying: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ means: except that they used to mock him — but the object was placed first, namely ﴿him﴾ (bihi), to convey restriction (ḥaṣr) and to match the rhythm of the verse-endings. It was placed first for two benefits: a verbal benefit, which is observing the verse-endings (fawāṣil), and a semantic benefit, which is restriction. It is as if He said: when the messenger comes to them, they mock no one except this messenger.

﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — that is, not someone else; they do mock others, but since these people had gone to excess in mocking the messengers, they became as though they mocked only the messengers. ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — and mockery is ridicule and derision.

* Benefits derived from these verses, from His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: first, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may send down angels to destroy the deniers. Its basis: the negation of sending down angels upon these people indicates that it is possible with others; otherwise the negation would not be valid.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the angels are armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿army﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the angels' place is the heavens, by His saying: ﴿from the heaven﴾, and this is the original state; but they may descend to earth, as in His saying concerning the Night of Decree: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4], and like the angels who guard the children of Adam, and who record their deeds, and similar things, and those who record those who arrive early for Friday prayer at the doors of the mosques.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the contemptibility of these people who denied the three messengers, by His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾, up to His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through mentioning Him in the plural form: ﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾. It should not be said that this indicates plurality, as the Christians argue, saying that the gods are many because Allah says ﴿We﴾ and similar verses. It is said to them: this plurality is for magnification (ta'ẓīm). How can you take proof from this ambiguous verse while being blind to clear verses such as: ﴿Indeed your God is one God﴾ [al-Saffat 4], ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171], ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73]? But the Christians, like other people of deviation, follow what is ambiguous in the Qur'an seeking discord and seeking its interpretation.

Whoever observes the following of doubts by the Christians and others in the texts of the Book and the Sunnah will be amazed at astonishing things, and it is obligatory upon us, with strong obligation, to seek knowledge to repel the doubts of these people; for these people, as you know, have spread among us now, and have multiplied in these lands of which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Expel the Jews and the Christians from the Arabian Peninsula" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Ma'rifat al-Sunan wa al-Athar (5538) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him]. These people spread poison among our youth and elders as well. Indeed they now—as we have heard—send pamphlets calling to Christianity, and send tapes calling to Christianity, because they have begun to know the addresses and know the locations, and then send to them. We have a number of these here: pamphlets and recorded tapes come to us calling to Christianity. If these fall into the hands of people who are ignorant, at least, their souls incline toward them. And although I think it very unlikely that any Muslim would become Christian, since the entire religion of the Christians as they are now is misguidance, nevertheless there is no doubt that it casts doubt, and produces inclination and reassurance toward these people. Therefore I see that today it is obligatory upon the youth of the Muslims to arm themselves with the weapon of knowledge: knowledge founded on transmitted text (athar) and reasoning (nazar); for those people are a people who make things resemble what they claim to be reason. It is no longer sufficient for us merely to learn transmitted text; there must be both transmitted text and reasoning. Transmitted text alone suffices for whom? For the believer about whom Allah said: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. But for the denier, transmitted text does not suffice, because he does not believe in transmitted text at all; he needs reasoning and intellect by which his argument may be refuted.

The point is that such a noble verse—﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾—is used as a comparison by the Christians to claim that Allah, glorified and exalted, is plural, more than one. We have already mentioned that they have been heedless, indeed blind, to the clear, explicit verses that Allah is one God, and that Allah declared disbelievers those who claim that Allah is plural: ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. In this verse is evidence that Allah destroyed these people with one shout, which was not repeated a second time: they were destroyed by one shout. But if someone asks: what kind of shout was it? Was it said, "Perish!"? We say: What? Allah knows this shout, may Allah protect us; it may be a cry, and it may be that they were commanded to perish. The point is that it was one shout, and they perished to the last of them. I said: there is in it a clarification.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Clarification of what? That they were destroyed. Good: by one shout.

Second: * Among its benefits: the explanation of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that whoever opposes Allah or wars against Allah, however great he may be, his destruction is easy for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything happens with one word: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar 49], ﴿And Our command is but one [word]﴾ [al-Qamar 50], and at this one command ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50]—it is neither delayed nor postponed; a glance of the eye is the swiftest thing there is. When Allah wills something He says to it, "Be," and it is—like a glance of the eye. Glory be to Allah! This indicates the greatness and power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these people who denied the three messengers were all destroyed, by His saying: ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. This indicates that whoever claims that this town to which the three were sent is Antioch, his claim is false; for the messengers of Jesus who were sent to Antioch came after Moses, and Allah, the Exalted, did not destroy a nation in a general manner after the Torah had been revealed. So said many scholars, based on His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43]. They said: this verse shows that Allah did not destroy any nation in a general manner after the revelation of the Torah. And this verse, as you know, in Surah Yasin—﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]—indicates that they were destroyed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 28–30 (part 2 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This is evidence of the intense regret of the servants who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾. For this reason the address came in indefinite form (tankir), to indicate that it is a great regret, since indefiniteness sometimes conveys magnitude and severity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, namely that He does not punish anyone except for his sin. From His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ So Allah, exalted is He, punishes no one except for a sin. Rather, He, the Mighty and Majestic, may pardon a sin if it is less than shirk.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of prophethood, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾, and that the message is general to every nation, because He said: ﴿to the servants﴾, then said: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾. So all the servants have had the proof established against them: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ [Fatir 24]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief that entails punishment. The context here concerns a people who denied the messengers and were all destroyed, then it was said: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This indicates that mocking the prophets or the messengers is disbelief. This is supported by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Was it Allah and His signs and His messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief."﴾ [At-Tawbah 65–66]

Is mocking the Books disbelief? Yes, from His saying: ﴿and His signs﴾. Mocking any single part of the Sharia, even one ritual (sha'irah), is disbelief, because mocking a single ritual is mocking the entire Sharia, just as disbelief in a single ritual is disbelief in the whole Sharia. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 85] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and wish to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers, truly.﴾ [An-Nisa 150–151] So whoever believes in the message but disbelieves in one ritual of it has fully disbelieved in all of it. Whoever mocks anything of the laws of the messengers, even something that is not obligatory, has disbelieved; even a recommended matter, if he mocks it, he has disbelieved, because it is not possible to believe in some and not others. Rather, whoever hates what Allah has sent down has disbelieved. What is the evidence? ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah revealed, so He made their deeds fruitless.﴾ [Muhammad 9] Deeds are rendered void only by disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 217] So this is a great matter, not a trivial one. For this reason, a person must be content with everything that Allah has legislated: he is content, for example, with the obligation of prayer, the prohibition of wine, the obligation of zakat, the prohibition of usury, and so on by analogy. That is, you must be content with and accept everything. Then, if you act upon it, you are rewarded; if you do not act upon it, you are punished if it is obligatory, or you deserve punishment, unless leaving that obligation is itself disbelief, in which case you have disbelieved by abandoning it. For example, a person must believe in the prohibition of usury. If he denies its prohibition, he disbelieves; or if he does not accept its prohibition, he disbelieves. If he believes in its prohibition, accepts it, and is content with the prohibition, but commits usury, does he disbelieve or not? He does not disbelieve; his ruling is the ruling of sinners.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, the scholars have derived this, and it appears that they derived it from this and from reality.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, before the Torah? The Torah was not revealed until after Allah had saved the Children of Israel.
* Student: The ruling on mocking the righteous (...)?
* Shaykh: Mocking the righteous is either directed at their persons or at their deeds. If it is at their deeds, it is mocking the Sharia. If it is at their persons, it is not disbelief, but it is a dangerous matter, except for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, for whoever mocks him, even only his person, is a disbeliever.
* Student: What indicates that this warner who...?
* Shaykh: Cried out to them.
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ when 'Abdullah ibn Salam came to him and asked him about things, and he answered him, and he asked him about the messenger who comes to him. Jibril said: "That is the enemy of (...) the angels." Also, when (...) Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, said: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [Al-Baqarah 98]", that these people said: "This is an enemy of the angels," when the Messenger ﷺ told them that he comes to him. [[Al-Bukhari (4480) narrated with his chain from Anas, who said: 'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in his orchard picking dates. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I will ask you about three things that none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And what causes a child to resemble its father or its mother?" He said: "Jibril informed me of them just now." He said: "Jibril?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels," and he recited this verse: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril — indeed, he has sent it down upon your heart by permission of Allah﴾"... the hadith.]]
* Shaykh: This would be if it were supposed that the Children of Israel were his enemies, because he brings punishment to them; it does not necessarily follow that these people are like him.
* Student: That is, what is derived from the verse is that he is the one who descends with punishment upon the Children of Israel.
* Shaykh: I say it does not follow, because are these people from the Children of Israel? We do not know; for we have preferred the view that they are not messengers of 'Isa, they are not messengers from the side of 'Isa.
* Student: The Children of Israel from when? From after...
* Shaykh: From after Ya'qub, because Israel is Ya'qub.

﴿All of them will be brought before Us.﴾ (Inna) here. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished.﴾

* Among the benefits of this verse: showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is able to destroy creation with a single shout alone, without any other act, a disturbing sound that tears hearts apart. From His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.
* And among them: showing the submission of everything to His greatness, such that He does not repeat or reiterate what He wills. From His saying: ﴿but one shout﴾. For this reason He emphasized it with "one", to show that they did not need the shout to be repeated a second time. Likewise, all that Allah commands in the cosmic order does not need repetition, as He said in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾ [Al-Qamar 50]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this shout destroyed them all, and none of them was spared, from His saying: ﴿and immediately they were extinguished﴾ [Ya-Sin 29]. Upon this there follows another benefit: that the seizing of human souls by the Angel of Death is greater than we imagine. One might say: how can he seize these souls while they die in a single instant? We say: the question "how" is not raised regarding unseen matters, for these are matters we do not perceive with our senses. So for every unseen matter, do not say "how." For this reason, when Imam Malik was asked, "How did He establish Himself?", he said: "The 'how' is unintelligible," meaning it is not possible for us to grasp it by reason so as to ask about it.

And He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ to the end. In this is evidence of the great regret of those who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾, for this indefinite form indicates magnitude.

* Among its benefits: that these deniers of the messengers will find their deeds to be regrets upon them, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾

* Among its benefits: that no prophet was sent, nor any messenger dispatched, except that he found someone who mocked him. And does he also find someone who believes in him? Yes, and someone who believes in him. But among them is one who finds no one believing in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of the seventy thousand: "And the prophet, with him no one [at all]."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5705) and Muslim (220), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] So mockery occurs for every messenger; every messenger who is sent finds someone who mocks him, and finds someone who believes in him, but not every messenger who is sent finds someone who believes in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "And the prophet, with him no one."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ [Ya-Sin 30]. Likewise, mocking the laws of the messengers is disbelief, and likewise mocking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is disbelief. The scholars differed concerning one who reviles Allah or His Messenger: is his repentance accepted? There are two opinions. Some said his repentance is not accepted, but he is to be killed as an apostate: he is not washed, not shrouded, not prayed over, and not buried with the Muslims; as for his affair in the Hereafter, it is up to Allah, so if Allah knows of his sincere repentance, He will not punish him, and if Allah knows that it is false, he will be punished in the Hereafter. This is the well-known position in the school of Imam Ahmad.

The second opinion: his repentance is valid, meaning the repentance of one who mocks Allah and His Messenger and reviles Allah and His Messenger. But with respect to one who mocks or reviles the Messenger ﷺ, he is killed; as for one who reviles Allah or mocks Him, he is not killed. This is the correct view: that if a person reviles Allah or His Messenger or mocks them, he becomes a disbeliever; if he repents, his repentance is accepted, but he is killed if the reviling or mockery was directed at the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and is not killed if it was directed at Allah. The difference between them is that mocking and reviling the Messenger is a right of a human being, whereas mocking and reviling Allah is a right of Allah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that He accepts repentance from all sins, and when Allah accepts his repentance, its consequence, which is death, is lifted from him. As for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, we do not know that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, pardoned his right, so it is obligatory upon us to apply the ruling.

Then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven, nor were We ever going to send down [one]﴾ [Yasin 28].

﴿And We did not send down﴾ — ﴿mā﴾ is negating. His saying ﴿upon his people﴾: the author said, "i.e., Habib," based on the premise that his name is Habib. It has already been mentioned that his name is not of concern to us; what matters is the story.

﴿upon his people after him﴾ — i.e., after he had been destroyed and had died at their hands. ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ — the ﴿min﴾ here is extra (ziyadah), because if it were removed the sentence would stand without it: if he had said, "And We did not send down upon his people an army from the heaven," the sentence would still be correct. His saying ﴿any army from the heaven﴾ means angels, for the angels are the armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none knows the armies of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 31], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed Our army, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat 173]. So the "jund" (army) are the angels. But [the author] said: "(for their destruction)" — ﴿and We were not ever going to send down﴾ angels to destroy anyone. So no angels were sent down to destroy anyone. It has also been said: "We were not going to send down [angels] to destroy these people, because they were too few and too insignificant for Allah to send angels from the heaven to destroy them." This is the closer view. So the negation here is specific to whom? To these people, because Allah sent down angels at Badr, and sent down angels at the battle of Hunayn, and Allah, the Exalted, sent down armies; likewise also at the battle of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see﴾ [al-Ahzab 9]. But ﴿and We were not going to send down armies﴾ against these people, out of contempt for them. And this which the author followed is the correct view.

Some scholars said: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾ means: any revelation or messengers, because revelation is brought down by the angels. But what the author followed is more correct, by the evidence that comes afterward. And Allah knows best.

(...) He said: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾. The author said: ﴿in﴾ here means ﴿mā﴾, and on this basis it is negating. ﴿In﴾ here is negating. We should keep in mind the meanings of ﴿in﴾: it comes as a negation, as here; and what else? And conditional, as when you say, "If Zayd stands, 'Amr stands." That is two.

* A student: And a lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah).

* The Shaykh: And a lightened form of the heavy, like:
"And if Malik was, noble of origins..." [poetic line incomplete in the source]
What else?

* A student: Interrogative.

* The Shaykh: No, it does not come as interrogative. ("In") does not come as interrogative.

* The student: Verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah).

* The Shaykh: No, that is ("ka'anna"). It also comes as extra (za'idah), as in his saying:
"Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold, nor silver, but you are the potsherd."
It comes in four aspects: negating, conditional, lightened form of the heavy, and extra. When ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating; it may also be negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in Allah's saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], meaning, "You do not have." But the rule is that when ﴿illa﴾ follows it, it is negating. Does it necessarily follow that it only comes as negating together with ﴿illa﴾? No, that is not necessary. It may come negating without ﴿illa﴾, as in: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾, meaning: "You do not have."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It was not﴾. The commentator said: "(their punishment)," meaning: their punishment with which Allah punished them for their disbelief was not ﴿but one shout﴾ — Jibril cried out at them, ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ — meaning: they did not need toil or armies; it was only a shout. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not specify who cried out. The author said it was Jibril, but we should not assert this without evidence, because it is obligatory upon us to leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified, unless its specification is reported by sound evidence; no sound evidence has come for specifying it. So we say: they were cried at, and we do not assert who this crier was. The point is that it was one shout; they were cried at and so they perished to the last of them. For this reason He said: ﴿then they were extinguished﴾. ﴿Idhā﴾ here is "fujā'iyyah" (sudden), indicating that what follows occurred immediately after what preceded it; that is, what follows happened directly after what came before. That is why it is called fujā'iyyah, because it comes suddenly and immediately: from the moment they were cried at, they were extinguished to the last of them.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿then they were extinguished﴾ — then they were silent and dead). From this we know that these people all died, because ﴿hum﴾ is a pronoun indicating plurality and comprehensiveness.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Oh, what regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 30] — these people and those like them who denied the messengers were destroyed, and it (i.e., regret, ḥasrah) is intense pain — intense pain and remorse is called ḥasrah — and calling to it is metaphorical, meaning: "This is your time, so come."

His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: ḥasrah is intense remorse, pain, grief, and sorrow over what has passed. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their means are cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and ﴿those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167] — meaning: remorse and pains — ﴿and they will not be removed from the Fire﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾: regret upon the servants — from whom? It has been said that the speakers are the deniers, who lament over themselves and say, "Oh, regret upon the servants!", then state the reason as will come. It has also been said that the regret belongs to the followers of the messengers; that is, this man and others like him lament over these servants. It has also been said that the lamentation is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but this does not mean He is characterized by it; rather, the meaning is that He describes the servants' regret over themselves, saying: "Oh, regret that befalls the servants," falling upon them, so that ﴿upon﴾ comes close in meaning to ﴿from﴾; that is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these servants...

That is, Allah, the Exalted, makes clear that these denying servants will lament over their denial. This is closer to the context of His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished. Oh, regret upon the servants!﴾ [Yasin 29–30]. The speech is the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but since lamentation is remorse and pain, Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from it, so it must be said that the meaning is: "Oh, regret befalling upon them," i.e., how intense is the servants' lamentation over what they did of denying the messengers, as its last part of the verse clarifies.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿upon the servants﴾ — the servants here refers to general servitude, not special servitude, because special servitude does not lead to lamentation for its people. We have already learned that servitude is general and special. The general is, as an example... we said "general servitude," because it includes only the deniers. Nevertheless, we say: it is general servitude, but a general term by which the specific is intended — who are they? The deniers of the messengers.

He said: (and calling to it is metaphorical), meaning not literal, because calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands. As for one who does not understand, calling to him is not literal. For this reason they said regarding the poet's verse:
"Oh you long night, will you not clear away / with dawn? And the morning is not the best of tidings."
This is meant as wishing, not a call in the sense of demanding, a demand for presence, because the night does not understand. Calling in its literal sense is directed only to one who understands; if it is directed to one who does not understand, it takes on another meaning by way of figurative usage (tajawwuz). The meaning is that the non-understanding is treated as if it understood, as though regret were a thing that comes and goes: you say, "Oh regret upon the servants, come!" ﴿What does not come to them﴾ [Yasin 30] — this explains its cause, the cause of the regret: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ [Yasin 30]. ﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is negating, and ﴿min﴾ is extra, because it occurs within a negated context. It is extra — extra in wording, adding to the meaning. This is the meaning of our saying "extra, extra": there is not a single letter in the Qur'an that conveys no meaning at all; everything in the Qur'an contains meanings, but it may be extra only in terms of grammatical parsing. For this reason we parse ﴿messenger﴾ in this verse as a subject (fā'il), and say: a subject in the nominative, marked by a presumed ḍammah at its end, its appearance prevented by the occupation of the position by the movement of the extra letter.

﴿There does not come to them any messenger﴾ — its benefit is to make the generality explicit, because ﴿messenger﴾ is an indefinite noun in a negated context and so generalizes. When ﴿min﴾ comes, it becomes more explicit and more indicative of generality than if it were omitted. For this reason they said that its benefit in such a context is: making the generality explicit.

His saying: ﴿from a messenger﴾ — the messenger, according to the general scholars, is a human being to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it. The term "messenger" is also applied to an angelic messenger, for Allah named Jibril a messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne secure﴾ [al-Takwir 19–20], to the end.

His saying: ﴿There does not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him﴾ means: except that they used to mock him — but the object was placed first, namely ﴿him﴾ (bihi), to convey restriction (ḥaṣr) and to match the rhythm of the verse-endings. It was placed first for two benefits: a verbal benefit, which is observing the verse-endings (fawāṣil), and a semantic benefit, which is restriction. It is as if He said: when the messenger comes to them, they mock no one except this messenger.

﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — that is, not someone else; they do mock others, but since these people had gone to excess in mocking the messengers, they became as though they mocked only the messengers. ﴿except that they used to mock him﴾ — and mockery is ridicule and derision.

* Benefits derived from these verses, from His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: first, that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may send down angels to destroy the deniers. Its basis: the negation of sending down angels upon these people indicates that it is possible with others; otherwise the negation would not be valid.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the angels are armies of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿army﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the angels' place is the heavens, by His saying: ﴿from the heaven﴾, and this is the original state; but they may descend to earth, as in His saying concerning the Night of Decree: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4], and like the angels who guard the children of Adam, and who record their deeds, and similar things, and those who record those who arrive early for Friday prayer at the doors of the mosques.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the contemptibility of these people who denied the three messengers, by His saying: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people after him any army from the heaven﴾, up to His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, through mentioning Him in the plural form: ﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾. It should not be said that this indicates plurality, as the Christians argue, saying that the gods are many because Allah says ﴿We﴾ and similar verses. It is said to them: this plurality is for magnification (ta'ẓīm). How can you take proof from this ambiguous verse while being blind to clear verses such as: ﴿Indeed your God is one God﴾ [al-Saffat 4], ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171], ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73]? But the Christians, like other people of deviation, follow what is ambiguous in the Qur'an seeking discord and seeking its interpretation.

Whoever observes the following of doubts by the Christians and others in the texts of the Book and the Sunnah will be amazed at astonishing things, and it is obligatory upon us, with strong obligation, to seek knowledge to repel the doubts of these people; for these people, as you know, have spread among us now, and have multiplied in these lands of which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Expel the Jews and the Christians from the Arabian Peninsula" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Ma'rifat al-Sunan wa al-Athar (5538) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him]. These people spread poison among our youth and elders as well. Indeed they now—as we have heard—send pamphlets calling to Christianity, and send tapes calling to Christianity, because they have begun to know the addresses and know the locations, and then send to them. We have a number of these here: pamphlets and recorded tapes come to us calling to Christianity. If these fall into the hands of people who are ignorant, at least, their souls incline toward them. And although I think it very unlikely that any Muslim would become Christian, since the entire religion of the Christians as they are now is misguidance, nevertheless there is no doubt that it casts doubt, and produces inclination and reassurance toward these people. Therefore I see that today it is obligatory upon the youth of the Muslims to arm themselves with the weapon of knowledge: knowledge founded on transmitted text (athar) and reasoning (nazar); for those people are a people who make things resemble what they claim to be reason. It is no longer sufficient for us merely to learn transmitted text; there must be both transmitted text and reasoning. Transmitted text alone suffices for whom? For the believer about whom Allah said: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. But for the denier, transmitted text does not suffice, because he does not believe in transmitted text at all; he needs reasoning and intellect by which his argument may be refuted.

The point is that such a noble verse—﴿And We did not send down﴾ and ﴿and We were not going to send down﴾—is used as a comparison by the Christians to claim that Allah, glorified and exalted, is plural, more than one. We have already mentioned that they have been heedless, indeed blind, to the clear, explicit verses that Allah is one God, and that Allah declared disbelievers those who claim that Allah is plural: ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. In this verse is evidence that Allah destroyed these people with one shout, which was not repeated a second time: they were destroyed by one shout. But if someone asks: what kind of shout was it? Was it said, "Perish!"? We say: What? Allah knows this shout, may Allah protect us; it may be a cry, and it may be that they were commanded to perish. The point is that it was one shout, and they perished to the last of them. I said: there is in it a clarification.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Clarification of what? That they were destroyed. Good: by one shout.

Second: * Among its benefits: the explanation of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that whoever opposes Allah or wars against Allah, however great he may be, his destruction is easy for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything happens with one word: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar 49], ﴿And Our command is but one [word]﴾ [al-Qamar 50], and at this one command ﴿like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50]—it is neither delayed nor postponed; a glance of the eye is the swiftest thing there is. When Allah wills something He says to it, "Be," and it is—like a glance of the eye. Glory be to Allah! This indicates the greatness and power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these people who denied the three messengers were all destroyed, by His saying: ﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]. This indicates that whoever claims that this town to which the three were sent is Antioch, his claim is false; for the messengers of Jesus who were sent to Antioch came after Moses, and Allah, the Exalted, did not destroy a nation in a general manner after the Torah had been revealed. So said many scholars, based on His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 43]. They said: this verse shows that Allah did not destroy any nation in a general manner after the revelation of the Torah. And this verse, as you know, in Surah Yasin—﴿and then they were extinguished﴾ [Yasin 29]—indicates that they were destroyed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 28–30 (part 2 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This is evidence of the intense regret of the servants who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾. For this reason the address came in indefinite form (tankir), to indicate that it is a great regret, since indefiniteness sometimes conveys magnitude and severity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, namely that He does not punish anyone except for his sin. From His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ So Allah, exalted is He, punishes no one except for a sin. Rather, He, the Mighty and Majestic, may pardon a sin if it is less than shirk.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of prophethood, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾, and that the message is general to every nation, because He said: ﴿to the servants﴾, then said: ﴿No messenger comes to them﴾. So all the servants have had the proof established against them: ﴿And there has been no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ [Fatir 24]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief that entails punishment. The context here concerns a people who denied the messengers and were all destroyed, then it was said: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾ [Ya-Sin 30] This indicates that mocking the prophets or the messengers is disbelief. This is supported by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Was it Allah and His signs and His messenger that you were mocking? Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief."﴾ [At-Tawbah 65–66]

Is mocking the Books disbelief? Yes, from His saying: ﴿and His signs﴾. Mocking any single part of the Sharia, even one ritual (sha'irah), is disbelief, because mocking a single ritual is mocking the entire Sharia, just as disbelief in a single ritual is disbelief in the whole Sharia. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 85] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others," and wish to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers, truly.﴾ [An-Nisa 150–151] So whoever believes in the message but disbelieves in one ritual of it has fully disbelieved in all of it. Whoever mocks anything of the laws of the messengers, even something that is not obligatory, has disbelieved; even a recommended matter, if he mocks it, he has disbelieved, because it is not possible to believe in some and not others. Rather, whoever hates what Allah has sent down has disbelieved. What is the evidence? ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah revealed, so He made their deeds fruitless.﴾ [Muhammad 9] Deeds are rendered void only by disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever — those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 217] So this is a great matter, not a trivial one. For this reason, a person must be content with everything that Allah has legislated: he is content, for example, with the obligation of prayer, the prohibition of wine, the obligation of zakat, the prohibition of usury, and so on by analogy. That is, you must be content with and accept everything. Then, if you act upon it, you are rewarded; if you do not act upon it, you are punished if it is obligatory, or you deserve punishment, unless leaving that obligation is itself disbelief, in which case you have disbelieved by abandoning it. For example, a person must believe in the prohibition of usury. If he denies its prohibition, he disbelieves; or if he does not accept its prohibition, he disbelieves. If he believes in its prohibition, accepts it, and is content with the prohibition, but commits usury, does he disbelieve or not? He does not disbelieve; his ruling is the ruling of sinners.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, the scholars have derived this, and it appears that they derived it from this and from reality.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, before the Torah? The Torah was not revealed until after Allah had saved the Children of Israel.
* Student: The ruling on mocking the righteous (...)?
* Shaykh: Mocking the righteous is either directed at their persons or at their deeds. If it is at their deeds, it is mocking the Sharia. If it is at their persons, it is not disbelief, but it is a dangerous matter, except for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, for whoever mocks him, even only his person, is a disbeliever.
* Student: What indicates that this warner who...?
* Shaykh: Cried out to them.
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ when 'Abdullah ibn Salam came to him and asked him about things, and he answered him, and he asked him about the messenger who comes to him. Jibril said: "That is the enemy of (...) the angels." Also, when (...) Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, said: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [Al-Baqarah 98]", that these people said: "This is an enemy of the angels," when the Messenger ﷺ told them that he comes to him. [[Al-Bukhari (4480) narrated with his chain from Anas, who said: 'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in his orchard picking dates. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I will ask you about three things that none knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And what causes a child to resemble its father or its mother?" He said: "Jibril informed me of them just now." He said: "Jibril?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels," and he recited this verse: "﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril — indeed, he has sent it down upon your heart by permission of Allah﴾"... the hadith.]]
* Shaykh: This would be if it were supposed that the Children of Israel were his enemies, because he brings punishment to them; it does not necessarily follow that these people are like him.
* Student: That is, what is derived from the verse is that he is the one who descends with punishment upon the Children of Israel.
* Shaykh: I say it does not follow, because are these people from the Children of Israel? We do not know; for we have preferred the view that they are not messengers of 'Isa, they are not messengers from the side of 'Isa.
* Student: The Children of Israel from when? From after...
* Shaykh: From after Ya'qub, because Israel is Ya'qub.

﴿All of them will be brought before Us.﴾ (Inna) here. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished.﴾

* Among the benefits of this verse: showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is able to destroy creation with a single shout alone, without any other act, a disturbing sound that tears hearts apart. From His saying: ﴿It was not but one shout﴾.
* And among them: showing the submission of everything to His greatness, such that He does not repeat or reiterate what He wills. From His saying: ﴿but one shout﴾. For this reason He emphasized it with "one", to show that they did not need the shout to be repeated a second time. Likewise, all that Allah commands in the cosmic order does not need repetition, as He said in Surah al-Qamar: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye.﴾ [Al-Qamar 50]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this shout destroyed them all, and none of them was spared, from His saying: ﴿and immediately they were extinguished﴾ [Ya-Sin 29]. Upon this there follows another benefit: that the seizing of human souls by the Angel of Death is greater than we imagine. One might say: how can he seize these souls while they die in a single instant? We say: the question "how" is not raised regarding unseen matters, for these are matters we do not perceive with our senses. So for every unseen matter, do not say "how." For this reason, when Imam Malik was asked, "How did He establish Himself?", he said: "The 'how' is unintelligible," meaning it is not possible for us to grasp it by reason so as to ask about it.

And He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ to the end. In this is evidence of the great regret of those who denied the messengers, from His saying: ﴿Alas﴾, for this indefinite form indicates magnitude.

* Among its benefits: that these deniers of the messengers will find their deeds to be regrets upon them, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him.﴾

* Among its benefits: that no prophet was sent, nor any messenger dispatched, except that he found someone who mocked him. And does he also find someone who believes in him? Yes, and someone who believes in him. But among them is one who finds no one believing in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of the seventy thousand: "And the prophet, with him no one [at all]."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5705) and Muslim (220), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] So mockery occurs for every messenger; every messenger who is sent finds someone who mocks him, and finds someone who believes in him, but not every messenger who is sent finds someone who believes in him, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "And the prophet, with him no one."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that mocking the messengers is disbelief, from His saying: ﴿No messenger comes to them but they mock him﴾ [Ya-Sin 30]. Likewise, mocking the laws of the messengers is disbelief, and likewise mocking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is disbelief. The scholars differed concerning one who reviles Allah or His Messenger: is his repentance accepted? There are two opinions. Some said his repentance is not accepted, but he is to be killed as an apostate: he is not washed, not shrouded, not prayed over, and not buried with the Muslims; as for his affair in the Hereafter, it is up to Allah, so if Allah knows of his sincere repentance, He will not punish him, and if Allah knows that it is false, he will be punished in the Hereafter. This is the well-known position in the school of Imam Ahmad.

The second opinion: his repentance is valid, meaning the repentance of one who mocks Allah and His Messenger and reviles Allah and His Messenger. But with respect to one who mocks or reviles the Messenger ﷺ, he is killed; as for one who reviles Allah or mocks Him, he is not killed. This is the correct view: that if a person reviles Allah or His Messenger or mocks them, he becomes a disbeliever; if he repents, his repentance is accepted, but he is killed if the reviling or mockery was directed at the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and is not killed if it was directed at Allah. The difference between them is that mocking and reviling the Messenger is a right of a human being, whereas mocking and reviling Allah is a right of Allah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that He accepts repentance from all sins, and when Allah accepts his repentance, its consequence, which is death, is lifted from him. As for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, we do not know that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, pardoned his right, so it is obligatory upon us to apply the ruling.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾

﴿Have they not seen﴾: that is, the people of Makkah who said to the Prophet ﷺ, "You are not a messenger." The interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), meaning: they know.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: They know. Yes. Strike out the hamza.

God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. The author explained "seeing" here as seeing in the sense of knowing, because they did not witness this with their own eyes; they knew it from the reports that reached them. As for his words "that is, the people of Makkah": the correct view is that this is not limited to the people of Makkah, but is general to everyone who denied the Messenger ﷺ. It seems the author restricted it to the people of Makkah because the verse is Meccan. But it may be said that even if the verse is Meccan, those who denied the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, were from Makkah and elsewhere. The people of Ta'if denied the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and many others did too, because people did not enter the religion of God in multitudes until after the conquest of Makkah.

﴿Have they not seen how many We destroyed﴾: he says "kam" is an informative (khabariyyah) particle meaning "many," governing what follows it, and suspending (mu'allaqah) what precedes it from acting.

﴿They saw﴾: seeing here means knowing. When seeing means knowing, it takes two objects. "Kam" suspended the verb from acting. That means it nullified its action both verbally and in position. Suspension (ta'liq) nullifies the action only verbally, not in position. Cancellation (ilgha') nullifies it both verbally and in position. Mental verbs either operate in both wording and position, or operate in position but not in wording, or do not operate at all, neither in wording nor in position. The third is called cancellation (ilgha'), the second is called suspension (ta'liq), and the first is called operation (i'mal). So here, "kam" suspended ﴿they saw﴾ from acting in wording or in position? In wording. As for position, the clause is in the accusative position, filling the place of the two objects of ﴿they saw﴾. Then it also has grammatical analysis (i'rab) in relation to what follows it. In relation to what follows, it is an object of what follows, and accordingly it is estimated, as the author said: that is, many.

And his words: (And the meaning is: We destroyed before them many of the generations, the nations.) And God, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿from the generations before them﴾: this "min" (from) explains "kam," clarifying the vagueness in "kam." ﴿Generations﴾ is the plural of "qarn." They are the community that shared one era, and it is called a qarn. An era is a hundred years, and accordingly a qarn is a hundred years, but it may be less than that. A community may last less than a qarn, which God destroys before this number of years is complete. But the rule is that we say: the qarn is the community that shared one era.

﴿How many We destroyed before them of the generations, that they﴾: that is, the destroyed, ﴿to them﴾: that is, the deniers, ﴿do not return﴾. How? ﴿That they﴾: that is, the destroyed, ﴿to them﴾: that is, to the deniers. Do you have a Makkan reading? In any case, the Makkans, according to the author's statement, since the address is to the people of Makkah, or the discussion is about the people of Makkah, then the deniers are the Makkans. What we have is more general: what we have is "the deniers," which is more general. So these nations that were destroyed, did they return to the nations after them? No. Rather, they went away and vanished as if they had never existed, and nothing remains of them except their deeds.

He says: ﴿they do not return﴾. Will they not then take warning from them? And ﴿that they﴾ and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it, in consideration of the meaning mentioned.

What precedes it is His words: ﴿How many We destroyed before them﴾. It is as if he said: "Have they not seen that they do not return?" So it is a substitute for what precedes it in terms of meaning. And his words "in terms of meaning" mean not in terms of grammatical analysis, because it is an independent clause and not subordinate to it in grammar, but it is subordinate to it in meaning. The summary is that God, in this verse, made a clarification by which He affirms to these deniers that He destroyed many of the earlier nations, and that these destroyed ones do not return to these deniers, because they have finished with this world and there is no return for them to it so that they might be allowed to make amends. So it is obligatory for these deniers to take warning from them.

Then He said: ﴿And indeed all of them, all together, will be brought before Us.﴾ He said: (﴿in﴾ is negating or lightened.) As for his words "negating": clear, in the sense of "ma" (not). "Lightened" means "in" but lightened. "Aw" (or) here is not for choice but for classification, because according to the reading that follows, it is "lamma." ﴿All﴾: that is, all creatures, is the subject (mubtada') under both interpretations, meaning whether it is negating or lightened, because the lightened "in," as we know, operates on the clause, and its subject is an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). So ﴿kull﴾ is the subject under both views, meaning whether ﴿in﴾ is negating or lightened. ﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except" (illa). Or with a light pronunciation, the lam is a distinguishing lam, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except," and accordingly "in" is negating, and the estimate is: "And every one is not except all brought before Us (...)."

(The benefits that were a help to him in disobedience: he began to seek help from God's blessings in his disobedience, and was not thankful, because he diverted them (...).)

(﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except," and accordingly "in" is negating, and the estimate is: "And every one is not except all brought before Us." He says: "And with lightening," and "and indeed all lamma all together." The lam is a distinguishing lam between the negating "in" and the lightened "in," and "ma" is extra. The estimate on this is: "And indeed all are, for all together, brought before Us." For "all together," since "ma" is extra. So if we want to analyze this verse, we say: "in" is negating on the reading with a shadda, and "lamma" means "except." Second analysis: "in" is lightened on the reading with lightening, and the lam is distinguishing and is for emphasis as is well known, and "ma" is extra. The estimate on this is: "And indeed all are, for all together, brought before Us.")

So then, in the author's statement, is the "or" in his words "negating or lightened" for choice or for classification?

* Students: For classification.

* The Shaykh: For classification. It is for classification: on the reading with a shadda it is negating, and on the reading with lightening it is lightened. He said: (﴿jami'un﴾ is the predicate of the subject, that is: gathered together.) The predicate of the subject. Where is the subject? ("Kullun jami'un.")

If someone says: How can it be a predicate of ﴿kull﴾, since ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality?

The answer: ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality, but its indicating totality does not necessarily require gathering together. You say: "Honor all the people," and the people may be scattered, each in a different direction. But ﴿jami'﴾ indicates gathering together. So it has an addition beyond totality, which is the gathering of people. All people will be brought before God, mighty and majestic. But is their presence scattered or gathered? The answer: their presence is gathered. The evidence? The verse ﴿jami'un﴾.

So will someone now say that the subject is the same as the predicate, because the word ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality and ﴿jami'﴾ indicates totality?

We say: No, because the difference between them is that ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality even if they are scattered, while ﴿jami'﴾ indicates totality together; that is, gathered.

(﴿Before Us﴾: in our presence at the place of standing after their resurrection. ﴿Brought before us﴾: for reckoning, a second predicate.) Why? ("Kull" now has two predicates: ﴿jami'﴾ and the second, ﴿muhdarun﴾.) I think the meaning is clear. God, mighty and majestic, says in this verse: Not one of these is except brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection, and people are all gathered.

* In this noble verse and the one before it:
