First: The affirmation of the deniers by what they acknowledge of the destruction of those who came before them, as in His words: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾

Second: Among the benefits of the verse: a person must look and take warning, so that when he considers the ends of people he takes a lesson from it. Because the interrogative here, although it is for affirmation, is also useful for rebuke, since it is obligatory for one who considers the end of the deniers to refrain from denial.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: there is no resurrection or return before the Day of Resurrection, according to His words: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾. So no one is resurrected before the Day of Resurrection, except by way of exception, as established in the Qur'an: that Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him, gives life to the dead by God's permission; and as in the story of the man whom God caused to die for a hundred years and then resurrected; and as in the story of the Children of Israel whom the thunderbolt seized, then God resurrected them after their death; and as in the story of the young man whom the Dajjal kills, then speaks to him, addresses him, and he rises alive. Otherwise, the basic rule is that whoever has died never returns, according to His words: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: the affirmation of resurrection, according to His words: ﴿And indeed all of them, all together, will be brought before Us.﴾

* Among its benefits: the perfection of God's power, mighty and majestic, in that He gathers all these creatures together in one place, according to His words: ﴿all together before Us﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to prepare for this day, because God, exalted is He, did not tell us about it merely for information, but told us so that we would prepare for it, so that we would be ready for what we will be held accountable for.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾

﴿Have they not seen﴾: that is, the people of Makkah who said to the Prophet ﷺ, "You are not a messenger." The interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), meaning: they know.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: They know. Yes. Strike out the hamza.

God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. The author explained "seeing" here as seeing in the sense of knowing, because they did not witness this with their own eyes; they knew it from the reports that reached them. As for his words "that is, the people of Makkah": the correct view is that this is not limited to the people of Makkah, but is general to everyone who denied the Messenger ﷺ. It seems the author restricted it to the people of Makkah because the verse is Meccan. But it may be said that even if the verse is Meccan, those who denied the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, were from Makkah and elsewhere. The people of Ta'if denied the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and many others did too, because people did not enter the religion of God in multitudes until after the conquest of Makkah.

﴿Have they not seen how many We destroyed﴾: he says "kam" is an informative (khabariyyah) particle meaning "many," governing what follows it, and suspending (mu'allaqah) what precedes it from acting.

﴿They saw﴾: seeing here means knowing. When seeing means knowing, it takes two objects. "Kam" suspended the verb from acting. That means it nullified its action both verbally and in position. Suspension (ta'liq) nullifies the action only verbally, not in position. Cancellation (ilgha') nullifies it both verbally and in position. Mental verbs either operate in both wording and position, or operate in position but not in wording, or do not operate at all, neither in wording nor in position. The third is called cancellation (ilgha'), the second is called suspension (ta'liq), and the first is called operation (i'mal). So here, "kam" suspended ﴿they saw﴾ from acting in wording or in position? In wording. As for position, the clause is in the accusative position, filling the place of the two objects of ﴿they saw﴾. Then it also has grammatical analysis (i'rab) in relation to what follows it. In relation to what follows, it is an object of what follows, and accordingly it is estimated, as the author said: that is, many.

And his words: (And the meaning is: We destroyed before them many of the generations, the nations.) And God, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿from the generations before them﴾: this "min" (from) explains "kam," clarifying the vagueness in "kam." ﴿Generations﴾ is the plural of "qarn." They are the community that shared one era, and it is called a qarn. An era is a hundred years, and accordingly a qarn is a hundred years, but it may be less than that. A community may last less than a qarn, which God destroys before this number of years is complete. But the rule is that we say: the qarn is the community that shared one era.

﴿How many We destroyed before them of the generations, that they﴾: that is, the destroyed, ﴿to them﴾: that is, the deniers, ﴿do not return﴾. How? ﴿That they﴾: that is, the destroyed, ﴿to them﴾: that is, to the deniers. Do you have a Makkan reading? In any case, the Makkans, according to the author's statement, since the address is to the people of Makkah, or the discussion is about the people of Makkah, then the deniers are the Makkans. What we have is more general: what we have is "the deniers," which is more general. So these nations that were destroyed, did they return to the nations after them? No. Rather, they went away and vanished as if they had never existed, and nothing remains of them except their deeds.

He says: ﴿they do not return﴾. Will they not then take warning from them? And ﴿that they﴾ and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it, in consideration of the meaning mentioned.

What precedes it is His words: ﴿How many We destroyed before them﴾. It is as if he said: "Have they not seen that they do not return?" So it is a substitute for what precedes it in terms of meaning. And his words "in terms of meaning" mean not in terms of grammatical analysis, because it is an independent clause and not subordinate to it in grammar, but it is subordinate to it in meaning. The summary is that God, in this verse, made a clarification by which He affirms to these deniers that He destroyed many of the earlier nations, and that these destroyed ones do not return to these deniers, because they have finished with this world and there is no return for them to it so that they might be allowed to make amends. So it is obligatory for these deniers to take warning from them.

Then He said: ﴿And indeed all of them, all together, will be brought before Us.﴾ He said: (﴿in﴾ is negating or lightened.) As for his words "negating": clear, in the sense of "ma" (not). "Lightened" means "in" but lightened. "Aw" (or) here is not for choice but for classification, because according to the reading that follows, it is "lamma." ﴿All﴾: that is, all creatures, is the subject (mubtada') under both interpretations, meaning whether it is negating or lightened, because the lightened "in," as we know, operates on the clause, and its subject is an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). So ﴿kull﴾ is the subject under both views, meaning whether ﴿in﴾ is negating or lightened. ﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except" (illa). Or with a light pronunciation, the lam is a distinguishing lam, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except," and accordingly "in" is negating, and the estimate is: "And every one is not except all brought before Us (...)."

(The benefits that were a help to him in disobedience: he began to seek help from God's blessings in his disobedience, and was not thankful, because he diverted them (...).)

(﴿Lamma﴾ with a shadda means "except," and accordingly "in" is negating, and the estimate is: "And every one is not except all brought before Us." He says: "And with lightening," and "and indeed all lamma all together." The lam is a distinguishing lam between the negating "in" and the lightened "in," and "ma" is extra. The estimate on this is: "And indeed all are, for all together, brought before Us." For "all together," since "ma" is extra. So if we want to analyze this verse, we say: "in" is negating on the reading with a shadda, and "lamma" means "except." Second analysis: "in" is lightened on the reading with lightening, and the lam is distinguishing and is for emphasis as is well known, and "ma" is extra. The estimate on this is: "And indeed all are, for all together, brought before Us.")

So then, in the author's statement, is the "or" in his words "negating or lightened" for choice or for classification?

* Students: For classification.

* The Shaykh: For classification. It is for classification: on the reading with a shadda it is negating, and on the reading with lightening it is lightened. He said: (﴿jami'un﴾ is the predicate of the subject, that is: gathered together.) The predicate of the subject. Where is the subject? ("Kullun jami'un.")

If someone says: How can it be a predicate of ﴿kull﴾, since ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality?

The answer: ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality, but its indicating totality does not necessarily require gathering together. You say: "Honor all the people," and the people may be scattered, each in a different direction. But ﴿jami'﴾ indicates gathering together. So it has an addition beyond totality, which is the gathering of people. All people will be brought before God, mighty and majestic. But is their presence scattered or gathered? The answer: their presence is gathered. The evidence? The verse ﴿jami'un﴾.

So will someone now say that the subject is the same as the predicate, because the word ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality and ﴿jami'﴾ indicates totality?

We say: No, because the difference between them is that ﴿kull﴾ indicates totality even if they are scattered, while ﴿jami'﴾ indicates totality together; that is, gathered.

(﴿Before Us﴾: in our presence at the place of standing after their resurrection. ﴿Brought before us﴾: for reckoning, a second predicate.) Why? ("Kull" now has two predicates: ﴿jami'﴾ and the second, ﴿muhdarun﴾.) I think the meaning is clear. God, mighty and majestic, says in this verse: Not one of these is except brought before Us on the Day of Resurrection, and people are all gathered.

* In this noble verse and the one before it:

First: The affirmation of the deniers by what they acknowledge of the destruction of those who came before them, as in His words: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾

Second: Among the benefits of the verse: a person must look and take warning, so that when he considers the ends of people he takes a lesson from it. Because the interrogative here, although it is for affirmation, is also useful for rebuke, since it is obligatory for one who considers the end of the deniers to refrain from denial.

* Also among the benefits of the verse: there is no resurrection or return before the Day of Resurrection, according to His words: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾. So no one is resurrected before the Day of Resurrection, except by way of exception, as established in the Qur'an: that Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him, gives life to the dead by God's permission; and as in the story of the man whom God caused to die for a hundred years and then resurrected; and as in the story of the Children of Israel whom the thunderbolt seized, then God resurrected them after their death; and as in the story of the young man whom the Dajjal kills, then speaks to him, addresses him, and he rises alive. Otherwise, the basic rule is that whoever has died never returns, according to His words: ﴿that they to them do not return﴾.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: the affirmation of resurrection, according to His words: ﴿And indeed all of them, all together, will be brought before Us.﴾

* Among its benefits: the perfection of God's power, mighty and majestic, in that He gathers all these creatures together in one place, according to His words: ﴿all together before Us﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to prepare for this day, because God, exalted is He, did not tell us about it merely for information, but told us so that we would prepare for it, so that we would be ready for what we will be held accountable for.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 33–36 (part 1 of 2):

(Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them﴾ is over the resurrection, a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam). ﴿The dead earth﴾ is read with light and heavy (tashdid) emphasis on the mim. ﴿We have revived it﴾ with water is the subject (mubtada').)

﴿A sign for them﴾: "āyah" in the language means a sign and a decisive proof of a thing. The author's words "a preposed predicate": where then is the subject? The subject is "the earth" (al-ardu), this subject is ﴿the earth﴾. As for his words ﴿the dead﴾, he says "with light and heavy emphasis", meaning that there are two readings: ﴿al-maytah﴾ and ﴿al-mayyitah﴾. This is evidence that "mayyit" (al-mayyitah), as it is applied to one whose soul has left his body, is also applied to one who is going to die, contrary to those who say that "mayyit" is for one who is going to die and "mayt" is for one who has already died. The dead earth has died, yet there are two readings here: ﴿al-mayyitah﴾ and ﴿al-maytah﴾.

﴿Al-ardu﴾ is the subject.
﴿Al-maytah﴾ is an adjective, and ﴿aḥyaynāhā﴾ is also an adjective. This is why the author said "subject", placing it after his words ﴿We have revived it﴾, to show that "the dead" and ﴿We have revived it﴾ are both adjectives of "the earth". However, the correct view is that ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah isti'nafiyyah), explaining the point of the sign concerning this earth, because the locus of the benefit is not the death of the earth but that God, exalted is He, revived it after its death.

As for the view of the author, if ﴿We have revived it﴾ is taken as an adjective, there is a difficulty for us, since this contradicts the known rule that clauses following definite nouns are circumstantial (ahwal). The answer to this is to say that "the earth" here is meant generically, so it has the meaning of an indefinite noun. A parallel to this is the words of the poet:

"And I pass by the base man who insults me,
so I go on and then say, 'It does not concern me.'"

He said "upon the base man who insults me". The estimate is "upon a base man who insults me". "So I go on, then say, 'It does not concern me.'" From this also, according to the view of some grammarians (mu'rabun) on the verse:
﴿Like the donkey who carries books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:5], the clause ﴿carries﴾ is an adjective of "donkey", because the intended meaning is the genus, so it means "like a donkey that carries books". As for the view we have chosen, we say that the clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is resumptive, to explain the point of the sign concerning this earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it﴾. The point of it being a sign is that this dead earth, whose trees are dry and which has no fruit, God sends down rain upon it and it comes alive after death. So the One who revived it and is able to revive it is able to revive the dead, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things Competent﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:39].

Accordingly, we say: the point of the sign is that you measure the witnessed by the unseen. The witnessed thing observed is this earth, dead with dried trees, upon which rain is sent down and it turns green. So the One who revived it is capable [of reviving the dead]. (...)

(God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ with light and heavy emphasis, ﴿We have revived it﴾ with water is the subject.) The author's style here, or his statement, has an evident problem, because the one who reads "subject" after his words ﴿We have revived it﴾ thinks that the subject is the phrase ﴿We have revived it﴾, whereas the subject is the word ﴿the earth﴾. But he delayed this to show you that ﴿We have revived it﴾ follows "the earth", so it is as if he says "subject" because it follows the subject. He thus postponed the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the governing word until after that of the following word. The correct and clearer and more eloquent expression would be: ﴿the earth﴾ is the subject, and "the dead" and ﴿We have revived it﴾ are adjectives.

He said: (﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We have revived it﴾). That is, We revived the dead earth with crops, so the crop stood up green and swaying. But merely being a crop does not benefit a human, rather it benefits livestock, and benefits humans in cases of necessity. But its greatest benefit is ﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾. ﴿From it﴾: from where? From the earth. We brought forth from it grain like wheat, ﴿and from it they eat﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33]. "From it" means from this grain they eat.

The benefit of His words ﴿and from it they eat﴾ is evidence of the ease of obtaining this grain and the greatness of its benefit, and that it is beneficial grain that is easy to obtain, because if it were difficult, they would not be able to eat from it except with great hardship. This is why He said ﴿and from it they eat﴾, placing the object before the verb to indicate restriction (hasr). But it is a relative restriction, due to its ease, as if they have no food except from this easily available source.

(﴿And We made in it gardens﴾, orchards, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34]). This is other than grain, because what comes out of the earth is grain and also fruit. Grain comes from crops and fruit from trees. ﴿And We made in it gardens﴾: ﴿made﴾ means "rendered", so it governs two objects. The second object is "in it", and the first object is ﴿gardens﴾. ﴿Gardens﴾ is the plural of "jannah", which is an orchard with many trees. It was so named because it conceals whoever enters it, and he is hidden by it. The root of this word, jīm and nūn, all revolves around this meaning, namely concealment and hiddenness. From it comes "janān" for the heart, because it is hidden; from it comes "jinn" because they are hidden and concealed; from it comes "junnah" for a shield, because a person is concealed by it. So all these derivatives indicate hiddenness and concealment. A garden with many intertwined trees, if someone is in it, is not seen, because these trees conceal him.

His words ﴿gardens of﴾, that is, orchards, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾: palm trees and grapevines are well known, and God specified them because they are food that needs no great effort, a staple food that requires no preparation. They are eaten fresh and dry: fresh like the fresh date and the fresh grape, and dry like the date that results from the fresh date, and like the raisin that results from the grape. God combined them because they are sweet staple food that needs no cooking, and can be benefited from both fresh and dry: ﴿of palm trees and grapevines. And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34].

(﴿We caused to gush forth in it﴾, that is, in the earth, ﴿springs﴾, that is, some of them). It is possible that "min" here is explanatory (li-bayān al-jins), and this is general and is the closer view; meaning We caused springs to gush forth in it, many springs and varied kinds. Among them are flowing abundant springs, and among them are stagnant springs that do not flow but well up on the surface of the earth, and among them are springs that come through an intermediary, like the well-known pipes nowadays which are set into the earth so that water comes out, and among them are springs that come without intermediary, like those that burst forth from the tops of mountains and otherwise. All of this is evidence of the power of God, mighty and majestic, and of His mercy towards His servants.

He says: ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and what their hands have made﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:35]. He said (with two fatḥahs and with two ḍammahs, i.e. variant readings: thamar and thumur). ﴿That they may eat﴾: the pronoun refers to people. ﴿Of its fruit﴾ and ﴿of its fruit (thumur)﴾, that is, the fruit of what was mentioned, from the palm trees and others.

His words ﴿That they may eat of its fruit﴾: this "li" (lām) is for causation, as is obvious, and the verb after it is in the subjunctive, either governed by it according to the Kufans, or by an implied "an" according to the Basrans.

His words ﴿of its fruit﴾ here are singular, and He did not say "of their fruit", because God mentioned palm trees and grapevines, which are two kinds. He did not say "of their two fruits", but said ﴿of its fruit﴾, that is, the fruit of what was mentioned; so the pronoun here refers to what was mentioned, the palm trees and grapevines.

The author said: He said: (from the palm trees and others). ﴿And what their hands have made﴾ (that is: they did not make the fruit). ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ (for His blessings upon them).

His words ﴿and what their hands have made﴾: concerning "mā" there are two views among the exegetes. The first view: it is negative, and this is the view the author adopted; that is, the fruit that comes out of palm trees and grapevines was not made by the hands of people (...).

What is it that their hands made? Because people do make things that they improve, such as grape juice, and likewise date syrup, and likewise the bread they bake from grains, and other things that people make by hand and enjoy. For example, there are kinds of sweets made by hand and manufactured by hand. So God, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon the servants in two matters: He bestowed upon them what He, mighty and majestic, brings forth from these fruits and crops, and He bestowed upon them what He taught them of what they make with their hands. The foods we eat are of two kinds: one kind we do not alter, we eat it, as they say, fresh; and another kind we work upon and combine, for example, from several fruits and the like. So God, mighty and majestic, bestowed favours upon the servants with both matters. Which of the two meanings is preferable? We say: the second is more general, so it is preferable. Moreover, we mentioned an earlier rule that if a verse is suitable for two meanings, there is no objection to taking it as both. So we say: God intended this and that: He intended that our hands did not make these fruits that come out of palm trees and grapevines, nor these grains that come out of crops, and He also intended what we make with our hands as we wish. All of this is a blessing.

His words ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:35]: the interrogative here is for rebuke, and the clause is coordinated with an implied element understood from the context; that is, have they been heedless of this and so do not give thanks? Or: have they disbelieved in it and so do not give thanks? Because the absence of thanks is either through heedlessness or through deliberate disbelief. Many people, regarding blessings, are either heedless, and consider this a customary matter, as if it were something ordinary with no favour from God in it. This happens to a believer who has not been afflicted with the opposite of those blessings, because a person does not know the value of a blessing except when he is afflicted with its opposite. So one does not know the value of being full except by being hungry, nor the value of drink except by being thirsty, nor the value of health except by being ill, nor the value of companionship except by losing a companion, and so on. This is heedlessness.

Or it may be disbelief, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They recognise the favour of God, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:83]: disbelief in the blessing and arrogance, saying: "I was given it on the basis of knowledge I possess," and similar things.

His words ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾: we have mentioned several times that gratitude (shukr) is performing the obedience of the Benefactor, and using His blessings for what God made them for. So whoever uses God's blessings for other than what God made them for is not grateful. If someone makes blessings a help for disobedience, and uses God's blessings to sin, he is not grateful, because he has used them for other than what they were given for. God bestowed these blessings upon us so that we may worship Him and be strengthened by them. We have also mentioned several times before that between praise (ḥamd) and gratitude (shukr) there is a general and specific relationship in one respect: praise is more general in terms of its cause, and more specific in terms of its object; gratitude is more specific in terms of its cause, and more general in terms of its object.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: (﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾, kinds, ﴿of what the earth produces﴾, such as grains and others, ﴿and of themselves﴾, males and females, ﴿and of what they do not know﴾, of wondrous and strange creatures).

God is greater! ﴿Glory be to Him who created﴾: "subḥāna" always comes in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) whose verb is necessarily omitted. Its original form is "tasbīḥan lillāh" (an extolling of God), and "tasbīḥ" is the verbal noun of "sabbaḥa". The governing verb is omitted, which is "sabbaḥa", and the verbal noun has been converted into a noun of the verbal noun (ism maṣdar), namely "al-tasbīḥ", which became "subḥān". Tasbīḥ is the glorifying of God, mighty and majestic, above what is not befitting to Him, derived from "sabaḥa", meaning he went far in the water. So the meaning of tasbīḥ in "subḥān Allāh" is the declaration of God, glorified and exalted, as free from what does not befit Him. Two things do not befit God, mighty and majestic: one is deficiency in His attributes, and the second is resemblance to created beings in them. However, one may refer the second to the first and say: resemblance to created beings is a deficiency, because the resemblance of the perfect to the deficient makes it (...).

We may say it like this. So His words ﴿Glory be to Him who created﴾ mean: exaltation of this One who created all the pairs.

His words ﴿He who created all the pairs, of what the earth produces and of themselves and of what they do not know﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:36]: this verse is like His words ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:49]. All created things subsist only by composition from two or more materials. There is nothing that comes from one single thing ever. Everything, whether from what the earth produces, or from human beings, or from livestock, or from what we do not know, is in this general sense composed of two things.

﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:49]: in glorification of God, mighty and majestic, above what does not befit Him. This is why the verse here came: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:36]. Created beings necessarily have plurality, and the Creator is exalted above plurality. This is the wisdom, God knows best, in His saying ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾, and not "Praise be to God who created the pairs". Because the fact that everything needs duality shows the perfection of the One, the unique, to whom none of His creatures is comparable. The children of Adam must have a duality of male and female; even the qualities and attributes in them are found to be paired: there is anger and contentment, dislike and love, strength and weakness, and so on. But the Creator, mighty and majestic, is One, singular, to whom nothing is comparable in His essence or in His attributes (...).

The relation is "distance", meaning that He is far from deficiency. What?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Praise is more general than gratitude in terms of cause, and more specific than it in terms of object; gratitude is more general in terms of object and more specific in terms of cause.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: God is praised for His blessings and for His perfection, so He is praised for two things; this is the cause of praise, and praise is only in the tongue, through commendation. Gratitude is only for blessings, not for excellence. You do not say "I thank God for the perfection of His attributes"; no, for His blessings. So its cause is more specific. But it relates to the heart, the tongue and the limbs, so it is more general in terms of its object.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of God's power, mighty and majestic, to revive the earth after its death; from His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33].
* Among them: the use of the witnessed to infer the unseen, since the revival of the earth after death is observed. It is cited as proof of God's reviving the dead at their resurrection on the Day of Judgement. God, exalted is He, pointed to this proof with His words: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things Competent﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:39]. He also said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and therewith We caused gardens and grain of harvest to grow, and tall palm trees with ranged spathes, as provision for the servants, and We revived therewith a dead land. Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qāf 50:9–11]. There are many verses on this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of describing inanimate matter as dead, and that this is not restricted to what has a moving spirit; from His words ﴿the dead, We have revived it﴾, where He described it with death and described it with life.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the greatness of God, glorified and exalted, from His words ﴿We have revived it, and We brought forth from it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the demonstration of God's blessing, mighty and majestic, in what He brought forth from the earth for people, of grains and fruits. The grains are in His words ﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33], and the fruits in His words ﴿And We made in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth in it. That they may eat of its fruit﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34–35].

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the servant's need for his Lord, as in His words: ﴿from it they eat﴾. This restriction (*hasr*) contains a kind of challenge to humanity, because you cannot eat except from what Allah has brought forth for you. This is one of the benefits of restriction, as if He is saying: If you are able, then bring forth for yourself what you eat. Indeed, you will never eat except from what We have brought forth for you.

It shows the greatness of Allah, in that He said ﴿We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We caused to gush forth﴾ using the plural of majesty (*damir al-'azamah*).

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the blessings Allah has bestowed upon His servants through these great, numerous trees that provide shade, as in His words: ﴿And We made therein gardens of date palms and grapevines﴾ [Ya-Sin 34–35]. How great are Allah's blessings upon the servant through these date palms and grapevines.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the excellence of date palms and grapevines, because they are fruit that is eaten without toil, and fruit that is eaten both fresh and dried.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in causing the earth to gush forth springs. This earth is dry and hard, yet from it comes this moist, flowing thing, which is water. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split open and water comes out of them﴾ [al-Baqarah 74]. This is from the immense power of Allah. Moses, peace be upon him, would strike a hard rock, either a specific rock, as it is said, which he carried with him, or any rock at all, and it would gush forth twelve springs, according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel. This is part of the perfect power of Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among them: showing that date palms and grapevines need water, and that their fruit increases in proportion to the water, because He said: ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth therein, [34] that they may eat of its fruit﴾ [Ya-Sin 34–35]. This indicates that water has an effect on fruits, in the abundance and goodness of the fruits, and this is the reality.

* Among them: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists, who deny human will and causation) by affirming causation (*'illah*) and wisdom (*hikmah*) in His words: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾.

The texts that establish the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are very numerous. Among them are those in which Allah the Most High explicitly stated it, such as His words: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings do not avail﴾ [al-Qamar 5].

* Among them: what Allah has stated in the form of negation and denial: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan 38], ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved, so woe to those who disbelieved from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27]. Nothing indicates an attribute more than affirming it and negating its opposite, for affirming it indicates its existence, and negating its opposite indicates its perfection, and that it is free from this deficiency that arises from its absence or from the absence of its perfection. There is no doubt that if we negate wisdom from the act of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or from the legislation of Allah, there follows from that a great deficiency, and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, would be doing something foolishly and purposelessly.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is showing the blessings Allah has bestowed upon His servants through this fruit that is eaten. Consider: if this fruit became bitter, would it be beneficial? No. This is why Allah the Most High said about water: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? [68] Is it you who brought it down from the rain clouds, or are We the producer? [69] If We willed, We could make it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 68–70]. So you would be unable to drink it. This fruit, Allah the Most High made it delicious to souls; you eat from it and your bodies are nourished by it. This is why He said: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾. If Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had willed, He could have made this fruit spoiled. It might be sweet and delicious and appetizing, but Allah would place in it a blight that spoils it. Isn't that so? It exists in abundance, but it is among the blessings of Allah that it remains and its fruit can be eaten.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that we do not possess the ability to bring this fruit into existence ourselves, and that this is merely a grace from Allah. This is because of His words: ﴿and that which their hands made﴾ [Ya-Sin 35]. For this is not of our making. If all people gathered together to produce a single date, they would not be able to do so, or a single grape, they would not be able to do so. Yet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, creates these countless clusters of grapes and these countless bunches of dates on the palm trees. We have not made these with our hands; the most that we do is direct these fruits according to what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has taught us. For example, we take pollen from the male palm and place it in the female palm's blossom so that the fruit becomes good. But as for creating and bringing them into existence, no. This is according to making *ma* a negation.

* Another benefit, which is: showing the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what He has taught us of what we do to these fruits, in a manner that differs from how they were created, so that from this there comes goodness upon goodness. This is because of His words: ﴿and that which their hands made﴾ [Ya-Sin 35]. Allah the Most High has taught us how to prepare these fruits in a way that we enjoy them and benefit from them more than they are in their natural state. This is according to making *ma* a relative pronoun (*maw�ulah*).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of thanking the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah rebuked those who do not give thanks. Thanking, besides being an act of obedience to Allah, is rewarded for the person, and through it he recognizes the value of Allah's blessing upon him, and it is a cause for more of these blessings. This is because of the words of Allah the Most High: ﴿And [recall] when your Lord proclaimed, "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe"﴾ [Ibrahim 7].

If someone says: We see many people upon whom Allah has lavished blessings while they disbelieve in them. So how do we answer this verse?

The answer to this is that we say: Allah the Most High has punished them with a great punishment, because punishment is not limited to the loss of blessings. Rather, punishment may come through the loss of blessings, and it may come through hardness of heart and sickness of the heart. Although most people think that punishments are only the removal of blessings, the reality is that punishments of the hearts are through sickness, hardness, and turning away from Allah and from His remembrance. These are the greatest punishment. Then, these people who are pampered in their bodies, you do not think at all that they are pampered in their hearts. In their hearts there is such constriction and distress, and a lack of patience with the decree and divine destiny (*qadar*), that it keeps them always in a fire. You will not find a better life than the life of the believer, even if he is the poorest of people: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 97].

This is one answer. What is the other answer now? We say: These people have been punished with a punishment greater than the destruction of wealth, fruits, and other things, which is the hardness of the heart, its sickness, and its turning away. This necessitates for the person constriction of the chest and weariness with life, because he is not content with Allah as Lord nor with His legislation as religion.

Second: we say these blessings were hastened to them as a punishment and as gradual deception (*istidraj*). This is why, when 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while he was lying on a mat of palm fiber, meaning woven with palm fiber, and it had left a mark on his side, he wept and said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "O Messenger, Persia and Rome are enjoying the luxuries they have been given of the world, while you are in this state?!" Then he said: "O 'Umar, these are people whose good things have been hastened to them in their worldly life." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4913), and Muslim (1479/31), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in which 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He was lying on a mat with nothing between him and it, and under his head was a cushion of leather stuffed with palm fiber, and at his feet was a tanned skin, and at his head were hanging water skins. I saw the mark of the mat on the side of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so I wept. He said: 'What makes you weep?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Chosroes and Caesar are in what they are in, and you are the Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Are you not pleased that they have the world and you have the Hereafter?'" It was also related in a similar form by Ahmad (7963) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So we say: These people are punished by these blessings that flow to them, because it is gradual deception; and because when they die and enter punishment, it becomes more severe for them, since they have departed from a world to which their hearts were attached and in which they were pampered, and then this punishment followed, and we seek refuge in Allah. So they become more full of regret.

It is mentioned about Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, may Allah have mercy on him, who was the Chief Judge in Egypt, that one day he passed by a Jewish oil merchant selling oil, tired from the oil, with dirty clothes, and he was Jewish, while the Chief Judge, the judges of Egypt, was riding in a carriage pulled by horses, with people around him on the right and left. This Jewish man stopped the procession and said to him: "O Chief Judge, how can you be in this state and I in this state, when your Prophet says: 'Indeed the world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever'?" [Related by Muslim (2956/1) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]

What is the meaning of this? Which of them is in paradise now? The Chief Judge, while this man is in trial and hardship. He said to him: "Yes. What I am in of bliss, in the world, compared to my bliss in the Hereafter, or to the bliss of the believer in the Hereafter, is a prison. And what you are in of hardship and trial, compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, is a paradise. You are now in paradise, because you are moving to a punishment, a punishment you cannot imagine." When he said that, the Jew said: "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," and he embraced Islam.

The main point is that we say: These pampered people, their bliss is in reality misery and punishment, and although their bodies are pampered, most people are heedless of this. Regrettably, this disease has crept into the Muslims, so most Muslims today seek only this bliss, I mean the bliss of this world, and are heedless of the bliss of the Hereafter. This is why you find them always talking about luxury, amusement, and the like, as if they were created for nothing but this. This is among the greatest things that turn a person away from his religion: that his heart is attached to the world, and he looks only to enjoying it.

We do not deny that a person may obtain from this world what he benefits from for the Hereafter. Rather, if the world is made a means to the Hereafter, it becomes in reality part of the Hereafter. But we deny that the world should be a person's greatest concern, as if he were created only for it. This is from the deficiency of his religion and also the deficiency of his intellect. How can you make yourself and your precious life so preoccupied to the utmost extent with a matter that is not guaranteed and is not everlasting?

Allah the Most High said, rebuking the people of Hud, peace be upon him: ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will live forever﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 129]. You are not eternal. How can you make this passage in which you live your greatest concern, when you do not know when you will depart from it?! Every one of these luxury-seekers does not know when he will die, isn't that so? But he knows that he will remain in the Hereafter, if he believes in it, and yet he works for the world, for which he was not created, and abandons the Hereafter, for which he was created (...).

﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾, to the end of the verse.

* In the noble verse: the glorifying of Allah the Most High Himself above every deficiency and defect, as in His words: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. And in it (...)

The alert to His oneness, the Mighty and Majestic, and His difference from creation, as in His words: ﴿He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. He did not say "Glory be to Allah" alone, but said: ﴿He who created all the pairs of what the earth produces﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. The combining of what is affirmed for the servants with what Allah is glorified above has come in more than one place in the Qur'an. Among them is His words: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish, [26] but there will remain the face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 26–27]. When He mentioned the state of creation, He mentioned the state of the Creator, because He, the Mighty and Majestic, remains while others perish. Similarly here: all creation is in pairs, and in it there must be two spouses. ﴿And of all things We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat 49]. As for the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, He is One. This is why He said: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that there is nothing created except (...); because of His words: ﴿and of that which they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin 36], and this is one of the most general of expressions.

And His words: ﴿of what the earth produces and of themselves﴾ [Ya-Sin 36] also contain benefits. * Another benefit of the verse: that the children of Adam are of diverse kinds, just as that is the case with what the earth produces, and even within the earth itself. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ [al-Ra'd 4]. Affirming that they are neighboring implies that each one differs from the other, because a neighbor is not his neighbor. Likewise here: ﴿of what the earth produces﴾ indicates that in the earth there are diverse kinds of plants. Similarly, ﴿and of themselves﴾: among what Allah the Mighty and Majestic created in them are kinds: male and female; black and white; tall and short; wretched and blessed; intelligent and dull; wise and foolish, and so on, so that a person may reflect on the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in creating these opposites.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of human ignorance, and that a person does not encompass everything. This is because of His words: ﴿and of that which they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. If you add to this His words, the Most High: ﴿And they ask you about the soul. Say, "The soul is of the affair of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little"﴾ [al-Isra' 85], it shows you the extent of human ignorance regarding matters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 33–36 (part 1 of 2):

(Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them﴾ is over the resurrection, a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam). ﴿The dead earth﴾ is read with light and heavy (tashdid) emphasis on the mim. ﴿We have revived it﴾ with water is the subject (mubtada').)

﴿A sign for them﴾: "āyah" in the language means a sign and a decisive proof of a thing. The author's words "a preposed predicate": where then is the subject? The subject is "the earth" (al-ardu), this subject is ﴿the earth﴾. As for his words ﴿the dead﴾, he says "with light and heavy emphasis", meaning that there are two readings: ﴿al-maytah﴾ and ﴿al-mayyitah﴾. This is evidence that "mayyit" (al-mayyitah), as it is applied to one whose soul has left his body, is also applied to one who is going to die, contrary to those who say that "mayyit" is for one who is going to die and "mayt" is for one who has already died. The dead earth has died, yet there are two readings here: ﴿al-mayyitah﴾ and ﴿al-maytah﴾.

﴿Al-ardu﴾ is the subject.
﴿Al-maytah﴾ is an adjective, and ﴿aḥyaynāhā﴾ is also an adjective. This is why the author said "subject", placing it after his words ﴿We have revived it﴾, to show that "the dead" and ﴿We have revived it﴾ are both adjectives of "the earth". However, the correct view is that ﴿We have revived it﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah isti'nafiyyah), explaining the point of the sign concerning this earth, because the locus of the benefit is not the death of the earth but that God, exalted is He, revived it after its death.

As for the view of the author, if ﴿We have revived it﴾ is taken as an adjective, there is a difficulty for us, since this contradicts the known rule that clauses following definite nouns are circumstantial (ahwal). The answer to this is to say that "the earth" here is meant generically, so it has the meaning of an indefinite noun. A parallel to this is the words of the poet:

"And I pass by the base man who insults me,
so I go on and then say, 'It does not concern me.'"

He said "upon the base man who insults me". The estimate is "upon a base man who insults me". "So I go on, then say, 'It does not concern me.'" From this also, according to the view of some grammarians (mu'rabun) on the verse:
﴿Like the donkey who carries books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:5], the clause ﴿carries﴾ is an adjective of "donkey", because the intended meaning is the genus, so it means "like a donkey that carries books". As for the view we have chosen, we say that the clause ﴿We have revived it﴾ is resumptive, to explain the point of the sign concerning this earth.

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it﴾. The point of it being a sign is that this dead earth, whose trees are dry and which has no fruit, God sends down rain upon it and it comes alive after death. So the One who revived it and is able to revive it is able to revive the dead, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things Competent﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:39].

Accordingly, we say: the point of the sign is that you measure the witnessed by the unseen. The witnessed thing observed is this earth, dead with dried trees, upon which rain is sent down and it turns green. So the One who revived it is capable [of reviving the dead]. (...)

(God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ with light and heavy emphasis, ﴿We have revived it﴾ with water is the subject.) The author's style here, or his statement, has an evident problem, because the one who reads "subject" after his words ﴿We have revived it﴾ thinks that the subject is the phrase ﴿We have revived it﴾, whereas the subject is the word ﴿the earth﴾. But he delayed this to show you that ﴿We have revived it﴾ follows "the earth", so it is as if he says "subject" because it follows the subject. He thus postponed the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of the governing word until after that of the following word. The correct and clearer and more eloquent expression would be: ﴿the earth﴾ is the subject, and "the dead" and ﴿We have revived it﴾ are adjectives.

He said: (﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We have revived it﴾). That is, We revived the dead earth with crops, so the crop stood up green and swaying. But merely being a crop does not benefit a human, rather it benefits livestock, and benefits humans in cases of necessity. But its greatest benefit is ﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾. ﴿From it﴾: from where? From the earth. We brought forth from it grain like wheat, ﴿and from it they eat﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33]. "From it" means from this grain they eat.

The benefit of His words ﴿and from it they eat﴾ is evidence of the ease of obtaining this grain and the greatness of its benefit, and that it is beneficial grain that is easy to obtain, because if it were difficult, they would not be able to eat from it except with great hardship. This is why He said ﴿and from it they eat﴾, placing the object before the verb to indicate restriction (hasr). But it is a relative restriction, due to its ease, as if they have no food except from this easily available source.

(﴿And We made in it gardens﴾, orchards, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34]). This is other than grain, because what comes out of the earth is grain and also fruit. Grain comes from crops and fruit from trees. ﴿And We made in it gardens﴾: ﴿made﴾ means "rendered", so it governs two objects. The second object is "in it", and the first object is ﴿gardens﴾. ﴿Gardens﴾ is the plural of "jannah", which is an orchard with many trees. It was so named because it conceals whoever enters it, and he is hidden by it. The root of this word, jīm and nūn, all revolves around this meaning, namely concealment and hiddenness. From it comes "janān" for the heart, because it is hidden; from it comes "jinn" because they are hidden and concealed; from it comes "junnah" for a shield, because a person is concealed by it. So all these derivatives indicate hiddenness and concealment. A garden with many intertwined trees, if someone is in it, is not seen, because these trees conceal him.

His words ﴿gardens of﴾, that is, orchards, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾: palm trees and grapevines are well known, and God specified them because they are food that needs no great effort, a staple food that requires no preparation. They are eaten fresh and dry: fresh like the fresh date and the fresh grape, and dry like the date that results from the fresh date, and like the raisin that results from the grape. God combined them because they are sweet staple food that needs no cooking, and can be benefited from both fresh and dry: ﴿of palm trees and grapevines. And We caused springs to gush forth in it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34].

(﴿We caused to gush forth in it﴾, that is, in the earth, ﴿springs﴾, that is, some of them). It is possible that "min" here is explanatory (li-bayān al-jins), and this is general and is the closer view; meaning We caused springs to gush forth in it, many springs and varied kinds. Among them are flowing abundant springs, and among them are stagnant springs that do not flow but well up on the surface of the earth, and among them are springs that come through an intermediary, like the well-known pipes nowadays which are set into the earth so that water comes out, and among them are springs that come without intermediary, like those that burst forth from the tops of mountains and otherwise. All of this is evidence of the power of God, mighty and majestic, and of His mercy towards His servants.

He says: ﴿That they may eat of its fruit, and what their hands have made﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:35]. He said (with two fatḥahs and with two ḍammahs, i.e. variant readings: thamar and thumur). ﴿That they may eat﴾: the pronoun refers to people. ﴿Of its fruit﴾ and ﴿of its fruit (thumur)﴾, that is, the fruit of what was mentioned, from the palm trees and others.

His words ﴿That they may eat of its fruit﴾: this "li" (lām) is for causation, as is obvious, and the verb after it is in the subjunctive, either governed by it according to the Kufans, or by an implied "an" according to the Basrans.

His words ﴿of its fruit﴾ here are singular, and He did not say "of their fruit", because God mentioned palm trees and grapevines, which are two kinds. He did not say "of their two fruits", but said ﴿of its fruit﴾, that is, the fruit of what was mentioned; so the pronoun here refers to what was mentioned, the palm trees and grapevines.

The author said: He said: (from the palm trees and others). ﴿And what their hands have made﴾ (that is: they did not make the fruit). ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ (for His blessings upon them).

His words ﴿and what their hands have made﴾: concerning "mā" there are two views among the exegetes. The first view: it is negative, and this is the view the author adopted; that is, the fruit that comes out of palm trees and grapevines was not made by the hands of people (...).

What is it that their hands made? Because people do make things that they improve, such as grape juice, and likewise date syrup, and likewise the bread they bake from grains, and other things that people make by hand and enjoy. For example, there are kinds of sweets made by hand and manufactured by hand. So God, exalted is He, bestowed a favour upon the servants in two matters: He bestowed upon them what He, mighty and majestic, brings forth from these fruits and crops, and He bestowed upon them what He taught them of what they make with their hands. The foods we eat are of two kinds: one kind we do not alter, we eat it, as they say, fresh; and another kind we work upon and combine, for example, from several fruits and the like. So God, mighty and majestic, bestowed favours upon the servants with both matters. Which of the two meanings is preferable? We say: the second is more general, so it is preferable. Moreover, we mentioned an earlier rule that if a verse is suitable for two meanings, there is no objection to taking it as both. So we say: God intended this and that: He intended that our hands did not make these fruits that come out of palm trees and grapevines, nor these grains that come out of crops, and He also intended what we make with our hands as we wish. All of this is a blessing.

His words ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:35]: the interrogative here is for rebuke, and the clause is coordinated with an implied element understood from the context; that is, have they been heedless of this and so do not give thanks? Or: have they disbelieved in it and so do not give thanks? Because the absence of thanks is either through heedlessness or through deliberate disbelief. Many people, regarding blessings, are either heedless, and consider this a customary matter, as if it were something ordinary with no favour from God in it. This happens to a believer who has not been afflicted with the opposite of those blessings, because a person does not know the value of a blessing except when he is afflicted with its opposite. So one does not know the value of being full except by being hungry, nor the value of drink except by being thirsty, nor the value of health except by being ill, nor the value of companionship except by losing a companion, and so on. This is heedlessness.

Or it may be disbelief, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They recognise the favour of God, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:83]: disbelief in the blessing and arrogance, saying: "I was given it on the basis of knowledge I possess," and similar things.

His words ﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾: we have mentioned several times that gratitude (shukr) is performing the obedience of the Benefactor, and using His blessings for what God made them for. So whoever uses God's blessings for other than what God made them for is not grateful. If someone makes blessings a help for disobedience, and uses God's blessings to sin, he is not grateful, because he has used them for other than what they were given for. God bestowed these blessings upon us so that we may worship Him and be strengthened by them. We have also mentioned several times before that between praise (ḥamd) and gratitude (shukr) there is a general and specific relationship in one respect: praise is more general in terms of its cause, and more specific in terms of its object; gratitude is more specific in terms of its cause, and more general in terms of its object.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: (﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾, kinds, ﴿of what the earth produces﴾, such as grains and others, ﴿and of themselves﴾, males and females, ﴿and of what they do not know﴾, of wondrous and strange creatures).

God is greater! ﴿Glory be to Him who created﴾: "subḥāna" always comes in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) whose verb is necessarily omitted. Its original form is "tasbīḥan lillāh" (an extolling of God), and "tasbīḥ" is the verbal noun of "sabbaḥa". The governing verb is omitted, which is "sabbaḥa", and the verbal noun has been converted into a noun of the verbal noun (ism maṣdar), namely "al-tasbīḥ", which became "subḥān". Tasbīḥ is the glorifying of God, mighty and majestic, above what is not befitting to Him, derived from "sabaḥa", meaning he went far in the water. So the meaning of tasbīḥ in "subḥān Allāh" is the declaration of God, glorified and exalted, as free from what does not befit Him. Two things do not befit God, mighty and majestic: one is deficiency in His attributes, and the second is resemblance to created beings in them. However, one may refer the second to the first and say: resemblance to created beings is a deficiency, because the resemblance of the perfect to the deficient makes it (...).

We may say it like this. So His words ﴿Glory be to Him who created﴾ mean: exaltation of this One who created all the pairs.

His words ﴿He who created all the pairs, of what the earth produces and of themselves and of what they do not know﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:36]: this verse is like His words ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:49]. All created things subsist only by composition from two or more materials. There is nothing that comes from one single thing ever. Everything, whether from what the earth produces, or from human beings, or from livestock, or from what we do not know, is in this general sense composed of two things.

﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:49]: in glorification of God, mighty and majestic, above what does not befit Him. This is why the verse here came: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:36]. Created beings necessarily have plurality, and the Creator is exalted above plurality. This is the wisdom, God knows best, in His saying ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾, and not "Praise be to God who created the pairs". Because the fact that everything needs duality shows the perfection of the One, the unique, to whom none of His creatures is comparable. The children of Adam must have a duality of male and female; even the qualities and attributes in them are found to be paired: there is anger and contentment, dislike and love, strength and weakness, and so on. But the Creator, mighty and majestic, is One, singular, to whom nothing is comparable in His essence or in His attributes (...).

The relation is "distance", meaning that He is far from deficiency. What?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Praise is more general than gratitude in terms of cause, and more specific than it in terms of object; gratitude is more general in terms of object and more specific in terms of cause.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: God is praised for His blessings and for His perfection, so He is praised for two things; this is the cause of praise, and praise is only in the tongue, through commendation. Gratitude is only for blessings, not for excellence. You do not say "I thank God for the perfection of His attributes"; no, for His blessings. So its cause is more specific. But it relates to the heart, the tongue and the limbs, so it is more general in terms of its object.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of God's power, mighty and majestic, to revive the earth after its death; from His saying ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth; We have revived it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33].
* Among them: the use of the witnessed to infer the unseen, since the revival of the earth after death is observed. It is cited as proof of God's reviving the dead at their resurrection on the Day of Judgement. God, exalted is He, pointed to this proof with His words: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells. Indeed, He who revived it is the reviver of the dead. Indeed, He is over all things Competent﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:39]. He also said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and therewith We caused gardens and grain of harvest to grow, and tall palm trees with ranged spathes, as provision for the servants, and We revived therewith a dead land. Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qāf 50:9–11]. There are many verses on this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of describing inanimate matter as dead, and that this is not restricted to what has a moving spirit; from His words ﴿the dead, We have revived it﴾, where He described it with death and described it with life.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the greatness of God, glorified and exalted, from His words ﴿We have revived it, and We brought forth from it﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the demonstration of God's blessing, mighty and majestic, in what He brought forth from the earth for people, of grains and fruits. The grains are in His words ﴿And We brought forth from it grain﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:33], and the fruits in His words ﴿And We made in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We caused springs to gush forth in it. That they may eat of its fruit﴾ [Yā Sīn 36:34–35].

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the servant's need for his Lord, as in His words: ﴿from it they eat﴾. This restriction (*hasr*) contains a kind of challenge to humanity, because you cannot eat except from what Allah has brought forth for you. This is one of the benefits of restriction, as if He is saying: If you are able, then bring forth for yourself what you eat. Indeed, you will never eat except from what We have brought forth for you.

It shows the greatness of Allah, in that He said ﴿We brought forth﴾ and ﴿We caused to gush forth﴾ using the plural of majesty (*damir al-'azamah*).

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the blessings Allah has bestowed upon His servants through these great, numerous trees that provide shade, as in His words: ﴿And We made therein gardens of date palms and grapevines﴾ [Ya-Sin 34–35]. How great are Allah's blessings upon the servant through these date palms and grapevines.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse is showing the excellence of date palms and grapevines, because they are fruit that is eaten without toil, and fruit that is eaten both fresh and dried.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is showing the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in causing the earth to gush forth springs. This earth is dry and hard, yet from it comes this moist, flowing thing, which is water. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split open and water comes out of them﴾ [al-Baqarah 74]. This is from the immense power of Allah. Moses, peace be upon him, would strike a hard rock, either a specific rock, as it is said, which he carried with him, or any rock at all, and it would gush forth twelve springs, according to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel. This is part of the perfect power of Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among them: showing that date palms and grapevines need water, and that their fruit increases in proportion to the water, because He said: ﴿And We caused springs to gush forth therein, [34] that they may eat of its fruit﴾ [Ya-Sin 34–35]. This indicates that water has an effect on fruits, in the abundance and goodness of the fruits, and this is the reality.

* Among them: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists, who deny human will and causation) by affirming causation (*'illah*) and wisdom (*hikmah*) in His words: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾.

The texts that establish the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are very numerous. Among them are those in which Allah the Most High explicitly stated it, such as His words: ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings do not avail﴾ [al-Qamar 5].

* Among them: what Allah has stated in the form of negation and denial: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan 38], ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved, so woe to those who disbelieved from the Fire﴾ [Sad 27]. Nothing indicates an attribute more than affirming it and negating its opposite, for affirming it indicates its existence, and negating its opposite indicates its perfection, and that it is free from this deficiency that arises from its absence or from the absence of its perfection. There is no doubt that if we negate wisdom from the act of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or from the legislation of Allah, there follows from that a great deficiency, and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, would be doing something foolishly and purposelessly.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is showing the blessings Allah has bestowed upon His servants through this fruit that is eaten. Consider: if this fruit became bitter, would it be beneficial? No. This is why Allah the Most High said about water: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? [68] Is it you who brought it down from the rain clouds, or are We the producer? [69] If We willed, We could make it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 68–70]. So you would be unable to drink it. This fruit, Allah the Most High made it delicious to souls; you eat from it and your bodies are nourished by it. This is why He said: ﴿that they may eat of its fruit﴾. If Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had willed, He could have made this fruit spoiled. It might be sweet and delicious and appetizing, but Allah would place in it a blight that spoils it. Isn't that so? It exists in abundance, but it is among the blessings of Allah that it remains and its fruit can be eaten.

* Another benefit of this noble verse is that we do not possess the ability to bring this fruit into existence ourselves, and that this is merely a grace from Allah. This is because of His words: ﴿and that which their hands made﴾ [Ya-Sin 35]. For this is not of our making. If all people gathered together to produce a single date, they would not be able to do so, or a single grape, they would not be able to do so. Yet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, creates these countless clusters of grapes and these countless bunches of dates on the palm trees. We have not made these with our hands; the most that we do is direct these fruits according to what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has taught us. For example, we take pollen from the male palm and place it in the female palm's blossom so that the fruit becomes good. But as for creating and bringing them into existence, no. This is according to making *ma* a negation.

* Another benefit, which is: showing the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in what He has taught us of what we do to these fruits, in a manner that differs from how they were created, so that from this there comes goodness upon goodness. This is because of His words: ﴿and that which their hands made﴾ [Ya-Sin 35]. Allah the Most High has taught us how to prepare these fruits in a way that we enjoy them and benefit from them more than they are in their natural state. This is according to making *ma* a relative pronoun (*maw�ulah*).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of thanking the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah rebuked those who do not give thanks. Thanking, besides being an act of obedience to Allah, is rewarded for the person, and through it he recognizes the value of Allah's blessing upon him, and it is a cause for more of these blessings. This is because of the words of Allah the Most High: ﴿And [recall] when your Lord proclaimed, "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe"﴾ [Ibrahim 7].

If someone says: We see many people upon whom Allah has lavished blessings while they disbelieve in them. So how do we answer this verse?

The answer to this is that we say: Allah the Most High has punished them with a great punishment, because punishment is not limited to the loss of blessings. Rather, punishment may come through the loss of blessings, and it may come through hardness of heart and sickness of the heart. Although most people think that punishments are only the removal of blessings, the reality is that punishments of the hearts are through sickness, hardness, and turning away from Allah and from His remembrance. These are the greatest punishment. Then, these people who are pampered in their bodies, you do not think at all that they are pampered in their hearts. In their hearts there is such constriction and distress, and a lack of patience with the decree and divine destiny (*qadar*), that it keeps them always in a fire. You will not find a better life than the life of the believer, even if he is the poorest of people: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl 97].

This is one answer. What is the other answer now? We say: These people have been punished with a punishment greater than the destruction of wealth, fruits, and other things, which is the hardness of the heart, its sickness, and its turning away. This necessitates for the person constriction of the chest and weariness with life, because he is not content with Allah as Lord nor with His legislation as religion.

Second: we say these blessings were hastened to them as a punishment and as gradual deception (*istidraj*). This is why, when 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while he was lying on a mat of palm fiber, meaning woven with palm fiber, and it had left a mark on his side, he wept and said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "O Messenger, Persia and Rome are enjoying the luxuries they have been given of the world, while you are in this state?!" Then he said: "O 'Umar, these are people whose good things have been hastened to them in their worldly life." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4913), and Muslim (1479/31), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in which 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He was lying on a mat with nothing between him and it, and under his head was a cushion of leather stuffed with palm fiber, and at his feet was a tanned skin, and at his head were hanging water skins. I saw the mark of the mat on the side of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so I wept. He said: 'What makes you weep?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Chosroes and Caesar are in what they are in, and you are the Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Are you not pleased that they have the world and you have the Hereafter?'" It was also related in a similar form by Ahmad (7963) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So we say: These people are punished by these blessings that flow to them, because it is gradual deception; and because when they die and enter punishment, it becomes more severe for them, since they have departed from a world to which their hearts were attached and in which they were pampered, and then this punishment followed, and we seek refuge in Allah. So they become more full of regret.

It is mentioned about Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, may Allah have mercy on him, who was the Chief Judge in Egypt, that one day he passed by a Jewish oil merchant selling oil, tired from the oil, with dirty clothes, and he was Jewish, while the Chief Judge, the judges of Egypt, was riding in a carriage pulled by horses, with people around him on the right and left. This Jewish man stopped the procession and said to him: "O Chief Judge, how can you be in this state and I in this state, when your Prophet says: 'Indeed the world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever'?" [Related by Muslim (2956/1) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]

What is the meaning of this? Which of them is in paradise now? The Chief Judge, while this man is in trial and hardship. He said to him: "Yes. What I am in of bliss, in the world, compared to my bliss in the Hereafter, or to the bliss of the believer in the Hereafter, is a prison. And what you are in of hardship and trial, compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, is a paradise. You are now in paradise, because you are moving to a punishment, a punishment you cannot imagine." When he said that, the Jew said: "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," and he embraced Islam.

The main point is that we say: These pampered people, their bliss is in reality misery and punishment, and although their bodies are pampered, most people are heedless of this. Regrettably, this disease has crept into the Muslims, so most Muslims today seek only this bliss, I mean the bliss of this world, and are heedless of the bliss of the Hereafter. This is why you find them always talking about luxury, amusement, and the like, as if they were created for nothing but this. This is among the greatest things that turn a person away from his religion: that his heart is attached to the world, and he looks only to enjoying it.

We do not deny that a person may obtain from this world what he benefits from for the Hereafter. Rather, if the world is made a means to the Hereafter, it becomes in reality part of the Hereafter. But we deny that the world should be a person's greatest concern, as if he were created only for it. This is from the deficiency of his religion and also the deficiency of his intellect. How can you make yourself and your precious life so preoccupied to the utmost extent with a matter that is not guaranteed and is not everlasting?

Allah the Most High said, rebuking the people of Hud, peace be upon him: ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will live forever﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 129]. You are not eternal. How can you make this passage in which you live your greatest concern, when you do not know when you will depart from it?! Every one of these luxury-seekers does not know when he will die, isn't that so? But he knows that he will remain in the Hereafter, if he believes in it, and yet he works for the world, for which he was not created, and abandons the Hereafter, for which he was created (...).

﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾, to the end of the verse.

* In the noble verse: the glorifying of Allah the Most High Himself above every deficiency and defect, as in His words: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. And in it (...)

The alert to His oneness, the Mighty and Majestic, and His difference from creation, as in His words: ﴿He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. He did not say "Glory be to Allah" alone, but said: ﴿He who created all the pairs of what the earth produces﴾ [Ya-Sin 36]. The combining of what is affirmed for the servants with what Allah is glorified above has come in more than one place in the Qur'an. Among them is His words: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish, [26] but there will remain the face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 26–27]. When He mentioned the state of creation, He mentioned the state of the Creator, because He, the Mighty and Majestic, remains while others perish. Similarly here: all creation is in pairs, and in it there must be two spouses. ﴿And of all things We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat 49]. As for the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, He is One. This is why He said: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that there is nothing created except (...); because of His words: ﴿and of that which they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin 36], and this is one of the most general of expressions.
