**Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin, Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim, on Surah Ya-Sin, verse 45:**

Then He, Exalted, said: (﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you"﴾ [Ya-Sin 45] "from the punishment of the worldly affliction"). According to me, is there no "worldly" (hamm) in your copy?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you"﴾ "from the punishment of the world"), because hamm is not only punishment (from the punishment of the world, like the others, ﴿and what is behind you﴾ from the punishment of the Hereafter, ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾ [Ya-Sin 45]; they turned away).

His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾. This sentence is conditional (shartiyyah). Its condition (fi'l al-shart) is ﴿it is said﴾, and its response (jawab) is omitted. The author estimated it with his words "they turned away." This estimate is without doubt a suggestion from the author; otherwise the matter may be broader than what the author said. Omitting such a response has the eloquence that the mind estimates everything that can follow from this saying. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that when people are told, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you," their responses differ. Some of them turn away and remain silent, some of them are arrogant and revile, some of them fight... and other matters that are not hidden. So in omitting this there is an eloquence that is evident, so that the mind may go in every direction in estimating this omitted element.

His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾. Who is the speaker? The speaker here is unspecified, because the verb is in the passive voice, to include anyone who says this statement to them, whether it is from the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His Book, or from the words of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his Sunnah, or from the words of the callers (du'at) after that. So these disbelievers, ﴿when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you"﴾, (﴿what is before you﴾ from the punishment of the world). Allah, Glorified and Exalted, may punish the disbeliever in this world, as He punished the earlier nations, and as He punished this nation too. But the punishment of this nation takes the form of some of them being tested by others: ﴿That [is so]. And if Allah had willed, He could have taken vengeance upon them, but [He ordained that] He would test some of you by means of others﴾ [Muhammad 4]. ﴿The Day We will seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 16]. This was at the Battle of Badr, when the chieftains of Quraysh were killed, and Allah, Exalted, named it "the greatest seizure." As for the earlier nations, their punishments are well known. So here, ﴿Fear what is before you﴾ means the punishment of this world, the varied punishment, whether it is at the hands of the believers, or is from the act of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, such as famine, earthquakes, drowning, and other things. ﴿And what is behind you﴾ means matters of the Hereafter, and the punishment of the Hereafter is harder, more severe, and more lasting.

Here He said: ﴿what is behind you﴾. Someone might say: if the matter were reversed, it would be closer to the correct meaning; He would say, "what is before you" is the punishment of the Hereafter, because it is future, and "what is behind you" is the punishment of this world, because the world is what a person leaves behind him.

But this is answered by saying that what is actually before them is the world. As for what is behind them, the words "khalf" and "waraa'" may be used in the sense of "in front," and from that is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force﴾ [Al-Kahf 79]. The scholars said its meaning is "in front of them." And like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And before him is Hell, and he will be given to drink of putrid fluid﴾ [Ibrahim 16–17]; that is, in front of him.

His saying: ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾. Here the particle (la'alla) indicates purpose (ta'lil), that is, so that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may show you mercy, when this matter is said to them. So He combined for them encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib): encouragement in His saying ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, and warning in His saying ﴿Fear what is before you and what is behind you﴾. He combined for them encouragement and warning, yet they do not respond. Rather they turn away, become arrogant, mock, and say: "This is only the fables of the former peoples," and other things like that, which are well known from these people when they are called to Allah.

In this noble verse: these disbelievers have had the proof established against them, the call has reached them, and they have been admonished, but that did not benefit them. This is because of His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear what is before you and what is behind you."﴾

* Among its benefits: when a person turns away from the religion of Allah and is arrogant, he becomes exposed to punishment, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both this world and the Hereafter. This is because of His saying: ﴿Fear what is before you and what is behind you.﴾

* Among its benefits: that turning toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and avoiding His disobedience, is a cause of mercy. This is because of His saying: ﴿that you may receive mercy.﴾

* Among its benefits also: the affirmation of causes and means (al-'ilal wal-asbab). This is because of His saying: ﴿la'allakum﴾; for this (la'alla) indicates purpose. No one denies that causes have an effect, except those who have turned away from the requirement of natural disposition (fitrah). People differed regarding causes and reasons in three opinions:

Some of them said: causes and reasons have effect by themselves, and every cause must have its effect on what it causes, and every reason must have its effect on what it results in.

Others said the opposite, and said: causes and reasons have no effect at all; they are only signs and indicators. So when the caused thing or the result is found, they do not say that it happened because of the cause or reason; rather they say that it happened at it, not by it. There is no doubt that these people opposed both transmitted texts and reason, and no one agrees with them in what they went to.

The third, middle opinion: they say that causes and reasons have an effect on what they cause and result in, but by Allah's making that effect in them. So they are not effective by themselves, but by what Allah, Exalted, has placed in them of the command that necessitates the caused thing or the result. This is the definite and correct view. The evidence is that Allah, Exalted, may strip this cause or this means of its effect, so that it has no effect at all. The story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, is not strange, when he was thrown into a fire blazing, and Allah said to this fire: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 69]. So it became coolness and safety, although it is a cause of burning. But it became coolness and safety upon Ibrahim. This shows that causes and reasons have effect only by what? By the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and by His making this cause or means effective.

* Among the benefits of this verse and the one before it also: the affirmation of mercy for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it is one of His attributes that are essential and active (dhatiyyah fi'liyyah). They are essential (dhatiyyah) because Allah has always been merciful to His servants and still is. They are active (fi'liyyah) in regard to their connection with the one who is shown mercy, for that is renewed in relation to the one shown mercy, not in relation to it being an attribute of Allah. So this one among mankind whom Allah has shown mercy is something newly occurring after he was not, so mercy became attached to him. It is not hidden from you what the Ash'aris (al-Ash'ariyyah) held: their denial of mercy in its true sense, and their claim that it means kindness (al-ihsan) or the will to show kindness. They interpreted it as will, because they affirm will for Allah, or as kindness, because it is a created, separate thing and not one of Allah's attributes. This is without doubt a false and weak view. We have already passed the explanation of their reasoning for denying it and the refutation of them. They said: mercy requires what? Softness, gentleness, and weakness, and this is not befitting for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They also said: reason does not indicate mercy, and we affirm among the attributes only what reason indicates. We have already explained that this statement is not correct:

First: mercy may occur from a person who is strong and powerful, and he is described as merciful, even among human beings.

Second: their claim that reason does not indicate it is false, for reason indicates it more clearly and more evidently than the indication of specification (takhsis) on will. This has passed with us many times.

Allah, Exalted, said (...). There is a third opinion which we will mention: that what is before them and what is behind them refers to the sins that lie in their future and which they fear they will commit, and what is behind them refers to past sins. So what is meant by what is before them and what is behind them is their deeds, not the punishment of Allah. We have previously said that if a verse can bear the meanings that have been stated for it without contradiction, then it is to be taken as including all of them.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾ [Yasin 46]. Have we already discussed this verse before?

Alright. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾. The pronoun here refers to those who deny the messengers. Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿There does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾, and the ﴿مِنْ﴾ (min, "from") here is extra in wording but adds to the meaning. It is extra in form and extra for meaning, meaning it gives the sentence a new sense. What is the new meaning? The new meaning is the emphasis of the negation and the explicit statement of its generality: that is, whatever sign comes to them, they will not accept it, but rather they turn away from it and act arrogantly.

The signs that come from Allah the Mighty and Majestic are divided into two types: cosmic signs (kawniyyah) and legislative signs (shar'iyyah).

As for the legislative signs, they are what the messengers, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, brought. Turning away from them takes the form of denial and arrogance: denial of the reports, and arrogance toward the rulings.

As for the cosmic signs, turning away from them means that a person does not care about them, they do not stir him at all, and his heart does not tremble at them, and he says what those who saw the punishment descending from the sky said: ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the sky falling, they would say, "Layered clouds."﴾ [At-Tur 44], or like those who say: the eclipse is not a frightening matter because it is a natural thing and should not frighten anyone — we ask Allah for well-being — or like those who see earthquakes, drownings and destruction from violent winds and other things, and then say: this is a natural matter that does not stir them at all. There is no doubt that this indicates hardness of hearts and their deadness; otherwise, it is obligatory for a person to take admonition from these signs. So turning away from the cosmic signs means what? It means not paying attention to them, not caring about them, and that they do not move a person at all or stir any feeling in him. This is turning away from the cosmic signs. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾, meaning: except that they meet them with aversion, do not reflect upon them, and do not think about them. When legislative signs come with a report, they deny it immediately and say: "This is a lie, this is magic, this is poetry." When legislative rulings come, they act arrogantly toward them, do not submit to them, and do not comply with them, without reflecting on them or on the benefits contained in them. Likewise, regarding the cosmic signs, they are unconcerned and do not care about them; ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾.

* In this verse there is evidence that Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentions or shows His servants signs of the kind on which humankind can believe; the reason is that, were it not so, the signs would have no benefit.

* Among its benefits: human beings may be heedless of the signs and turn away from them without consideration. A person must first consider and then judge. For this reason it is said: "Judgment on a thing is a branch of conceiving it." So look first at the signs: see whether they are convincing and compelling to righteousness. Be righteous by them. If they are of no benefit, then one is excused for turning away from them.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the explanation of the hardness of the hearts of these people, for they did not accept any sign. Its proof is: ﴿There does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of general lordship (rububiyyah 'ammah), by His saying ﴿from the signs of their Lord﴾. Allah the Exalted thus affirms that He is the Lord of these people, and He, glorified and exalted, is the Lord of everything: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred, and to whom belongs everything﴾ [An-Naml 91]. Everything has Allah as its Lord, even the disbelievers. But we say: sometimes lordship is specific, meaning a special lordship in which there is greater care and attention, such as His saying: ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [Al-A'raf 122]. This lordship is other than the general lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the condemnation of the condition of these people and a warning against their action, by His saying ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾, even though it came from whom? From their Lord, who is their Owner, their Creator, and whose command is to Him, and yet they turn away.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 47 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed? You are not but in clear error."﴾ [Ya-Sin 47]

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ The author said: (That is, the poor among the Companions said, ﴿Spend﴾ upon us ﴿from what Allah has provided you﴾ of wealth). In this way the author proceeded in explaining the verse, making the speakers the poor. Accordingly, the verse concerns the poor asking the wealthy to spend; that is, when the poor come asking the wealthy to spend, they mock them and say: "How shall we feed you when Allah, the Exalted, has not willed that we feed you?! And had He willed that we feed you, He would have given you without your asking." This is the interpretation of the verse according to what the author adopted.

However, what should be adopted is that the verse is general, because the agent is left unspecified in it, and leaving the agent unspecified is sometimes intended to indicate generality. So ﴿when it is said to them﴾ means: when anyone among people says to them, whether the poor are asking them to spend or the wealthy are urging them to spend. For the wealthy among the Companions, for example, do spend, and they urge the wealthy among the disbelievers to spend as well. Therefore, the correct view is to leave the verse in its unspecified form so that it is more comprehensive.

As for His saying ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you﴾: "spending" means giving and bestowing. His saying ﴿from what He has provided you﴾ means: from what Allah has given you. In their saying ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you﴾, rather than saying "spend from your wealth," there is an alert that what is in your hands is not in reality from your own earning but from the provision of Allah. So it was incumbent upon you to spend from what Allah has provided you, because Allah commands you to do so. The One who commanded you to spend is the One who gave you this wealth, so how can you deny His bounty and be arrogant toward His command, so that you do not spend?! This is the benefit in His saying ﴿from what Allah has provided you﴾.

The answer: ﴿Those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed?"﴾ As for His saying ﴿Those who disbelieve say to those who believe﴾, this lam (in lilladhina) is, most correctly, in its original sense, and what is meant by it is attribution; that is, they uttered a statement that reached those who believed. Who are those who believed? They are the ones who were told, ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you﴾.

"They say": the author said: (in mockery of them). What the author mentioned may be mockery, and it may also be from the category of invoking divine decree out of obstinacy and pretext.

He says: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed?﴾ Here ﴿man﴾ means "the one who," and it is permissible for it to be an indefinite qualified noun; i.e., "Shall we feed someone whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed, apart from us?" or "Shall we feed the one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed?" Here ﴿law﴾ is a particle of non-occurrence due to non-occurrence; its condition is His saying ﴿willed﴾, and its response is ﴿fed him﴾. It has come contrary to the more common usage, in that the lam was omitted from the response. The original would be: "whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed" (la-atamahu). When the response of (law) is affirmative, the more common usage includes the lam, though the lam may be omitted. Both usages were combined in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who grow it, or are We the growers? If We willed, We could make it into debris, and you would remain astonished﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 63-65]. Then He said: ﴿Have you considered the water which you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the rain clouds, or are We the sender? If We willed, We could make it bitter, so why are you not grateful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 68-70]. So the lam came in the response of ﴿law﴾ in the former verse and was omitted in the second verse. The verse before us belongs to the category of the omitted lam: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed?﴾

The author said: They say this in mockery and derision; that is: "Shall we feed a people whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed? So is their feeding up to us or up to Allah?" Up to Allah.

It may also be from the category of what? The invoking of divine decree to escape blame; that is: "Shall we feed a people whom, if Allah had willed, He would have fed, so we fed them? But Allah, the Exalted, has not willed that we feed them, so we do not feed them." These are two aspects.

The third aspect: it may be that they said this as an objection to divine decree, as the socialists and communists say: "Why does Allah make this one poor and not give him?" As if in this answer they object against Allah, saying: "Who feeds them? Allah. We are not responsible for them; Allah is responsible for them, and it was incumbent upon Allah to feed them, but He has not willed that." So this contains a kind of objection to decree. These are three aspects: mockery, the second: invoking decree, and the third: objecting to decree.

Then they said: ﴿You are not but in clear error﴾, i.e., (you, in your saying this to us together with this belief of yours, are not but in clear error, evident). That is, these disbelievers who were commanded to spend on the poor say to the one who commanded them: "Do you believe that Allah, if He willed, would have fed them?" He says: "Yes, I believe that." They say: "Then how do you command us to feed them when the matter is by the will of Allah?! You are nothing but in clear error."

As for His saying ﴿You are not﴾, is ﴿in﴾ here negating or conditional?
* The students: Negating.
* The Shaykh: In the sense of (ma)?
* The students: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that it is negating? The presence of (illa) after it; and when (illa) comes after (in), it is evidence that (in) is negating. A few days ago we went over that (in) comes in the Arabic language in four aspects:
The first?
* A student: It comes as an extra particle.
* The Shaykh: Good, and its example?
* The student: The poet's saying:
Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold ∗∗∗ .............................
* The Shaykh:
Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold ∗∗∗ nor refined silver, but you are clay.
Good. Does it also come as?
* A student: Conditional.
* The Shaykh: Conditional. Its example?
* The student: "If Zayd stands, I stand."
* The Shaykh: And will you not bring us evidence from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, or the speech of the Arabs?
* The student: From the Qur'an?
* The Shaykh: Yes: ﴿If he is rich or poor, Allah is more deserving of both﴾ [an-Nisa' 135]. This is conditional (in). Good. Third?
* A student: Negating.
* The Shaykh: It also comes negating. Its example?
* The student: ﴿You are not but in clear error﴾ [Ya-Sin 47].
* The Shaykh: Good.
* The student: A lightened form of the heavy (inna).
* The Shaykh: A lightened form of the heavy (inna). Its example?
* The student: ....................... ∗∗∗ and indeed Malik's people were noble in origins
* The Shaykh: The poet's saying: ....................... ∗∗∗ and indeed Malik's people were noble in origins. Good.

As for the author's saying ﴿clear﴾, he said: i.e., (evident). Is it from (abana), intransitive, or from (abana), transitive? (Abana) comes both transitive and intransitive: one says (abana al-shay'a), meaning he made it manifest, and one says (abana al-subhu), meaning it appeared. So ﴿mubin﴾ is from the quadriliteral, from abana yubinu, so he is mubin. Can it mean (bayyin) on the basis that it is from the intransitive or the transitive?
* A student: Intransitive.
* The Shaykh: From the intransitive. And in other contexts it may mean (abana) like: ﴿And a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr 1]; the meaning is not "a manifest Qur'an," but "a Qur'an making the truth manifest."

The author said: (And the explicit statement of their disbelief has a great effect). Where? ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieve say﴾, and He did not say: "they said." ﴿Those who disbelieve say﴾, so it has a great effect. What is this great effect? This great effect is:
* First: the explicit declaration of the disbelief of these people. Had He said "they said," we would say: perhaps they said that not because of disbelief but because of stinginess. This is the benefit that this explicit mention in place of the pronoun in this verse is to declare their disbelief.
* The second benefit: that such a statement is not uttered except by a disbeliever, so that disbelief is general to everyone who makes this statement.

It has previously passed us that explicit mention in place of the pronoun has three benefits:
The first benefit: declaring the ruling upon those to whom the pronoun refers.
The second: that whoever says the like of this is a disbeliever or a wrongdoer, according to context.
The third: the cause, and that this statement's cause is such-and-such, according to what is described.

The commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 47 (part 2 of 2):

(...) The lam here means "about" ('an). That is, "those who disbelieved said about those who believed," meaning they said concerning those who were commanded to spend on them, namely the believers: ﴿Shall we feed one whom Allah could feed if He willed?﴾
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Its meaning is that the lam is for connection (al-ṣilah, a connecting particle). That is, this statement is connected to those who spoke. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you,"﴾ this statement, ﴿those who disbelieved said﴾ (the ones to whom it was said) ﴿to those who believed﴾ (the speakers). So the lam is for connection, meaning it links this statement to the speaker who presented to them the words: ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you.﴾
* Student: The belief (...) ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Shall we feed one whom Allah could feed if He willed?"﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Because he is saying: if you believe that affairs are in the hand of Allah, then how do you order us to spend on these people? If Allah willed, He would feed them without us. So by your ordering us, while you believe that the matter is in the hand of Allah, this is considered misguidance from you.
(...) Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you," ...﴾ to the end.
* From this noble verse it is derived that those who disbelieved are admonished and alerted, but they are arrogant. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what Allah has provided you,"﴾ so the proof is established against them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when a person spends by the command of Allah, he has no favor upon Allah, because Allah, the Exalted, is the One who gave him. This is from His saying: ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is fitting for the speaker and preacher to explain the reasons that motivate him to do what he preaches. This is from His saying: ﴿from what Allah has provided you.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those who said this statement, ﴿Shall we feed one whom Allah could feed if He willed?﴾ are disbelievers, from His saying: ﴿those who disbelieved said.﴾
* Among its benefits: stinginess is a trait of the disbelievers, from His saying: ﴿those who disbelieved said.﴾ If it is a trait of the disbelievers, then it is not befitting for the believer to be characterized by it. Every trait that belongs to the disbelievers, such as Jews, Christians and others, it is proper for the Muslim not to do it, because if he does, he becomes one who imitates the disbelievers in that characteristic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person may say a word of truth while intending falsehood. ﴿Shall we feed one whom Allah could feed if He willed?﴾ We believe that if Allah willed, He would feed these people. But His wisdom, Mighty and Majestic is He, required that He make these people poor and those people rich.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the polytheists acknowledge the will of Allah and that it takes effect in everything. This is from their saying: ﴿one whom Allah could feed if He willed,﴾ and the polytheists, or disbelievers, do not deny lordship (rububiyyah), meaning they do not deny the lordship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Rather, they affirm it. Even those who pretended to deny it only deny it with their tongues. This is due to the saying of Allah, the Exalted, about the people of Pharaoh: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml 14], and Moses' saying to Pharaoh: ﴿He said, "You know well that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence"﴾ [al-Isra 102]. But they deny lordship out of arrogance and obstinacy, and otherwise their inner selves bear witness to it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the methods of propaganda used by the polytheists since ancient times. They said to these believers, or to these speakers, ﴿Spend from what Allah has provided you,﴾ they said to them: ﴿You are only in clear error.﴾ This disgraceful description of the believers by the disbelievers has not ceased and does not cease to exist until our day. They describe the people of goodness with many repulsive descriptions, either to make people shun them, or to incite the rulers against these believers. They say: "These are reactionaries, these are backward, these are extremists, these are rigid."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, and whatever is similar to that of the bad words with which they revile the friends of Allah, the Exalted. We do not deny that among the people of goodness and religion there are those who go to extremes and exaggerate in their deeds or in their description of others, with takfir (declaring someone a disbeliever) and tafsiq (declaring someone a sinner), so that they declare a disbeliever whom Allah has not declared a disbeliever, and declare a sinner whom Allah has not declared a sinner. We do not deny that this exists. But it seems to me, and Allah knows best, that the existence of such extremists came only as a result of the extremism of others in sins and wickedness, so they want to produce a reaction against them. If all people were upright in religion, this extremism would not have happened. But when they see a side extreme in wickedness and disobedience, and that it continues and is approved by some rulers, a counter-reaction arises against them. So these became strict in response to the laxity of those. But moderation is the good. Nevertheless, moderate people are not safe from the tongues of the misguided extremists nor from the tongues of the excessive extremists. For example, the excessive ones say to these moderates: "You are negligent, you are compromisers, you approve of the people of evil." And those (the people of evil) say: "These are strict, these want people to be like them, otherwise they are disbelievers." And whatever is similar to that. The point is that the offensive titles by which the enemies of Allah label the friends of Allah have not ceased to exist and do not cease to exist until our day. Even the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) label the people of the Sunnah with offensive titles. They say: "These are mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) when they affirm the attributes literally; these are ḥashwiyyah; these are nawābit," and whatever is similar to that of the words that necessitate aversion to them and belittling and demeaning their status. But does this harm the people of goodness?
No, it does not harm them, but it hurts them, and hurt is not the same as harm. A person may be hurt by something without being harmed by it. Here, a person is hurt by the smell of onions, leeks and any disgusting thing, yet he is not harmed by it. Allah has affirmed for Himself that He is hurt by the hypocrites and others, and negated for Himself being harmed. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who hurt Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57]. In the ḥadīth qudsī He said: "The son of Adam hurts Me; he curses time" [agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246), from the ḥadīth of Abu Hurayrah]. And in another ḥadīth qudsī He said: "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me" [narrated by Muslim (2577), from the ḥadīth of Abu Dharr]. The point is that such titles undoubtedly hurt the believers, and they are hurt by them, and their hearts are constricted by them, but they do not harm them. Rather, they benefit them, because if they are patient with them, they are rewarded for patience, and if they are hurt without patience, they become an expiation for them, because no fatigue, nor harm, nor sorrow, nor grief, nor hurt, nor distress befalls the believer, even a thorn that pricks him, except that Allah expiates his sins by it. [Al-Bukhari, in its wording, (5641), and Muslim (2573/52), from the ḥadīth of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "No fatigue, nor illness, nor anxiety, nor sorrow, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even a thorn that pricks him, except that Allah expiates some of his sins by it."] Especially since he is hurt here for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So this is a virtue for him, and this person who was hurt for Allah's sake has attained what the friends of Allah attained: the prophets, the truthful (ṣiddīqīn) and the martyrs. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the righteous are tested, the most excellent first, then the next most excellent [narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2398) and Ibn Majah (4023), from the ḥadīth of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas]. So if there is strength in his religion, he is hurt more, so that the test is more complete. If his religion is weaker, Allah may show him mercy and he does not suffer the hurt that the other suffers. Allah, the Exalted, may also test him: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is reassured by it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. We ask Allah for safety.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exaggeration of the enemies of Allah in what they describe the friends of Allah with. This is from their saying: ﴿You are only in clear error.﴾ As if they restricted their state from every aspect to what? To clear error. As if there is no guidance in them at all. "You are only in error." This is the utmost of aggression from these people.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the will of Allah. It is mentioned many times in the Qur'an. But every will of Allah that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned is accompanied or restricted by what? By wisdom. Since the will of Allah is not mere will; rather, it is accompanied by wisdom.
Alright, the principle we mentioned, brother?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Well done.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yasin 48] Who says it? The disbelievers who deny Allah's promise, which includes the Resurrection.

Here ﴿متى﴾ (matā, "when") is an interrogative of disapproval and challenge. That is, they say, deeming this matter far-fetched and challenging whoever speaks of it: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ This ﴿متى﴾ is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿هذا﴾ (hādhā, "this") is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). That is because ﴿متى﴾ has the status of an indefinite noun, while ﴿هذا الوعد﴾ ("this promise") is definite, and the known rule is that the definite word is the subject, while the predicate is typically indefinite (though it may be definite). But when there is an indefinite and a definite word, and the definite can be the subject, it is the subject. Why? Because the subject is the thing about which a judgment is made, so it must be definite, and definiteness, as you know, specifies and particularises the referent. Hence the scholars stated this rule: when there are two words, one definite and the other indefinite, and the definite can be the subject, let it be the subject. The reason is that the subject is that about which a judgment is made, so it must be known and specified.

He says: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ He said: (﴿the promise﴾ refers to the resurrection; ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾). What are they saying? Disapproval and challenge. That is why He said: ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾; i.e., if you are truthful that we will be resurrected, then when will it be? Without doubt this is a baseless doubt, because those who spoke of the resurrection did not specify a particular day so that they could say: "Come on, give us the resurrection!"

Look at their argument in another verse that is clearer: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, their argument is only that they say, "Bring our fathers, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Jathiyah 25]. Did those who said they would be resurrected say that you will be resurrected in this world, so that they would say, "Bring our fathers"? Not at all, they did not say that. Rather they said you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. So their saying ﴿"Bring our fathers"﴾ means "Raise them for us," which is a challenge misplaced, because they were not told that they would be resurrected in this world, but on the Day of Resurrection. They say: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ What is the answer? Allah mentions this in the Qur'an: ﴿Say, "Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then gathers you to the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt."﴾ [al-Jathiyah 26]. So the promise has not yet come at its time; wait, and this promise will come.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They await nothing but one blast﴾ [Yasin 49]. This is the answer; in this verse too He answered. He said: (﴿They await nothing﴾ means they wait for ﴿nothing but one blast﴾, which is the blast of Israfil.)

(نظر) is used transitively in itself, and when it is transitive by itself it means "to await"; like: ﴿They await nothing but one blast﴾ [Yasin 49], ﴿Then do they await anything but the way of the former peoples?﴾ [Fatir 43], and there are other examples.

If it is followed by (في) it means reflective looking; you say: nazara fī kadhā, i.e., he pondered it and considered it.

If it is followed by (إلى) it means looking with the eye; you say: nazartu ilayhi (I looked at him), and from it the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah 22–23].

What these people await is ﴿nothing but one blast﴾, which is the first blast of Israfil. ﴿Blast﴾ means they will be cried at, and that is in the first blast on the Trumpet, because this blast has a great, disturbing sound that terrifies all creatures. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills﴾ [an-Naml 87]. All creatures are terrified except whom Allah the Exalted wills, and they will be terrified with a severe terror that leads to swooning, to death; and then there will be one blast in which there is terror and there is swooning.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They await nothing but one blast that will seize them﴾, seizing them as an enemy seizes his enemy, such that it gives them no respite and no reprieve.

(﴿وهم يخَصِّمون﴾ with the shadda; its origin is (يختصمون): the vowel of the tā' was moved to the khā' and the tā' was assimilated into the ṣād; i.e., they are heedless of it while disputing, trading, eating, drinking and other things.)

The origin of ﴿يَخَصِّمُونَ﴾ is (يختصمون). The author says: (the vowel of the tā' was moved to the khā'), and the khā' was originally sukūn, so it became ﴿يَخَصِّمُونَ﴾. Yes, and this is one of the readings: with a fatha on the yā', ﴿يَخَصِّمُونَ﴾, because he said: (the vowel of the tā' was moved to the khā'), and the tā' has a fatha, and he mentioned nothing else.

The reading in the Mushaf is ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾, and it seems the khā' was kasra out of consideration for the kasra of the ṣād: ﴿يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾.

There is a third reading: ﴿يَخْصِمُونَ﴾ like (يَضْرِبون), so the readings are now three.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: He mentioned ﴿يَخْصِمُونَ﴾.

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, but may Allah guide you, this is ﴿يَخْصِمُونَ﴾; we now have three readings, he mentioned only two.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Glory be to Allah the Mighty! If only you would not hurry. I have only two readings here, and you have the glossary with you; what does it say?

* Student: His saying: ﴿يَخَصِّمُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the yā', present tense of (خَصَّم) like (عَلَّمَ), originally (اخْتَصَمَ); the vowel of the tā' was moved to the khā', then the tā' was changed into ṣād and assimilated into the ṣād, and the hamzat al-waṣl was dropped as the khā' was vocalised. So the modification occurred in the past tense as it occurred in its present tense, which he indicated by saying: (its origin is yakhtaṣimūn). His saying: (the vowel of the tā' was moved) means wholly or partly; it was given a fatha. These are two readings: full fatha on the khā', and ikhtilās, i.e., pronouncing part of its fatha. (And in a reading: ﴿يَخْصِمُونَ﴾ like (يَضرِبون), i.e., some of them dispute with others), so victory goes to the one stronger in dispute, not to the one in the right, because they are in confusion and uproar, and they have no faith, no manliness and no character; they are the worst of creation. (...) the obstinacy and arrogance of these people: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ [Yasin 48].

* Benefitted from this: that the children of Adam reach the point of challenging the Lord of the worlds and the one who conveyed His message, in their saying: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾.

* Among its benefits: the Messengers conveyed the clear message and explained to people that they will be resurrected and recompensed, and that they were promised this; as shown by their saying:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾.

* Among its benefits: those who said this in challenge and disapproval did not believe the messengers, but denied them; and would that they had considered the matter and reflected; as shown by his saying here: ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾.

* Among its benefits: a warning to these deniers by this blast which will seize them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that this blast will come upon them suddenly; as shown by ﴿while they are disputing﴾, heedless of it.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: an explanation of the state of those upon whom the Hour will arrive and whom the blast will seize, namely disputing and contention, which indicates the evil of their conditions and the evil of their characters, and that their only concern is this matter: nothing but contention and quarrelling, out of greed and covetousness for the world and heedlessness of the Hereafter. That is why the authentic hadith states that the Hour will not arrive except upon the worst of creation[[Related by Muslim (1924/176) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]], and it is known that these people eat and drink; but Allah mentions only this disputing to show the evil of their state at that time.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yasin 48] Who says it? The disbelievers who deny Allah's promise, which includes the Resurrection.

Here ﴿متى﴾ (matā, "when") is an interrogative of disapproval and challenge. That is, they say, deeming this matter far-fetched and challenging whoever speaks of it: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ This ﴿متى﴾ is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿هذا﴾ (hādhā, "this") is the postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). That is because ﴿متى﴾ has the status of an indefinite noun, while ﴿هذا الوعد﴾ ("this promise") is definite, and the known rule is that the definite word is the subject, while the predicate is typically indefinite (though it may be definite). But when there is an indefinite and a definite word, and the definite can be the subject, it is the subject. Why? Because the subject is the thing about which a judgment is made, so it must be definite, and definiteness, as you know, specifies and particularises the referent. Hence the scholars stated this rule: when there are two words, one definite and the other indefinite, and the definite can be the subject, let it be the subject. The reason is that the subject is that about which a judgment is made, so it must be known and specified.

He says: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ He said: (﴿the promise﴾ refers to the resurrection; ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾). What are they saying? Disapproval and challenge. That is why He said: ﴿"if you are truthful"﴾; i.e., if you are truthful that we will be resurrected, then when will it be? Without doubt this is a baseless doubt, because those who spoke of the resurrection did not specify a particular day so that they could say: "Come on, give us the resurrection!"

Rather they said you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection. Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 50–51:

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their families.﴾ [Ya-Sin 50] That is, when it seizes them, they will not go beyond their places, and they will not even be able to speak because of the intensity of the terror they are in.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest﴾ means: they will not be able to give instructions to their families, their children or their foolish ones, because the matter is too great for them to speak about it.

﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾ because they will not go beyond their places. They will neither reach their families and see them, nor will they be able to bequeath anything to anyone about them. This shows that the event that seizes them is a great matter, and it is so, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills; and all will come to Him in humility.﴾ [An-Naml 87]

He said: (﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾ from their markets and their occupations; rather, they will die right there.)

(﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾ [Ya-Sin 51]: it is the horn of the second blowing for resurrection, and between the two blowings is forty years.)

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. Allah, the Exalted, always mentions the blowing of the Trumpet in the passive form ﴿is blown﴾ (nufikha), because leaving the agent unspecified is more emphatic in conveying awe and grandeur than naming it. This is why you find that the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then there covered them that which covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha 78] is more eloquent than if what covered them had been specified. So leaving things vague sometimes conveys awe and grandeur.

Here the one who blows is left unspecified, and in all the verses it is unspecified: the blower is unnamed to show the magnitude of this matter. It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the one entrusted with blowing the Trumpet is Israfil, one of the bearers of the Throne. [Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (348) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]

The author said: (the second blowing for resurrection, and between the two blowings is forty years. ﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾) and so on to the end.

﴿The Trumpet is blown﴾ for resurrection. Allah, the Exalted, has mentioned the blowing of the Trumpet in this verse, in Surah az-Zumar, in Surah an-Naml, and likewise in Surah al-An'am and elsewhere.

The point is that the scholars differed over whether the blowings are three or two. Some said they are two, and some said they are three. The apparent meaning is that there are only two, but the first of them involves terror and swooning, and the second involves raising, and this is the apparent view of the author when he said: (the second blowing for resurrection), so there are two blowings, but in the first of them a great terror occurs, then death.

Some scholars said there are three: the first blowing is terror, the second blowing is swooning and death, and the third blowing is raising.

In Surah az-Zumar Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom Allah wills. Then it is blown again, and behold, they are standing, looking on.﴾ [Az-Zumar 68] So He mentioned two blowings.

In Surah an-Naml: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills; and all will come to Him in humility.﴾ [An-Naml 87] Then He mentioned the Day of Resurrection and omitted mention of the second blowing. So this terror is before death, then death, then resurrection.

He said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. The Trumpet (aṣ-ṣūr) is a great, wide horn. It is reported in a hadith that its width is as the distance between the heaven and the earth. [Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'n-Nushur (609) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.] It is blown for resurrection, and the spirits come out of it, and each spirit returns to the body it used to inhabit in the world, and never mistakes it. Despite the great number of spirits coming out of this Trumpet, no spirit mistakes its body that it used to inhabit in the world. Even if it were assumed that dozens of people were buried in one place, each person's spirit returns only to its own body. This is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing, may He be exalted.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Then, behold﴾, that is, the buried ones, ﴿they will emerge from the graves﴾, the tombs, ﴿to their Lord, hastening﴾, they will come out quickly.)

His saying ﴿Then behold﴾: the fa' is conjunctive, (idha) is a particle indicating suddenness, and ﴿hum﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿yansilun﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿ilā rabbihim﴾ is connected to ﴿yansilun﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then, behold﴾, meaning that as soon as the blowing occurs, no time passes between them, that is, between the blowing of the Trumpet and the emergence from the graves.

﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾: from the tombs, they will come out to Allah, the Exalted, hastening.

As for His saying ﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾, the pronoun in ﴿hum﴾ (they): the author said (that is, the buried ones). How do we know that the intended meaning is the buried ones? From His saying ﴿from the graves﴾, because al-ajdath (the graves) are the tombs.

As for His saying ﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾, this is based on what is most common, because some people are not in a grave. Rather, they are cast into the sea, or cast onto the surface of the earth, or eaten by predators, or burned and scattered by the winds. But the general and most common case is that they are in graves.

As for His saying ﴿to their Lord﴾, there is a fronting of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul) to convey restriction (hasr), meaning they will not hasten to a worldly life, or to a relative, or to a friend, but they will hasten only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Al-nasalan means moving swiftly, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they, from every elevated place, will hasten﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 96], that is, they will come out quickly.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse before this one and this one as well: that the blowing of the Trumpet, when it occurs (...).

Despite the great number of spirits coming out of this Trumpet, no spirit mistakes its body that it used to inhabit in the world. Even if it were assumed that dozens of people were buried in one place, each person's spirit returns only to its own body. This is the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing, may He be exalted.

Allah, the Exalted, said: (﴿Then, behold﴾, that is, the buried ones, ﴿they will emerge from the graves﴾, the tombs, ﴿to their Lord, hastening﴾, they will come out quickly.)

His saying ﴿Then behold﴾: the fa' is conjunctive, (idha) is a particle indicating suddenness, and ﴿hum﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿yansilun﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿ilā rabbihim﴾ is connected to ﴿yansilun﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then, behold﴾, meaning that as soon as the blowing occurs, no time passes between them, that is, between the blowing of the Trumpet and the emergence from the graves.

﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾: from the tombs, they will come out to Allah, the Exalted, hastening.

As for His saying ﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾, the pronoun in ﴿hum﴾ (they): the author said (that is, the buried ones). How do we know that the intended meaning is the buried ones? From His saying ﴿from the graves﴾, because al-ajdath (the graves) are the tombs.

As for His saying ﴿Then, behold, they will emerge from the graves﴾, this is based on what is most common, because some people are not in a grave. Rather, they are cast into the sea, or cast onto the surface of the earth, or eaten by predators, or burned and scattered by the winds. But the general and most common case is that they are in graves.

As for His saying ﴿to their Lord﴾, there is a fronting of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul) to convey restriction (hasr), meaning they will not hasten to a worldly life, or to a relative, or to a friend, but they will hasten only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Al-nasalan means moving swiftly, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they, from every elevated place, will hasten﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 96], that is, they will come out quickly.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse before this one and this one as well: that the blowing of the Trumpet, when it occurs (...).

The commonly known view is that the returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) mentioned is not omitted except when the governing word of the relative pronoun (mawṣūl) matches the governing word of the omitted element, both in form and meaning. This is the view known among the grammarians (al-naḥwiyyīn). However, the preferred view is that the ʿāʾid may be omitted whether its governing word is of the same kind as the governing word of the relative pronoun or of a different kind. The rule that Ibn Malik stated in his line:

*"The omission of what is known is permissible......"*

is general, covering everything and not limited to the subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar), but applying to everything.

As for His saying ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ [Yasin 52], "al-Raḥmān" is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, among the names specific to Him that may not be applied to anyone else. No one is named Raḥmān. As for "raḥīm," it may be used to describe created beings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿لَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ عَزِيزٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَنِتُّمْ حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُمْ بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [al-Tawbah 128] ("There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is your distress; [he is] anxious over you and to the believers [is] kind and merciful"). However, "raḥmān" may not be applied to anyone else. The difference between them is that "raḥīm" is considered in terms of the act, while "raḥmān" is considered in terms of the attribute. So when He says "al-Raḥmān," it means the One possessing vast mercy, and "al-Raḥīm" means the One whose mercy reaches whomever He wills of His servants.

Here He mentioned ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ and did not say "what Allah promised," because Allah's mercy on the Day of Resurrection will manifest far more than in this world. Allah the Exalted has one hundred mercies, of which He placed one mercy on earth. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will have the full hundred mercies: the remaining ninety-nine and the first mercy. [Ibn Abi Shaybah (35210) reported with his chain from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah created, on the day He created the heavens and the earth, one hundred mercies. He placed one mercy in the earth, and by it the mother shows compassion to her child, and the animals show compassion to one another. He withheld ninety-nine mercies until the Day of Resurrection. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy into one hundred mercies." Muslim (2753) also reported it, from the hadith of Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him), in similar wording.] This indicates the manifestation of Allah's mercy on that Day, and for this reason He said here: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾.

﴿al-Raḥmān﴾ is a derived noun (mushtaqq) that indicates what? It indicates the attribute of mercy. It is obligatory for us, regarding the names of Allah the Exalted, to affirm the name, and what it indicates of attribute and of the effect that follows from it. It is also permissible to say: and the judgement. So here "al-Raḥmān" is His name, "mercy" is His attribute, and "He has mercy on whom He wills" is His act, glorified and exalted be He, and it is the effect of mercy.

He said: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾, ﴿وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ [Allah promised], because there will be a day on which people are resurrected, and on which the doer of good is rewarded for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. The reward of a good deed is ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

He said: (﴿وَصَدَقَ﴾ فيه ﴿الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾) ["and the Messengers spoke the truth"]. "Ṣadaqa" means "he informed with truth," and "ṣaddaqa" means "he confirmed the speaker." So affirmation (taṣdīq) is from the addressee, and truthfulness (ṣidq) is from the speaker. It is said ṣadaqa, and it is said ṣaddaqa. "Ṣadaqa" means "he informed with truth." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 152] ("And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission"). And "ṣaddaqa" means "he confirmed the speaker"; that is, he acknowledged his words and accepted them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَالَّذِي جَاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ﴾ [al-Zumar 33] ("And the one who brought the truth and believed in it"). So he is truthful (ṣādiq) and one who affirms (muṣaddiq). And Allah knows best.

* Benefits: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿قَالُوا يَا وَيْلَنَا مَنْ بَعَثَنَا مِنْ مَرْقَدِنَا﴾ ["They will say, 'Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?'"] [Yasin 52]. In this is evidence of the intensity of the regret of the deniers, those who denied resurrection: when they are resurrected they say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" The evidence for this is their saying "Woe to us!" This phrase is a call for destruction and regret upon whoever utters it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the barzakh (the intermediate state) is light compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, to the extent that it is like sleep to a sleeper.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rebuke of these deniers when it is said to them: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Exalted is truthful in His promise and does not break it. This is because breaking a promise happens from one of two things: either lying or incapacity. Both are negated for Allah the Mighty and Majestic. There is no lying in His promise, and no inability to carry it out. For this reason He, the Mighty and Majestic, does not break the appointed promise, because of the perfection of His truthfulness and power.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the truthfulness of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, in what they reported concerning resurrection and other matters, by His saying: ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾.

* Among its benefits: the polytheists used to acknowledge the truth, but when? When they witnessed it. And acknowledging the truth after witnessing it does not benefit, because acknowledging the truth when it is not unseen means the person is not a believer in the unseen, but only a believer in what is witnessed.

If you say: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتُهُمْ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا وَاللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [al-Anʿām 23] ("Then their [response] will not be but to say, 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'"). Here they denied polytheism, although they were polytheists. Indeed they acknowledge their polytheism, as He said: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَعَصَوُا الرَّسُولَ لَوْ تُسَوَّى بِهِمُ الْأَرْضُ وَلَا يَكْتُمُونَ اللَّهَ حَدِيثًا﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 42] ("On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that they were leveled with the earth, and they will not conceal from Allah a [single] statement"). So how do we reconcile them?

The reconciliation between them is that the Day of Resurrection is not a moment or a short hour, but fifty thousand years. They fluctuate: at times they acknowledge everything they did, and at times they deny. When they see the salvation of the believers, they say: ﴿وَاللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ ["By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"], perhaps they will be saved as others were saved. But their mouths will be sealed, and their hands and feet will speak. At that point they acknowledge, and they do not conceal from Allah a statement. And Allah knows best.

* * *

* Student: (...) two readings (...) ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾. The reading with the fatḥa is clear.
* The Shaykh: We do not have two readings here, do we?! There are no two readings.
* Student: You recited it, sir.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: "Ṣaddaqa," "ṣadaqa."
* The Shaykh: No, I said: it is said ṣaddaqa, and it is said ṣadaqa.
* Student: Is it not a reading?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not a reading.
* Student: Which is preferred regarding the number of blasts: are they two or three?
* The Shaykh: The preferred view is that they are two.
* Student: And the blast that the Messenger (ﷺ) spoke of, that he is the first to see Musa [Moses]? [Al-Bukhari (7472) and Muslim, with his wording (2373/160), with their chains, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: Two men quarrelled, one a Jew and one a Muslim. The Muslim said: "By the One who chose Muhammad (ﷺ) above the worlds." The Jew said: "By the One who chose Musa (peace be upon him) above the worlds." He said: The Muslim raised his hand at that moment and slapped the face of the Jew. The Jew went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of what had happened between him and the Muslim. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not prefer me over Musa, for the people will fall unconscious, and I will be the first to regain consciousness, and behold, Musa will be holding onto the side of the Throne. I do not know whether he was among those who fell unconscious and regained consciousness before me, or whether he was among those whom Allah excepted."]?
* The Shaykh: That is the blast of the swoon (ṣaʿq).
* Student: The swoon.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Shaykh, is there evidence that (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Abu Hurayrah said: forty, between them forty. Abu Hurayrah was asked and said: "I refused" [Muttafaq ʿalayh; al-Bukhari (4814) and Muslim (2955/141), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. But perhaps the author (al-Mu'allif) took it from another evidence. Otherwise, Abu Hurayrah, the narrator of the hadith, refused to state anything definitively; that is, he did not hear it from the Messenger. But Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in al-Nuniyya that between them is forty years or forty days. Do you see, I forgot whether in the Nuniyya he mentioned forty days or forty years.

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. (...).
* The Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ["So today no soul will be wronged at all, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do"] [Yasin 54]. ﴿الْيَوْمَ﴾ ["today"] means the Day of Resurrection, when people are brought forth for judgement and decision. So the "al-" here is for the presential definite (al-ʿahd al-ḥuḍūrī); that is: in their presence on that Day, when they are brought forth, no soul will be wronged at all.

And His saying ﴿لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا﴾ means: it will not be diminished. Diminution occurs in one of two ways: either by an increase in bad deeds or by a decrease in good deeds, and both are negated, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصَّالِحَاتِ وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ فَلَا يَخَافُ ظُلْمًا وَلَا هَضْمًا﴾ [Ṭāha 112] ("And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer will not fear wrongdoing or deprivation"). That is: he will not fear deprivation of his right in good deeds, nor wrongdoing by an increase in bad deeds.

He says: ﴿لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا﴾, and ﴿نَفْسٌ﴾ ["soul"] is indefinite in a negative context, so it includes every soul. Even the disbeliever's punishment is according to his deeds. For this reason He said: ﴿وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾, meaning: you will not be repaid for your deeds except what you used to do.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون) ["except the recompense for what you used to do"]. He estimated "recompense" (jazāʾ) so that the verb would not fall directly upon the deed itself, since the deed has passed and ended, while what exists on the Day of Resurrection is the recompense. For this reason he said: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم), not the deed itself, for the deed was in the day of the world, not the Day of Resurrection, and what is on the Day of Resurrection is the recompense. Therefore the author estimated: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون).

If someone says: Is the author's statement here not open to criticism, since it appears as a correction upon the words of Allah, the Almighty?

The answer to this is: No, it is not open to criticism, and its implication is not a correction of Allah's words, because the author intended to explain the intended meaning, and did not intend that there is a deficiency in the speech. It is known in rhetoric (al-balāgha) that brevity (al-ījāz) is of two kinds: brevity of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf) and brevity of compactness (ījāz al-qiṣar). Brevity of omission means that the sentence contains something omitted that is known from the context. Brevity of compactness means that the sentence has few words that carry many meanings. So according to the author's statement, there is brevity of omission in the speech.

If someone says: Is there some clumsiness in this construction that the author mentioned (لا تُجزون إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون) when compared with His saying: ﴿وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾?

The answer: Yes. The Qur'an is more eloquent without doubt, clearer and more forceful, because expressing the recompense by the deed itself has greater effect upon the soul. When a person knows that on the Day of Resurrection he will be recompensed only for his deed, he will restrain himself from forbidden things and will be strong in doing what is commanded, because he knows that this very deed is what he will be recompensed for on the Day of Resurrection. What appears to me is that the speech does not need this estimation the author mentioned, because making the thing itself, which is the deed, the thing by which a person is recompensed, is more effective in stirring the soul, as we have established.

As for His saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾, ﴿كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [you used to do]: when? In the world. And ﴿تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ is the predicate of "kāna." The clause requires a returning pronoun referring back to the antecedent, which is ﴿مَا﴾, because it is established in the science of grammar that every relative noun (ism mawṣūl) requires a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) that connects it to its clause (ṣila), just as every predicate (khabar) of a subject (mubtada') that is a clause requires a connecting element that links the predicative clause to the subject it is predicated of. Here we say: the returning pronoun is omitted; that is: "what you used to do." The word "deed" (ʿamal) without doubt applies to action, and it also applies to speech, and it applies to the deed of the heart, which is inclining toward a thing, being at ease with it. When the word "deed" is used absolutely, it includes these three.

The word "deed" is for the three:
The deed of the heart: which is its inclining toward a thing, its contentment with it, and its tranquillity in it. This is called the deed of the heart.
Speech: that is, the deed of the tongue.
Action: the deed of the limbs.

This applies when "deed" is used absolutely. But when it is said "deed and speech," or "speech, belief, and deed," then deed here is interpreted as what? As action, the deed of the limbs. This occurs frequently in the Arabic language and in the Qur'an: when a thing is mentioned alone it is comprehensive, and when it is paired with something else it becomes specific, because when it is paired with something else the speech takes the form of division (taqsīm), and division requires a divided whole, each part of which is the opposite of the other part.

The summary now is that what is meant by "deed" here is what? The deed of the heart, of the limbs, and of the tongue, which is speech. This includes all of it, because a person will be recompensed for all of this on the Day of Resurrection.

If someone says: Does "deed" include abstention? That is: if a person abandons a sin, is this called a deed for which he is recompensed?

The answer: Yes, it is said to be a deed for which he is recompensed. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, Allah writes it for him as a complete good deed" [Muttafaq ʿalayh; al-Bukhari (6491) and Muslim (131/207), from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas], because he abandoned it for Allah's sake. So what is the sense in which abandonment is a deed? Because abandonment is restraining the soul from its impulse and its advance. It is therefore a deed. And then we say: the word ﴿تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [you do] includes four things, which are:

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is a deed, and a person is recompensed for it: ﴿إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّ أَصْحَابَ الْجَنَّةِ الْيَوْمَ فِي شُغُلٍ فَاكِهُونَ﴾ ["Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in enjoyment"] [Yasin 55], then He said: ﴿وَامْتَازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ ["And stand apart today, O criminals"] [Yasin 59].

When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned that on that Day the doer is recompensed for his deed, He mentioned the categories of doers, and they are two categories. The first category: the companions of Paradise. The second category: the criminals. The criminal (al-mujrim) is the one who commits a sin, as will come. The companions of Paradise: He did not mention their deeds, but He mentioned in many verses their deeds, which are the cause of their entering Paradise.

He said: ﴿إِنَّ أَصْحَابَ الْجَنَّةِ الْيَوْمَ فِي شُغُلٍ فَاكِهُونَ﴾. ﴿أَصْحَابَ﴾ ["companions"] is the plural of ṣaḥb, and ṣaḥb is a collective noun for ṣāḥib ["companion"]. The companion (ṣāḥib) is the one who accompanies his companion. A thing is not called a companion of another except after lasting association, according to what custom requires. The only exception the scholars made is the Companions (ṣaḥāba) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for their companionship is established by mere meeting, even for a moment. So whoever met the Prophet (ﷺ) while believing in him and died upon that, even for a moment, is a Companion (ṣaḥābī) of his.

The word ﴿الْجَنَّةِ﴾ ["Paradise"]: it has passed that in the Arabic language it is a name for a garden with many trees, and it was named so because, due to the abundance of its trees, it conceals whoever and whatever is in it. "Yajunnu" means what? It means "conceals." This root (jīm and nūn) all revolves around this meaning, which is concealment. From it the fetus (janīn) is named, for its concealment in its mother's womb, and the jinn are named for their concealment from the eyes, and the shield (junna) is named because the fighter is concealed by it from arrows.

So al-jannah in language is every garden with many trees, named so because it conceals whoever is in it and what is in it: whoever is in it of inhabitants and what is in it of small trees that are beneath the large trees. This is the original meaning of this word in language.

But its meaning in the Sharia is: the abode that Allah, glorified and exalted, prepared for the God-fearing: ﴿وَسَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا السَّمَاوَاتُ وَالْأَرْضُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 133] ("And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous"). Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted prepared for the God-fearing. In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is not correct to say that Paradise in the Hereafter is a garden with many trees. If you said this, you would lower its value in people's souls. But when you say: it is the abode that Allah prepared for the God-fearing, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, this becomes a motivation to work for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 52–61 (part 2 of 5):

His saying: ﴿Al-yawm﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, and the (al) here is for specific reference (al-'ahd). Which kinds of 'ahd are there?
* Students: The mentioned (al-dhikri).
* Other students: The present (al-huduri).
* The Shaykh: The mentioned (al-dhikri), the reference to something already mentioned, because its referent has already been mentioned. The (al) is for the mentioned reference when the thing it prefixes has already been mentioned, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15–16]. So when the referent of (al) has already been mentioned, it is the mentioned reference.
﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy﴾. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) is the predicate of inna.
﴿Fi shughul﴾. The author says: (with the ghayn pronounced with sukun and with damma) ﴿shughl﴾ and ﴿shughul﴾. Are the two readings both canonical (sab'iyyah), or is one of them shadhdh (irregular)?
* The students: Both are canonical.
* The Shaykh: Both are canonical. This is because the author, may Allah have mercy on him, by his method, when he says (in a reading) and (and in a reading), both are equal, meaning both are canonical readings of the seven. But if he says (and it was read), this reading is irregular (shadhdh). So his terminology should be known, lest there be confusion.
(...) You have seen in the author's words this (and in a reading). Know that this reading is canonical, meaning it is among the sound readings: if you wish, recite with it, and if you wish, recite with the second reading. So it is permissible for us now to say: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in shughl fakihun﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in shughul fakihun﴾.
Is it better to confine ourselves to one reading, or to recite sometimes with this and sometimes with that?
The correct view is that it is better to recite with this at times and with that at times, because all of them are authentically transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. If we remain on one reading, we abandon the rest of the readings, though they are legislated and authentically transmitted from the Messenger, peace be upon him. So it is preferable that you recite once with this and once with that, except in front of the common people, where you should not do so, because if you recite with a reading different from what is in the copies of the Qur'an in their hands, it will cause fitnah and shake their confidence in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But if you are reciting to yourself or reciting among students of knowledge, it is better to recite sometimes with this and sometimes with that.
The author said: (﴿fi shughul﴾ with the ghayn pronounced with sukun and with damma, from what the people of the Fire are occupied with, from what they enjoy). So they are occupied away from what the people of the Fire have. Had the author left it absolute, as it is, it would have been better: they are occupied, away from everything, by what they enjoy. That is, as if they do not think about anything else, because this bliss they are in has occupied them and they are absorbed in it, away from anything else. This is like His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever, they desire no removal from it﴾ [al-Kahf 108], meaning they do not desire any transfer or descent from what they are in, nor even ascent. Even the lowest of them sees himself as the most complete of people in bliss. So it is better to keep it absolute and say: ﴿fi shughul﴾, meaning they are absorbed in the bliss they have, away from everything, none of them looks for or awaits a bliss higher than what he has, such that he sees his bliss as deficient, and he never turns to anything at all.
﴿Fi shughul﴾. The author said: (like the deflowering of virgins). The kaf here is for comparison, not for restriction. That is, among the things they are occupied with is delighting in the deflowering of virgins, meaning women of the worldly women, and likewise the wide-eyed houris. The author gave this example only because of His saying: ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin 56].
He said: (like the deflowering of virgins, not a labour in which they toil, because there is no fatigue in Paradise). That is, there is no toil in it. It is known that this occupation is not one in which they toil, but one in which they rest, because it is an occupation in what delights and what brings about enjoyment.
He said: (﴿fakihun﴾ enjoying, a second predicate of inna, and the first being ﴿fi shughul﴾).
﴿Fakihun﴾ is a second predicate of inna. Where is the first?
* The students: ﴿fi shughul﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Fi shughul﴾, the prepositional phrase, so inna here has two predicates. Is it permissible for the predicate to be multiple?
The answer: Yes, the predicate may be multiple. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving (14), Owner of the Throne, the Glorious (15), Doer of whatever He wills﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. These are five predicates. So the predicate may be multiple, but multiplicity of predicates may be such that each word has an independent meaning, or two words may be in the meaning of a single word. For example, if you say: this orange is sweet-sour. These are two words, but they are in the meaning of one word, i.e., bitter-sweet, meaning combining sweetness and sourness.
But if you say: so-and-so is standing, joyful. Are the two predicates in the meaning of one predicate? No, each one has an independent meaning, as evidenced by the fact that one of them is separate from the other in meaning.
The conclusion now is that we understood from the author's words that the predicate may be multiple, whether it is abrogated as in the verse or not.
He said: (﴿hum﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), ﴿wa azwajuhum﴾ is conjoined to it, ﴿fi zilal﴾ [Ya-Sin 56] is the predicate of the subject).
﴿Hum﴾ means the companions of the Garden, ﴿wa azwajuhum﴾ is the plural of zawj, and it is applied to the male and female, so one says: this is the zawj of so-and-so (a woman), and one says: this is the zawj of so-and-so (a man). But the scholars said: it is necessary to distinguish, though it is a weak usage in the field of inheritance (al-fara'id), so one says zawjah for the female and zawj for the male, why? So that the student is not confused about whether the deceased case involves a male spouse or a female spouse. Otherwise, in the classical Arabic language, the tā' is dropped from zawj whether for a female or a male.
(﴿hum wa azwajuhum fi zilal﴾, plural of zullah or zill, predicate), meaning that ﴿fi zilal﴾ is a predicate of the subject ﴿hum﴾, and ﴿zilal﴾ is the plural of zullah or the plural of zill, and the meaning does not differ much: they are in shades, where there is no sun to scorch them or heat the air, but rather light. Some scholars said: like the light that exists between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun, a bright light but gentle, because the gentlest is such a time. It is a shade that is ample (zill zalil).
(﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾ plural of arika, which is a couch in the canopy or the bedding in it). ﴿ʿAla al-ara'ik﴾ is a fronted predicate, and ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is a delayed subject, and what the author mentioned may also be permitted later.
