What we have mentioned is more general, because what we have mentioned includes that they recline on couches with their wives or without their wives, whereas on the author's statement it requires that they recline on couches with the wives.
Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said (﴿lahum fiha fakiha﴾ and ﴿lahum﴾ in it ﴿ma yaddaʿun﴾ [Ya-Sin 57], what they wish for).
* Student: The attachment of ʿala (...).
* The Shaykh: The attachment of ʿala, attached; that is, ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is attached to ﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾.
(﴿lahum fiha fakiha﴾ and ﴿lahum﴾ in it ﴿ma yaddaʿun﴾)
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Tafsir. ﴿Lahum fiha fakiha wa lahum ma yaddaʿun﴾ and so on.
﴿Lahum﴾ means for the companions of the Garden. ﴿Fiha﴾ means in the Garden. ﴿Fakiha﴾ means that with which they enjoy fruit. Every food of the people of Paradise is fakiha, because they eat it by way of enjoyment, not by way of need or necessity. In this world we sometimes eat for enjoyment, sometimes out of need, and sometimes, what? out of necessity. But in Paradise, everything we eat is for enjoyment, because there is no need or necessity there. For this reason a person eats and the food comes out as perspiration, more fragrant than the scent of musk, and there is no urine in it and no excrement.
If someone says: you make fakiha a name for everything they eat because they eat it by way of enjoyment, so how do you answer His saying: ﴿In both there is fakiha, date palms and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman 68], when the basic principle in conjunction is difference? Are date palms and pomegranates eaten or not? They are eaten.
The answer is known from what we mentioned just now: when a thing is mentioned alone it has a general meaning, and when it is joined with something else it has a specific meaning contrasting with what is joined with it, because division requires that the divided part from one side be different from the divided part from the other side.
We say: date palms and pomegranates were mentioned specifically for a distinctive quality in them; otherwise they are of the fakiha. This is of the type of conjoining the specific to the general, and conjoining the specific to the general is common in the Arabic language, like what?
* The student: (...) the verse.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and other than the verse, because you cannot cite what you are judging.
* Student: ﴿And what was given to Musa and Isa and the prophets from their Lord﴾ [Ali 'Imran 84].
* The Shaykh: No, this is of the type of conjoining the general to the specific; we want conjoining the specific to the general.
* Student: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾ [al-Qadr 4].
* The Shaykh: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾, and "the Spirit" is Jibril, who is among the angels.
He said: ﴿Lahum fiha fakiha wa lahum﴾. The mufassir said: (therein ﴿ma yaddaʿun﴾, they wish for).
Whatever they wish for is attained; indeed Allah gives them more than what they wish for, because a person's wish is limited. He may think that this is the greatest thing while there is something greater that he does not perceive. When we were children we used to say: a million is the most. Who has a million! And now a million has become the most?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: Above it there are things: billions, and above billions, other things. The point is that in the Hereafter a person is given everything he wishes, and more than he wishes. If someone asks: is...
The answer is that this is a matter with possibilities: it may be that when a person desires something, it is attained for him; and it may be that he must claim it, and the claim in the sense of request means he must ask for it, and the benefit of the request is to show the sincerity of the intention, just as the deed shows the sincerity of intention. If someone says: I want to visit so-and-so, this intention does not appear unless he actually visits him; and as long as he has not acted, the intention may not be sincere.
In any case, it suffices us that Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And therein is whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf 71], for the apparent meaning of the verse is that whatever you desire, even if you do not ask for it, will be attained for you.
Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 58]. ﴿Salam﴾: the author said: (a subject (mubtada'); ﴿qawlan﴾ meaning by speech; its predicate is ﴿min rabbin rahim﴾, toward them, meaning He says to them: peace be upon you). That is, the meaning of the author's statement is that Allah, glorified and exalted, says to them: peace. And ﴿qawl﴾ here is in the accusative by his explanation through the omission of the preposition, because he said: (meaning: by the speech). Accusative by omission of the preposition is not regular except with inna and an (that), but is transmitted; that is, if the Arabs are heard using the accusative, it is acted upon, and if it is not heard, it is not acted upon. The rule is that the preposition may be omitted, meaning the prepositional particle; when the preposition is omitted, what follows it becomes accusative, and it is said of it: accusative by what? By omission of the preposition. But as Ibn Malik said:
Transmitted, and with inna and an it is regular, with safety from ambiguity, like: I wondered that they would give.
I think you have found this in what came before: (with inna and an it is regular), but also on condition that ambiguity is avoided (like: I wondered that they would give). In any case, the author went with ﴿qawlan﴾ being accusative by omission of the preposition, meaning: it is said to them: peace be upon you, and this speech proceeds from a Lord Most Merciful. The remainder of the commentary on the verse will come, Allah willing, in the next lesson.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Whether the Garden in which Adam was is disputed: is it the Garden of Eternity, or a garden of this world? On the view that it is the Garden of Eternity, which is what you raised as the difficulty, it is said: this is an exception, and perhaps Allah brings about kinds and categories of bliss that did not exist in the time of Adam.
* Student: Are there ranks in Paradise, O Shaykh (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The one in a lower rank does not see that he is (...).
* The Shaykh: He does not see that he is higher than him, but he does not covet that, nor grieve and regret that he was not in his rank. When we pass by palaces, each of us says: by Allah, my house is nothing compared to this palace, and wishes that he had this palace if he is of the people of this world. But if he is of the people of the Hereafter it does not concern him, and there it does not happen in (...) at all. Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we mentioned exactly this in His saying: ﴿In both there is fakiha, date palms and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman 68], and we answered it.
* Student: Date palms and pomegranates (...).
* The Shaykh: Not at all. Meat is also enjoyed as fakiha. When you are served the meat of a camel that has grown very old, and the meat of a small bird from (...), what is the bird's meat compared to camel meat? Yes: it is a fruit one enjoys, because camel meat you chew for two hours without it breaking down, let alone swallowing it, whereas this one, as soon as it touches the mouth, crumbles and melts; there is a difference between them.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Doubt, if one leans toward it. But if he repels it and does not lean toward it, and seeks refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan, it does not harm him. For example: I doubted whether so-and-so had arrived; he has arrived, but I do not have knowledge of it; this is doubt. If I lean toward it, that is a problem. But a man has arrived, then I doubted his arrival; I do not lean toward this, even though it may occur to the soul. The matters the believer believes in are for him like direct witnessing. If something that causes doubt occurs to his soul, he repels it. But if he is in doubt, and we seek refuge in Allah, you find that he is reassured by this doubt, and it becomes a judgment of reality in his heart.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, if he repels it. The Companions complained to the Messenger that they find in themselves what they would prefer to fall from the sky rather than speak of it, and he said: «This is clear faith»[[Narrated by Muslim (132/209) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 52–61 (part 3 of 5):

* In the preceding part of the noble verse, Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned that when the Trumpet is blown, people will rise from their graves (al-ajdath), that is, from the tombs, and they will hasten to their Lord, [and] the disbelievers will say: ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin 52]. In this there is evidence, or there are benefits to be drawn from this verse:
* Among them: the disbelievers' calling down woe upon themselves when they witness the reckoning on the Day of Resurrection, due to their saying: ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?﴾.
* And among its benefits: that staying in the graves is nothing but like the sleep of one who sleeps, then wakes and leaves the place; due to their saying: ﴿from our sleeping place﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, mighty and majestic, makes clear to them, as a rebuke, that this is what the Most Merciful promised of resurrection and recompense.
* And also in it: that they will acknowledge, according to the second possibility, that what Allah promised will come to pass, based on the view that His saying: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Ya-Sin 52] is part of their speech.
* And among its benefits also: that the Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, are truthful in what they report about Allah, the Exalted, and about others; due to His saying: ﴿and the Messengers spoke truly﴾ [Ya-Sin 52].
Then He said: ﴿It will be but one shout, and behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin 53].
* In this verse: evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, the Exalted, and that He, mighty and majestic, will cry out to the occupants of the graves with a single shout, saying for example: "Come out!", and they will all come out, none of them left behind; therefore He said: ﴿behold, they will all be brought before Us﴾.
* And among its benefits also: that when Allah, the Exalted, commands something, He does not repeat the command a second time; rather the thing happens at the first command. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 50]. The one who repeats a command or a statement is the incapable one, whereas the capable one does not repeat it.
* And among its benefits also: an indication that Allah, the Exalted, descends for judgment among His servants; it is drawn from His saying: ﴿brought before Us﴾; i.e., "with Us," and "with" (al-indiyah) indicates nearness. It has been established by the texts that Allah, mighty and majestic, descends to judge among His servants, and He judges between them.
Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in anything, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ [Ya-Sin 54].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the absolute negation of injustice on the Day of Resurrection, for it is a day of justice, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya' 47].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person is not wronged, neither by a little nor by a lot; because ﴿shay'an﴾ ("anything") is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it is general. If someone says: "Is anyone wronged on other than this day?" The answer: No, no one is wronged; but the mention of this day is to clarify the reality, for this day is the day of recompense, so it is as if He said: this day, which is the day of recompense, has no injustice in it. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no injustice today﴾ [Ghafir 17].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed; due to His saying: ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. From this is derived the perfection of Allah's justice, mighty and majestic; and this benefit branches from the preceding one.
If someone says: Does not the person who does a good deed get rewarded tenfold? The answer: Yes, but this is part of the recompense that Allah promised, so it does not contradict the apparent meaning of the verse; for Allah promised that whoever comes with a good deed, He will give him ten times its like, so it falls under His saying: ﴿except for what you used to do﴾.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of expressing the cause by the effect (ta'bir bi-al-sabab 'an al-musabbab). From where is it taken?
* A student: ﴿except for what you used to do﴾.
* The Shaykh: How so?
* A student: That the recompense is for the deed (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the deed is a cause of the recompense, so there is the expression of the cause for the effect.
Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in their enjoyment, [they and their spouses] reclining in the shade on couches﴾ up to the end of the verses [Ya-Sin 55].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that people on that day are divided into two groups: a group who are the people of Paradise, and a group who are the people of the Fire. The people of Paradise, this is their recompense: ﴿busy in their enjoyment﴾.
* And from His saying: ﴿fakihun﴾ ("enjoying") is derived the perfection of their bliss; for whenever bliss is perfected, the enjoyment of this blessing with which a person is made happy is perfected.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: that the people of Paradise have spouses; due to His saying: ﴿they and their spouses in the shade﴾ [Ya-Sin 56]. Allah has described these spouses with many attributes; He, mighty and majestic, said in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿In them are those restricting their gaze, untouched by man or jinn before them﴾ [al-Rahman 56], and He said: ﴿In them are good and beautiful [women]﴾ [al-Rahman 70]. "Restricting their gaze" means that she restricts her gaze to her husband and does not look at anyone else, because she sees that her husband is the most perfect of husbands, so her gaze does not extend to others; and she is also restricted in regard to her husband's gaze upon her, so her husband does not transgress or extend his gaze to others besides her; thus each of them is content with the other. And they are also "good and beautiful", good in character, beautiful in faces and bodies; and their attributes are many in the noble Qur'an.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that Paradise has no sun; due to His saying: ﴿they and their spouses in the shade﴾.
* And among its benefits: the perfect comfort of the people of Paradise; due to His saying: ﴿reclining on couches﴾, for the one who reclines is usually at rest and at ease, and whenever a person is more at ease, his comfort increases; and reclining on couches is undoubtedly a sign of peace of mind and freedom from preoccupation.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the people of Paradise have fruit in it, which is everything one enjoys; and we have mentioned that all their food is fruit which they enjoy.
* And among its benefits also: that the people of Paradise have whatever they desire, and indeed they are given more than they desire; and "therein is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3244), and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that this noble Qur'an is mathani, in which meanings are repeated: a thing is mentioned and its opposite is mentioned; for if it mentioned only what produces hope without what produces fear, hope would dominate fear and a person would fall into feeling secure from Allah's plan; and if it mentioned only the aspect of fear without the aspect of hope, a person would fall into despair of Allah's mercy. Thus when Allah mentions bliss, He mentions its opposite, and when He mentions the companions of Paradise, He mentions the companions of the Fire, and so on. This is one of the meanings of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating [its teachings]﴾ [al-Zumar 23], meaning that meanings are repeated in it so that travel to Allah, glory be to Him, in the required manner becomes easy.
Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. It has already been stated that the author parsed ﴿salam﴾ as a subject (mubtada') and its predicate ﴿qawlan﴾ as accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "peace by word from a Lord, Most Merciful"; and this is one of the possible readings of the noble verse. It may also be that ﴿salam﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject; i.e., "it is peace," meaning Paradise is peace, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus 25]. It may also be that the predicate is His saying: ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾, i.e., "peace by word, from Allah, issued from Allah, mighty and majestic." These possibilities do not contradict one another in meaning, for the whole meaning is one: that Allah greets them with words, saying: "Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise."
As for His saying: ﴿from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾, the word "Rabb" in the Arabic language is used with several meanings: it is used for the Lord of the worlds, mighty and majestic, and with this meaning it includes creation, sovereignty and management; so the Rabb is the Creator, the Owner, the Manager. "Rabb" is also used for the possessor, as in the expression "rabb al-bayt," i.e., the owner of the house; and like His saying, upon him be blessings and peace, concerning the found property (luqatah): "Its water-skin and its sandal are with it; it comes to the water and eats the trees until its owner (rabbuha) finds it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (91), and Muslim (1722/1) from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid.]], i.e., its owner. This refers to stray camels.
As for His saying: ﴿from a Lord﴾, what is meant is the first meaning, i.e., Allah, mighty and majestic; Allah is the Rabb, meaning the Creator, the Owner, the Manager. "Rahim" (Most Merciful) is from mercy, which is an essential attribute that Allah, glory be to Him, has not ceased and does not cease to possess; but its effects are renewed in relation to the one who is shown mercy. Allah, mighty and majestic, shows mercy to whom He wills, and it is known that the one shown mercy is renewed, so Allah's mercy toward this person is renewed; as for the essence of the meaning, Allah has not ceased and does not cease to be Most Merciful.
The People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah, who are the Salaf, interpret mercy in a manner befitting Allah, mighty and majestic, whereas the People of Distortion (ahl al-tahrif) interpret mercy either as beneficence (al-ihsan) or as the will to do good; they say: the meaning of "Rahim" is "benefactor" or "one who wills benefaction." Why? They say: because Allah cannot be described with mercy, for mercy indicates weakness, tenderness and softness, and this does not befit Allah, glory be to Him. They interpreted it as will, because they affirm will; or as beneficence, because beneficence is separate from Allah, mighty and majestic, being created. There is no doubt that this is distortion. If mercy necessarily entails tenderness and softness, this applies to the mercy of creatures; as for the mercy of the Creator, this meaning is not necessarily implied. Moreover, we deny that tenderness and softness necessarily follow from it; why? Because we find a strong, brave king who has mercy, and this does not diminish his strength or authority in the least. But even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that it entails tenderness and softness, this would be with respect to the mercy of created beings.
﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ upon them, i.e., He says to them: "Peace be upon you," and He says: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾ [Ya-Sin 59]. The author's words "and He says" mean Allah, mighty and majestic; but there is room for examination in asserting this, for it may be Allah who says to the criminals: ﴿Separate yourselves﴾, and it may be that the speaker is one of the angels. The point is that it is said to the criminals: ﴿Separate yourselves today﴾; therefore, had the author said "and it is said" (wa-yuqal), it would have been more appropriate; because asserting that the speaker is Allah requires a textual basis, i.e., an explicit text from the Lawgiver.
He says: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾. What is meant by ﴿today﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, and the "al" here is for prior mention (al-'ahd al-dhikri).
﴿O criminals﴾: the author said: "(i.e., withdraw from the believers when they are mixed with them)". That is: it is said on the Day of Resurrection: "Separate yourselves, O criminals; distinguish yourselves from the believers, withdraw from them," for the path of the criminals is not the path of the righteous; the righteous have their path to Paradise, and these have their path to the Fire, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation, and drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam 85–86]. Thus these are separated from those; it is said to them in a manner of rebuke and humiliation, for when you see a gathering you say, for example: "O such-and-such group, separate yourselves, move away," and in this there is clear humiliation and disgrace of them.
As for His saying: ﴿O criminals﴾, who is the criminal? The criminal is the doer of crime (ijram), and ijram is sin and wrongdoing; i.e., "O sinners, O wrongdoers, separate yourselves from the believing obedient ones."
Then He said: (﴿Did I not charge you﴾ — I command you — ﴿O children of Adam﴾ — through My messengers — ﴿that you not worship Satan﴾ — not obey him — ﴿indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ — manifest in enmity — ﴿and that you worship Me﴾ — affirm My oneness and obey Me — ﴿this is a straight path﴾ — the way). ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam﴾ [Ya-Sin 60]: the interrogative here is for affirmation (taqrir), and generally when a negation follows the interrogative particle, the interrogative is for affirmation; like ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1], this is for affirmation; ﴿Did you not come to them messengers from among yourselves?﴾ [al-An'am 130], for affirmation; ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar 36], for affirmation; ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8], for affirmation; and so whenever something indicating negation comes after the interrogative particle, the interrogation is generally for affirmation.
Here it is affirmation: Allah, mighty and majestic, affirms that He charged them; therefore it is valid, outside the Qur'an, to convert it into a past verb, saying: "I have charged you."
If someone asks: What is the purpose of this affirmation? Its purpose is rebuke; i.e., Allah affirms this matter as a rebuke to them and to establish the proof against them that Allah charged them not to worship Satan.
The author glossed "al-'ahd ila" (charging) as "command"; i.e., "Did I not command you?" But in reality it is more emphatic than a command, for "al-'ahd ila" seems to include a covenant and pact; and indeed it does, for Allah has taken from us the covenant that we worship none but Him and do not worship Satan, for he is an enemy.
His saying: ﴿O children of Adam﴾: this includes males and females, although "ibn" (son) originally refers to a male and "banun" (sons) originally refers to males; but when what is meant is a tribe or a kind, it includes male and female. Indeed the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, said: if one makes a waqf for "the sons of Tamim," it includes their males and females; but if one makes a waqf for "the sons of so-and-so," where so-and-so is an individual person and not a tribe, it is restricted to whom? To males only. "Banu Adam" here is a tribe, indeed inclusive of all tribes, so it includes males and females.
His saying: ﴿that you not worship Satan﴾: the author interpreted worship here as obedience, for obeying others in what opposes Allah's prohibitions is a form of worship, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary; but they were commanded not to worship except one God﴾ [al-Tawbah 31], not that they should worship many lords. Adi ibn Hatim said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not worship them" — i.e., we do not pray to them, bow or prostrate to them. He said: "Do they not make lawful what Allah has made unlawful, and you make it lawful, and make unlawful what Allah has made lawful, and you make it unlawful?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is their worship"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3095) from the hadith of Adi ibn Hatim.]]. Although this hadith is weak, the reality is that obeying other than Allah in opposing Allah's command is indeed a form of worship; for worship in origin is humility and submission, and obeying a command is humility and submission.
His saying: ﴿Satan﴾: is what is meant the genus or a specific Satan? The apparent meaning is that the genus is intended, including the satans of mankind and the satans of jinn; just as the jinn have satans, mankind also has satans, there are among mankind satans who command people to sin and transgression and forbid them from righteousness and kindness.
His saying: (﴿that you not worship Satan, indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾ — manifest in enmity): ﴿indeed he﴾ — i.e., Satan — ﴿is to you a clear enemy﴾. Every person or every individual who commands you to oppose Allah's command is an enemy to you, whether he perceives it or not, and at their head is the first Satan who leads every satan.
He said: ﴿indeed he is to you an enemy﴾: the enemy is the opposite of the ally (wali), and the ally is one who takes you under his protection, watches over you and cares for you; so the enemy, its opposite, is one who does not want good for you but wants evil for you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 52–61 (part 4 of 5):

Regarding His words, ﴿mubin﴾, he said: "(clearly hostile)." How did he explain ﴿mubin﴾ as "(clear)"? We say: it derives from (abana), and (abana) comes with the meaning of "made clear" (transitive, *muta'addi*) and with the meaning of "became clear" (intransitive, *lazim*). If it means "made clear," it is transitive; if it means "became clear," it is intransitive. We cannot determine whether it is transitive or intransitive except by an indicator from the context (*qarina*). Here we say: if we explain ﴿mubin﴾ as the tafsir of the author does, "(clearly hostile)," does it become intransitive or transitive? It is intransitive. Yet it is possible to make it transitive and say: ﴿mubin﴾ means "one who makes his enmity manifest," because he commands you to evil. But this is weak, since if he had made his enmity manifest, no one would have followed him. Rather, he deceives people, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ [Al-A'raf 22]. So we take ﴿mubin﴾ here as intransitive, from (abana) in the sense of "became clear."

﴿And that you worship Me. This is a straight path.﴾ [Ya-Sin 61] "Do not worship Satan; and that you worship Me" is a negation and an affirmation, and this is the reality of monotheism (tawhid). The word ﴿an﴾ in ﴿wa an u'budooni﴾ is verbal (*masdariyya*), and it may also be explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), because ﴿a'ahd﴾ includes the meaning of saying. When it is established that what includes the meaning of saying, without its letters, becomes explanatory, as in His words: ﴿So We revealed to him, "Build the ship..."﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 27].

In any case, ﴿And that you worship Me﴾ means that Allah has charged us to worship Him alone, that is: humble yourselves to Me in obedience.

The author said: "(Affirm My oneness and obey Me)," and this is a correct meaning, for worship is affirming the oneness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, humbling oneself to Him by carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibition.

﴿This is a straight path.﴾ The referent of ﴿this﴾ is abandoning the worship of Satan and singling out Allah for worship. ﴿A straight path.﴾ The author explained ﴿sirat﴾ as "the road," but the correct view is that not every road is a *sirat*; rather, the *sirat* is the wide, smooth road, because it is derived from (al-sarṭ) or (al-sarṭ), and (al-sarṭ), as we know, is swallowing something quickly. A road cannot be a road for swift travel unless it is wide and easy.

As for His words ﴿straight﴾, this is its description, and straightness includes the evenness of the course, and also the flatness of the ground. If it were assumed that the road turns to the right and left, it would not be correct to say it is straight; and if it has heights and depths, it is not straight, because part of it is raised and part of it descends. So straightness means that it is free from deviation to the right and left, and free from differences in its elevation and depression.

His words ﴿a straight path﴾: to whom? To Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Allah attributed the *sirat* to Himself, and attributed the *sirat* to His creatures, saying in Surat al-Fatihah: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [Al-Fatihah 6–7]. So He attributed the path to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, and He said: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ash-Shura 52–53]. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, or "and the earth"? ﴿and whatever is on the earth.﴾ How then do we reconcile the two attributions? We say: Allah attributed the path to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour because they are the ones who travel upon it; they are its travellers. And He attributed it to Himself because He is the One who established it for His servants, and it leads to Him, just as you say: "This is the road to Makkah." What is the meaning of "the road to Makkah"? It is the one that leads to Makkah. And you say: "This is the road of so-and-so" if he is the one who laid it out for people and paved it for them, or the one who travelled it and walked upon it.

In any case, the attribution of the path to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour is because they travel it; the attribution of the path to Allah is because He is the One who established it for His servants and prescribed it for them, and it—the path—leads to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And that you worship Me. This is a straight path. (61) And he had already led astray a great multitude of you. Did you not then understand?﴾ [Ya-Sin 61–62]. ﴿And indeed﴾: this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics. What are they?
* Student: The *waw*.
* Shaykh: What? Where is the *waw*?
* Student: The *lam* and (qad).
* Shaykh: Yes, the *lam* and (qad).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: And the implied oath.
* Shaykh: The implied oath. Because this *lam* is a preface to the oath (*mutawwi'a lil-qasam*), so this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics?
* Student: The oath, the *lam*, and (qad).
* Shaykh: The oath. Where is the oath?
* Student: "By Allah, he had already led astray a great multitude of you."
* Shaykh: Well done. The implied phrase is: "By Allah, he had already led astray..." Good. Now, if someone says: how does Allah the Mighty and Majestic swear, when He is the most truthful in speech without any oath?

We answer this with several points:
The first point: an indication that this is a important matter that requires what? An oath to be sworn upon it; because if it were not important, He would not have sworn about it.

Second: the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and among the methods of the Arabic language is that when something is intended to be affirmed and confirmed, an oath is sworn about it; and the Qur'an, as we know, was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue.

Third: when the one sworn by is explicit, meaning it is expressly stated, then swearing by it indicates its greatness; for Allah does not swear by anything except for the greatness of that thing, such as His words: ﴿By the sun and its brightness. (1) And by the moon when it follows it﴾ [Ash-Shams 1–2], and so on to the end, and what is similar to that of what Allah has sworn by, for it indicates the greatness of the one sworn by.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, he has a way.
* Student: His words, the Exalted: ﴿that you not worship Satan﴾ (...) *la* is negating (...).
* Shaykh: How? It is possible that it is negating, and the verb is in the subjunctive governed by (an); or that (la) is prohibitive.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is meant by it is generality; for this reason He said: ﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude of you.﴾
* Student: (...) O children of Adam, did I not charge you that you not worship Satan, and the believers (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, He has made clear that He charged all creation that they not worship Satan, and that they worship Him alone. But Satan led astray a great multitude of them, as in the verse we began with; so the address is general.
* Student: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿they and their spouses﴾ [Ya-Sin 56]: those young men who did not marry (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, they have spouses. Even those who did not marry will have spouses in Paradise from the *hur al-'in* (wide-eyed maidens), and from the women of this world who did not marry.
* Student: (...) their spouses?
* Shaykh: The *hur al-'in*.
* Student: The young women.
* Shaykh: The young women; they have spouses. First, it is apparent that the women of the world will not exceed the men, because most of the people of the Fire are women; women are the majority of the people of the Fire. And if it were assumed that the number of women of this world exceeded the number of men, then a person may combine two wives or more. In any case, when you reach there, God willing, there will be no hardship; and Allah is the One whose help is sought.
* Student: It has been said, O Shaykh, that they will be given a choice; the wives of this world, meaning the women of this world, will be given a choice between their husbands in Paradise.
* Shaykh: This is when a woman has married two men, so she is given the choice between them; meaning: if she married two men and entered Paradise with both of them, she will be given a choice between them.
* Student: If she was divorced?
* Shaykh: Even if she was divorced. The Prophet ﷺ informed that she will choose the better of the two in character.[[Narrated by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (6631), and by 'Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad (1210), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]
* Student: Regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾ (...) the blowing of the Trumpet (...).
* Shaykh: No; because Allah said in another verse: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface﴾ [An-Nazi'at 13–14], and a shout does not come from blowing; blowing is a sound, not a shout.
* Student: "Do not worship except Allah" (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is in the accusative governed by (an).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed; if we make (la) negating, it is in the accusative governed by (an); and if we make it prohibitive, it is in the jussive governed by it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it may be said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾; so when they separate, Allah says to them: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam...﴾
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a possibility, but we do not affirm it definitively. There is a possibility that it is the speech of Allah, that Allah says to them: "Separate yourselves, O criminals"; and there is a possibility that it is the speech of one of the angels. So when they separate, they are addressed. This is among the things that indicates what our brother has taken, that His words: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam﴾ are specific to the disbelievers. But His words: ﴿And he had already led astray a great multitude of you...﴾ [would contradict this], because if they were the disbelievers, He would have led all of them astray.
* Student: Shaykh, I mean...
* Shaykh: I understand you, may Allah bless you, I understand; but certainty requires a transmitted text (*tawqif*).

﴿A great multitude of you, did you not then understand?﴾ Do you have it like this, ﴿jibillan﴾?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: *Jublan*. The problem I have: ﴿jibillan﴾, we have reached this?

His words, the Exalted: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾, in it are benefits...

﴿Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful﴾ * In this noble verse is evidence of what the people of Paradise enjoy: safety from all afflictions, not from illnesses, nor from fatigue, nor from death, nor from anything else. ﴿Peace﴾, because Allah the Exalted says to them: "Peace be upon you." This utterance from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is not a supplication, but a report from Allah. Such a thing is only a supplication when it comes from a created being; but when it comes from the Creator, it is a report, meaning that Allah the Exalted informs them that He will grant them safety from every calamity.
* And among its benefits: the affirmation of lordship (*rububiyyah*), which here, as it appears, is the specific lordship. Lordship is divided into two kinds: specific and general. The general is that which encompasses all creation, for all creation is under the lordship of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: He is their Creator, their Owner, their Manager. Among its examples is His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2]. As for the specific lordship, it is that which is particular to the sincere servants of Allah from among the believing servants of Allah, the messengers and their followers, and it is more specific than the first; because it entails special care for the one under lordship, and granting him success, and reforming his condition. Among its examples is His words: ﴿Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [Al-A'raf 122], for Moses and Aaron were among the sincere servants of Allah, so lordship with respect to them was specific. Among it is the supplication of the believers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic by this name, such as: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us﴾ [Ali 'Imran 16], for what is meant by it is the specific lordship; because seeking a means through the more specific is more specific for supplication than seeking a means through the more general. And both kinds are combined in His words: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, (121) the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ [Al-A'raf 121–122]. The first is general, and the second is specific. So, how many kinds of lordship are there? A specific question.
* Student: Two: general lordship and specific lordship. General lordship (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, the sincere servants of Allah. The difference between them is that the general is for the comprehensive general management, such as creation, sovereignty, and management; and this is specific lordship that entails special care.
Now, this verse: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful﴾. I say: the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is from the specific lordship, because it is addressed to the sincere people.
* And in this noble verse: the affirmation of mercy to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, by His words ﴿Most Merciful﴾; and the affirmation of lordship in His words ﴿Lord﴾. Is "the Lord" one of the names of Allah? Yes, "the Lord" is one of the names of Allah. This is shown by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "As for bowing, glorify the Lord therein,"[[Narrated by Muslim (479/207), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and his ﷺ saying about the siwak: "It purifies the mouth and pleases the Lord."[[Narrated by al-Nasa'i (5) and al-Darimi (711), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] As for "the Most Merciful," that it is one of the names of Allah is not hidden.
* And in this verse: an indication that they reached this station only by the mercy of Allah, by His words: ﴿from a Lord Most Merciful﴾. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5673) and Muslim (2816/72), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] O Allah, cover us with Your mercy. So the Messenger ﷺ informed that no one enters Paradise except that Allah covers him with His mercy, that is: He bestows mercy upon him in abundance, and then he enters.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals.﴾
* In this noble verse, among the benefits: that criminals will be humiliated on the Day of Resurrection, in that they will be distinguished from the believers by the wording of expulsion. ﴿And separate yourselves today﴾ means: withdraw and go far away.
* And among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted distinguishes between the criminals and the righteous on the Day of Resurrection, just as He distinguished between them in this world; for the path of these is other than the path of those.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that whoever undertakes an action should mention the description appropriate to that action. Here, when they were commanded to separate and were expelled, it was fitting to mention the reason for that, when He said: ﴿O criminals﴾, as if He said: "Separate yourselves because of your crime." And there is no doubt that mentioning the cause of a ruling removes doubt, confusion, and objection. So we say: attaching a ruling to a description is a benefit based on the principle we mentioned: that attaching a ruling to a description indicates the causality (*'illiyyah*) of that description, meaning that this description is the cause of that ruling. So if you say, for example: "The diligent student is honoured." Here the honouring is attached to diligence, which indicates that the cause of the honouring is diligence. This principle is beneficial for the seeker of knowledge: that attaching a ruling to a description indicates its causality, meaning that it is the cause of that ruling.

His words: ﴿O criminals﴾: the particle of address (*ya*) has been omitted from it. Why? The scholars of rhetoric may claim that it was omitted as a form of humiliation for them, so that the speech is not lengthened; for lengthening speech with the addressee is a form of kindness toward him and a delight in addressing him. So when it is shortened, it is a kind of humiliation. This is not absolute, but depends on the context: sometimes it is honouring to shorten speech, and sometimes it is honouring to lengthen it; but the situation here does not call for that, rather it calls for shortening the speech and not prolonging it as a form of humiliation for them.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy. (60) And that you worship Me. This is a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin 60–61].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah the Exalted loves to establish proof against Himself; that is, He loves to establish an excuse for Himself, so that the proof may be established against His creation. This is shown by His words: ﴿Did I not charge you﴾, for whoever has charged us not to worship Satan and to worship Allah has established the proof against us and established the excuse for Himself. This is like His words: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, so that mankind will not have any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [An-Nisa' 165].
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward creation, in that He did not leave their sincerity toward Him to their intellects, but charged them with it through the tongues of the messengers. For if Allah had left sincerity to the intellects, the intellects would have differed greatly about it, because desires are not restrained. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic made this something He Himself guaranteed for His servants. Therein is the affirmation of the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic through this covenant which He made with His servants.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is necessary to clear away (al-takhliyah, emptying) before adorning (al-tahliyah, filling). Or someone may say: takhliyah before tahliyah, since He said ﴿that you should not worship Satan﴾ — what is this? It is takhliyah — ﴿and that you worship Me﴾ — this is tahliyah. That is, negation and affirmation, and this is tawhid. Tawhid is built on negation and affirmation, because bare negation is pure nullification and nonexistence, and bare affirmation does not prevent sharing. Therefore tawhid is not achieved except through negation and affirmation. Let me give an example of this: if you say, "There is no standing person in the house," this is bare negation, meaning the absence of anyone standing in the house. And if you say, "Zayd is standing in the house," this is bare affirmation, which does not prevent sharing, i.e., there may be another man standing in the house. But if you say, "There is no one standing in this house except Zayd," then exclusivity is established and tawhid is realized, and no one stands in this house except Zayd.

So tawhid necessarily involves these two matters: negation and affirmation. But with which does it begin? It begins first with negation, so that affirmation falls upon a place free of impurities, pure and fit for affirmation to settle in. For this reason it begins with negation and then with affirmation. This is abundant in the Qur'an. Listen to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free of what you worship (26) except He who originated me"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 26–27]. So he disavowed every object of worship first, then affirmed worship for Allah alone, ﴿He who originated me, for He will guide me﴾ [al-Zukhruf 27].

Among the benefits of this noble verse: obedience to Satan in disobedience to Allah is a form of worship, since obedience to Satan in disobedience to Allah is not possible except as a kind of worship, because His saying ﴿that you should not worship Satan﴾ — for obedience involves a kind of humbling, and worship is humbling. Whoever obeys Satan in disobedience to Allah has worshipped him.

Among its benefits: worship is not confined to bowing, prostration, sacrifice, and vows, and the like; rather it is general and comprehensive of every act of obedience in which complete humility is found, and so it is worship.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to beware of obeying Satan, since Allah, exalted is He, named his obedience "worship," and every person must beware of worshipping another alongside Allah. In it is a warning against obeying Satan in disobedience to Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to worship Allah alone, in His saying ﴿and that you worship Me﴾. Worship is applied to two meanings: the first is ta'abbud (the act of worshipping), and the second is al-muta'abbad bihi (that by which one worships). Ta'abbud means humbling oneself before Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and in this sense it is the servant's action: his prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, zakah, and the like. Worship is also applied to what is worshipped by, and in this sense it is every comprehensive term for what Allah loves and is pleased with of statements and actions; worship is a comprehensive term for everything Allah loves and is pleased with, of sayings and deeds, inward and outward, of the heart and of the limbs. So, worship is applied to what?

* Students: Two meanings.
* The Shaykh: The first: ta'abbud, which is the act of the worshipper; and the second: al-muta'abbad bihi, which are the well-known established acts of worship.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the straight path is tawhid, since He said ﴿This is a straight path﴾. ﴿This﴾ refers to abandoning the worship of Satan and adhering to the worship of Allah; ﴿a straight path﴾ means a direct road with no crookedness in it. It is so because it leads to the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, and His Garden, so it is a straight path.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the path may be straight, and it may be crooked. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153]. Every human being has a path; if it is in accordance with the law of Allah, it is straight, and if it is contrary to it, it is crooked.

The commonly known view is that the returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) mentioned is not omitted except when the governing word of the relative pronoun (mawṣūl) matches the governing word of the omitted element, both in form and meaning. This is the view known among the grammarians (al-naḥwiyyīn). However, the preferred view is that the ʿāʾid may be omitted whether its governing word is of the same kind as the governing word of the relative pronoun or of a different kind. The rule that Ibn Malik stated in his line:

*"The omission of what is known is permissible......"*

is general, covering everything and not limited to the subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar), but applying to everything.

As for His saying ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ [Yasin 52], "al-Raḥmān" is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, among the names specific to Him that may not be applied to anyone else. No one is named Raḥmān. As for "raḥīm," it may be used to describe created beings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿لَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ عَزِيزٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَنِتُّمْ حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُمْ بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [al-Tawbah 128] ("There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is your distress; [he is] anxious over you and to the believers [is] kind and merciful"). However, "raḥmān" may not be applied to anyone else. The difference between them is that "raḥīm" is considered in terms of the act, while "raḥmān" is considered in terms of the attribute. So when He says "al-Raḥmān," it means the One possessing vast mercy, and "al-Raḥīm" means the One whose mercy reaches whomever He wills of His servants.

Here He mentioned ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ and did not say "what Allah promised," because Allah's mercy on the Day of Resurrection will manifest far more than in this world. Allah the Exalted has one hundred mercies, of which He placed one mercy on earth. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will have the full hundred mercies: the remaining ninety-nine and the first mercy. [Ibn Abi Shaybah (35210) reported with his chain from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah created, on the day He created the heavens and the earth, one hundred mercies. He placed one mercy in the earth, and by it the mother shows compassion to her child, and the animals show compassion to one another. He withheld ninety-nine mercies until the Day of Resurrection. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy into one hundred mercies." Muslim (2753) also reported it, from the hadith of Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him), in similar wording.] This indicates the manifestation of Allah's mercy on that Day, and for this reason He said here: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾.

﴿al-Raḥmān﴾ is a derived noun (mushtaqq) that indicates what? It indicates the attribute of mercy. It is obligatory for us, regarding the names of Allah the Exalted, to affirm the name, and what it indicates of attribute and of the effect that follows from it. It is also permissible to say: and the judgement. So here "al-Raḥmān" is His name, "mercy" is His attribute, and "He has mercy on whom He wills" is His act, glorified and exalted be He, and it is the effect of mercy.

He said: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾, ﴿وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾ [Allah promised], because there will be a day on which people are resurrected, and on which the doer of good is rewarded for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. The reward of a good deed is ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

He said: (﴿وَصَدَقَ﴾ فيه ﴿الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾) ["and the Messengers spoke the truth"]. "Ṣadaqa" means "he informed with truth," and "ṣaddaqa" means "he confirmed the speaker." So affirmation (taṣdīq) is from the addressee, and truthfulness (ṣidq) is from the speaker. It is said ṣadaqa, and it is said ṣaddaqa. "Ṣadaqa" means "he informed with truth." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 152] ("And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission"). And "ṣaddaqa" means "he confirmed the speaker"; that is, he acknowledged his words and accepted them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَالَّذِي جَاءَ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ﴾ [al-Zumar 33] ("And the one who brought the truth and believed in it"). So he is truthful (ṣādiq) and one who affirms (muṣaddiq). And Allah knows best.

* Benefits: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿قَالُوا يَا وَيْلَنَا مَنْ بَعَثَنَا مِنْ مَرْقَدِنَا﴾ ["They will say, 'Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?'"] [Yasin 52]. In this is evidence of the intensity of the regret of the deniers, those who denied resurrection: when they are resurrected they say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" The evidence for this is their saying "Woe to us!" This phrase is a call for destruction and regret upon whoever utters it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the punishment of the barzakh (the intermediate state) is light compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, to the extent that it is like sleep to a sleeper.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rebuke of these deniers when it is said to them: ﴿هَذَا مَا وَعَدَ الرَّحْمَنُ﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Exalted is truthful in His promise and does not break it. This is because breaking a promise happens from one of two things: either lying or incapacity. Both are negated for Allah the Mighty and Majestic. There is no lying in His promise, and no inability to carry it out. For this reason He, the Mighty and Majestic, does not break the appointed promise, because of the perfection of His truthfulness and power.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the truthfulness of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, in what they reported concerning resurrection and other matters, by His saying: ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾.

* Among its benefits: the polytheists used to acknowledge the truth, but when? When they witnessed it. And acknowledging the truth after witnessing it does not benefit, because acknowledging the truth when it is not unseen means the person is not a believer in the unseen, but only a believer in what is witnessed.

If you say: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتُهُمْ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا وَاللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [al-Anʿām 23] ("Then their [response] will not be but to say, 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists'"). Here they denied polytheism, although they were polytheists. Indeed they acknowledge their polytheism, as He said: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوَدُّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وَعَصَوُا الرَّسُولَ لَوْ تُسَوَّى بِهِمُ الْأَرْضُ وَلَا يَكْتُمُونَ اللَّهَ حَدِيثًا﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 42] ("On that Day, those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that they were leveled with the earth, and they will not conceal from Allah a [single] statement"). So how do we reconcile them?

The reconciliation between them is that the Day of Resurrection is not a moment or a short hour, but fifty thousand years. They fluctuate: at times they acknowledge everything they did, and at times they deny. When they see the salvation of the believers, they say: ﴿وَاللَّهِ رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ ["By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"], perhaps they will be saved as others were saved. But their mouths will be sealed, and their hands and feet will speak. At that point they acknowledge, and they do not conceal from Allah a statement. And Allah knows best.

* * *

* Student: (...) two readings (...) ﴿وَصَدَقَ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾. The reading with the fatḥa is clear.
* The Shaykh: We do not have two readings here, do we?! There are no two readings.
* Student: You recited it, sir.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: "Ṣaddaqa," "ṣadaqa."
* The Shaykh: No, I said: it is said ṣaddaqa, and it is said ṣadaqa.
* Student: Is it not a reading?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not a reading.
* Student: Which is preferred regarding the number of blasts: are they two or three?
* The Shaykh: The preferred view is that they are two.
* Student: And the blast that the Messenger (ﷺ) spoke of, that he is the first to see Musa [Moses]? [Al-Bukhari (7472) and Muslim, with his wording (2373/160), with their chains, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: Two men quarrelled, one a Jew and one a Muslim. The Muslim said: "By the One who chose Muhammad (ﷺ) above the worlds." The Jew said: "By the One who chose Musa (peace be upon him) above the worlds." He said: The Muslim raised his hand at that moment and slapped the face of the Jew. The Jew went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of what had happened between him and the Muslim. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not prefer me over Musa, for the people will fall unconscious, and I will be the first to regain consciousness, and behold, Musa will be holding onto the side of the Throne. I do not know whether he was among those who fell unconscious and regained consciousness before me, or whether he was among those whom Allah excepted."]?
* The Shaykh: That is the blast of the swoon (ṣaʿq).
* Student: The swoon.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Shaykh, is there evidence that (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. Abu Hurayrah said: forty, between them forty. Abu Hurayrah was asked and said: "I refused" [Muttafaq ʿalayh; al-Bukhari (4814) and Muslim (2955/141), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. But perhaps the author (al-Mu'allif) took it from another evidence. Otherwise, Abu Hurayrah, the narrator of the hadith, refused to state anything definitively; that is, he did not hear it from the Messenger. But Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in al-Nuniyya that between them is forty years or forty days. Do you see, I forgot whether in the Nuniyya he mentioned forty days or forty years.

* * *

* Student: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. (...).
* The Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ["So today no soul will be wronged at all, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do"] [Yasin 54]. ﴿الْيَوْمَ﴾ ["today"] means the Day of Resurrection, when people are brought forth for judgement and decision. So the "al-" here is for the presential definite (al-ʿahd al-ḥuḍūrī); that is: in their presence on that Day, when they are brought forth, no soul will be wronged at all.

And His saying ﴿لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا﴾ means: it will not be diminished. Diminution occurs in one of two ways: either by an increase in bad deeds or by a decrease in good deeds, and both are negated, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِنَ الصَّالِحَاتِ وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ فَلَا يَخَافُ ظُلْمًا وَلَا هَضْمًا﴾ [Ṭāha 112] ("And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer will not fear wrongdoing or deprivation"). That is: he will not fear deprivation of his right in good deeds, nor wrongdoing by an increase in bad deeds.

He says: ﴿لَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْئًا﴾, and ﴿نَفْسٌ﴾ ["soul"] is indefinite in a negative context, so it includes every soul. Even the disbeliever's punishment is according to his deeds. For this reason He said: ﴿وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾, meaning: you will not be repaid for your deeds except what you used to do.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون) ["except the recompense for what you used to do"]. He estimated "recompense" (jazāʾ) so that the verb would not fall directly upon the deed itself, since the deed has passed and ended, while what exists on the Day of Resurrection is the recompense. For this reason he said: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم), not the deed itself, for the deed was in the day of the world, not the Day of Resurrection, and what is on the Day of Resurrection is the recompense. Therefore the author estimated: (إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون).

If someone says: Is the author's statement here not open to criticism, since it appears as a correction upon the words of Allah, the Almighty?

The answer to this is: No, it is not open to criticism, and its implication is not a correction of Allah's words, because the author intended to explain the intended meaning, and did not intend that there is a deficiency in the speech. It is known in rhetoric (al-balāgha) that brevity (al-ījāz) is of two kinds: brevity of omission (ījāz al-ḥadhf) and brevity of compactness (ījāz al-qiṣar). Brevity of omission means that the sentence contains something omitted that is known from the context. Brevity of compactness means that the sentence has few words that carry many meanings. So according to the author's statement, there is brevity of omission in the speech.

If someone says: Is there some clumsiness in this construction that the author mentioned (لا تُجزون إلا جزاء ما كنتم تعملون) when compared with His saying: ﴿وَلَا تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾?

The answer: Yes. The Qur'an is more eloquent without doubt, clearer and more forceful, because expressing the recompense by the deed itself has greater effect upon the soul. When a person knows that on the Day of Resurrection he will be recompensed only for his deed, he will restrain himself from forbidden things and will be strong in doing what is commanded, because he knows that this very deed is what he will be recompensed for on the Day of Resurrection. What appears to me is that the speech does not need this estimation the author mentioned, because making the thing itself, which is the deed, the thing by which a person is recompensed, is more effective in stirring the soul, as we have established.

As for His saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾, ﴿كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [you used to do]: when? In the world. And ﴿تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ is the predicate of "kāna." The clause requires a returning pronoun referring back to the antecedent, which is ﴿مَا﴾, because it is established in the science of grammar that every relative noun (ism mawṣūl) requires a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) that connects it to its clause (ṣila), just as every predicate (khabar) of a subject (mubtada') that is a clause requires a connecting element that links the predicative clause to the subject it is predicated of. Here we say: the returning pronoun is omitted; that is: "what you used to do." The word "deed" (ʿamal) without doubt applies to action, and it also applies to speech, and it applies to the deed of the heart, which is inclining toward a thing, being at ease with it. When the word "deed" is used absolutely, it includes these three.

The word "deed" is for the three:
The deed of the heart: which is its inclining toward a thing, its contentment with it, and its tranquillity in it. This is called the deed of the heart.
Speech: that is, the deed of the tongue.
Action: the deed of the limbs.

This applies when "deed" is used absolutely. But when it is said "deed and speech," or "speech, belief, and deed," then deed here is interpreted as what? As action, the deed of the limbs. This occurs frequently in the Arabic language and in the Qur'an: when a thing is mentioned alone it is comprehensive, and when it is paired with something else it becomes specific, because when it is paired with something else the speech takes the form of division (taqsīm), and division requires a divided whole, each part of which is the opposite of the other part.

The summary now is that what is meant by "deed" here is what? The deed of the heart, of the limbs, and of the tongue, which is speech. This includes all of it, because a person will be recompensed for all of this on the Day of Resurrection.

If someone says: Does "deed" include abstention? That is: if a person abandons a sin, is this called a deed for which he is recompensed?

The answer: Yes, it is said to be a deed for which he is recompensed. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, Allah writes it for him as a complete good deed" [Muttafaq ʿalayh; al-Bukhari (6491) and Muslim (131/207), from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas], because he abandoned it for Allah's sake. So what is the sense in which abandonment is a deed? Because abandonment is restraining the soul from its impulse and its advance. It is therefore a deed. And then we say: the word ﴿تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [you do] includes four things, which are:

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is a deed, and a person is recompensed for it: ﴿إِلَّا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّ أَصْحَابَ الْجَنَّةِ الْيَوْمَ فِي شُغُلٍ فَاكِهُونَ﴾ ["Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in enjoyment"] [Yasin 55], then He said: ﴿وَامْتَازُوا الْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا الْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾ ["And stand apart today, O criminals"] [Yasin 59].

When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned that on that Day the doer is recompensed for his deed, He mentioned the categories of doers, and they are two categories. The first category: the companions of Paradise. The second category: the criminals. The criminal (al-mujrim) is the one who commits a sin, as will come. The companions of Paradise: He did not mention their deeds, but He mentioned in many verses their deeds, which are the cause of their entering Paradise.

He said: ﴿إِنَّ أَصْحَابَ الْجَنَّةِ الْيَوْمَ فِي شُغُلٍ فَاكِهُونَ﴾. ﴿أَصْحَابَ﴾ ["companions"] is the plural of ṣaḥb, and ṣaḥb is a collective noun for ṣāḥib ["companion"]. The companion (ṣāḥib) is the one who accompanies his companion. A thing is not called a companion of another except after lasting association, according to what custom requires. The only exception the scholars made is the Companions (ṣaḥāba) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for their companionship is established by mere meeting, even for a moment. So whoever met the Prophet (ﷺ) while believing in him and died upon that, even for a moment, is a Companion (ṣaḥābī) of his.

The word ﴿الْجَنَّةِ﴾ ["Paradise"]: it has passed that in the Arabic language it is a name for a garden with many trees, and it was named so because, due to the abundance of its trees, it conceals whoever and whatever is in it. "Yajunnu" means what? It means "conceals." This root (jīm and nūn) all revolves around this meaning, which is concealment. From it the fetus (janīn) is named, for its concealment in its mother's womb, and the jinn are named for their concealment from the eyes, and the shield (junna) is named because the fighter is concealed by it from arrows.

So al-jannah in language is every garden with many trees, named so because it conceals whoever is in it and what is in it: whoever is in it of inhabitants and what is in it of small trees that are beneath the large trees. This is the original meaning of this word in language.

But its meaning in the Sharia is: the abode that Allah, glorified and exalted, prepared for the God-fearing: ﴿وَسَارِعُوا إِلَى مَغْفِرَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا السَّمَاوَاتُ وَالْأَرْضُ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 133] ("And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous"). Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted prepared for the God-fearing. In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is not correct to say that Paradise in the Hereafter is a garden with many trees. If you said this, you would lower its value in people's souls. But when you say: it is the abode that Allah prepared for the God-fearing, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, this becomes a motivation to work for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 52–61 (part 2 of 5):

His saying: ﴿Al-yawm﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, and the (al) here is for specific reference (al-'ahd). Which kinds of 'ahd are there?
* Students: The mentioned (al-dhikri).
* Other students: The present (al-huduri).
* The Shaykh: The mentioned (al-dhikri), the reference to something already mentioned, because its referent has already been mentioned. The (al) is for the mentioned reference when the thing it prefixes has already been mentioned, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15–16]. So when the referent of (al) has already been mentioned, it is the mentioned reference.
﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy﴾. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) is the predicate of inna.
﴿Fi shughul﴾. The author says: (with the ghayn pronounced with sukun and with damma) ﴿shughl﴾ and ﴿shughul﴾. Are the two readings both canonical (sab'iyyah), or is one of them shadhdh (irregular)?
* The students: Both are canonical.
* The Shaykh: Both are canonical. This is because the author, may Allah have mercy on him, by his method, when he says (in a reading) and (and in a reading), both are equal, meaning both are canonical readings of the seven. But if he says (and it was read), this reading is irregular (shadhdh). So his terminology should be known, lest there be confusion.
(...) You have seen in the author's words this (and in a reading). Know that this reading is canonical, meaning it is among the sound readings: if you wish, recite with it, and if you wish, recite with the second reading. So it is permissible for us now to say: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in shughl fakihun﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in shughul fakihun﴾.
Is it better to confine ourselves to one reading, or to recite sometimes with this and sometimes with that?
The correct view is that it is better to recite with this at times and with that at times, because all of them are authentically transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. If we remain on one reading, we abandon the rest of the readings, though they are legislated and authentically transmitted from the Messenger, peace be upon him. So it is preferable that you recite once with this and once with that, except in front of the common people, where you should not do so, because if you recite with a reading different from what is in the copies of the Qur'an in their hands, it will cause fitnah and shake their confidence in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But if you are reciting to yourself or reciting among students of knowledge, it is better to recite sometimes with this and sometimes with that.
The author said: (﴿fi shughul﴾ with the ghayn pronounced with sukun and with damma, from what the people of the Fire are occupied with, from what they enjoy). So they are occupied away from what the people of the Fire have. Had the author left it absolute, as it is, it would have been better: they are occupied, away from everything, by what they enjoy. That is, as if they do not think about anything else, because this bliss they are in has occupied them and they are absorbed in it, away from anything else. This is like His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever, they desire no removal from it﴾ [al-Kahf 108], meaning they do not desire any transfer or descent from what they are in, nor even ascent. Even the lowest of them sees himself as the most complete of people in bliss. So it is better to keep it absolute and say: ﴿fi shughul﴾, meaning they are absorbed in the bliss they have, away from everything, none of them looks for or awaits a bliss higher than what he has, such that he sees his bliss as deficient, and he never turns to anything at all.
﴿Fi shughul﴾. The author said: (like the deflowering of virgins). The kaf here is for comparison, not for restriction. That is, among the things they are occupied with is delighting in the deflowering of virgins, meaning women of the worldly women, and likewise the wide-eyed houris. The author gave this example only because of His saying: ﴿They and their spouses are in shade﴾ [Ya-Sin 56].
He said: (like the deflowering of virgins, not a labour in which they toil, because there is no fatigue in Paradise). That is, there is no toil in it. It is known that this occupation is not one in which they toil, but one in which they rest, because it is an occupation in what delights and what brings about enjoyment.
He said: (﴿fakihun﴾ enjoying, a second predicate of inna, and the first being ﴿fi shughul﴾).
﴿Fakihun﴾ is a second predicate of inna. Where is the first?
* The students: ﴿fi shughul﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Fi shughul﴾, the prepositional phrase, so inna here has two predicates. Is it permissible for the predicate to be multiple?
The answer: Yes, the predicate may be multiple. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving (14), Owner of the Throne, the Glorious (15), Doer of whatever He wills﴾ [al-Buruj 14–16]. These are five predicates. So the predicate may be multiple, but multiplicity of predicates may be such that each word has an independent meaning, or two words may be in the meaning of a single word. For example, if you say: this orange is sweet-sour. These are two words, but they are in the meaning of one word, i.e., bitter-sweet, meaning combining sweetness and sourness.
But if you say: so-and-so is standing, joyful. Are the two predicates in the meaning of one predicate? No, each one has an independent meaning, as evidenced by the fact that one of them is separate from the other in meaning.
The conclusion now is that we understood from the author's words that the predicate may be multiple, whether it is abrogated as in the verse or not.
He said: (﴿hum﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), ﴿wa azwajuhum﴾ is conjoined to it, ﴿fi zilal﴾ [Ya-Sin 56] is the predicate of the subject).
﴿Hum﴾ means the companions of the Garden, ﴿wa azwajuhum﴾ is the plural of zawj, and it is applied to the male and female, so one says: this is the zawj of so-and-so (a woman), and one says: this is the zawj of so-and-so (a man). But the scholars said: it is necessary to distinguish, though it is a weak usage in the field of inheritance (al-fara'id), so one says zawjah for the female and zawj for the male, why? So that the student is not confused about whether the deceased case involves a male spouse or a female spouse. Otherwise, in the classical Arabic language, the tā' is dropped from zawj whether for a female or a male.
(﴿hum wa azwajuhum fi zilal﴾, plural of zullah or zill, predicate), meaning that ﴿fi zilal﴾ is a predicate of the subject ﴿hum﴾, and ﴿zilal﴾ is the plural of zullah or the plural of zill, and the meaning does not differ much: they are in shades, where there is no sun to scorch them or heat the air, but rather light. Some scholars said: like the light that exists between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun, a bright light but gentle, because the gentlest is such a time. It is a shade that is ample (zill zalil).
(﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾ plural of arika, which is a couch in the canopy or the bedding in it). ﴿ʿAla al-ara'ik﴾ is a fronted predicate, and ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is a delayed subject, and what the author mentioned may also be permitted later.
He said: (﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾ plural of arika). The arika is a couch in the canopy or the bedding in it, but the more common usage is that it is a couch. A canopy (hajalah) is a small tent in the middle of the large house; that is, it is in the position of the private sleeping chamber as we know it among ourselves. So a house, for example, includes many separate rooms, and the room for sleeping is like the hajalah: a small tent specific to the man and his family, or to the man alone, or to the woman alone.
(﴿muttaki'un﴾ a second predicate, attached to ﴿ʿala﴾). That is, ﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾ is attached to ﴿muttaki'un﴾. According to the author's statement, the subject is ﴿hum﴾, ﴿fi zilal﴾ is a predicate, and ﴿muttaki'un﴾ a second predicate. Is the sentence then one or multiple? The sentence is one: they are in shades, reclining. The sentence is one, but its predicate is multiple. And ﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾, according to the author's statement, is attached to ﴿muttaki'un﴾, and the reason for fronting it over its governing word is consideration of the fawasil (verse endings). You know that the Noble Qur'an takes the fawasil into account, even if this leads to placing the less excellent before the more excellent, as in His saying in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿By the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha 70]; He placed Harun before Musa though Musa is more excellent, for the sake of the fawasil, because when the endings are uniform they have an effect on listening and attentiveness, and the Qur'an is the most eloquent speech. This is what the author adopted.
We have a second opinion on the matter in terms of grammatical analysis: that ﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾ is a fronted predicate and ﴿muttaki'un﴾ a delayed subject. On this view we have two sentences: the sentence ﴿hum wa azwajuhum fi zilal﴾, and the second: (reclining upon couches). What we have mentioned is more general, because what we have mentioned includes that they recline on couches with their wives or without their wives, whereas on the author's statement it requires that they recline on couches with the wives.
Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said (﴿lahum fiha fakiha﴾ and ﴿lahum﴾ in it ﴿ma yaddaʿun﴾ [Ya-Sin 57], what they wish for).
* Student: The attachment of ʿala (...).
* The Shaykh: The attachment of ʿala, attached; that is, ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is attached to ﴿ʿala al-ara'ik﴾.
(﴿lahum fiha fakiha﴾ and ﴿lahum﴾ in it ﴿ma yaddaʿun﴾)
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Tafsir. ﴿Lahum fiha fakiha wa lahum ma yaddaʿun﴾ and so on.
﴿Lahum﴾ means for the companions of the Garden. ﴿Fiha﴾ means in the Garden. ﴿Fakiha﴾ means that with which they enjoy fruit. Every food of the people of Paradise is fakiha, because they eat it by way of enjoyment, not by way of need or necessity. In this world we sometimes eat for enjoyment, sometimes out of need, and sometimes, what? out of necessity. But in Paradise, everything we eat is for enjoyment, because there is no need or necessity there. For this reason a person eats and the food comes out as perspiration, more fragrant than the scent of musk, and there is no urine in it and no excrement.
If someone says: you make fakiha a name for everything they eat because they eat it by way of enjoyment, so how do you answer His saying: ﴿In both there is fakiha, date palms and pomegranates﴾ [al-Rahman 68], when the basic principle in conjunction is difference? Are date palms and pomegranates eaten or not? They are eaten.
