However, in any case there is no doubt that if he had mentioned them it would have been better, because sometimes he mentions several readings concerning the manner of pronouncing a letter, just as he mentions several readings that reach up to six readings, as in ﴿a-andhartahum﴾ [Ya-Sin 10] regarding facilitation, verification, omission and the like. But man is human, and sometimes he overlooks and neglects what should be mentioned, or mentions what need not be mentioned.

﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude﴾, that is, a creation ﴿kathiran﴾ (great, many). This does not mean that the majority were not led astray by Shaytan; rather, he led astray most of creation, since most of creation were led astray by Shaytan. For it is established in the authentic hadith: "Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam! He will say: Here I am at Your call and Your pleasure. He will say: Bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire. He will say: O Lord, what is the group for the Fire? He said: Of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine." All of these are in the Fire from the children of Adam, and one is in Paradise. This was difficult for the Companions and weighed heavily on them, and they said: Which of us is that one, O Messenger of Allah? He said: "Rejoice, for you are among two peoples, neither of which has ever been (in a matter) but it has outnumbered it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj." [Reported by at-Tirmidhi (3169) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn.] And indeed, whoever observes creation now, although we are in a small part of the ages, finds that nine hundred and ninety-nine of them are all in error, even those who ascribe themselves to the Islamic religion, among whom there is great error that reaches the point of disbelief, even though they are ascribed to Islam.

Now, is the meaning of "kathir" here "the majority" or not? Yes, the meaning is the majority: ﴿a great multitude﴾. He said: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾. The hamzah here is for interrogation, and the purpose of the interrogation is reproach, rebuking them for not using their reason. The fa' here is conjunctive, and the element it conjoins is either what preceded or an implied clause suited to the context. There are two opinions among the scholars: some say that the particle of conjunction conjoins what follows to what precedes, but in the wording there is an inversion between the particle of conjunction and the hamzah, and if each were placed in its own position the wording would be "a-lam takunu ta'qilun" (did you not use your reason).

Others said: the hamzah is in its proper place, and the fa' conjoins an implied element understood from the context or the setting. In reality this may be closer to the rules, but it is more difficult, since in some places you cannot estimate anything and do not know what fits; in that case the second is easier. My rule is that when the grammarians differ on a question, the preferred view is the easier one, so long as it does not entail a difference in meaning and the meaning that follows from the easier view is not sound. In that case we do not follow the easier view, because it would harm the meaning and lead to an unsound meaning. But as long as the meaning is correct on both readings, the easier is the preferred one. "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (69) and Muslim (1734/8) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]

﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ means that He rebuked them for not using their reason. Reason is of two kinds: reason in the sense of perception, which is what obligation (taklif) depends upon, and reason in the sense of conduct, which is what praise or blame depends upon. Reason is of two kinds: reason in the sense of perception, which is what obligation depends upon, or if you wish, say: it is the basis of obligation, and what the jurists say about it: among the conditions of worship is reason. The other reason is in the sense of conduct, which is what praise and blame depend upon. Which is intended here? The second, decisively; because if the reason of perception were absent from them, they would not be under obligation and blame would not be directed at them. But the reason of conduct was absent from them, so they did not act well, and they became rational yet not rational: rational with respect to perception, which entails obligation, and not rational with respect to conduct, which entails praise or blame. In reality, although they were given minds, or in other words were given intelligence (dhaka') but were not given reason ('aql). How excellent is the expression of Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning the theologians (mutakallimun) when he described them: they were given intelligence but were not given purity of soul (zaka'), they were given understanding but were not given knowledge, and they were given hearing, sight and hearts: ﴿Their hearing, nor their sight, nor their hearts availed them anything, since they used to deny the signs of Allah, and there encompassed them that which they used to ridicule﴾ [al-Ahqaf 26]. Note: they were given intelligence but not purity of soul, may Allah grant us well-being. Their intelligence became a proof against them. They were given understanding: they had comprehension, but they had no knowledge, and when a person speaks from his understanding and not from knowledge, he goes astray and is lost. So there must be knowledge upon which your belief and worship are built. The point is that these people were given minds through which the proof is established against them, but they were deprived of the minds which bring praise and blame, which are right guidance and good conduct. They did not employ their minds which Allah had bestowed upon them; they did not employ them in what would benefit them. ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ He, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ his enmity and his misguiding, or what befell them of punishment, so that you would believe). That is: if you had reasoned about his enmity and his misguidance, or if you had reasoned about the punishment that befell those who followed him of torment and chastisement, you would have opposed him, you would not worship him, and you would have believed in Allah alone. But desire covered over guidance, as the Exalted said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾ [Fussilat 17].

Then He, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿This is Hell﴾ [Ya-Sin 63]. The author said regarding the implied meaning: (And it will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿This is Hell﴾). The demonstrative ﴿hadhihi﴾ here indicates something near, since the demonstrative for the distant is ﴿ulaika﴾ (those) in this sense, and the demonstrative for the distant in the plural is ﴿ula'i﴾, and the demonstrative for the distant in the singular is ﴿tilka﴾ or ﴿dhalika﴾, for example. Now here He says: ﴿This is Hell﴾, indicating its nearness to them, because it will be brought on the Day of Resurrection: "It is led by seventy thousand bridles, each bridle led by seventy thousand angels," [Reported by Muslim (2842/29) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. It will be led and brought, and people will see it, and there will befall them a tremendous terror which the describers cannot describe. And it will be said to these criminals: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾. In another verse, Allah says concerning it: ﴿On the Day when they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push. This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see? Burn in it, so be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [at-Tur 13–16]. At first, before they were pushed toward it, they were told: ﴿which you were promised﴾. When they are pushed toward it, the pushing indicates that they retreat on their heels out of fear of it, but they are driven into it with force, may Allah protect us. It will be said: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [at-Tur 14]. Denial is violence in rejecting the truth, and pushing is violence, is it not? It is violence. So the recompense became of the same kind as the deed. As for when it is displayed to them and brought near them, it will be said to them: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾. Here there is a difficulty, which is that it has been said: promise (wa'd) is used for good and threat (i'yad) for evil, and upon this is the saying of the poet:

"And I, if I threaten him or promise him, am one who breaks my threat and fulfils my promise."

Here He said: ﴿you were promised﴾. We say: yes, the matter is as the exegete said, with an implied element which is known, namely his saying: (by it), "you are promised by it" not "you are promised it." If he had said "you are promised it," there would be room for the difficulty. As for Paradise, Allah said of it: ﴿the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Furqan 15]. Allah promised those who believed and did righteous deeds gardens; but these were promised with it, meaning it was said to them: you will certainly encounter it, and this is what happens.

* Student: In His saying, Exalted is He.
* Shaykh: What? His saying or His saying (the pronoun)?
* Student: In His saying..
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿Did you not then be...﴾ (...).
* Shaykh: Conjoining an imperative clause to an indicative clause is permissible, there is no obstacle. There is a difference of opinion, but its permissibility is valid absolutely so long as the meaning is sound: ﴿He said: O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah, and you have taken Him behind your backs?﴾ [Hud 92]. This is conjoining a declarative to an imperative, and likewise the reverse, with no obstacle.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, "taqrir" (affirmation) means that this thing has occurred. But it is an affirmation which may include reproach; sometimes it includes reproach. The point is that this is an established thing, that is: fixed. The meaning of taqrir is that it is a fixed matter. Then it may be a favour or a trial; if it is a trial, it is reproach and blame; if it is a favour, it is praise: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [ash-Sharh 1]. ﴿Alam﴾: they say it is for taqrir. Does it indicate reproach and blame, or praise and commendation? Praise and commendation, because the meaning of taqrir is that the thing is established; then it may be the one or the other, according to what the context requires.
* Student: (...) the disbelievers, lest it be said..
* Shaykh: Allah loves what?
* Student: (...) lest it be said: Allah, Glorified and Exalted; that is: He does not need (...).
* Shaykh: No, this and that, all of it, as in the hadith: "There is no one to whom excuse is more beloved than from Allah." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7416) and Muslim (1499/17) from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.] Allah, Glorified and Exalted, loves to excuse Himself and establish the proof against others. Both, or both of them, are correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Abu Hurayrah only obeyed him when the Messenger said to him: "He told you the truth, though he is a liar." [Reported by al-Bukhari (2311) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Furthermore, he (Shaytan) also commanded him to do something which Abu Hurayrah knew to be good, which is the recitation of the Qur'an; but he did not know that it would protect him from Shaytan until after the Messenger's affirmation of it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, three questions, (...) Ya'juj and Ma'juj (...) those who think that they.. Some of the common people say that these Ya'juj and Ma'juj are not from the children of Adam, and that they are of differing kinds, a race which differs enormously; among them are those who are ten or twenty to a mudd of food and do not reach its limit, and among them are those of huge bodies, long ears, having two ears, one of which they spread as a mattress and the other they use as a blanket. They differ, but the correct view is that they are from the children of Adam; there is no doubt about that.

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾, that is: (you were promised by it), but they used to deny it, as Allah said in Surah at-Tur: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [at-Tur 14]. So they were promised it, that is: they were threatened with it, but they denied it, and Allah's refuge is sought. On the Day of Resurrection they will be reproached for this denial and it will be said: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾ and ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾ [Ya-Sin 64]. That is: it will be said to them: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾. Is this command a cosmic command or a legislative command? If it is from Allah, it is a cosmic command; and if it is from those whom Allah commanded to say it, the angels, it is likewise a cosmic command. The intent is humiliation and abasement, since it is known that they will not be able to burn in it; but it is said as a form of humiliation and abasement.

﴿Today﴾: the "al" here is for the mention of a previously referred thing (al-'ahd al-dhikri), and it may, with respect to addressing these disbelievers, be for the presence of a thing before one (al-'ahd al-huduri), that is: this present day, burn in the fire therein.

The distinction between al-'ahd al-dhikri, al-'ahd al-huduri and al-'ahd al-dhihni often comes up for us, so what is the difference between them?

* Student: The al-'ahd al-huduri means that the thing is present before him.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...), and the al-'ahd al-dhikri means that it was previously mentioned in speech, like His saying, Exalted is He..
* Shaykh: Good, no (...) examples.
* Student: Meaning..
* Shaykh: The dhihni?
* Student: And the al-'ahd al-dhihni means that it is known in the mind..
* Shaykh: Known, but enough, that's it?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 62–67 (part 2 of 3):

So the presential definiteness (al-'ahd al-hudūrī) is what is definite because it is present, the mentioned definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhikrī) is what is definite because it was previously mentioned, and the mental definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhihnī) is what is definite in the minds. For example, if we say: "Go to the judge," while you are in a town, which judge do you go to? To the judge of that same town, because this is known in the mind. The presential, if you say, for instance, "Today we honour you," this is presential; like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. The mentioned definiteness is what was previously mentioned, such as: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15–16], meaning the messenger already mentioned, not another messenger. Here, ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾ appears to be the presential definiteness.

As for His saying, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, (mā) is a verbal-source particle (mā maṣdariyyah), meaning "for your having disbelieved," and the bā' (bi-) denotes causation, meaning "because of." His saying, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, means: you used to disbelieve in it in the world. They disbelieved in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, the prophets, and everything Allah informed of. For this reason they did not perform obedience to Him, since they had no faith. They are only told, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, to establish the proof against them and to show that they were not wronged. Hence, ﴿Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them, "Did no warner come to you?" (8) They say, "Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything. You are only in a great error.'"﴾ [al-Mulk 8–9].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾: ﴿Today﴾ means the Day of Resurrection. (﴿We will seal over their mouths﴾ refers to the disbelievers, because of their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 23]. ﴿And their hands will speak to Us and their feet will testify﴾, and others, ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. So every limb speaks of what proceeded from it.)

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾: sealing over something means closing it and preventing access to it. From it comes "I sealed the bag" when I secured its tying, and "I sealed over it" with wax or the like. The meaning of ﴿We will seal over their mouths﴾ is that We close them so they cannot speak. That is because the polytheists, on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the monotheists have been saved, speak and disown polytheism and say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾

They acknowledge it, because they were not polytheists, hoping they will be saved as the people of monotheism were saved. At that point their mouths are sealed, because their mouths have begun speaking with what? With falsehood. So their mouths are sealed, and the limbs and skins speak: the limbs speak of what they did, and the skins speak of what they touched. The skin touches prohibited things, like a man touching a woman out of desire, for example, and the limbs testify against them. For this reason, the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us﴾ [Ya-Sin 65]. The very hand speaks, saying: "I did such-and-such, I did such-and-such, I did such-and-such."

﴿And their feet will testify﴾ [Ya-Sin 65]: the very feet testify, saying: "I testify that he did such-and-such." Consider the difference between the hand and the foot. For the hand He said, ﴿their hands will speak to Us﴾; for the feet He said, ﴿will testify﴾. This is because the hand reports what it itself did, while the foot reports what something other than it did. They said: this is because the basic form of direct action is by the hand. For this reason, earning is always attributed to the hand: "for what your hands have earned," or ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41], or "for what their hands have earned." So the hands are the doers, and the feet are witnesses, because the witness is the one who reports what another did, while the doer is the one who reports what he himself did. This is what some scholars have said, and it is a distinction that is acceptable, though a person may also testify against himself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 135]. So a person's acknowledgment against himself is a testimony against himself. But the distinction that some scholars pointed out, which we have conveyed to you, is an acceptable distinction.

﴿And their feet will testify for what they used to earn﴾: is it like this in your copies?

﴿for what they used to earn﴾. He said: (﴿And their feet will testify﴾ and others). The author said "and others," and this does not mean that he is correcting the Qur'an, but he is alerting to another place in the Qur'an. In another verse, Allah explained that the skins will testify against them: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves from your hearing, your sight, or your skins from testifying against you﴾ [Fussilat 22]. Not only that, but before it: ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight, and their skins will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat 20]. Hearing and sight were mentioned here or not? Here they were not mentioned; here the hands and feet were mentioned, and hearing, sight, and skins were not. This is why the author said "and others," indicating that there are other members that testify besides the hands and feet. ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing and their sight will testify against them﴾: hearing by what it heard, sight by what it saw, and skin by what it touched. ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ He did not say, "They will say to their sight and hearing, 'Why did you testify?'" This is because the punishment of the skin is general, encompassing the whole body, but the punishment of hearing and sight is specific to hearing and sight. Therefore, ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾, because the punishment will fall upon the skins, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa' 56]. The summary is that it testifies besides the hands and feet, so the witnesses are how many? Five: the hands, the feet, the hearing, the sight, and the skins.

He says: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. The phrase ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ is governed by two governing verbs: the first is (yukallimu, "speak"), and the second is (yashhadu, "testify"). Tanāzu' (grammatical contention) is when two governing words act upon one and the same governed word, such as saying: "I honoured and saw Zayd." Here "I honoured" and "I saw" are two governing words acting upon one governed word, which is Zayd. As for which of them governs it, the first or the second, the scholars differed on this. Ibn Malik says:

*"The second is preferred among the people of Basra, and others chose the reverse, namely the family of ..."*

The second governing word is the one preferred by the Basrans and the Kufans, the one that governs is the first.

﴿And their feet will testify for what they used to earn﴾, and He did not say "what they used to do," because doing may not be something a person earns. An action may be a mistake, so a person is not held accountable for it, and so it is not part of his earning. Rather, what counts as earning is the action that results in reward or punishment. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], and He did not say "what it did." So earning is more specific than doing, since not every action is necessarily earning. An action may happen by inadvertence or ignorance, so a person is not held accountable for it, or it may happen without intention, so a person is not held accountable for it. Nevertheless, sometimes "doing" is used to mean the action that is earning, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself, and whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾ [Fussilat 46]. He says: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. So every limb speaks of what proceeded from it: the hand speaks of what it seized, the foot of what it walked, the eye of what it saw, the ear of what it heard, and the skin of what it touched. In Surat al-Nur, Allah mentioned that the tongues testify: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur 24].

So we add this to the five, and they become six. The tongue also testifies against them, because the tongue is the greatest of the limbs in danger, as the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh: "Shall I not direct you to the head of all this?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He took hold of his own tongue and said: "Restrain this." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we say?" He said: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Mu'adh! Do people get thrown on their faces, or on their noses, into the Fire, except for the harvest of their tongues?"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2616) and Ibn Majah (3973), from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]] Every morning the limbs disown the tongue, meaning they make the matter depend upon it. For this reason, in Surat al-Nur He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues will testify against them﴾, and He specified the tongues in Surat al-Nur because He mentioned in it matters related to that, such as slander, and the greatest of them is the slander of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Therefore, tongues were mentioned in Surat al-Nur, because slander is speech. So He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾, and every limb speaks of what proceeded from it.

He said: (﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾: We would have blinded them with obliteration. ﴿And they race to the path﴾: they hasten toward the way, going as is their custom. ﴿But how could they see?﴾: how could they see then? That is, they cannot see. ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ into monkeys and swine or into stones ﴿in their places﴾. In another reading, ﴿in their places﴾ (makānātihim), plural of makānah, meaning place; that is, in their dwellings. ﴿So they would not be able to proceed or to return﴾: they would not be able to go or come.)

His saying: ﴿And if We willed﴾ [Ya-Sin 66]. (Law) here is a particle of prohibition for existence. What was prohibited? The obliteration. It was prohibited because of the prohibition of willing. So it is a particle of prohibition for prohibition, like: "If Zayd had come, I would have honoured you." The coming and the honouring were prohibited. But (lawla) is a particle of prohibition for existence, and (lamma) is a particle of existence for existence. These three tools contend over existence and non-existence.

"If Zayd had come, I would have honoured you": prohibition for prohibition.
"Were it not for Zayd, I would have honoured you": prohibition for existence.
And if you wish, say: "Were it not for the coming of Zayd, I would have honoured you," so that it matches the two examples. Here, ﴿And if We willed﴾, so it is a particle of prohibition for prohibition: the transformation was prohibited because the willing was prohibited. So His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. ﴿We willed﴾ is in the plural; the pronoun is a plural pronoun: "if We willed," meaning We. This is one of the ambiguous matters, because the Christian claimed the plurality of gods by means of such a pronoun. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refers to Himself as "We," "will," "desire," and similar. So he is plural. But we respond that the plural here is for magnification, not for plurality. You have blinded your eye and blinded your insight to the clear, decisive verses indicating that Allah is one God: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171]. But as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7]. So the pronoun "We will" is a plural pronoun; (we) here is for magnification and definitely not for plurality, because Allah is One.

﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾: he said, "We would have blinded them with obliteration." Obliteration is more emphatic than blinding, because obliteration is the removal of the eye at once, leaving no trace, while blindness can occur while the eye remains, though it may still be intact in appearance or may differ. The point is that obliteration is the complete removal of the eye and its features. If Allah willed, He would do that even after the eye exists; otherwise He would not create eyes for them.

We said "after the eye exists," because Allah said: ﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, and Allah is over all things capable. As He was capable of cleaving the eye, He is capable of obliterating that cleft. If a human may sew a cut until it heals, how much more so the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, who says to a thing: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]!

﴿So they race to the path, but how could they see?﴾ [Ya-Sin 66]: that is, their eyes are obliterated, and they hasten to find the path that leads them to their goal, as if you picture them now jostling like frightened donkeys, hoping to find the way. Is this possible? Can a blind person be guided to the path? No; in terms of visual guidance it is not possible. For this reason He said: ﴿but how could they see?﴾, meaning: how could they see the path when Allah has obliterated their eyes! The intended meaning of this verse is that Allah, glorified and exalted, obliterated the hearts of these people. And if He willed, He would have obliterated their eyes, so the obliteration would be sensory and known. Just as one whose eye is obliterated cannot see, so one whose insight is obliterated cannot see the truth. How could a person whose insight Allah has obliterated see the truth and be guided? That is impossible, just as one whose sight Allah has obliterated cannot be guided to the path.

He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ [Ya-Sin 67]. The first, ﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, is the absence of guidance; the second is the absence of movement: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. ﴿Transformed them﴾: it has been said that the meaning of transformation is what the author said: "monkeys, swine, and stones." It has also been said that the meaning of transformation is leaving them as they are; that is, they would be transformed in their places, unable to move. They would be human but transformed, unable to move. Whichever it is, Allah is over all things capable, and Allah has turned the children of Adam into monkeys and swine.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The children of Israel, yes: ﴿And you had already known those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath. So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and repelled"﴾ [al-Baqarah 65]. ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and upon whom He became angry and made of them apes and swine, and who worshipped false deities"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 60]. So Allah, glorified and exalted, is over all things capable. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Does he who raises his head before the imam not fear that Allah will turn his head into the head of a donkey, or make his form the form of a donkey?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (691) and Muslim (427/114), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] The matter is easy for Allah, glorified and exalted; He says: ﴿Be, and it is﴾.

He says: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾: that is, We would have changed their forms into other forms, such as monkeys and swine, or made them stones, or left them remaining like inanimate objects. The point is that if Allah, glorified and exalted, willed, He would have transformed them and kept them in their places, unable to move. For this reason He said: ﴿So they were not able to proceed or to return﴾, meaning they were not able to see. Why? Because they were transformed in their places and remained fixed, unable to go forward or return. One who cannot proceed or return is like a pillar that neither advances forward nor retreats backward. If Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed, He would have transformed them in this manner, until their state became manifest to the senses. As for good and moral progress, they did not advance toward goodness, but rather lagged behind toward evil. For this reason, the course they followed in their deeds was the opposite of the correct direction, indeed entirely contrary to it: ﴿So they were not able to proceed or to return﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whomever We cause to live long, We reverse him in creation. Then will they not reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin 68] (...).

What do you say about it? (The interrogative particle, meaning negation; that is, "then do they not see.")

(...) We have reached His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that worship Me; this is a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin 61].

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin 62]. This is the beginning of the benefits.

* From this noble verse the following benefits are derived:

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 62–67 (part 3 of 3):

* First: an explanation of the enmity of Satan toward the children of Adam, in that he has led astray from among them a great multitude (jibillan kathiran), meaning a great number of creatures.
* Among its lessons: caution, indeed warning, against Satan and his seduction, because he cannot seek to guide creation or the children of Adam; he seeks only to mislead them.
* Among its lessons: whoever follows Satan in his seduction and misguidance is lacking in reason, based on His saying: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾
* Among its lessons: whoever's conduct is corrupt may rightly be described as lacking reason, even if he possesses comprehension-reason ('aql idrak). His saying here, ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾, supports this. It has already been explained to us that reason is of two kinds: reason which is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif), namely comprehension-reason ('aql idrak), and reason which is the basis of praise and blame, namely the reason of conduct ('aql al-tasarruf), by which rectitude is attained.
* Among its lessons: a rebuke and reproach of those who followed Satan in his misguidance, for being lacking in reason, based on His saying: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ [Yasin 63] In this is an affirmation of the Fire of Hell, and that it will be witnessed with the eye on the Day of Resurrection, based on His saying ﴿This﴾, since the demonstrative refers to something perceptible that is pointed to.

* Among its lessons: a description of the Fire, that it is, may Allah protect us, entirely darkness and entirely blackness, based on His saying ﴿Jahannam﴾ (Hell), because it derives from al-jahmah, meaning darkness and blackness.
* Also among its lessons: the affirmation of these people and the exposure of their error in denying it, based on His saying ﴿which you were promised﴾.
* Among the lessons of the verse: the truthfulness of the promise of Allah, the Exalted, in that He fulfilled what He promised these deniers, until they witnessed with their own eyes what they had been promised.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ [Yasin 64]

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: an explanation that these deniers are commanded in a manner of humiliation and degradation to enter the Fire, based on His saying ﴿Burn in it today﴾.
* Among its lessons: the affirmation of causes, based on His saying ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾. The affirmation of causes is established by the Shari'ah, by reason, and by the senses. None denies the affirmation of causes except one who is ignorant of the reality of things. No one denies that if you strike a glass bottle with a stone, it breaks, and if you throw rags into fire, they burn. Only one who obstinately denies what is evident would deny this. Yet, despite this, are causes effective in themselves, or do they act by their own essence? No; rather, Allah, the Exalted, creates the effect within them. Accordingly, affirming causes does not involve any shirk, contrary to those who claim that affirming the effect of causes is a kind of shirk, because the occurrence of these causes produces effects only by what? By the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who causes the effect in them. For this reason, if Allah wills that they not produce an effect, they will not. The nature of fire is to burn, yet it did not burn Abraham, peace be upon him; rather it became cool and safe for him, because Allah said: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham.﴾ [al-Anbiya 69]
* Among its lessons: the perfect justice of Allah, the Exalted, based on His saying ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: you were not wronged; rather, it is you who did this to yourselves.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that Allah, the Exalted, seals the mouths of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection so that they do not speak. We have already discussed how to reconcile this verse with His saying about them: ﴿Then their discourse will be only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not associators."﴾ [al-An'am 23]. What is the reconciliation?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. So the Resurrection has states: a state in which they deny, and a state in which they confess, but only after their hands and tongues have testified against them.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the power of Allah, the Exalted, based on His saying ﴿and their hands speak to Us and their feet bear witness﴾, for it is contrary to custom that hands and feet should speak. But Allah is capable of all things. For this reason, when Allah mentioned that they will say to their skins: ﴿"Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has made us speak, He who makes everything speak."﴾ [Fussilat 21]
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that a person's limbs may testify against one another, since this individual's limbs bear witness against him for what he did. Does it follow from this that a person in this world may bear witness against himself? Yes, it is possible, and his testimony against himself is his acknowledgment against himself.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that what matters in action is the acquisition (kasb) that accompanies it, not mere action, based on His saying ﴿for what they used to acquire﴾. We have mentioned in the exegesis the difference between His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat 20] and ﴿for what they used to earn﴾, because mere action may not be an acquisition, as when it proceeds from one who is ignorant, or one who is heedless or asleep, or the like.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path, but how could they see?﴾, and the two verses that follow.

* In this noble verse: an affirmation of the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying ﴿And if We willed﴾. But everything dependent on the will of Allah is also joined with wisdom, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not will a bare will; rather His will follows His wisdom. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [al-Insan 30]. His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ indicates that His will is joined with knowledge and wisdom.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's power, ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. These seeing eyes, if Allah willed, He would obliterate them and they would become as though they had never existed.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the striking of a parable, by likening intelligible things to perceptible things. These people, if their eyes were obliterated, could not find the way. Likewise, if Allah obliterates the insight of the heart, may Allah protect us, one cannot reach the truth or recognize it.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfect eloquence of the Qur'an. For if Allah had willed, He could have said: "And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they could neither go forward nor return." But He presented it in this expansive, flowing style, which is more effective in impact, and which has a fine melodious cadence that the ears yearn for and delight in hearing.

Then He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places, and they would not be able to proceed, nor could they return.﴾ Here too is an affirmation of the will and of the perfect power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Also among its lessons: that Allah, the Exalted, if He willed, would have fixed them in their places so that they could neither go forward nor return, based on ﴿and they would not be able to proceed, nor could they return﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 62–67 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. I will recite it as it is in the Mushaf. I think we stopped at this verse, and we spoke about its beginning, which is His saying: ﴿And he had already led astray﴾.

He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. ﴿Led astray﴾: idlal (misguidance) means causing loss and turning away from the straight path. Before we begin, what do you want to ask?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a benefit here. ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾. In it is the affirmation that Allah speaks and utters speech, and this is the truth. The people of the qibla (ahl al-qibla, the Muslims) have differed about the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Some of them said: He speaks with a letter and a sound in a manner befitting Him, and His sound does not resemble the sounds of created beings. Others said: He does not speak, but He creates speech which He attributes to Himself as an honour and dignity. Others said: He speaks, but His speech is only what He conceives within Himself, and what is heard is created. The first is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), the second is the position of the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazila) and those who agree with them, and the third is the position of the Ash'ariyyah (Ash'arites). The reality of the matter is that the position of the Ash'arites is the position of the Mu'tazilah, because all of them agree that the Mushaf in our hands is created. But the Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilah said: it is the speech of Allah. Those (the Ash'arites) said: it is an expression of the speech of Allah. So they are worse than them in this respect, because the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah say: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah as Allah said of it that it is the speech of Allah: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the speech of Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah 6]. But they say: ﴿until he hears the speech of﴾, meaning: the speech which is an expression of the speech of Allah. So which of them is closer to the truth? The Jahmiyyah and the Mu'tazilah. But each of them is in manifest error. The correct view is that it is the speech of Allah, which He spoke with Himself, and Jibril heard it from Him and conveyed it to Muhammad ﷺ. This is an important and good benefit.

But I want you, when I am extracting the benefits, not to say anything, because you know that a person whose thinking is arranged on something and who proceeds along it, and then a stone is placed in front of him so that he stumbles, what was in his mind is removed.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Whatever it is, until the benefits are finished. Once more, fine.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you﴾. ﴿Led astray﴾ means ﴿adalla﴾ in the sense of wasted and brought; that is: he led you to misguidance in which there is no guidance. ﴿He had led astray from among you a great multitude﴾. The author said: (khalqan, the plural of jabil like qadim; and in one reading with a damma on the ba'). ﴿Jubulan﴾. Is this reading sab'iyyah (of the seven canonical readings) or shadhdhah (irregular)? (And in one reading) is sab'iyyah, yes. If he says "and in one reading", or says for example "with a damma on the ba' and with its sukun", then it is sab'iyyah; but if he says "and it was read (wa-quri'a)", then it is shadhdhah. This is the author's terminology.

So there are two canonical readings: ﴿jubulan﴾ and ﴿jubulan﴾ (with damma). There is a third reading which the author did not mention: ﴿jibillan kathiran﴾, and there is a fourth reading: ﴿jibalan﴾ without the shaddah on the lam. But the author, may Allah have mercy on him, did not intend his tafsir to be a collection of the readings; he mentions what he sees the benefit as requiring. However, in any case there is no doubt that if he had mentioned them it would have been better, because sometimes he mentions several readings concerning the manner of pronouncing a letter, just as he mentions several readings that reach up to six readings, as in ﴿a-andhartahum﴾ [Ya-Sin 10] regarding facilitation, verification, omission and the like. But man is human, and sometimes he overlooks and neglects what should be mentioned, or mentions what need not be mentioned.

﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude﴾, that is, a creation ﴿kathiran﴾ (great, many). This does not mean that the majority were not led astray by Shaytan; rather, he led astray most of creation, since most of creation were led astray by Shaytan. For it is established in the authentic hadith: "Allah will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Adam! He will say: Here I am at Your call and Your pleasure. He will say: Bring forth from your progeny a group for the Fire. He will say: O Lord, what is the group for the Fire? He said: Of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine." All of these are in the Fire from the children of Adam, and one is in Paradise. This was difficult for the Companions and weighed heavily on them, and they said: Which of us is that one, O Messenger of Allah? He said: "Rejoice, for you are among two peoples, neither of which has ever been (in a matter) but it has outnumbered it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj." [Reported by at-Tirmidhi (3169) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn.] And indeed, whoever observes creation now, although we are in a small part of the ages, finds that nine hundred and ninety-nine of them are all in error, even those who ascribe themselves to the Islamic religion, among whom there is great error that reaches the point of disbelief, even though they are ascribed to Islam.

Now, is the meaning of "kathir" here "the majority" or not? Yes, the meaning is the majority: ﴿a great multitude﴾. He said: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾. The hamzah here is for interrogation, and the purpose of the interrogation is reproach, rebuking them for not using their reason. The fa' here is conjunctive, and the element it conjoins is either what preceded or an implied clause suited to the context. There are two opinions among the scholars: some say that the particle of conjunction conjoins what follows to what precedes, but in the wording there is an inversion between the particle of conjunction and the hamzah, and if each were placed in its own position the wording would be "a-lam takunu ta'qilun" (did you not use your reason).

Others said: the hamzah is in its proper place, and the fa' conjoins an implied element understood from the context or the setting. In reality this may be closer to the rules, but it is more difficult, since in some places you cannot estimate anything and do not know what fits; in that case the second is easier. My rule is that when the grammarians differ on a question, the preferred view is the easier one, so long as it does not entail a difference in meaning and the meaning that follows from the easier view is not sound. In that case we do not follow the easier view, because it would harm the meaning and lead to an unsound meaning. But as long as the meaning is correct on both readings, the easier is the preferred one. "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (69) and Muslim (1734/8) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]

﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ means that He rebuked them for not using their reason. Reason is of two kinds: reason in the sense of perception, which is what obligation (taklif) depends upon, and reason in the sense of conduct, which is what praise or blame depends upon. Reason is of two kinds: reason in the sense of perception, which is what obligation depends upon, or if you wish, say: it is the basis of obligation, and what the jurists say about it: among the conditions of worship is reason. The other reason is in the sense of conduct, which is what praise and blame depend upon. Which is intended here? The second, decisively; because if the reason of perception were absent from them, they would not be under obligation and blame would not be directed at them. But the reason of conduct was absent from them, so they did not act well, and they became rational yet not rational: rational with respect to perception, which entails obligation, and not rational with respect to conduct, which entails praise or blame. In reality, although they were given minds, or in other words were given intelligence (dhaka') but were not given reason ('aql). How excellent is the expression of Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning the theologians (mutakallimun) when he described them: they were given intelligence but were not given purity of soul (zaka'), they were given understanding but were not given knowledge, and they were given hearing, sight and hearts: ﴿Their hearing, nor their sight, nor their hearts availed them anything, since they used to deny the signs of Allah, and there encompassed them that which they used to ridicule﴾ [al-Ahqaf 26]. Note: they were given intelligence but not purity of soul, may Allah grant us well-being. Their intelligence became a proof against them. They were given understanding: they had comprehension, but they had no knowledge, and when a person speaks from his understanding and not from knowledge, he goes astray and is lost. So there must be knowledge upon which your belief and worship are built. The point is that these people were given minds through which the proof is established against them, but they were deprived of the minds which bring praise and blame, which are right guidance and good conduct. They did not employ their minds which Allah had bestowed upon them; they did not employ them in what would benefit them. ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ He, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ his enmity and his misguiding, or what befell them of punishment, so that you would believe). That is: if you had reasoned about his enmity and his misguidance, or if you had reasoned about the punishment that befell those who followed him of torment and chastisement, you would have opposed him, you would not worship him, and you would have believed in Allah alone. But desire covered over guidance, as the Exalted said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them﴾ [Fussilat 17].

Then He, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿This is Hell﴾ [Ya-Sin 63]. The author said regarding the implied meaning: (And it will be said to them in the Hereafter: ﴿This is Hell﴾). The demonstrative ﴿hadhihi﴾ here indicates something near, since the demonstrative for the distant is ﴿ulaika﴾ (those) in this sense, and the demonstrative for the distant in the plural is ﴿ula'i﴾, and the demonstrative for the distant in the singular is ﴿tilka﴾ or ﴿dhalika﴾, for example. Now here He says: ﴿This is Hell﴾, indicating its nearness to them, because it will be brought on the Day of Resurrection: "It is led by seventy thousand bridles, each bridle led by seventy thousand angels," [Reported by Muslim (2842/29) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. It will be led and brought, and people will see it, and there will befall them a tremendous terror which the describers cannot describe. And it will be said to these criminals: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾. In another verse, Allah says concerning it: ﴿On the Day when they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push. This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see? Burn in it, so be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [at-Tur 13–16]. At first, before they were pushed toward it, they were told: ﴿which you were promised﴾. When they are pushed toward it, the pushing indicates that they retreat on their heels out of fear of it, but they are driven into it with force, may Allah protect us. It will be said: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [at-Tur 14]. Denial is violence in rejecting the truth, and pushing is violence, is it not? It is violence. So the recompense became of the same kind as the deed. As for when it is displayed to them and brought near them, it will be said to them: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾. Here there is a difficulty, which is that it has been said: promise (wa'd) is used for good and threat (i'yad) for evil, and upon this is the saying of the poet:

"And I, if I threaten him or promise him, am one who breaks my threat and fulfils my promise."

Here He said: ﴿you were promised﴾. We say: yes, the matter is as the exegete said, with an implied element which is known, namely his saying: (by it), "you are promised by it" not "you are promised it." If he had said "you are promised it," there would be room for the difficulty. As for Paradise, Allah said of it: ﴿the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Furqan 15]. Allah promised those who believed and did righteous deeds gardens; but these were promised with it, meaning it was said to them: you will certainly encounter it, and this is what happens.

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾, that is: (you were promised by it), but they used to deny it, as Allah said in Surah at-Tur: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [at-Tur 14]. So they were promised it, that is: they were threatened with it, but they denied it, and Allah's refuge is sought. On the Day of Resurrection they will be reproached for this denial and it will be said: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾ and ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾ [Ya-Sin 64]. That is: it will be said to them: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾. Is this command a cosmic command or a legislative command? If it is from Allah, it is a cosmic command; and if it is from those whom Allah commanded to say it, the angels, it is likewise a cosmic command. The intent is humiliation and abasement, since it is known that they will not be able to burn in it; but it is said as a form of humiliation and abasement.

﴿Today﴾: the "al" here is for the mention of a previously referred thing (al-'ahd al-dhikri), and it may, with respect to addressing these disbelievers, be for the presence of a thing before one (al-'ahd al-huduri), that is: this present day, burn in the fire therein.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 62–67 (part 2 of 3):

So the presential definiteness (al-'ahd al-hudūrī) is what is definite because it is present, the mentioned definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhikrī) is what is definite because it was previously mentioned, and the mental definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhihnī) is what is definite in the minds. For example, if we say: "Go to the judge," while you are in a town, which judge do you go to? To the judge of that same town, because this is known in the mind. The presential, if you say, for instance, "Today we honour you," this is presential; like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. The mentioned definiteness is what was previously mentioned, such as: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (15). But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil 15–16], meaning the messenger already mentioned, not another messenger. Here, ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾ appears to be the presential definiteness.

As for His saying, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, (mā) is a verbal-source particle (mā maṣdariyyah), meaning "for your having disbelieved," and the bā' (bi-) denotes causation, meaning "because of." His saying, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, means: you used to disbelieve in it in the world. They disbelieved in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, the prophets, and everything Allah informed of. For this reason they did not perform obedience to Him, since they had no faith. They are only told, ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾, to establish the proof against them and to show that they were not wronged. Hence, ﴿Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them, "Did no warner come to you?" (8) They say, "Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything. You are only in a great error.'"﴾ [al-Mulk 8–9].

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾: ﴿Today﴾ means the Day of Resurrection. (﴿We will seal over their mouths﴾ refers to the disbelievers, because of their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 23]. ﴿And their hands will speak to Us and their feet will testify﴾, and others, ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. So every limb speaks of what proceeded from it.)

﴿Today We will seal over their mouths﴾: sealing over something means closing it and preventing access to it. From it comes "I sealed the bag" when I secured its tying, and "I sealed over it" with wax or the like. The meaning of ﴿We will seal over their mouths﴾ is that We close them so they cannot speak. That is because the polytheists, on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the monotheists have been saved, speak and disown polytheism and say: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾

They acknowledge it, because they were not polytheists, hoping they will be saved as the people of monotheism were saved. At that point their mouths are sealed, because their mouths have begun speaking with what? With falsehood. So their mouths are sealed, and the limbs and skins speak: the limbs speak of what they did, and the skins speak of what they touched. The skin touches prohibited things, like a man touching a woman out of desire, for example, and the limbs testify against them. For this reason, the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And their hands will speak to Us﴾ [Ya-Sin 65]. The very hand speaks, saying: "I did such-and-such, I did such-and-such, I did such-and-such."

﴿And their feet will testify﴾ [Ya-Sin 65]: the very feet testify, saying: "I testify that he did such-and-such." Consider the difference between the hand and the foot. For the hand He said, ﴿their hands will speak to Us﴾; for the feet He said, ﴿will testify﴾. This is because the hand reports what it itself did, while the foot reports what something other than it did. They said: this is because the basic form of direct action is by the hand. For this reason, earning is always attributed to the hand: "for what your hands have earned," or ﴿for what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41], or "for what their hands have earned." So the hands are the doers, and the feet are witnesses, because the witness is the one who reports what another did, while the doer is the one who reports what he himself did. This is what some scholars have said, and it is a distinction that is acceptable, though a person may also testify against himself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 135]. So a person's acknowledgment against himself is a testimony against himself. But the distinction that some scholars pointed out, which we have conveyed to you, is an acceptable distinction.

﴿And their feet will testify for what they used to earn﴾: is it like this in your copies?

﴿for what they used to earn﴾. He said: (﴿And their feet will testify﴾ and others). The author said "and others," and this does not mean that he is correcting the Qur'an, but he is alerting to another place in the Qur'an. In another verse, Allah explained that the skins will testify against them: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves from your hearing, your sight, or your skins from testifying against you﴾ [Fussilat 22]. Not only that, but before it: ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight, and their skins will testify against them for what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat 20]. Hearing and sight were mentioned here or not? Here they were not mentioned; here the hands and feet were mentioned, and hearing, sight, and skins were not. This is why the author said "and others," indicating that there are other members that testify besides the hands and feet. ﴿Until, when they reach it, their hearing and their sight will testify against them﴾: hearing by what it heard, sight by what it saw, and skin by what it touched. ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ He did not say, "They will say to their sight and hearing, 'Why did you testify?'" This is because the punishment of the skin is general, encompassing the whole body, but the punishment of hearing and sight is specific to hearing and sight. Therefore, ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾, because the punishment will fall upon the skins, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa' 56]. The summary is that it testifies besides the hands and feet, so the witnesses are how many? Five: the hands, the feet, the hearing, the sight, and the skins.

He says: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. The phrase ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ is governed by two governing verbs: the first is (yukallimu, "speak"), and the second is (yashhadu, "testify"). Tanāzu' (grammatical contention) is when two governing words act upon one and the same governed word, such as saying: "I honoured and saw Zayd." Here "I honoured" and "I saw" are two governing words acting upon one governed word, which is Zayd. As for which of them governs it, the first or the second, the scholars differed on this. Ibn Malik says:

*"The second is preferred among the people of Basra, and others chose the reverse, namely the family of ..."*

The second governing word is the one preferred by the Basrans and the Kufans, the one that governs is the first.

﴿And their feet will testify for what they used to earn﴾, and He did not say "what they used to do," because doing may not be something a person earns. An action may be a mistake, so a person is not held accountable for it, and so it is not part of his earning. Rather, what counts as earning is the action that results in reward or punishment. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], and He did not say "what it did." So earning is more specific than doing, since not every action is necessarily earning. An action may happen by inadvertence or ignorance, so a person is not held accountable for it, or it may happen without intention, so a person is not held accountable for it. Nevertheless, sometimes "doing" is used to mean the action that is earning, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself, and whoever does evil, it is against himself﴾ [Fussilat 46]. He says: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾. So every limb speaks of what proceeded from it: the hand speaks of what it seized, the foot of what it walked, the eye of what it saw, the ear of what it heard, and the skin of what it touched. In Surat al-Nur, Allah mentioned that the tongues testify: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur 24].

So we add this to the five, and they become six. The tongue also testifies against them, because the tongue is the greatest of the limbs in danger, as the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh: "Shall I not direct you to the head of all this?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He took hold of his own tongue and said: "Restrain this." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be held accountable for what we say?" He said: "May your mother be bereaved of you, O Mu'adh! Do people get thrown on their faces, or on their noses, into the Fire, except for the harvest of their tongues?"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2616) and Ibn Majah (3973), from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]] Every morning the limbs disown the tongue, meaning they make the matter depend upon it. For this reason, in Surat al-Nur He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues will testify against them﴾, and He specified the tongues in Surat al-Nur because He mentioned in it matters related to that, such as slander, and the greatest of them is the slander of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Therefore, tongues were mentioned in Surat al-Nur, because slander is speech. So He said: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿for what they used to earn﴾, and every limb speaks of what proceeded from it.

He said: (﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾: We would have blinded them with obliteration. ﴿And they race to the path﴾: they hasten toward the way, going as is their custom. ﴿But how could they see?﴾: how could they see then? That is, they cannot see. ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them﴾ into monkeys and swine or into stones ﴿in their places﴾. In another reading, ﴿in their places﴾ (makānātihim), plural of makānah, meaning place; that is, in their dwellings. ﴿So they would not be able to proceed or to return﴾: they would not be able to go or come.)

His saying: ﴿And if We willed﴾ [Ya-Sin 66]. (Law) here is a particle of prohibition for existence. What was prohibited? The obliteration. It was prohibited because of the prohibition of willing. So it is a particle of prohibition for prohibition, like: "If Zayd had come, I would have honoured you." The coming and the honouring were prohibited. But (lawla) is a particle of prohibition for existence, and (lamma) is a particle of existence for existence. These three tools contend over existence and non-existence.

"If Zayd had come, I would have honoured you": prohibition for prohibition.
"Were it not for Zayd, I would have honoured you": prohibition for existence.
And if you wish, say: "Were it not for the coming of Zayd, I would have honoured you," so that it matches the two examples. Here, ﴿And if We willed﴾, so it is a particle of prohibition for prohibition: the transformation was prohibited because the willing was prohibited. So His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. ﴿We willed﴾ is in the plural; the pronoun is a plural pronoun: "if We willed," meaning We. This is one of the ambiguous matters, because the Christian claimed the plurality of gods by means of such a pronoun. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refers to Himself as "We," "will," "desire," and similar. So he is plural. But we respond that the plural here is for magnification, not for plurality. You have blinded your eye and blinded your insight to the clear, decisive verses indicating that Allah is one God: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171]. But as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7]. So the pronoun "We will" is a plural pronoun; (we) here is for magnification and definitely not for plurality, because Allah is One.

﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾: he said, "We would have blinded them with obliteration." Obliteration is more emphatic than blinding, because obliteration is the removal of the eye at once, leaving no trace, while blindness can occur while the eye remains, though it may still be intact in appearance or may differ. The point is that obliteration is the complete removal of the eye and its features. If Allah willed, He would do that even after the eye exists; otherwise He would not create eyes for them.

We said "after the eye exists," because Allah said: ﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, and Allah is over all things capable. As He was capable of cleaving the eye, He is capable of obliterating that cleft. If a human may sew a cut until it heals, how much more so the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, who says to a thing: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]!

﴿So they race to the path, but how could they see?﴾ [Ya-Sin 66]: that is, their eyes are obliterated, and they hasten to find the path that leads them to their goal, as if you picture them now jostling like frightened donkeys, hoping to find the way. Is this possible? Can a blind person be guided to the path? No; in terms of visual guidance it is not possible. For this reason He said: ﴿but how could they see?﴾, meaning: how could they see the path when Allah has obliterated their eyes! The intended meaning of this verse is that Allah, glorified and exalted, obliterated the hearts of these people. And if He willed, He would have obliterated their eyes, so the obliteration would be sensory and known. Just as one whose eye is obliterated cannot see, so one whose insight is obliterated cannot see the truth. How could a person whose insight Allah has obliterated see the truth and be guided? That is impossible, just as one whose sight Allah has obliterated cannot be guided to the path.

He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾ [Ya-Sin 67]. The first, ﴿We would have obliterated their eyes﴾, is the absence of guidance; the second is the absence of movement: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾. ﴿Transformed them﴾: it has been said that the meaning of transformation is what the author said: "monkeys, swine, and stones." It has also been said that the meaning of transformation is leaving them as they are; that is, they would be transformed in their places, unable to move. They would be human but transformed, unable to move. Whichever it is, Allah is over all things capable, and Allah has turned the children of Adam into monkeys and swine.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The children of Israel, yes: ﴿And you had already known those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath. So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and repelled"﴾ [al-Baqarah 65]. ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and upon whom He became angry and made of them apes and swine, and who worshipped false deities"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 60]. So Allah, glorified and exalted, is over all things capable. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Does he who raises his head before the imam not fear that Allah will turn his head into the head of a donkey, or make his form the form of a donkey?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (691) and Muslim (427/114), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] The matter is easy for Allah, glorified and exalted; He says: ﴿Be, and it is﴾.

He says: ﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them in their places﴾: that is, We would have changed their forms into other forms, such as monkeys and swine, or made them stones, or left them remaining like inanimate objects. The point is that if Allah, glorified and exalted, willed, He would have transformed them and kept them in their places, unable to move. For this reason He said: ﴿So they were not able to proceed or to return﴾, meaning they were not able to see. Why? Because they were transformed in their places and remained fixed, unable to go forward or return. One who cannot proceed or return is like a pillar that neither advances forward nor retreats backward. If Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed, He would have transformed them in this manner, until their state became manifest to the senses. As for good and moral progress, they did not advance toward goodness, but rather lagged behind toward evil. For this reason, the course they followed in their deeds was the opposite of the correct direction, indeed entirely contrary to it: ﴿So they were not able to proceed or to return﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whomever We cause to live long, We reverse him in creation. Then will they not reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin 68] (...).

What do you say about it? (The interrogative particle, meaning negation; that is, "then do they not see.")

(...) We have reached His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that worship Me; this is a straight path﴾ [Ya-Sin 61].

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Did you not then use reason?﴾ [Ya-Sin 62]. This is the beginning of the benefits.

* From this noble verse the following benefits are derived:

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verses 62–67 (part 3 of 3):

* First: an explanation of the enmity of Satan toward the children of Adam, in that he has led astray from among them a great multitude (jibillan kathiran), meaning a great number of creatures.
* Among its lessons: caution, indeed warning, against Satan and his seduction, because he cannot seek to guide creation or the children of Adam; he seeks only to mislead them.
* Among its lessons: whoever follows Satan in his seduction and misguidance is lacking in reason, based on His saying: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾
* Among its lessons: whoever's conduct is corrupt may rightly be described as lacking reason, even if he possesses comprehension-reason ('aql idrak). His saying here, ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾, supports this. It has already been explained to us that reason is of two kinds: reason which is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif), namely comprehension-reason ('aql idrak), and reason which is the basis of praise and blame, namely the reason of conduct ('aql al-tasarruf), by which rectitude is attained.
* Among its lessons: a rebuke and reproach of those who followed Satan in his misguidance, for being lacking in reason, based on His saying: ﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ [Yasin 63] In this is an affirmation of the Fire of Hell, and that it will be witnessed with the eye on the Day of Resurrection, based on His saying ﴿This﴾, since the demonstrative refers to something perceptible that is pointed to.

* Among its lessons: a description of the Fire, that it is, may Allah protect us, entirely darkness and entirely blackness, based on His saying ﴿Jahannam﴾ (Hell), because it derives from al-jahmah, meaning darkness and blackness.
* Also among its lessons: the affirmation of these people and the exposure of their error in denying it, based on His saying ﴿which you were promised﴾.
* Among the lessons of the verse: the truthfulness of the promise of Allah, the Exalted, in that He fulfilled what He promised these deniers, until they witnessed with their own eyes what they had been promised.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ [Yasin 64]

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: an explanation that these deniers are commanded in a manner of humiliation and degradation to enter the Fire, based on His saying ﴿Burn in it today﴾.
* Among its lessons: the affirmation of causes, based on His saying ﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾. The affirmation of causes is established by the Shari'ah, by reason, and by the senses. None denies the affirmation of causes except one who is ignorant of the reality of things. No one denies that if you strike a glass bottle with a stone, it breaks, and if you throw rags into fire, they burn. Only one who obstinately denies what is evident would deny this. Yet, despite this, are causes effective in themselves, or do they act by their own essence? No; rather, Allah, the Exalted, creates the effect within them. Accordingly, affirming causes does not involve any shirk, contrary to those who claim that affirming the effect of causes is a kind of shirk, because the occurrence of these causes produces effects only by what? By the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who causes the effect in them. For this reason, if Allah wills that they not produce an effect, they will not. The nature of fire is to burn, yet it did not burn Abraham, peace be upon him; rather it became cool and safe for him, because Allah said: ﴿O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham.﴾ [al-Anbiya 69]
* Among its lessons: the perfect justice of Allah, the Exalted, based on His saying ﴿Burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning: you were not wronged; rather, it is you who did this to yourselves.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that Allah, the Exalted, seals the mouths of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection so that they do not speak. We have already discussed how to reconcile this verse with His saying about them: ﴿Then their discourse will be only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not associators."﴾ [al-An'am 23]. What is the reconciliation?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. So the Resurrection has states: a state in which they deny, and a state in which they confess, but only after their hands and tongues have testified against them.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: the power of Allah, the Exalted, based on His saying ﴿and their hands speak to Us and their feet bear witness﴾, for it is contrary to custom that hands and feet should speak. But Allah is capable of all things. For this reason, when Allah mentioned that they will say to their skins: ﴿"Why did you testify against us?" They will say, "Allah has made us speak, He who makes everything speak."﴾ [Fussilat 21]
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that a person's limbs may testify against one another, since this individual's limbs bear witness against him for what he did. Does it follow from this that a person in this world may bear witness against himself? Yes, it is possible, and his testimony against himself is his acknowledgment against himself.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: that what matters in action is the acquisition (kasb) that accompanies it, not mere action, based on His saying ﴿for what they used to acquire﴾. We have mentioned in the exegesis the difference between His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾ [Fussilat 20] and ﴿for what they used to earn﴾, because mere action may not be an acquisition, as when it proceeds from one who is ignorant, or one who is heedless or asleep, or the like.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, and they would race to the path, but how could they see?﴾, and the two verses that follow.

* In this noble verse: an affirmation of the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying ﴿And if We willed﴾. But everything dependent on the will of Allah is also joined with wisdom, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, does not will a bare will; rather His will follows His wisdom. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ [al-Insan 30]. His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ indicates that His will is joined with knowledge and wisdom.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's power, ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾. These seeing eyes, if Allah willed, He would obliterate them and they would become as though they had never existed.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the striking of a parable, by likening intelligible things to perceptible things. These people, if their eyes were obliterated, could not find the way. Likewise, if Allah obliterates the insight of the heart, may Allah protect us, one cannot reach the truth or recognize it.
* Also among the lessons of this noble verse: the perfect eloquence of the Qur'an.
