The second meaning is that it is a dhikr through which Allah is remembered, and this is the most noble type of remembrance. How so? Because the Qur'an is the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; so, as soon as you recite it while feeling that it is the speech of Allah, you will remember the greatness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Also, because the Qur'an includes reports which are the most truthful of reports and the most beneficial for hearts; and because it includes stories which are the best, most beautiful and most complete of stories; and because it includes rulings from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware, which are the most just and most upright of rulings for the welfare of the servants; and because it includes the attributes of Allah the Exalted and His names, which are the most excellent names and the most noble attributes. All of this in reality is dhikr, so the Qur'an itself is a remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because it includes all these meanings which Allah the Exalted has explained in His Book.

The third meaning of dhikr is that it is elevation and honour for the one who upholds it and acts by it, due to His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَذِكْرٌ لَكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ وَسَوْفَ تُسْأَلُونَ﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44], "And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people, and you will be questioned." The meaning of dhikr as elevation and honour is present in the Qur'an, as in the verse I have just recited, and as in His saying: ﴿وَرَفَعْنَا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ﴾ [al-Sharḥ 4], "And We raised high your remembrance," i.e., We raised your name with honour, esteem and glorification.

So the meaning of dhikr here becomes: the remembrance which is admonition; the dhikr which is the remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic through what the Qur'an contains, of which we have pointed out some; and the third, honour. For there is no doubt that whoever holds fast to this Qur'an, he will have honour and dominion over all creation. For this reason I urge you to hold fast to this Qur'an, and if you hold fast to it in creed, action and guidance, then the final outcome will be yours. Do not think that you are few; even if you were few, guidance by the Qur'an necessitates that people will be drawn to the one guided by it, so that they increase little by little, like a stone you throw into the sea, and then the circle widens until it encompasses the whole sea. The gist is that what matters is that when a person holds fast to this noble Qur'an, he will have honour, dominion and supremacy over all creation.

He said: ﴿إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ وَقُرْآنٌ مُبِينٌ﴾. The word ﴿قُرْآنٌ﴾ may be taken in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl) and may be taken in the sense of the active participle (fāʿil), since qur'ān is a verbal noun like shukrān, ghufrān, nukrān and the like, and a verbal noun comes in the sense of the active participle and comes in the sense of the passive participle. Accordingly, the Qur'an is both "reciter" and "recited." As for it being a reciter, it is from al-qarʾ, meaning gathering; it gathers the rulings, morals and etiquettes found in the earlier books before it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَأَنْزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ﴾ [al-Mā'idah 48], "And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what is before it of the Book and as a guardian over it." It also gathers everything by which the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter are established. As for it being recited, i.e., read, that is because it is recited, and qirāʾah means tilāwah (recitation).

So we say: qur'ān is a verbal noun used in the sense of both the active and passive participle. Is there a parallel to it, i.e., a verbal noun coming on the pattern faʿlān?

* Student: Yes, there is a parallel.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, there is a parallel; we mentioned: ghufrān, shukrān, nukrān and what is similar to them.

He said: ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (muẓhir lil-aḥkām wa-ghayrihā), "making clear the rulings and other things." So ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ here is from (abāna), meaning "to make clear." We have previously mentioned many times that (abāna) can be intransitive and can be transitive. It is intransitive in the sense of "to become clear," and this is frequent in the Qur'an, such as: ﴿وَإِنْ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلُ لَفِي ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 164], meaning: clearly and manifestly. And mubīn may come from (abāna) in the sense of "to make clear," i.e., the transitive form, as in this verse.

﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ means: making clear. Making clear what? It makes clear the rulings and other than rulings, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ تِبْيَانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-Naḥl 89], "And We sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things." There is nothing that people need except that it is found in the Qur'an; everything people need is present in the Qur'an, but its presence there is either explicitly, or apparently, or by allusion and indication, or by general inclusion, or by necessary implication.

The gist is that the Qur'an clarifies everything: at times it mentions the evidence for a matter, and at times it points to the evidence for a matter. For example, in many matters that are not found in the Qur'an, and which are among the most important rulings of Islam, such as the number of units (rakaʿāt) in the prayers, the determination of the shares of zakāt and what is obligatory in it, and similar things, yet the Qur'an contains an indication to them, such as His saying: ﴿وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانْتَهُوا﴾ [al-Ḥashr 7], "And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from." If you direct this verse to the Sunnah, it encompasses the entire Sunnah, and our whole Shariah does not go beyond the Book and the Sunnah. Therefore the Qur'an is a clarification of everything; for this reason He said: ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ in rulings and other things. It also clarifies everything that preceded us of events in which there is benefit in their explanation, such as the stories of the prophets, the stories of the righteous, the stories of those who denied the messengers, and other things. Everything that preceded and in whose mention there is benefit for us is mentioned; as for what has no benefit for us, there is no need to mention it. This thing that is not mentioned may be left to people's intellects and experiments, as in many natural phenomena, whether celestial or geological or otherwise. We find that the Qur'an did not detail them or clarify them. Why? Because there is no benefit in them; their benefit lies in people seeking them, looking into the signs of Allah, and striving until they grasp them.

For this reason you find that some matters over which people dispute, such as the question of the rotation of the earth, are they present in the Qur'an explicitly? They are not present. If this were something we were obligated to believe, affirmatively or negatively, Allah the Mighty and Majestic would have clarified it plainly, as He clarified the matters we must believe in explicitly. So these are left to people to extract what is in the earth of minerals and other great benefits which were only discovered recently. This too is not mentioned in the Qur'an, although there is an allusion to it in the Qur'an, but it is not mentioned in detail. Rather Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَفِي الْأَرْضِ قِطَعٌ مُتَجَاوِرَاتٌ﴾ [al-Raʿd 4], "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts." And ﴿قِطَعٌ﴾ is from the forms of the plural of abundance; if you say that they are millions of pieces, you do not go outside its indication. If these pieces did not differ in their benefits, their essences and everything related to them, Allah would not have said ﴿قِطَعٌ مُتَجَاوِرَاتٌ﴾. So in this verse they are differentiated; you may, for example, say: Allah guided us to extracting what from the earth? Minerals, because Allah explained that they are pieces. What are the pieces above the ground? This is only the case with many things that are not known, and perhaps they will become known in the future, and perhaps their knowledge has appeared now. The gist is that the Qur'an is clarifying what? It is clarifying everything.

And if you contemplate the Qur'an again and again, you will not reflect a second time without a new meaning appearing to you that is different from the first. No one can encompass the meanings of the Qur'an, but whenever a person contemplates it, seeking the truth and desiring what is correct, he will be guided to many meanings.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked: "Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entrust you with anything?" This was circulating at that time, from the time of ʿAlī and the Shīʿah, who claimed that the Prophet ﷺ had entrusted the caliphate to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him. So he was asked: "Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entrust you with anything?" meaning: of the caliphate, or of the knowledge he withheld from people? He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding which Allah the Exalted gives whomever He wills in His Book, and what is in this sheet. What is in this sheet: the blood-money, the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever." [Narrated by al-Bukhārī (3047) from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.] The evidence is his first statement: "except an understanding which Allah the Exalted gives whomever He wills in His Book." This understanding differs greatly among people, very greatly indeed. You see some scholars speak on a verse and extract from it limited and countable benefits, while another speaks on it and extracts many times more than the first. All of this depends on the person's readiness, understanding and insight, and the more a person grows in faith and piety, the more guidance he gains from the Qur'an: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا زَادَهُمْ هُدًى وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ﴾ [Muḥammad 17], "And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety."

He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿لِيُنْذِرَ﴾ with the yāʾ and the tāʾ). ﴿لِيُنْذِرَ﴾ with the yāʾ: the pronoun refers to what? To the Qur'an. ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. But on the reading with the tāʾ, the author supplied: (bihi), "to warn by it"; therefore he said: (with the yāʾ and the tāʾ, bihi), the word (bihi) refers to the second reading, which is ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾. As for the first reading, it does not need this supplied word. There is no doubt that the Qur'an itself is a warner, and that the Prophet ﷺ warned by it. The Qur'an contains a threat and contains descriptions of those who deserve this threat, and this is warning; just as it also contains good tidings and descriptions of those who are given good tidings, and this is giving glad tidings. The Qur'an contains both good tidings and warning, and the Prophet ﷺ came with the Qur'an, warned by it, frightened by it and encouraged by it. ﴿مَنْ كَانَ حَيًّا﴾: the author said: (yaʿqilu mā yukhāṭabu bihi, wa-hum al-mu'minūn), "who understands what is addressed to him, and they are the believers."

﴿مَنْ كَانَ حَيًّا﴾: Is the life intended here the spiritual life, which is the life of the heart, or the sensory life, which is the life of the body? The apparent meaning is that it includes both; for this reason Ibn Kathīr, may Allah have mercy on him, said: ﴿مَنْ كَانَ حَيًّا﴾ "upon the face of the earth," meaning: whoever is alive in bodily life, because the message of the Messenger ﷺ is a general message for all creation; so he warns whoever is alive, meaning he warns every living being. Or it means whoever is alive in spiritual life, meaning the life of the heart, where it is intended to refer to one who understands, perceives and believes. Its opposite is the dead: the dead of body and the dead of heart. As for the dead of body, he cannot be warned by the Qur'an, because he has passed to the abode of recompense and cannot understand or know. As for the dead of heart, because his heart has been sealed—may Allah protect us—the light does not reach him and the truth does not reach him.

(﴿وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ﴾: the punishment, ﴿عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾: and they are like the dead, who do not understand what is addressed to them.) Here He said: ﴿لِيُنْذِرَ مَنْ كَانَ حَيًّا﴾, so that he may benefit from the warning, be admonished, avoid the prohibited things and perform the obligatory duties; ﴿وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ﴾. What do you expect to be said? You would expect it to say: "and the word may be realized against the dead," or "against those who are dead," since this is what the contrast requires. Yes, but He turned away from this to mention the disbelievers: ﴿وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ [Yā-Sīn 70]. The benefit of turning away from mentioning the counterpart by its own wording is two things:

The first: that what is meant by the dead is the disbeliever, and that the disbeliever cannot benefit from the Qur'an.

The second: a record that whoever does not benefit from the Qur'an is a disbeliever, and whoever benefits from it in some matters but not others has in him a trait of disbelief; for this reason every act of disobedience is a trait of disbelief, though it may be few and may be many. Therefore Allah the Mighty and Majestic turned away from this to His saying: ﴿وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ rather than saying "and the word will be realized against the dead," but rather He said: ﴿عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

And of this—meaning of these examples, and there are many in the Qur'an—is His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقْضِي بِالْحَقِّ وَالَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِهِ لَا يَقْضُونَ بِشَيْءٍ﴾ [Ghāfir 20], "And Allah judges with truth, while those they call upon besides Him do not judge anything." He did not say "they do not judge with falsehood," but rather He said: "they do not judge anything," to include falsehood and what is other than falsehood; meaning they have no judgement at all, since they are subjects and owned, so they judge nothing. ﴿وَيَحِقَّ الْقَوْلُ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا خَلَقْنَا لَهُمْ مِمَّا عَمِلَتْ أَيْدِينَا أَنْعَامًا﴾ [Yā-Sīn 71], to the end.

﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾: the interrogation here is for what? For confirmation (taqrīr), since whenever the interrogative enters upon a negation, it is for confirmation, whether the negative particle is a letter such as (lam) or a verb such as (laysa). The point is that the interrogative here is for confirmation, the wāw is a conjunction particle, and the thing conjoined to is what preceded, or the thing conjoined to is implied between the hamzah and the wāw according to what the context requires.

He says: ﴿يَرَوْا﴾: he said (yaʿlamū, "they know"), so he interpreted the seeing here as seeing of knowledge. It may also be intended as seeing by the eye, and seeing by the eye is stronger in confirmation than seeing of knowledge, because a person may deny seeing of knowledge and say: "I do not know of this." But with seeing by the eye, if the thing is in front of him, such as seeing camels, he cannot deny it. In reality the word is open to both. In view of the fact that Allah created these things, it is undoubtedly seeing of knowledge, since we did not witness the creation of these things, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿مَا أَشْهَدْتُهُمْ خَلْقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَا خَلْقَ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ [al-Kahf 51], "I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation." And in view of the created thing, it is seeing by the eye, because it is observed and known and cannot be denied.

The author said: (the interrogative is for confirmation, and the wāw entering upon it is for conjunction). The wāw entering upon it now: is the wāw the entering particle or the entered-upon? That is: "Speak with knowledge"; do not be like the child who, when you mention two things to him, always takes the last one, and if the expression is reversed on him he takes the last, which is the first in the first expression. So now, is the wāw the entered-upon or the entering?

* Students: Entering.

* The Shaykh: "And the wāw entering upon it is for conjunction"? Is the wāw entering upon it, or entered upon?

* Student: Entering.

* The Shaykh: Which is the entering one: the earlier or the later?

* Student: The later.

* The Shaykh: O brothers, the earlier, without doubt. The one that enters upon a thing is the earlier. For example, if the wāw comes to us, the hamzah and the wāw: you say, "the hamzah entered upon the wāw," or "the wāw entered upon the hamzah"?

* Student: The wāw upon the hamzah.

**Shaykh:** The author says it this way, but we say: the hamzah (interrogative particle) has entered upon the waw. When you say *sawfa yaqumu* (he will stand), does *yaqumu* enter upon *sawfa*, or does *sawfa* enter upon *yaqumu*? *Sawfa* enters upon *yaqumu*, so the one that enters is the first. The author says "and the waw entering upon it," pointing to the second opinion regarding this kind of ordering, which is that the implied meaning is "*wa-alam yaraw annā khalaqnā lahum*" (and have they not seen that We created for them). This is one of the two well-known opinions. Here the author, may God have mercy on him, takes the waw as entering upon the hamzah, whereas in fact, by the normal order, the hamzah enters upon the waw. But he, may God have mercy on him, holds that in this matter there is a transposition, and that the waw originally enters upon the hamzah, so the original form is *wa-alam yaraw*.

(﴿That We created for them﴾ among the people, ﴿of what Our hands have made﴾, meaning: what We made without any partner or helper, ﴿cattle﴾, which are camels, cows and sheep.) ﴿That We created for them﴾ means: We brought into existence for them, from non-existence, cattle. God, glorified and exalted, is exclusive in creating; there is no creator except God, glorified and exalted. Attributing "creation" to a created being means that the created being has a kind of creation which is not in the same sense as God's. God's creation of things is creation of bringing into existence from nothing. The creation of a created being is not bringing into existence; it is only changing from one state to another or from one attribute to another. If you carve a piece of wood into a door, you have "created" it as a door, but did you bring this wood into existence? The answer is no; you have only shaped it into a specific form, and this is a kind of creation. For this reason, it will be said to the image-makers on the Day of Resurrection: "Give life to what you have created" (Bukhari, Muslim). Although they did not bring the image into existence from nothing, they changed and transformed it from one state to another. So the creation proper to God is creation of bringing into existence, whereas the creation that comes from a created being is only change and transformation.

﴿That We created for them﴾: is the *lam* here for ownership or for entitlement?

**Student:** For entitlement.

**Shaykh:** For entitlement. It is also valid for it to be for ownership, as will come in the same verse.

﴿Of what Our hands have made, cattle﴾: meaning, of what We made of blessings. The meaning is not that God, glorified and exalted, created these cattle with His hand. If that were what He meant, and the reality were so, He would have said "of what We made with Our hands," as He said, exalted is He, addressing Iblis about Adam: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad 75]. Here He attributed the creation to Himself and made the created thing "with the hands." Here, however, He attributed the making to the hands: ﴿of what Our hands have made﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30] and similar verses, in which an action is attributed to the hands while the intended meaning is the person. Likewise here, God attributed the making to His hands, and what is intended is what? The intended meaning is Himself: "of what We made." And here He said "Our hands" in the plural. Does God have more than one hand? The answer is no. Does God have more than two hands? The answer is no. God does not have more than two hands; He has only two. Why then did He use the plural here? He used it for the sake of harmony, because the more eloquent usage, when a dual is attached to a plural pronoun, is to use the plural. Have you not considered His saying: ﴿If you two turn to God in repentance, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim 4], although a person has only one heart?

Here, since He attached it to the pronoun which denotes plurality, and here it is undoubtedly for glorification, the plural fits. Also, the plural is more expressive of glorification; therefore it is pluralized. Moreover, these cattle cannot be counted except by God, glorified and exalted; they are many multitudes, and each of them needs an action, does it not? A specific action, because each one has a specific creation. So the plural is also used in consideration of the object made, which is these cattle.

Well, in any case, this verse undoubtedly establishes the hand for God, glorified and exalted, but it does not establish that He has more than two hands, for the reasons of plurality you have known. It does not establish that God has more than two hands, for the reason of plurality you have known.

If someone says: What is the evidence that God has only two hands?

We say: The evidence is that God praised Himself with them in the context of praise, giving and provision. Had He possessed more, He would have mentioned it, since the context calls for it. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Jews say, "The hand of God is chained up." Their own hands are chained up, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64]. Had He had more than two, He would have said "rather, His hands," because the more hands there are, the more giving there is. This applies to created beings; as for the Creator, glorified and exalted, His giving does not run out and cannot be counted. He has only two hands. This is what the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah) hold.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** The criterion for avoiding forced interpretation of verses (...).

**Shaykh:** One looks: if the wording requires it and indicates it according to the rules of the Arabic language, it is established by the Qur'an.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** With respect to the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, it is undoubtedly a deficiency. Had he been a poet, that would be a deficiency. Even if poetry is not in itself a deficiency, it is a deficiency because of the doubts it entails. Just as illiteracy is a deficiency in itself, yet with respect to the Prophet, peace be upon him, it is an attribute of perfection; for this reason God praised him for it in His saying: ﴿the Prophet, the unlettered﴾ [al-A'raf 157]. Something may be perfection in one respect and deficiency in another. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, among poetry there is wisdom" (Bukhari, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b). So that poetry which contains wisdom is undoubtedly a perfection.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, there is a prohibition in it. The prohibition is that if we said so, the cattle would be more noble than the Prophets.

**Student:** His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾. Why do we say that ﴿reminder﴾ means revelation, which is the Sunnah, and that the clear Qur'an is the Qur'an?

**Shaykh:** Because the polytheists said that the Qur'an is poetry, but they did not say that about the speech of the Messenger, peace be upon him. God refuted their claim and said: what you say, that it is poetry and that the Messenger was taught it, is only a reminder. In the Qur'an there is much description of the Qur'an as "reminder": ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr 9].

In the verse that follows, there is a fifth benefit: the establishment of causation, or if you wish, of wisdom, through His saying: ﴿so that he may warn﴾. The *lam* here. Whenever you see a *lam* of causation in the Book of God, it establishes wisdom in God's actions or His legislation.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle?﴾ [Ya-Sin 71], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this verse: confirming God's blessing upon His servants through these cattle, from His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle?﴾.

* And among its benefits: these cattle are our property, which we benefit from in all ways of benefit, from His saying: ﴿We created for them﴾. So for every way of benefiting from them, it is permissible for us to benefit, since they are ours, and we are free regarding them except where evidence prohibits something.

* It follows from this benefit that it is permissible to ride what is not customarily ridden, such as riding cows. For this reason the jurists said: it is permissible to benefit from these animals in ways other than those for which they were created.

If you say: What is the answer to the authentic hadith: "While a man was riding a cow and driving it, it turned to him and said: 'We were not created for this.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'I believe in this, and so do Abu Bakr and Umar'" (Bukhari, Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah)?

The answer to this is that we say: this man rode it in a way that burdened it, and it was not created to be tortured, and he was doing that. Even if a person rode camels in a manner that tormented them, we would tell him: they were not created for this.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the attribution of action to God is valid, from His saying: ﴿of what Our hands have made﴾. But is God called "the Doer"? No, just as He is not called "the Maker," based on His saying: ﴿the handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾ [al-Naml 88]. This is because the domain of information is broader than the domain of naming and designation. It is permissible to derive an attribute from every name, but it is not permissible to derive a name from every attribute. For this reason we say: the attributes are broader than the names. That is, the domain of attributes, the attributes of God, is broader than the domain of names, because every name includes an attribute, but not every attribute includes a name.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the establishment of the hand for God, glorified and exalted, from His saying: ﴿of what Our hands have made, cattle﴾. This hand, which God described Himself with or attributed to Himself, is a real hand that is established, but without being similar to the hands of created beings, because the likeness of the Creator to the created is impossible in the extreme, both by reason and by revelation. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura 11], and He said: ﴿So do not strike examples for God﴾ [al-Nahl 74]. As for reason, every intelligent person perceives the difference between the Creator and the created, in essence and in attributes. So it is obligatory for us to believe in everything God described Himself with, without likening Him to anything.

Know further that what God described Himself with is divided into necessary attributes and non-necessary attributes, and into those whose counterpart for us is parts and portions.

For example, hearing, knowledge, power and life are necessary attributes, and the scholars call them the essential attributes (*al-sifat al-dhatiyyah*). And such as being established on the Throne, descending to the lowest heaven, creating, and similar things, are non-necessary attributes.

God has not ceased and will not cease being a Creator, but the created thing renews. So every creation connected with this created thing is something that comes into being after it was not. But this is a renewal of type, not a renewal of genus, because God has not ceased and will not cease being a Creator. But being established on the Throne is undoubtedly something that came into being, because before the Throne He was not established upon it.

As for what has counterparts that are parts and portions, such as the hand, the face, the leg, and the eye: for us, its counterpart is a part of the essence or a portion of it. But it is not valid to say that it is a part of God or a portion of God, because God, mighty and majestic, is not divisible and does not have portions. A part is that whose existence can be without the existence of its whole; this part, with respect to God, mighty and majestic, cannot be like that. That is, it is impossible for the hand, for example, to become separated from Him—God forbid—or the face, or the like. With respect to created beings, is it possible for these to become separated or not? It is possible. For this reason it is obligatory for us to say: what has counterparts that are parts and portions for us; and we do not say: what is parts and portions for God, because this is utterly denied.

As for the hand, we say: it is a real hand, truly established for God in a manner befitting Him, but not resembling the hands of created beings. This is the position of the Salaf (the early pious generations), and the leading scholars of the Muslims have followed it.

But some people were afflicted with distortion (*tahrif*) of the hand, and they said: it means blessing or power, on the basis that their intellects consider it impossible for God, mighty and majestic, to be described with a real hand. There is no doubt that this is error and a crime against the texts. As for its being error, it is because they judged the Creator by their deficient intellects, and this is undoubtedly error. How can you judge the Creator by your own intellect?!

The Creator, mighty and majestic, says of Himself: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64], and He says: ﴿What I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad 75], and He says: ﴿of what Our hands have made﴾ [Ya-Sin 71], and you say: He has no hand. Glory be to God! Were it not for their interpretation, while saying "we affirm the hand, but the intended meaning is such-and-such," this would be a denial of the texts, and we know that one who denies the texts is a disbeliever.

It is a crime against the texts from two angles. They say: God did not intend such-and-such, and He intended such-and-such. So they negated what God intended and affirmed what He did not intend. Thus it was a crime against the texts from both angles: the negative, and what after the negative? And the affirmative. The negative, in that they negated what God affirmed; and the affirmative, in that they affirmed what God did not intend.

When God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿What I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad 75], and someone says: He meant by the two hands blessing or power, we say: Glory be to God! What made you know this? God says: ﴿What I created with My two hands﴾ [Sad 75], and you say: He has no hand, rather it is blessing. Who told you this? Your negation is speaking about God without knowledge, and your affirmation of what He affirmed is also speaking about God without knowledge. So it was a crime against the texts from two angles.

The truth is that a person is amazed to an extreme that such a path is taken by leading scholars who are recognized for goodness, righteousness and benefit to the Ummah. Yet through this one recognizes the complete wisdom of God, mighty and majestic, and that a human, whoever he is, is weak and deficient. Otherwise, glory be to God! God, glorified and exalted, speaks about Himself with a speech which is the truest speech and the best speech, and comes from the One most knowing of what He says; then we say: "By God, He did not intend this!"

So must we believe that God has a real hand or a metaphorical one? A real hand befitting Him, not resembling the hands of created beings in any way whatsoever. Likewise, it is obligatory upon us to let all the verses and hadiths about the attributes stand upon their apparent meaning.

It remains for us to say: what do you say about the interpretation of some scholars of His saying: ﴿And the heaven We built with hands﴾ [al-Dhariyat 47], meaning: with power?

The answer: we say this is correct; *ayd* here means power, because *ayd* is the verbal noun of (*ada, ya'idu, aydan*). But it is not permissible to say that it is like His saying: ﴿Our hands﴾ [Ya-Sin 71]. It is forbidden for us to say that it is like His saying "Our hands," because God did not attribute it to Himself. He did not say: "We built the heaven with Our hands." And since God did not attribute that to Himself, it is forbidden for us to attribute it to Him. So it was necessary to interpret His saying: ﴿And the heaven We built with hands﴾ as meaning "with power." And *ayd* here is the verbal noun of (*ada, ya'idu*), like (*baa'a, yabi'u, bay'an*) and (*kaala, yakilu, kaylan*). This is its meaning. And when God does not attribute a thing to Himself, it is forbidden for us to attribute it to Him, because if we attributed it to Him when He did not attribute it to Himself, we would be speaking about God without knowledge.

Have you not considered His saying: ﴿On the Day when the shin will be uncovered, and they will be called to prostrate, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam 42]? The early scholars differed regarding His saying: ﴿the shin﴾: is the intended meaning "a severe hardship," or is the intended meaning "the shin of God, mighty and majestic"? If we take the rule we have just established, that what God did not attribute to Himself it is forbidden for us to attribute to Him, we say: the intended meaning of "shin" here is hardship, necessarily, and it cannot be interpreted as the shin of God, because God did not attribute it to Himself. He did not say "the day We uncover Our shin," but said: ﴿on a day when the shin will be uncovered﴾.

However, if you reflect on the context of the noble verse, and what has come in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, you will find that this requires that the intended meaning be the shin of God. For in the long, well-known hadith of Abu Sa'id: God uncovers His shin, and everyone who used to prostrate to God in this world prostrates to Him, while whoever did not prostrate to God in this world is unable to prostrate (Bukhari, Muslim). Here: ﴿On the Day when the shin will be uncovered, and they will be called to prostrate, but they will not be able. Their eyes will be humbled, humiliation will cover them, and they used to be called to prostrate while they were sound﴾ [al-Qalam 42-43]. We find that the context of the verse agrees with the context of the hadith. In that case, we say: the speech of God is explained by the speech of God, and it is explained by the speech of His Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him. So if the context of Abu Sa'id's hadith indicates what the context of the verse indicates, then the verse is explained by it. And in that case, the preponderant opinion is that the shin mentioned in indefinite form is intended as the shin of God, mighty and majestic, but it was made indefinite for the sake of glorification, because indefiniteness may be intended to express glorification.

**Part 4 of 5**

If someone asks: the verse before us in Surah Ya-Sin says, ﴿Of what Our hands have made, livestock﴾ [Ya-Sin 71]. Do you then describe Allah as having many hands, or what?

We say: what Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) hold is that Allah has only two hands. We then need to reconcile this with the statement indicated by His words, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad 75], and His words, ﴿The Jews say, "Allah's hand is chained up." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they said. Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64]. We need to reconcile this with the verse ﴿Of what Our hands have made﴾ [Ya-Sin 71], and with the singular form in His words, ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Mulk 1], and similar verses.

The scholars said: reconciling them is easy, and all praise is due to Allah, because there is no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful, nor is there any discrepancy in His speech. His speech does not contradict itself, just as His creation does not contradict itself. Creation is harmonious with itself, and likewise the Law (shari'ah) is harmonious with itself. How is that? They said: the singular noun in the construct state (al-mufrad al-mudaf) is inclusive, because it denotes generality. Have you not considered His words, ﴿If you were to count Allah's blessings, you could not enumerate them﴾ [al-Nahl 18]? How many blessings are there that cannot be counted? Yet He said, ﴿Allah's blessing﴾ in the singular. But the singular in the construct state denotes generality: it includes everything that this singular noun signifies, however many it may be.

So, ﴿in His hand is the dominion﴾ [al-Mulk 1]: if we suppose that there are many hands, would that be included or not? The two hands are included. Therefore there is no contradiction between the singular and the number, whether plural or dual. ﴿In His hand is the dominion﴾: "hand" (yad) is a singular noun in the construct state, "yad" is the construct, and the pronoun is the genitive. What does a singular construct noun convey? It conveys generality: any singular construct noun conveys generality.

Let me pause here to clarify. If a man says, "My wife is divorced," and he has four wives, who is divorced? All the wives, unless he intended only one. If he says, "My slave is free," and he has more than one slave, all of them become free, unless he intended one. If he says, "My house is an endowment (waqf)," then all his houses become endowments, unless he intended one. So the singular construct noun is general.

Is there an example from the Qur'an or the Sunnah that supports what I have said? Yes, such as His words, ﴿If you were to count Allah's blessing, you could not enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl 18]. Here "blessing" (ni'mah) is a singular construct noun, so it includes all the blessings that cannot be counted. Therefore, regarding ﴿in His hand is the dominion﴾, we say that this does not preclude that the intended "hand" here is the two hands.

We are left with reconciling the two hands with the plural form in ﴿Our hands﴾. How do we reconcile them? The answer to this has two aspects.

The first aspect: many scholars of the Arabic language say that the least plural is two. They cite as evidence His words, ﴿If you two (plural of two) repent to Allah, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim 4], where a plural form is used although the intended meaning is two. And His words, ﴿If he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾ [al-Nisa' 11], although the mother is blocked by two (siblings) from a third to a sixth. And the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two or more are a congregation in prayer." [Narrated by Ibn Majah (972) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]

But most scholars of the language say that the least plural is three. In that case the reconciliation is by the second aspect: we say that the plural in His words, ﴿Of what Our hands have made﴾, is intended to express magnificence (ta'zim), because the plural denotes magnificence. For this reason the plural pronoun "na" (we/Our) is used in contexts of magnificence. Every pronoun that Allah attributes to Himself, which is "na," does not mean plurality; it means magnificence. So the plural here is for magnificence, and also for suitability (munasabah). What is the suitability? Because it is attached to something that conveys plurality, so the more fitting form is plural. This suitability is verbal (lafzi), and intending magnificence is a suitability of meaning (ma'nawi). By this the difficulty is removed.

If someone asks: why do you not say that Allah has many hands?

The answer is that the meaning prevents this, because when Allah praised and extolled Himself with giving, He mentioned only two hands. If He had more, He would have mentioned the greater number, because that is more eloquent in praise. When He said, ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64], it is known that He has only two hands.

Similar to this is His words, ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar 67]. He affirmed the handful with one hand, and "the heavens folded in His right hand," with the other hand. The texts on this are numerous, and for this reason we believe that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has only two hands.

We say the same about the attribute of the eye. The eye is mentioned in the plural and mentioned in the singular: ﴿and that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha 39], ﴿running under Our eyes﴾ [al-Qamar 14]. We say: "eye" ('ayn) is a singular construct noun, so it is general. As for ﴿running under Our eyes﴾, either we say it is for magnificence, or that the least plural is two, and Allah, exalted is He, does not have more than two eyes. The evidence for this is the hadith about the Dajjal (Antichrist). When the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke about him and described his deceptions, he said: "Indeed he is one-eyed, and indeed your Lord is not one-eyed." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3439) and Muslim (169/273) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.] So he clarified the clear sensory sign, which is the blindness of the Dajjal's eye.

It is strange that some people said: the meaning of "one-eyed" here is "defect." They wanted to establish that Allah has many eyes, based on the plural in His words, ﴿running under Our eyes﴾. But this is a blindness on their part, a blindness of this speaker, because the hadith is explicit that the meaning is blindness of the eye, when he said, "one-eyed of the right eye." He did not say only "one-eyed." If he had only said "one-eyed," perhaps what he said would be possible, though it is weak, because the Arabic language uses "blind" ('awar) to express the eye. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Four are not permissible for sacrificial animals: the sick, the emaciated, the one-eyed (al-'awra'), and the lame." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (2802), al-Tirmidhi (1497), al-Nasa'i (4369), and Ibn Majah (3144) from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn Azib.] He made "al-'awar" something other than a defect; the other three are all defects, but he placed "al-'awar" in the eye. So we say to them: the root of "al-'awar" is in the eye. Then when the hadith says, "one-eyed of the right eye," it becomes decisive, eliminating any possibility that it means a defect.

If someone asks: what is its significance?

We say: its significance is that if Allah had more than one eye, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have mentioned it, because it is more indicative of Allah's magnificence, and clearer in distinguishing: it is more indicative of magnificence if He has many eyes, and clearer in distinction than saying the difference is that this one is one-eyed while the Lord, mighty and majestic, is not one-eyed.

Thus it is clear that the indication of the hadith of the Dajjal, which is sound, is a clear and evident indication that Allah has two eyes. Also, a hadith is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), mentioned by Ibn al-Qayyim in Mukhtasar al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah: "When one of you stands to pray, he is between the two eyes of the Most Merciful." [Narrated by al-Marwazi in Ta'zim Qadr al-Salah (128) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] This hadith has weakness, but in reality we do not need it, because the hadith in the two Sahihs about the Dajjal is clear, and praise is due to Allah. (...)

* From the benefits of the noble verse: ﴿Did they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, livestock?﴾
* From its benefits: the affirmation of the hand for Allah, mighty and majestic, in His words ﴿Our hands﴾. This was discussed thoroughly in the previous lesson.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: that we possess these livestock with both legal ownership (mulk shar'i) and actual, decreed ownership (mulk hissi qadari). As for legal ownership, we own their bodies and benefits by sale, purchase, leasing, and other means. As for actual, sensory ownership, we control their reins and tethering, and they are subjected to us: we make them stand and kneel, we take them away and bring them back. This is part of the completion of Allah's blessing upon us through this ownership.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: that He used the words ﴿so they are their owners﴾, a nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) that conveys stability and continuity, meaning settled and complete ownership.

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We subjected them to them, so some of them they ride, and some of them they eat﴾ [Ya-Sin 72].

* From its benefits: the clarification of Allah's blessing upon us by making these livestock tractable. Had they been unmanageable, we would not have been able to benefit from them. For this reason, when a camel bolted during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), a man brought it down with an arrow. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed these camels have wild tendencies like wild animals. Whichever of them bolts, do to it this way." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5509) and Muslim (1968/20) from the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij.] This camel had rebelled against its owners, and they could not catch it except with an arrow.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: the clarification that the actions of creatures are created by Allah. His words ﴿and We subjected them to them﴾ show this. Although they are the direct doers, their acts are attributed to Allah in terms of decree and creation, and attributed to the doer in terms of acquisition (kasb) and action. So these tractable camels were made tractable by Allah, and therefore their acts proceed by the creation of Allah, mighty and majestic.

This is the correct position on this issue, namely the question of human actions: are they created by Allah, or do they belong to the servants independently? There are three positions on this, or rather three schools of thought.

The first school: the Jabriyyah (determinists), who say that the creation of Allah, mighty and majestic, encompasses every movement in the heavens and the earth, and that a person is compelled in his deeds, having no choice in them. Even voluntary, chosen movement is like compelled movement in which he has no will. They say: a person's actions are like the movement of a palm frond in the wind, not by its own choice.

It is said to them: this entails chaos, such that every person would do whatever he wishes and say, "This is not by my choice, and I am compelled to it." It also entails that if Allah punishes a person for disobedience, He would be unjust to him. It also entails that praising the obedient is pointless, since one does not praise a person for an act he is compelled to do without choice. It further entails that blaming the disobedient is unjust, since it blames someone who did not choose the act.

Just as these false consequences follow from it, it also contradicts reality, for a person finds the difference between his voluntary action and his involuntary action. He finds the difference between descending a ladder step by step, calmly and by choice, and someone pushing him so that he cannot stand. The matter is clear from the rational, practical standpoint that this view is false, one of the most false views.

But what deceived its adherents is that Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned that He created everything, that He decreed everything, and that nothing happens in His dominion that He does not will, and other such matters that they use as a pretext. Yet in reality they looked at these and neglected the other texts indicating that a person acts by his own choice.

For this reason, a group opposed them: they looked at the texts indicating that a person acts by his own choice, and at the reality, and they denied that Allah, mighty and majestic, has any will or creation in the actions of servants. They said: the servant is independent in his deeds; he does what he wishes and leaves what he wishes, and Allah, glorified and exalted, has no connection to the servant's action. These people are closer to reason than those others, because a person undoubtedly finds that he acts by choice: he enters his house, leaves his house, comes to the mosque, leaves the mosque, and chooses this action over that action, in a voluntary way, never feeling that anyone compels him to it.

But these people went astray by denying the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, and His creation of the actions of creatures, and by believing that a person is independent in what he brings about. For this reason they were called the Magians (Majus) of this Ummah, because they resemble the Magians (Zoroastrians) in affirming two agents for events. They affirm that whatever is from Allah's action is from Allah, and whatever is from a person's action is from the person, independently. For this reason they were named the Magians of this Ummah. These people are undoubtedly misguided, because they removed something from the dominion of Allah out of the dominion of Allah.

Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) took a middle position between the two views, and they acted upon both sets of evidence. They said: a person undoubtedly acts by his own choice and abstains by his own choice, and he has complete will by means of capacity (qudrah). The One who created this will and capacity is Allah, mighty and majestic. If Allah, glorified and exalted, willed, He would deprive him of will; if He willed, He would deprive him of capacity. Therefore, if Allah deprives the servant of will, no ruling applies to his act. For example, is an insane person held accountable for his actions? No, because he performs them without intention. The incapable person is not held to account: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun 16].

So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who created will and capacity in a person. They said: will and capacity are the cause of the existence of the act. Without will the act would not have occurred, and without capacity it would not have occurred. So will and capacity are the cause of the act's existence. If these two are created by Allah, then the Creator of the cause is the Creator of the effect. Thus the servant's act is attributed to Allah from this aspect: that is, Allah is the One who brought into existence in him the cause of the act, and so he became the doer. Just as burning, for example, in fire is attributed to whom? To the fire. But the One who placed this power in it is Allah, mighty and majestic. Thus the burning by the fire is directly the act of the fire, but by the decree of Allah, glorified and exalted, as creation.

This is what Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah adopted, and it agrees with transmitted texts, reason, and reality, because it combines the textual evidences and affirms the sensory evidences. When you gather the legal evidences from all their sides, you find that they all flow into one channel, which is the view adopted by Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. Without this belief, activity would be paralyzed, and a person would become dependent: he would neither say nor do anything. Without this belief, a person would not turn to his Lord, mighty and majestic, in his needs and afflictions. He, as a willing, acting being who moves and works, returns to Whom as a created, managed being? To Allah, mighty and majestic. So he is neither dependent nor self-centered; that is, he will not be self-sufficient apart from his Lord, nor will he be passive, saying, "If something is decreed for me, it will happen." Rather, he works, seeking help from Allah and relying on Him.

He said: ﴿And We subjected them to them, so some of them they ride, and some of them they eat.﴾

* From the benefits of the noble verse: we may benefit from these livestock by riding them, but on condition that this does not cause them hardship. If it causes them hardship, it is forbidden, because hardship is punishment of them in an improper place.
* From the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of riding two on one animal (al-irtidaf 'ala al-dabbah), based on the generality of His words, ﴿so some of them they ride﴾. But this is restricted by what we have indicated: that there be no hardship in it.
* Also from the benefits of the noble verse: the lawfulness of these livestock, or of some of them if we take "min" (some of) as partitive and take "livestock" more generally than the grazing animals. The ruling for all livestock is permissibility, which is the default. For this reason, if two persons dispute whether an animal is lawful, the word of the one who says it is lawful is accepted until evidence for prohibition is established. First: due to the generality of His words, ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 29].

Secondly, based on the general application of His words: ﴿and from them they eat﴾. The basic ruling is permissibility, unless evidence establishes prohibition. However, this permissibility is in fact restricted. Restricted by what? By the well-known conditions of slaughter (dhakah, the lawful ritual slaughter), for if a permissible animal is not slaughtered in the lawful Islamic manner, it becomes forbidden and is no longer lawful. So this unrestricted statement ﴿and from them they eat﴾ is restricted by conditions, namely that it be slaughtered in the lawful manner. Nevertheless, if a person is compelled to it, it becomes lawful for him even if it was not slaughtered, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But whoever is forced [by necessity], neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, then there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah 173].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is permissible to inflict suffering upon animals if the benefit cannot be achieved except by it. Eating [meat] requires slaughter, and slaughter is among the most painful things; and because the Shari'ah permitted branding (wasm), branding animals with fire for the sake of preserving their value; and because the Shari'ah prescribed marking (ish'ar) camels and cattle as offerings (hady) so that it is known that they are offerings, and ish'ar is to cut the side of their hump until blood flows from it. On this basis, if we need to inflict suffering on an animal for the sake of preserving its value or for other reasons, there is no harm in it, just as some people do today with pigeons: when one wants to raise them in a place, he plucks the front feathers of the wings so that they do not fly away until they become accustomed to the place and are raised there. They say: if we clipped them, the feathers would not grow back quickly, so they choose to pluck them out so that the feathers grow quickly and they become ready to fly.

He said: ﴿And from them they eat (72). And for them in them are benefits and drinks; so will they not be grateful?﴾ [Ya-Sin 72, 73].

* Also derived from this noble verse is what has already been mentioned: that Allah the Mighty and Majestic created these things for our benefit; any benefit that can be obtained from these animals is permissible for us ﴿and for them in them are benefits﴾, but on condition, as we have already stated, that it involves no hardship. If there is hardship in it, then it is prohibited.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of the milk of these animals, based on His words: ﴿and drinks﴾.

Then He said: ﴿so will they not be grateful?﴾
* From this sentence is derived: the obligation to thank Allah the Exalted for these blessings. Its basis is that He rebuked those who do not give thanks, and rebuke is only directed at doing what is forbidden or abandoning what is obligatory. Thanking is thanking the Benefactor, as the Shari'ah indicates, and reason also indicates it; for every person is indebted to the one who has bestowed favour upon him, and it is incumbent on him to thank him according to what the situation requires. This is why the authentic hadith states: "Whoever does you a kindness, reciprocate it; and if you cannot find anything to reciprocate with, then pray for him until you see that you have reciprocated."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1672) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]]

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And they have taken besides Allah gods, that they might be helped﴾ [Ya-Sin 74]. Among the benefits of this verse:
* Firstly: the validity of applying the term "god" (ilah) to other than Allah the Mighty and Majestic, based on His words: ﴿they have taken besides Allah gods﴾.

But are these gods true? The answer: No, they are false gods, based on Allah's words: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62]. Although they name them gods and worship them as they worship the Lord the Mighty and Majestic, they are not gods: ﴿They are not but names which you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [an-Najm 23].
* Secondly: those who took these gods imagined that they would help them, but Allah refuted this delusion by His words: ﴿they are not able to help them﴾ [Ya-Sin 75].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person in falsehood must cling to something to justify his falsehood. What is it here? The hope of victory: ﴿that they might be helped﴾. Every person in falsehood must give a reason for what he has adopted of falsehood, as has often passed before you in the statements of the people of innovation, and as has also passed before you in (...).
A devotional ruling; that is, a person will not be accepted if he says: "This is lawful and this is unlawful" until he states his evidence and proof.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿that they might be helped﴾ [Ya-Sin 74] ﴿they are not able to help them﴾ [Ya-Sin 75].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these gods cannot help their worshippers, based on His words: ﴿they are not able to help them﴾.

If you say: Do they not call upon the gods for help, and are sometimes helped?
* A student: That is a test.
* The Shaykh: It is a test. But did this help come through them?
* The student: From Allah.
* The Shaykh: That is, sometimes he calls upon the idol and is helped.
* The student: A trial.
* The Shaykh: A trial. But did this aid come by his calling for help?
* The student: At the time of calling for help.
* The Shaykh: It occurred at them, not by them.
* The student: Not by them.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it occurred at them, not by them. There is a difference between something happening through a thing and something happening at it while the cause is other than it. The cause of this aid is the trial, as you said, and not the invoking of these idols, based on Allah's words: ﴿And who is more astray than one who invokes other than Allah, those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and they are unaware of their invocation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these worshippers are a mobilised army for their idols, defending the idols and supporting them, based on His words: ﴿while they are for them an army brought forward﴾.

In this there is, as is evident, a proclamation of their foolishness: they seek help from one who cannot help them, while they are the ones who support him. This is folly. How can you support something that cannot help you and from which you gain nothing? For this reason, His words ﴿while they are for them an army brought forward﴾ are considered as evidence of the foolishness of these people: that they defend these gods and support them, although they cannot help them.

What I have just established is based on our chosen interpretation, that the meaning of the verse is: these worshippers of the worshipped are an army brought forward. As for the opinion of the author (al-Mu'allif), he holds otherwise: he sees that these idols are an army for these people, but that they will all be brought forward into the Fire; and the weakness of this view has already been explained.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 68–75 (part 1 of 5):

Then He said: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68]

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation; will they not then reason?﴾ This sentence is conditional. The protasis (fi'l al-shart) is His saying ﴿We grant him long life﴾, and its apodosis (jawab) is ﴿We reverse him﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿whomever We grant long life﴾, meaning: We make his life long. For this reason the author said: (by lengthening his term; ﴿We reverse him﴾; and in another reading with doubling, from al-tankis). The reading that the author took as the basis is from inkas [[The correct form is ﴿nankusuhu﴾ from (al-naks), not from inkas, and this will be pointed out later.]], and inkas and tankis both mean returning from a complete state to a deficient state.

As for His saying ﴿nunakkisuhu﴾ or ﴿nankusuhu fi al-khalq﴾, the author explains it as: (meaning, He creates him so that after his strength and youth he becomes weak and senile). Yes, whenever a person's life is prolonged, he goes back, not only in physical strength but in physical strength, mental strength and intellectual strength; he becomes weak and returns to the lowest age, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said. The purpose of this reminder, although it is a known matter that everyone knows, is that a person should hasten to use his life while he is still in his strength and youth, because there will come a day when he will not have that physical capacity, nor that intellectual capacity, nor that mental capacity. His thinking will be limited like the thinking of a child, who thinks only about what is enclosed by the walls of his house, and his mind will likewise be limited, unable to look, understand, think about matters, weigh them and judge them. Likewise his memorization of things will be limited, so that something may pass him in the morning and he cannot express it in the evening. All of this is a clear and manifest reality. Indeed, some people lose their minds completely, and may reach a state resembling madness, harming their families with shouting, wailing and chanting, and similar things, according to what they were like in childhood. Even a man who was, for example, a camel driver and used to recite poetry, you will find that when he grows old and senile he begins to recite these poems. All of this is a matter that cannot be avoided. For this reason the poet said:

There is no pleasure in life while its delights are troubled
By remembrance of death and senility.

Every intelligent person, when he remembers that his end is either sudden death or senility, life will not be pleasant for him. But the meaning of "life will not be pleasant for him" is not that he remains regretful and grieving; no, rather he strives and prepares for this state which cannot be avoided.

Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation; will they not then reason?﴾ (That the One who is able to do that, which is known to them, is able to resurrect, so that they believe in it; and in another reading with the letter ta', ﴿will you not then reason?﴾), which is a seven-fold reading, as is well known. Thus the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the intended meaning is to argue from the change of a person's condition into this lowly state that Allah, Most High, is able to resurrect you. What he said is possible, but it is better to say that the meaning of His saying ﴿will you not then reason?﴾ is: will you not have intellect, so that you hasten your lives before you reach this state? Hasten it with what? With faith and righteous deeds as much as you can, so that when you reach this condition you are in the best state of readiness for it. Generally, the person who spends his time in obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted, when he becomes senile you find that he cares only for acts of obedience. Many Muslims, when they become senile, you find them saying: Where is the water? I want to perform ablution. Or you find them praying constantly, or reading the Qur'an constantly, or remembering Allah constantly. This is among the blessings of Allah, glorified and exalted, that a person grows old in the state he was in. The opposite will be the case: whoever in his strength and youth was not occupied with righteous deeds, his delirium when he grows old will be with that evil deed. He said: ﴿will you not then reason?﴾

(﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾, meaning the Prophet, ﴿nor is it proper for him﴾; this is a rejection of their saying that what he brought of the Qur'an is poetry. ﴿Poetry﴾ comes easily ﴿to him﴾; ﴿it is only a reminder﴾, an admonition, ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾, that makes the rulings and other matters manifest.)

As for His saying ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it proper for him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69]: the "We" in "We taught" refers to Allah, Most High, and the pronoun "him" refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

If someone says: where is the referent of the pronoun, since none of the preceding verses mentions the Prophet ﷺ?

We say: the referent of a pronoun is known from the preceding context or the following context, and this resembles the mental familiarity (al-'ahd al-dhihni) in the definite article "al", or it is known from understanding, such that the matter is understood by the listener. This is like the al-'ahd, what is it? It is like the al-'ahd al-dhihni.

Here the referent of the pronoun in His saying ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ is known, and it is well known that the one who brought this reminder and clear Qur'an is Muhammad ﷺ.

Allah, Most High, says: ﴿And We did not teach him﴾, meaning We did not teach the Prophet ﷺ poetry; for if Allah had taught the Prophet ﷺ poetry, that would have been a proof for the falsifiers and deniers, and they would have said: this Qur'an is among the poetry he was taught. For this reason he was not taught poetry, nor was he taught writing, as Allah, Most High, said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48].

He says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾. The Prophet ﷺ never composed poetry at all. And if it is supposed that metrical speech flowed from his tongue, it was not intentional or deliberate, but came unintentionally; and what comes unintentionally is not intended, so it is not considered knowledge. Like his saying ﷺ: "I am the Prophet, there is no lie, I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2864) and Muslim (1776/78), from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]].

This is rajaz, but it was not intentional, so it is not teaching. As for poetry (shi'r), it is metrical, rhymed speech, and it was named shi'r because it takes hold of the feelings (shu'ur). For this reason you find that verse takes hold of the heart more than prose does. That is, you may hear an excellent and eloquent sermon, and find something similar in meaning in verse, but you see that the effect of verse is stronger and its grip on the feelings greater; for this reason it was called shi'r. By this we know that what is now called "prose poetry" (al-shi'r al-manthur) is not poetry, because it does not take hold of the feelings. It is neither poetry nor prose, but is like the hypocrite, belonging neither to these nor to those; those who delight in prose and sermons are not moved by it, nor are those who delight in poetry and qasidas. In reality it is nothing, but "every person is accustomed to his age". Those who invented it delight in it and consider it more poetic than the poetry of Imru' al-Qays. So we say: poetry is what takes hold of the feelings, by being metrical, rhymed speech that takes hold of the heart.

He says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾. The author said: (a rejection of their saying that what he brought of the Qur'an is poetry). The deniers and those who stand against any person must describe his speech with defects. Why? In order to repel people from him. But, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32]. Allah, glorified and exalted, said in Surat al-Dhariyat: ﴿Likewise, no messenger came to those before them except that they said: a sorcerer or a madman﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52].

All the messengers were described by their enemies with these two descriptions: sorcery and madness. Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was also described thus; they described him as a sorcerer, a poet, a madman, a soothsayer and a liar, all of it in order to repel people from him. But did the matter succeed? Did people flee from him? Never; for the truth, praise be to Allah, will prevail however much it is confronted with blows, for the final outcome belongs to it.

If someone says: does this description of the Messenger, peace be upon him, extend to his followers?

The answer: Yes, everything with which the messengers were described, their followers are described with its like. Do you not know that the criminals, when they see the believers, say: ﴿Indeed, these have strayed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 32], describing them with misguidance? In our age they describe them with reaction, backwardness and similar words by which they repel people from the truth. And the people of innovation describe the People of the Sunnah and the Community with derogatory labels: they say they are "nawabit" (upstarts), "ghuthaa'" (scum), "hashw" (filler), "hashwiyya", "mujassima" (anthropomorphists), "mushabbiha" (likeners), and similar things. All of this is in order to repel people from what they are upon. But, praise be to Allah, the matter becomes a reward for those who are described with these faults, and a trial for them through patience upon the truth they hold; then the final outcome will be theirs.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (and poetry comes easily to him). That is, it is not easy for him; rather it is difficult for him to compose and difficult for him to recite. That is, when he, peace and blessings be upon him, recited the poetry of others, he sometimes recited it in a meter other than the known one, because he had no interest in poetry or memorizing it. As for composing it himself, he did not recite it. But it is better to interpret here ﴿nor is it proper for him﴾ as: it is not possible, nor suitable for him, nor fitting for him. For wherever ﴿mā yanbaghī﴾ appears in the Qur'an, it refers to something impossible to the utmost degree, as in His saying: ﴿And it is not proper for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. The meaning of ﴿mā yanbaghī﴾ is not that it is not good, but that it is impossible to the utmost degree of impossibility. Similarly His saying: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40], meaning this is something impossible, that the sun should overtake the moon, and this is according to the normal course of things concerning the sun. ﴿Nor is it proper for him﴾, meaning it is not possible nor fitting for him, peace and blessings be upon him, to be a poet.

﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾. The author said: (it is not what he brought ﴿except a reminder﴾). He informed us that ﴿in﴾ here is negating; that is, it is nothing but a reminder. ﴿In﴾ with a kasra on the hamza comes with several meanings, which we will now recall, though they have passed us before. The first:

* Student: negating.
* Shaykh: Yes, negating as here, and its sign is usually that it is followed by "illa" (except). Good, and the second?
* Student: conditional.
* Shaykh: Conditional, like?
* Student: "in tudhākir tanjaḥ" (if you study, you will succeed).
* Shaykh: "In tudhākir tanjaḥ," good. And it comes...
* Student: superfluous (zā'ida).
* Shaykh: Superfluous, like?
* Student: "mā in" (mā inna).
* Shaykh: "Mā in," bring the verse.
* Student:
Banī Ghudāna mā in antum dhahabun ∗∗∗ wa lā ṣarīfun wa lākin antum al-kharafu
* Shaykh:
Banī Ghudāna mā in antum dhahabun ∗∗∗ wa lā ṣarīfun wa lākin antum al-kharafu
Good, that is three.
* Student: a lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafa min al-thaqīla).
* Shaykh: A lightened form of the heavy, like?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good, ﴿in hādhāni la-sāḥirāni﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63].
................... ∗∗∗ wa in mālikun kānat kirāmu al-ma'ādin
Good. ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, he said: (an admonition).
* Student: (...) for obedience, is he rewarded for this (...)?
* Shaykh: It is not apparent; the apparent is that it is not a condition.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt; because having this thing in his heart is better than having love of the world in his heart, and similar things.
* Student: (...) meaning he is rewarded for it (...).
* Shaykh: By Allah, I doubt the reward unless he has an intention; if he has an intention. But in reality he intends this matter; but did he intend it for drawing near to Allah? Allah knows best.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is known (...) intended for drawing near; he intends the deed and drawing near to Allah by it. But here, does he intend drawing near, or is it something that flows on his tongue because it is what is in his mind from before?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What I have, I have ﴿nunakkisuhu﴾, and in another reading with doubling, from al-tankis. We will review. We now have two readings; we will review the two readings now. You do not have it.
* Student: His saying: ﴿nunakkisuhu fi al-khalq﴾, meaning We turn him around in it, so his weakness and the deficiency of his body and powers continue to increase (...).
And 'Asim and Hamza read ﴿nunakkisuhu﴾ from al-tankis, which is more intensive (...), ﴿nankusuhu﴾. 'Asim and Hamza read with a damma on the first nun, a fatha on the second, and a kasra on the kaf, doubled, from nakkasa for intensification; and the rest with a fatha on the first nun, a sukun on the second, and a damma on the kaf, lightened, from nakasa, and it allows both intensification and its absence.
* Shaykh: ﴿nankusuhu﴾. Good. The one we have, the third, ﴿nunkisuhu﴾ at the end, did not mention it. Repeat.
* Student: And 'Asim and Hamza read ﴿nunakkisuhu﴾ from al-tankis, which is more intensive.
* Shaykh: No, what is before it? He said: "and it is more intensive."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Or did you vocalize it?
* Student: I vocalized it.
* Shaykh: The text: ﴿nankusuhu﴾.
* Student: (...) And 'Asim and Hamza read ﴿nankusuhu﴾ from al-tankis, which is more intensive, (...) 'Asim and Hamza read with a damma on the first nun, a fatha on the second, and a kasra on the doubled kaf, from nakkasahu and ghalabahu, and the rest with a fatha on the first and a sukun on the second, and a damma on the kaf, lightened.
* Shaykh: ﴿nankusuhu﴾ with this vocalization.
* Student: And it allows intensification and its absence (...) from the door of qatala (...), and from it it is said..
* Shaykh: We will see later. Do you not have the Mushaf with the readings?
* Student: Why did the pre-Islamic Arabs describe the Qur'an as poetry, when the difference between poetry and prose is clear to their common people, let alone their poets? Did they not know that it is not poetry?
* Shaykh: In any case, you know that the falsifier disguises everything, and when propaganda and talk and speech multiply, the matter may be reversed. They understood that this is not poetry, but they might say, for example: this is poetry brought in a new way, and similar things, and they promote their propaganda until the matter becomes confused.
* Student: Because the promoters of modern poetry...
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: They said: poetry was among the Arabs and was revealed (...), evidence being that they described the Qur'an as poetry while it is not metrical or rhymed.
* Shaykh: No, we say this is from the door of promotion; for this reason you cannot bring a single qasida of the earlier poets resembling this poetry of theirs at all.

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it proper for him; it is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾ for what?

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it proper for him﴾, meaning: We did not teach Muhammad ﷺ poetry; ﴿nor is it proper for him﴾, that is, it is not valid nor possible that he learn poetry, because his learning poetry would give the falsifiers an argument, as in His saying: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. So if the Prophet ﷺ had learned poetry, they would have said: this Qur'an is poetry of what he learned, just as if he had been writing, they would have said: this is something he wrote. Allah, Most High, said: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾. I think we have stopped at this sentence and explained that ﴿in﴾ comes with several meanings; what are they?

* Student: Conditional, negating, superfluous, and a lightened form of the heavy.
* Shaykh: From the heavy. Good. What determines the multiple meanings of a single word is the context, and this is a rule for every word with multiple meanings: it is determined by context and the indication of the situation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 68–75 (part 2 of 5):

He said: ﴿إِنْ هُوَ﴾ meaning: what He has taught him, ﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ وَقُرْآنٌ مُبِينٌ﴾. So His saying ﴿إِنْ هُوَ﴾ is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun (maṣdar) understood from (ʿallamnā, "We taught"). That the referent of a pronoun be a verbal noun known from the preceding verb is not a strange matter. Have you not seen the saying of the Exalted: ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ [al-Mā'idah 8], "Be just; that is nearer to piety." ﴿هُوَ﴾ means: the justice understood from the word ﴿اعْدِلُوا﴾. So here, ﴿وَمَا عَلَّمْنَاهُ الشِّعْرَ وَمَا يَنْبَغِي لَهُ إِنْ هُوَ﴾ means: that which We taught him, ﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ وَقُرْآنٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ means: what We taught him is nothing but a reminder and a clear Qur'an.

As for His saying ﴿إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ﴾, the author said: (ʿiẓah), meaning: an admonition by which whoever takes heed is reminded. And who is it that takes heed? The one who is reminded by this Qur'an has been explained by Allah the Exalted in His saying: ﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَذِكْرَى لِمَنْ كَانَ لَهُ قَلْبٌ أَوْ أَلْقَى السَّمْعَ وَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ﴾ [Qāf 37], and this is with regard to readiness and acceptance. In another verse, He the Exalted said something indicating that all the God-fearing (muttaqūn) are admonished by this Qur'an, so there is a clarification in it for those who are admonished by it in terms of conduct. Thus in Surah Qāf there is a clarification for those who are admonished by it in terms of acceptance and readiness to remember.

In the other verses that link remembrance with the Qur'an to faith, piety and the like, there is evidence for those who are admonished by it in terms of conduct and action, and the more a person acts by the Qur'an, the more he is reminded by it. What the author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned regarding the meaning of "dhikr" is one of its meanings; for the dhikr by which the Qur'an is described contains several meanings:
