They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and they have no share in them, and He has no supporter among them. And intercession with Him will not benefit, except for one whom He permits"﴾ [Saba' 22-23].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: all created beings return to Allah, as He says: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [Yasin 83]. This return includes both the return to Allah Most High on the Day of Resurrection and the return to Him in His decrees over creation, both the universal (kawniyyah) and the legislative (shar'iyyah), as He says: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment rests with Allah﴾ [al-Shura 10], and He says: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more favorable in outcome﴾ [al-Nisa' 59].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it shows the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, in that there must be a return to Him. Were there no such return, the creation of creatures would be pointless and without purpose. For if there were no return and no recompense for deeds in that return, creation would have been made so that whoever causes corruption would corrupt the earth, and trials, evils and nothing at the end would occur.

In all these verses there is proof of Allah's power to revive bones when they have become decayed, and this is from ten aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿Say: He will revive them who produced them the first time﴾ [Yasin 79]. In this there is an argument from the greater to the lesser.

The second: His saying: ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾ [Yasin 79]. His knowledge of every creation requires that He, the Exalted, is able to revive bones when they have decayed.

The third: His saying: ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Yasin 80]. Whoever can make fire from this green, cool, moist tree, when fire is dry and burning, is able to restore creation, because this is more eloquent in power, namely, the making of fire from a green tree.

The fourth: the creation of the heavens and the earth. His power to create the heavens and the earth is proof of His power to revive bones when they have decayed, because the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Yasin 81].

The fifth and sixth: ﴿the Creator, the Knowing﴾ [Yasin 81]. "Al-Khallaq" (the Creator) is an inherent attribute of Him. His being Creator includes that He creates everything, and His being Knowing indicates that nothing of creation is hidden from Him so that He could be incapable of it.

The seventh: that nothing resists Him. Rather, when He commands something, it happens immediately, as He says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yasin 82].

The eighth: the glorification of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, above every deficiency. It is well known that one who is incapable of restoring creation is deficient. So when He is exalted above every deficiency, it is possible that what He promised, the reviving of bones when they have decayed, will occur.

The ninth: that the dominion (malakut) of everything is in His hand. Whoever has the dominion of everything in his hand, meaning that He is the Owner of everything, is able to bring into existence what does not exist and to cause the existent to cease.

The tenth: His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [Yasin 83]. This is the outcome of creation: that the creatures are resurrected and returned to Allah so that He may recompense them for what they did.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. On the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"), the author says: "Surat al-Saffat is Meccan, one hundred and eighty-two verses." The Meccan (makkiyyah) surah is that which was revealed before the Hijrah (migration to Madinah). So everything revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, even if it was revealed outside Makkah, and everything revealed after the Hijrah is Medinan, even if it was revealed in Makkah. Accordingly, His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3], which was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ while he was standing at 'Arafah, is Medinan. This is the most correct of the opinions on the Meccan and Medinan, that what was revealed after the Hijrah is Medinan and what was revealed before it is Meccan.

As for the basmalah ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, it is an independent verse of the Book of Allah. For this reason it is not counted among the verses of the surah that follows it, and even in al-Fatihah, according to the preferred opinion, it is not part of the surah. Accordingly, the numbering found in the mushafs is contrary to the preferred opinion, since in the numbering of al-Fatihah the basmalah is counted as one of its verses. The correct view is that, like the rest of the surahs, the basmalah in it is an independent verse that is not counted among its verses.

It is mentioned before every surah except Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). Surat Bara'ah was not preceded by the basmalah. Why? It was said: because it was revealed with the sword, and the basmalah is mercy, so it is not fitting for the basmalah to be mentioned before it. But this is not correct. Rather, the correct view is that when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, compiled the mushaf, they were uncertain whether Bara'ah was part of al-Anfal or not, so they left it, leaving out the basmalah, and placed a dividing line between it and Surat al-Anfal without the basmalah. We know that if the basmalah had been revealed before Surat Bara'ah it would have been preserved, because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr 9]. Thus the Companions' ijtihad in this matter conformed to reality, i.e., conformed to the fact that it was not revealed at the beginning of this surah.

As for its meaning: when someone says "bismillah" (in the name of Allah), it means "with every name of Allah." We say "with every name of Allah" because "ism" (name) is a singular noun in the construct state, so it is general. Thus the saying of one who says "bismillah" does not mean one name of Allah, but all the names of Allah. This shows you the greatness of this basmalah: you begin seeking blessing and help through every name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The "ba'" in it is for accompaniment and for seeking help. It is for accompaniment in order to obtain its blessing, for the basmalah contains blessing. For this reason, when it is mentioned over an animal for slaughter, the animal becomes lawful and pure, and when it is not mentioned, it becomes unlawful and impure. When it is mentioned before wudu', the wudu' is valid, and when it is not mentioned, the wudu' is invalid according to the view of those who hold that the basmalah is a condition of wudu' or one of its obligations. But the preferred view regarding the basmalah in wudu' is that it is sunnah, based on the saying of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him: "Nothing is established in this matter," meaning the matter of saying the basmalah in wudu'. When it is mentioned over food, it drives Satan away from it, and if it is not mentioned, Satan shares in the food of the eater and the drink of the drinker.

The essential point is that it is blessing. Therefore we say: the "ba'" is for accompaniment, meaning that the one who says the basmalah is accompanied by blessing and help through his basmalah, because it assists a person in his affairs.

As for "Allah," it is the proper name (al-'alam al-khass) of Allah, the Exalted. It is not named by it other than Allah. Its meaning is the One possessing divinity (uluhiyyah) and worship over all His creatures. That is, "ilah" (god) in the sense of "ma'luh" (one who is worshipped), i.e., one who is worshipped.

If someone says: where is the hamzah, if you say that its origin is "ilah"?

The answer: it was dropped for lightness, because of frequent use, just as it was dropped from "nas" (people), whose origin is "unas," and it was dropped from "shar" (evil) and "khayr" (good), whose origins are "ashar" and "akhyar."

As for "al-Rahman," it is one of the names of Allah, and "al-Rahim" is likewise one of His names. The difference between them is that "al-Rahman" is considered in terms of attribute, and "al-Rahim" in terms of action. For this reason "al-Rahman" came in this form, which indicates breadth. The mercy of Allah, the Exalted, is broad and encompasses everything. As for "al-Rahim," it is the One who conveys His mercy to His creatures. Mercy is divided, in terms of the name "al-Rahim," into two kinds: general and specific. As for "al-Rahman," in terms of attribute, it is general, because it is (...)

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is a dependent element that must have a governing element ('amil), which is called the complement (al-muta'alliq). That is, the governing element of the prepositional phrase is what is called the complement. One says, for example: "The prepositional phrase is dependent on such-and-such." So where is the complement of the basmalah? The scholars said: the complement of the basmalah is a deleted verb, placed later, agreeing with the word with which one begins in its root. A later verb agreeing with the word with which one begins in its root. So if you want to make wudu', the deleted element is: "In the name of Allah I make wudu'." If you want to read, it is: "In the name of Allah I read." And so on by analogy. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1690/1), from the hadith of Jundub ibn Sufyan]. So he estimated the verb: "I slaughter in the name of Allah."

Why did he estimate a verb? Because it is the basis of action. For this reason verbs act without condition, whereas nouns act only under conditions, such as the active participle (ism al-fa'il), the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), the adjective of similarity (sifah mushabbahah), and others. It was estimated as coming later for two reasons. The first: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah. The second: for the sake of specification, because placing the governing element after the governed element indicates specification and restriction. It was estimated to agree with the word with which one begins in its root, because it is more specific and more indicative of the intended meaning. So if you want to make wudu' and you say "In the name of Allah I make wudu'," this is more specific than if you estimated "In the name of Allah I begin."

In any case, if we are asked: how do we estimate the governing element in the basmalah? The answer: we estimate it as a later verb agreeing with the word with which one begins in its root. If what one begins with is wudu', we say "I make wudu'"; if it is reading, we say "I read"; if it is entering, we say "I enter"; and so on.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿By those ranked in lines, and those who drive away with violent driving, and those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat 1-3], and so on to the end. The "wa" here is a particle of oath (harf qasam), and an oath is the affirmation of a matter by mentioning something revered in a specific form. This is the oath.

Our saying "affirmation of a matter": this is what the oath is for, that it gives emphasis. By mentioning something revered, it is as if the one swearing says: "I affirm this just as I affirm the greatness of the one sworn by." One cannot swear by this great one in my view except over a matter that is certain.

Our saying "in a specific form" refers to the form of the oath. The particles of oath are three: the "wa," the "ba'," and the "ta'." The "wa" is the most frequently used, and the "ba'" is the most varied in form; that is, the "ba'" is used for swearing with the verb present or omitted, and it is used with both an explicit noun and a pronoun. The "ta'" is more specific than the "wa."

So which of the oath particles is most common in use?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the most common is the "ba'," because it is used with the verb present, as you say: "I swear by Allah you will do such-and-such," and with the verb omitted, as you say: "By Allah you will do such-and-such."

It is also used with an explicit noun, such as: "I swear by Allah," and with a pronoun, such as: "Indeed Allah... and by Him I swear, surely over everything He is Capable." Here the "ba'" entered on a pronoun. As for the "wa," it is the most frequently used but it enters only on the explicit noun, and the verb of swearing is not mentioned with it.

The "ta'" is the least used. It is restricted to the explicit noun and is also restricted to specific names, namely Allah and Rabb. Ibn Malik said:

........................ ∗∗∗ .......... And the "ta'" is for Allah and Rabb

So you say: "Ta-llahi, I will surely do such-and-such," and you say: "Ta-rabbi al-Ka'bah, I will surely do such-and-such," or "Ta-rabbi, I will surely do such-and-such." Is the verb of swearing mentioned with it? It is not mentioned with it. So it is the most restricted in use.

The "wa" here is a particle of oath. ﴿al-Saffat﴾ [al-Saffat 1] is a noun in the genitive by the "wa" of oath, since particles of oath govern in the genitive. ﴿al-Saffat﴾ has a meaning and a purpose. The meaning of ﴿al-Saffat﴾ is things standing in a single straight line. Every multiple thing that stands in one straight line is called "saff." He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row (saffan)﴾ [al-Saff 4], meaning in a straight line. This is the meaning of al-Saffat. But what is its intended referent?

The author said the intended referent is "the angels," and it is feminine because they are considered as groups, and "jama'at" (groups) is feminine. The deviants have seized upon this resemblance, namely the feminine form of the angels, and said that the angels are the daughters of Allah. For this reason they are mentioned in the feminine form. But there is no doubt that this is a form of deception and comparison, for Allah mentioned the angels in the masculine form: ﴿And the angels glorify their Lord with His praise﴾ [al-Shura 5], and He did not say "yusabbihna" (feminine plural).

In any case, the angels are feminine because they are considered as groups, since the angels, peace be upon them, are different groups, and each group has a specific duty. Among them are those whose duty is specific worship of Allah, such as glorification, bowing, and prostration and other things. Among them are angels appointed to guard the children of Adam, angels appointed to guard their deeds and record them, and angels appointed to other matters, some of which we know and some of which we do not know.

If someone says: who are the angels?

The answer: they are an unseen world, created from light, and Allah, the Exalted, made them servants obeying Him. They carry out His commands in the most perfect manner. They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.

If someone says: this definition is objected to, because the angels are sometimes seen; the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form, with six hundred wings, which filled the horizon [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3232), and Muslim (174/280), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. And sometimes Jibril comes in the form of a man?

The answer: this is a rare occurrence, and what is rare does not break the rule or invalidate the definition. And the rare, as the scholars say, has no ruling.

What is the reason the angels are described as "al-Saffat"?

The author said: (they arrange themselves in worship, or their wings in the air, awaiting what they are commanded). This "al-Saffat" is the description applied to the angels, because they line themselves up for worship, meaning they prepare themselves for it. Or they stand in rows before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah says: ﴿And indeed, we are those who stand in rows, and indeed, we are those who glorify﴾ [al-Saffat 165-166]. Or they spread their wings in the air, awaiting what they are commanded, as Allah says: ﴿Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings?﴾ [al-Mulk 19]. A bird in the air that has put its wings out like this and does not move is said to be "saff" (spread out).

If someone says: is "aw" (or) here for variety, or for doubt, or what?

It is possible that it is for variety, meaning that they line up in this way and in that way. Or it is for doubt, meaning for hesitation between two opinions held by the exegetes. But the first meaning is better, because this is a description of the angels: they line themselves up for worship, and likewise they spread their wings in the air, awaiting what they are commanded.

﴿Then those who drive away with violent driving﴾ [al-Saffat 2]: the angels drive the clouds, meaning they drive them onward. So the described thing is one and the same: the "al-Saffat" are the "al-Zajirat."

His saying ("they drive the clouds, i.e., drive them onward") perhaps is given as an example of the driving of the angels, because the angels drive the clouds, i.e., they drive them onward. Likewise they drive the soul of the dying disbeliever when he dies, driving his soul to come out. They say: "Come out, O evil soul." Perhaps they also drive other things that we do not know. The point is that the intended referent of "al-Zajirat" is: the angels. And how are they driving? We say: there are several aspects to this, among them: driving the clouds, driving the souls of disbelievers at death, and other things that Allah commands them to drive.

﴿Then those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat 3]: (i.e., readers of the Qur'an who recite it, "dhikran" being a verbal noun from the meaning of "al-Taliyat").

His saying: (﴿Then those who recite the reminder﴾). The author shifted with this description from the first referent, i.e., from the first described thing, and said "al-Taliyat" (...)

﴿By those ranked in lines, and those who drive away with violent driving, and those who recite the reminder. Indeed, your God is one﴾ [al-Saffat 1-4]. We spoke yesterday about the Meccan and the Medinan. What is the Meccan? (...)

(﴿dhikran﴾ is a verbal noun from the meaning of "al-Taliyat"). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, parsed "dhikran" as a verbal noun from the meaning of "al-Taliyat." From this we gain a grammatical benefit: a verbal noun may come from the word or from the meaning. If it comes from the meaning, it is a semantic verbal noun (masdar ma'nawi), and if it comes from the word, it is a verbal noun of the same root (masdar lafzi). So if you say "qa'adtu juluusan" (I sat a sitting), then "juluusan" is a semantic verbal noun, and "qa'adtu qu'uudan" (I sat sitting) is a verbal noun of the same root.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 36, verse 76–83 (part 5 of 5):

﴿وَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا﴾ [al-Saffat 3]. The author says: "Inna al-taliyat asluha al-dhakirat dhikran" (the reciters are originally "those who remember with remembrance"). "Al-taliyat dhikran" means "al-dhakirat dhikran," so according to him "al-taliyat" carries the meaning of "al-dhakirat," and ﴿ذِكْرًا﴾ is its verbal noun (masdar) derived from its meaning. However, what appears to be correct differs from the author's statement: ﴿ذِكْرًا﴾ is the direct object (maf'ul bihi) of ﴿التَّالِيَاتِ﴾, because ﴿التَّالِيَاتِ﴾ is an active participle (ism al-fa'il) that has fulfilled the conditions for governing an object, being definite with the article (al-). ﴿ذِكْرًا﴾ is its direct object. That is: "fa-al-taliyat," meaning "those who recite the Remembrance." By "the Remembrance" is meant the Qur'an. It is called a remembrance (dhikr) for several reasons: because it is a remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is among the best forms of remembrance; because it reminds a person of his Lord; because it reminds a person of the rulings of his Lord; because it reminds a person of the blessings of his Lord; and because it is a remembrance (dhikr) for the one who acts by it, meaning a source of honour and elevation, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is a remembrance for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 44]. It is also a remembrance because it admonishes its possessor and reminds him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad 29]. So the Qur'an is a remembrance in these five respects. Will you repeat them?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: In what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: For those who passed? Good. And the blessings of Allah? And it is itself also a remembrance of Allah, among the best types of remembrance.

﴿فَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا (٣) إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾ [al-Saffat 3–4]. This sentence is the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam). For this reason the letter nun in ﴿إِنَّ﴾ is pronounced with a kasra here, because it falls in the response to an oath. Also, its predicate is linked with the lam (of emphasis): ﴿لَوَاحِدٌ﴾ "surely one." When inna is the response to an oath, it must take a kasra. When its predicate is preceded by the lam, or its delayed subject, or a complement of one of them is preceded by the lam, it must take a kasra.

﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ﴾ The address. The author says: "O people of Makkah." But the correct view is that it is general, including everyone who is mentioned. What led the author to make it specific to the people of Makkah is that this verse is Meccan and the polytheists were the people of Makkah. However, the general meaning should not be restricted to the place of its revelation. If the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specific cause, then the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specific place. So the correct view is that ﴿إِلَهَكُمْ﴾ means: O people, ﴿لَوَاحِدٌ﴾ "one," meaning without partner. The words "al-Wahid" (the One) and "al-Ahad" (the Unique) and similar terms indicate singularity, meaning that He, the Mighty and Majestic, has no partner.

﴿إِلَهَكُمْ﴾ is of the pattern (fi'al) in the sense of (maf'ul), meaning "your ma'luh," that is, the one worshipped (al-ma'luh). The ma'luh is the one who is worshipped out of love and veneration. By His love a person performs the commands, and by His veneration he refrains from the prohibitions. Therefore: your Lord, O people, is one, with no partner. Allah the Mighty and Majestic has no partner in His lordship (rububiyyah), no partner in His divinity (uluhiyyah), and no partner in His names and attributes. So whoever brings evidence that He has no partner in His lordship—
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Where is "surely your Lord is one"? (...) We are speaking about lordship.
* Student: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd 16].
* Shaykh: Yes. Divinity: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾ [Muhammad 19]. Names and attributes: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11]. So Allah the Exalted is one in His divinity, His lordship, His names and His attributes, glorified and exalted is He.

Then he said: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [al-Saffat 5], "the Lord of the heavens and the earth." ﴿رَبُّ﴾ here is either an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan), meaning a clarifying appositive, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). The estimate is: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. ﴿رَبُّ﴾ means creator, owner and manager. He is the One who created the heavens and the earth, He is the One who owns the heavens and the earth, and He is the Manager of the heavens and the earth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. This is His singularity in creation and management. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 189]. This is His singularity in dominion. "Al-Samawat" is the plural of "sama'" (sky), which is well known. Their number is seven heavens, by the explicit text of the Qur'an: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 86]. ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. The earth is likewise seven, according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit Sunnah. As for the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, it is in His saying?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, we said: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that they are seven earths.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: His saying: ﴿and of the earth the like thereof﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. The likeness here is in number, because it is impossible for the earth to be like the heaven in its essence, nor in its extent and greatness. The heaven is wider and greater, and its material is different from the material of the earth. So it is necessary that the likeness be in number.
As for the Sunnah, it is explicit, such as his saying ﷺ: "Whoever usurps a span of land, Allah will encircle him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."[Recorded by Muslim (1610/137) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd.]

﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾ [al-Saffat 5], "the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them." That is, and the Lord of what is between them. What is between them? There is no doubt that what is between them consists of great creatures, as evidenced by the fact that they are placed as a counterpart and equal to the heavens and the earth. So it must be a great thing, not merely the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth. Rather, there are great things between the sky and the earth that are among the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Among them we know the clouds, which are between the sky and the earth. The stars are between the sky and the earth, the sun is between the sky and the earth, and the moon is between the sky and the earth, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾ [al-Anbiya' 33].

As for what was widely known among the astronomers of the past, that the sun is in the fourth heaven, the moon in the lowest heaven, and Mercury, Saturn and Jupiter in the other heavens, in this order:
"Zuhal (Saturn) bought its Mirrikh (Mars) from its Shams (Sun), so the Aqmar (moons) became radiant with 'Utarid (Mercury)."
How many is this? Seven, arranged from highest to lowest.
The highest is "Zuhal" (Saturn), in the seventh heaven. "Shara" (Jupiter, al-Mushtari) is in the sixth. "Mirrikh" (Mars) is in the fifth heaven. "Min shamsih" (the sun) is in the fourth. "Fa-tazaharat" (Venus, al-Zuhrah) is in the third. "Bi-'Utarid" (Mercury) is in the second heaven. "Al-aqmar" (the moon) is in the lowest heaven. This is what was well known among the astronomers of the past. But this is contrary to the correct view, because the apparent meaning of the texts is that the sun, the moon and the stars are all below the heaven, not fixed in the heavens. Rather they are in an orbit that revolves between the sky and the earth. The moon is the nearest of them to the earth, as evidenced by its eclipsing what is above it, as we have witnessed and as others have witnessed at times. You find it passing beneath a star so that the star disappears behind it. This shows that it is beneath the stars.

In any case, we say: between the seven heavens are the clouds, the sun, the moon, the stars, the planets and other things, some of which we may not know. We may not know these matters, and perhaps later knowledge will reveal to us much of them.

He said: ﴿وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾ [al-Saffat 5], "and the Lord of the easts." That is, and the wests of the sun. For it there is an east and a west each day. He said: "al-Mashariq" (the easts). He said: "(that is: and the wests)." So it is as if this is from the method of mentioning one of two opposites and leaving out the other, similar to His saying: ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold, since the garments, which are shirts and the like, protect from both heat and cold. Here He said: ﴿وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾ and the author said: "(i.e., and the wests)."

In any case, "al-Mashariq" is the plural of "mashriq" (east). So what is meant by the easts? Is it, as the author said, "the easts of the sun," because each day it has an east? Or do we say that "al-mashariq" is more general, so that it includes the easts of the sun, the easts of the moon, the easts of the stars, and the easts of everything that rises? Which of them? The second is more general. So we say: Lord of the easts, meaning the easts of the sun, the easts of the moon, the easts of the stars, and the easts of everything that rises. Allah mentioned the easts without the wests because the easts are more indicative of power than the wests, since rising is a beginning and setting is an end. In rising, especially the rising of the sun, there is also illumination and light, in which the completeness of the blessing fully appears.

His saying: ﴿الْمَشَارِقِ﴾ here is in the plural. In some verses it came in the dual, such as His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman 17]. In some verses it came in the singular: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, as Allah said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil 9]. So is this a contradiction or what?

The answer: No. There is no contradiction in the Qur'an: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa' 82]. The Qur'an cannot contradict itself, nor can it contradict authentic Sunnah.

We say: with authentic Sunnah, because a weak Sunnah may contradict the Qur'an, and its contradicting the Qur'an indicates its weakness. But it is impossible with authentic Sunnah. If something is found whose apparent meaning is conflict, there must be a way to reconcile the conflict: either by possible harmonization (jam'), which is the first level for acting upon texts whose apparent meaning conflicts; or by abrogation (naskh) if the chronology is known and the text is of a kind that admits abrogation; and the third is preponderance (tarjih), where one of them is stronger than the other. These three levels are necessary. But sometimes the one considering it may not find any of these ways. He may be unable to harmonize, may not know the abrogation, and may not be able to prefer one over the other. What then is his position? Suspension (tawaqquf), so that he says: "Allah knows best." It is not permissible under any circumstances to believe that there is a contradiction in the Qur'an or in authentic Sunnah at all. But is it permissible for him to try to know these levels, or if it is difficult for him the first time, should he stop? He should try. He must consider repeatedly until it becomes clear, lest doubt enter his heart and he deviate, and Allah forbid.

So this benefit came incidentally: there is no contradiction in the Qur'an, neither within itself nor with authentic Sunnah. If something is found whose apparent meaning is conflict or contradiction, we must apply the three levels: first, harmonization; if that is not possible, abrogation; if that is not possible, preponderance; and if we cannot reach that, then suspension, but with an attempt to reach one of these levels.

Therefore, based on this rule, we can apply the difference mentioned concerning the east and the west as follows: "the east" with regard to direction, meaning the direction of the east: ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him﴾ [al-Muzzammil 9], meaning the direction of the east and the direction of the west, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115], that is, the direction of Allah according to one of the two interpretations. As for "the two easts" and "the two wests" ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman 17], what is meant is the easts of summer and winter, and the wests of summer and winter. The sun, for example, has a limit in its rising in summer, which is the Tropic of Cancer, and it has a limit in its course in winter, which is the Tropic of Capricorn. The difference between the two easts is great, and no created being can move the sun from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn, nor can he shift it by a single hair's breadth. Likewise we say regarding the moon, since it revolves through the two easts and the two wests.

If someone says: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman 17]. In which other place of the Qur'an is the dual form mentioned?
* Student: In Surat al-Rahman.
* Shaykh: In Surat al-Rahman. Elsewhere?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is not in al-Isra'. This is in the surah of the...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, in "Hal Ata" I think.
* Student: Al-Muzzammil.
* Shaykh: Al-Muzzammil, yes. I meant the dual. Did it occur in other than al-Rahman? In any case, the reason for mentioning it in the dual in al-Rahman is that this surah addresses two groups, or not? Mankind and the jinn. So this was a meaningful fit for the context of the whole surah.

(The easts and the wests) The plural is clear in this, either by considering the easts of everything that rises and the wests of everything that sets, such as the sun, the moon, the stars and the planets, or because they are the daily easts of the sun, since each day it has an east. This is the level of the three levels: the level of harmonization.

So the harmonization between them is that we say: "the easts" refers to the easts of everything that rises, or to the easts of the sun each day. "Al-mashriqayn" (the two easts) refers to the easts of summer and winter and their wests. "Al-mashriq wal-maghrib" (the east and the west) refers to the direction.

He said: ﴿وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾ (i.e., and the wests). ﴿إِنَّا زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِزِينَةٍ الْكَوَاكِبِ﴾ [al-Saffat 6], "Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars." The pronoun ﴿إِنَّا﴾ refers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. The plural pronoun is used for Allah out of glorification, not out of plurality, because the verse says: ﴿Indeed your God is One﴾ [al-Saffat 4]. But this is from the category of glorification.

His saying: ﴿زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِزِينَةٍ﴾ [al-Saffat 6], that is, We placed on it what adorns it..

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So let not their speech grieve you﴾ [Yasin 76]. That is: let it not bring you into grief. Grief (huzn) is regret and worry over what has passed, and its opposite is fear (khawf), which is worry over what is yet to come. What did they say? They said many things. For example: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 5]. This is an attack on the divinity (uluhiyyah). They also said: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd 43]. This is an attack on the prophethood (risalah). And they said that Muhammad ﷺ is possessed, a poet, a soothsayer and a sorcerer. This too is a defect in the character of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

It is well known that a human being is a human being who is affected when his call is struck at its core and its root. And it was said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 5]. When a person's jurisprudential opinion is struck, for example, he feels in himself some disturbance; but if what is struck is his foundation, it is greater and more severe; and if he is defamed in his very essence, it is more and more severe. For this reason Allah consoles His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with directions of this kind.

﴿So let not their speech grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ [Yasin 76]. The sentence is a resumptive clause explaining the state of those who say what they say about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and what he brought. Their state is that they are threatened by what? By the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of what they conceal and what they reveal: what they conceal among themselves and what they make known to people; what they hide within themselves and what they show to others. So we have two kinds of secrecy: the first is a person's concealing what is in his soul, so that no one knows of it; the second is the secrecy of a matter among themselves, so that it does not go out to others.

Let us give an example: there are ten people who talk among themselves about some matter, but it does not go out to anyone else. Is this secrecy or not? It is secrecy. And one of these ten has concealed something in himself and has not informed his companions; this is also secrecy.

So His saying ﴿what they conceal﴾ includes both this and that: what each person hides in himself, and what they keep secret among themselves without making it known to others. In this there is clear warning, for Allah the Exalted knows what they conceal and what they reveal, and He will repay them for it on the Day of Resurrection.

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop [of semen], and then he is an open adversary?﴾ [Yasin 77]. And: ﴿And he presents for Us an example and forgets his [own] creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ [Yasin 78]. He says: ﴿Does not man see﴾. ﴿Yara﴾ here means "know": ﴿Did he not know?﴾ The interrogation here is for affirmation, and its purpose is rebuke. The waw is a conjunctive particle, and the element it is conjoined to is either implied after the hamzah, or it is what preceded; on the second view the hamzah has been moved from its place, and its original form on the second view is: "wa-alam yara".

As for His saying ﴿al-insan﴾ [Yasin 77], the author said: "and he is al-'As ibn Wa'il". On the author's view the (al) here is for the mental (ahd) reference. But the correct view is that (al) is for the genus, i.e., the human race, and among them is al-'As ibn Wa'il; because the basic function of (al) is to indicate the genus. This is its basic use: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who have believed﴾ [al-'Asr 1-3], meaning the genus of man.

The reason that this is the basic use is that the reference (ahd) restricts it to a specific thing, while the original is that the word remains on its generality. So if someone says of ﴿Does not man see﴾ that it refers to so-and-so son of so-and-so, we say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said "al-insan", and it is comprehensive. Therefore the correct view is that it is general; but we may take al-'As ibn Wa'il as an example of whoever held this view or adopted this opinion.

(﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop﴾ — semen — "until We made him strong and powerful; ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾ — intensely contentious toward Us; ﴿open﴾ — clear in denying resurrection.)

Man was created from a drop, which is this despised semen as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described it: this despised water from which man was created. If a person returns to his origin, he finds that it is like phlegm, nothing. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brings him into being, giving him eloquence, rhetoric and strength of argument, after he has been nurtured by the blessings of Allah in his mother's womb, then at his mother's breast, then by the various kinds of food and drink Allah has bestowed on him, so that he grows strong and his intellect, thought and mind become firm, and he becomes a contentious adversary.

﴿Then he is an open adversary﴾: that is, intensely contentious; because (fa'il) carries the sense of (fa'il) but indicates intensity.

His saying ﴿mubin﴾: that is, clear, showing its own nature; meaning, displaying his contentiousness, being strong and intense in it. Later, if Allah wills, there will be an explanation of a type of human argumentation and contentiousness.

﴿Does not man see that We created him from a drop, then he is an open adversary?﴾ We have already said that this interrogation is for affirmation, the purpose of which is rebuke, and that the intended meaning of "man" is more general than what the author restricted it to, namely al-'As ibn Wa'il.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾, that is, one who displays contention, contrary to the author's statement: "clear in contention."

He said: ﴿And he presents for Us an example﴾. That is: this man who was an open adversary struck an example for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intending to challenge and deny. The content of his denial is explained by His saying: ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ This sentence is separated from what came before because it serves as an explanation of something vague in His saying ﴿and he presents for Us an example﴾.

﴿And he forgets his creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones"﴾: ﴿And he forgets his creation﴾ means the beginning of his creation, that he was created from despised water, and then became this human, an open adversary. The clause ﴿and he forgets his creation﴾ may be a declarative sentence, or it may be a circumstantial clause, i.e., "while he has forgotten his creation"; that is, in striking this example he has forgotten his origin, that he was from semen, then became a complete human being, an open adversary. The example is explained by His saying: ﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿And he forgets his creation﴾ from the semen, and it is more strange than his example.) How so? Because his example was the restoration of something that already existed, while the creation from semen was the beginning of his creation. And which of the two is more impossible, if there were any impossibility for Allah? The beginning. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum 27]. If that is so, then this man who is an open adversary is astray in two respects:

The first: his astonishment at Allah's power to restore.
The second: his forgetting the first creation, in that he forgot that he was created from despised water until he became a complete human being and an open adversary.

(﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ — that is, rotten.) What is the form of ﴿man﴾? It is interrogative, and the purpose is negation or denial: no one gives life to bones when they are decayed. When a person dies and decays — that is, his flesh and sinews disappear and his bones crumble with age — then they are decayed. These decayed bones are the furthest thing from life, for they resemble dust; so how can these bones be brought to life? This is the ground of the astonishment of this denying man.

(﴿He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decayed?"﴾ — that is, rotten. It is not said "ramimah" with a feminine ending because it is a noun, not an adjective.) The word ramim is sometimes used as an adjective, i.e., a passive or active participle: marmum or rimm; and sometimes it is used as a noun, meaning that a bone when it has rotted is called ramim. Since it is used as a noun, it does not need the feminine ta'. It is like asad, hajar, shajar, and the like, which do not take ta'. But if it were intended as an adjective, it would take the feminine, because "bones" is a plural, and every plural may take the feminine, especially since He said ﴿wa-hiya﴾, and this is a feminine pronoun.

He said: ﴿while they are decayed﴾. (It is narrated that he took a decayed bone, crumbled it, and said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Do you think Allah will bring this back to life after it has rotted and decayed?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes, and He will cause you to enter the Fire." [Recorded by 'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Tafsir (2498) from the narration of Qatadah ibn Di'amah.])

The author related this report with the weak form "it is narrated" (ruwiya), and he is right to do so, because this denying man, whether he denied in front of the Prophet ﷺ or behind his back, is a denier in any case; and it is not the custom of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to address people in this manner, saying "Yes, and He will cause you to enter the Fire." So this report requires examination of its chain and its authenticity.

Allah the Exalted said, clarifying His power to do this: ﴿Say﴾ [Yasin 79]. To whom is the address? To the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿Say﴾: that is, to this one who denied that Allah could give life to bones while they are decayed: ﴿He who initiated them the first time will give them life﴾.

Know that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, "Say," it is a command to him to convey. It is well known that the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to convey the Qur'an in general, as in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67]. But when He specifies something of the rulings or the reports with "Say," there is special emphasis on what he is commanded to say, because he is commanded to convey it in a particular manner; and what is in a particular manner is more emphatic than what falls under the general.

The summary of this principle: when Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to say "Say," this is a specific command to convey this matter, whether it is a report or a ruling.

﴿He who initiated them the first time will give them life﴾: the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, did not say "Allah will give them life," but said ﴿He who initiated them the first time﴾, so that the answer would contain the proof. For if He had said "Say, Allah will give them life," a person would understand that Allah is the one who gives them life. But when He says ﴿He who initiated them the first time﴾, the answer contains what? The proof: ﴿He who initiated them the first time﴾. And who initiated them the first time? He who initiated them the first time is Allah, Mighty and Majestic; no creature created these bones or originated them the first time. So if Allah, Mighty and Majestic, originated them the first time, He is able to restore them, for restoration is easier than beginning. This is a proof; that is, Allah mentioned in the verses that follow the evidence for the possibility of giving life to these bones while they are decayed. This is the first proof: ﴿He who initiated them the first time﴾. The inference from this that one who is able to begin is able to restore a fortiori.

Second, He said: (﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾ — created thing — ﴿Knowing﴾ in summary and in detail, before its creation and after its creation.) This sentence ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾: the author said that (khalq) here means "created thing" (makhluq), making the verbal noun act as the passive participle. What appears is that the intended meaning is the verbal noun itself. It is well known that there is no created thing except by a creation. But when He says ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾, there is a text on His knowledge of creation: how He creates and how He originates creation. This is more indicative of His power to revive the dead than if we said "knowing of every created thing," because if you say "knowing of every created thing," His knowledge of the created thing would be after its creation. But if the verse is taken at face value, ﴿of every creation﴾ means that He knows how to create. One who knows how to create, when He wills something, is not unable to do it, for if He knows, nothing remains but the will: when He wills it, and He is Knowing of every creation, He does what He knows, Mighty and Majestic. So His being ﴿Knowing of every creation﴾ is a proof that He is able to restore it, for one who is incapable is either incapable because of his incapacity, or because of his ignorance. If you say to someone, "Make us a tape recorder," and he does not know how to make one, will he make one?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: Why? Because of his ignorance. If you say, "Make us a tape recorder," and he knows how to make it but has no power, he will not make it. Here, when He says He is ﴿the One who initiated them the first time﴾, this is power.

﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾ is the negation of ignorance. So when the incapacity implied by His saying ﴿initiated them the first time﴾ is negated, and the ignorance implied by His saying ﴿Knowing of every creation﴾ is negated, the creation becomes possible. These are two proofs: ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation.﴾

(﴿He who made for you﴾ [Yasin 80] — that is, among people — ﴿from the green tree﴾: the markh and the 'ifar, or every tree except the jujube — ﴿fire, and then from it you kindle.﴾)

﴿He who made for you from the green tree fire﴾: ﴿made﴾ means "caused to be," and the one who made for us from the green tree fire is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

As for the author's saying "for you" — "among people" — the author intended by "among people" that this making is not specific to the addressees, that is, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions, but is general for everyone; so it is made for them among people.

﴿From the green tree﴾: the author says: (from the markh and the 'ifar). On his statement, (al) is for the mental reference, and it would be general with a specific intention. But we have already noted that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and that the basic function of (al) is to indicate the genus, i.e., generality. So the correct view is that what is meant is ﴿from the tree﴾, i.e., from every tree, as he said.

As for his saying "except the jujube": we know nothing about this, whether it is excluded and the jujube cannot produce fire. Allah knows best. In any case, we say that the basic statement ﴿from the green tree fire﴾ is general.

﴿The green tree﴾ contains moisture, does it not? Moisture entails coldness, and the fire that comes out of this moist, cold tree is dry and hot. This dry, hot thing is produced from something moist and cold, and the great contrariness between moisture and coldness on the one hand and heat and dryness on the other is evident. If Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produces from something a thing that is so contrary to what it comes from, then He is able to give life to bones while they are decayed; for creating an opposite from its opposite is more emphatic in power than creating a thing from nothing opposite. This is clear. So this is the third proof of the possibility of giving life to bones while they are decayed.

His saying ﴿then from it you kindle﴾: the "fa'" here is conjunctive, and "idha" is sudden; that is, as soon as you strike one stick against another from this tree, fire springs forth and is kindled from it. That is, it requires no great effort; rather kindling is an easy and sudden operation. The suddenness we derive from the word "idha."

In His saying ﴿then from it you kindle﴾ there is proof that this action is continuous, for a nominal sentence indicates stability and continuity. No one denies this: no one denies that fire arises from green wood from which people kindle. Well, ﴿then from it you kindle.﴾

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (You strike, and this indicates the power to resurrect, for He combined in it water, fire and wood: water does not extinguish the fire, nor does the fire burn the wood.)

He said: (﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ — despite their greatness — ﴿able to create the likes of them﴾ — that is, the humans in their smallness? — ﴿Yes﴾ [Yasin 81].)

This is also a fourth proof: "Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?" (36:81). The answer is "Yes" (balā). Allah answered Himself: yes, the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, as Allah the Exalted said: "The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind" (40:57). This is a matter known by the senses and by observation. All of mankind does not equal one of the stars, so what of these stars and constellations which none can count except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the great heavens about which Allah the Exalted said: "And the heaven We built with power, and indeed, We are expanding it" (51:47). He who created the heavens and the earth is surely able to create the likes of people? The answer: "Yes, by Allah, yes, and more so!" He who created these great celestial bodies, with the great benefits He placed in them, is also able to create their likes all the more and with greater reason. This is the fourth proof.

He said: "Yes, He is the Creator, the All-Knowing" (Yes, He is able to do that; He answered Himself, Mighty and Majestic; "He is the Creator": the One of abundant creation; "the All-Knowing": knowing of everything).

As for "He is the Creator" (al-Khallāq), the author said: "the One of abundant creation." He took fa''āl to be an intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālagha). There is no doubt that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates abundantly. But we should also say: the fa''āl here is a form of attribution (nisba); that is, He is described as having creation as an attribute. Describing Him with creation is more eloquent than describing Him as one who brings creation into existence or performs creation; that is, He is one who possesses (...). That is, if we say, "So-and-so is a carpenter" (najjār), what does our saying that he is a carpenter convey? If we take it as an attribution, and what does it convey if we take it as an intensive form? If we take it as an intensive form, the meaning is that he does much carpentry, a carpenter, that is, one who does much carpentry; but is he skilled at it? And is he deserving of being described by this profession, so that he is called a carpenter? He may be, and he may not be. He may do much carpentry, but his doors come out and are of no use at all, a sham; they break their hinges and are useless, and every day one or two doors come out for us, may God preserve, but they are ruin. We say this is an intensive form, but does carpentry describe him in the sense that he is skilled and proficient in it? No, it is not necessarily so; he may be, and he may not be. But if you say najjār, with the form of attribution, meaning one who has the craft, then it is more eloquent as a description, and the najjār, meaning one who has the craft and is proficient in it, whether he does a lot or a little of carpentry, is a proficient carpenter.

Here we can say: "He is the Creator" (al-Khallāq): on what do we take it? On the attribution that conveys the description of Allah with this great attribute; that is, the One possessing perfected creation in the most complete manner. Along with this, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, combines in His case both the description and the act; that is, abundance of creation. There is no doubt that the creation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cannot be counted in kinds, let alone in species, let alone in individuals. Who can count the kinds of creation? Who can count the species of these kinds? And who can count the individuals of these species? No one can count that. Thus both matters are combined in the right of Allah, Glorified and Exalted. What are they? The attribution, that is, the descriptive quality, the perfection of the description; and second, the abundance conveyed by the intensive form.

If Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is Creator (khallāq), that is, creation is a description of Him, a necessary attribute of His.

And likewise, the One of abundant creation, would He be incapable of giving life to bones when they are decayed? No. So take this as a fifth proof.

"The All-Knowing": this too is a proof, for we have said that the non-restoration is either due to incapacity or due to ignorance. Whenever Allah describes Himself with knowledge, this means that He is capable, for He does not lack knowledge of how to create and how to bring into being. So this can be counted as a sixth proof.

Then He said: "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (36:82).

The author said: ("His command" means: His affair), that is, His matter and state. "When He intends a thing, He says to it, 'Be,' and it is": He does not need to bring building tools, for example, nor soldiers to help Him, nor to work with His own hand, Mighty and Majestic. Rather, He says, "Be," and it is.

As for his saying "His affair," it may be disputed, and it is said that what is meant by the command is the command of origination (amr al-takwīn); that is, His command is to say "Be" without repetition, as in His saying: "And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye" (54:50). So the command is taken as one of what? Of affairs (umūr) or one of commands (awāmir)? One of commands. He takes "command" as "one of commands," while the author wants to take it as "one of affairs." We can say: both together. We say: His affair, Mighty and Majestic, in the perfection of His power, is that He says to a thing, "Be," and it is; and His command, when He intends a thing, is to say "Be" without repetition: "It is but a single shout, and at once they are on the surface" (79:13–14).

As for "when He intends a thing": the author, may God have mercy on him, said: (that is, creates a thing, "that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is").

It is better not to restrict "a thing" to creation, but to say: when He intends a thing, creation or annihilation; that is, things either He intends to bring into existence, that is to create, or He intends to annihilate, and annihilation is destruction, not bringing into being. So it is better to leave the verse on its apparent meaning, in its generality: "a thing," whether it is creation and bringing into being or annihilation and destruction.

But what moved the author to say "creates a thing" is that the context is the proof of creation, which is bringing into being, so he restricted it to that. But if we say it is in its generality, it does not exclude creation any more than it excludes annihilation. So it is better to say: "when He intends a thing," that is, the bringing into being of a thing and its creation, or its annihilation.

Some may excuse the author by saying: annihilation contains a kind of creation, because destroying an existing thing is a creation; and for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "He who created death and life" (67:2), although death is nonexistence and extinction. "That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed" (11:7). The matter here is easy.

He said: "a thing, that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is." "Be" here: is it complete (tāmma) or incomplete (nāqisa)? Complete. This is the apparent meaning. If we take it as incomplete, the meaning becomes: "Be such-and-such," that is, transform into such-and-such. But if we take it as complete, it becomes more comprehensive, to include what Allah, Exalted, intends to transform from one thing into another, and what Allah, Exalted, intends to bring into existence from the outset. That is, "Be" means: come into being, so that it exists and comes to be; or "Be such-and-such," that is, the tall becomes short and the short becomes tall, and similar things. When we take it as complete, this is more comprehensive.

"And it is": he says, "So it is" (fa-yakūn). In a reading with a nasb (accusative), it is coordinated with "to say" (an yaqūla). Are these two Seven readings, or is one of them irregular (shādhdha)?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Why? Because he said, "In a reading," and the author's terminology, when the two readings are both Seven, is to say "and in a reading," and when one of them is irregular, he says of the irregular one: "it has been read."

In His saying "fa-yakūn" there are two readings: "fa-yakūna" and "fa-yakūnu." As for the reading with raf' (nominative), the fa here is for resumption (isti'nāf), and the clause "yakūnu" is the predicate of an omitted subject, the implied meaning being: "so He is one who becomes."

As for the reading with nasb (accusative), it is coordinated with "an yaqūla": "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says, so it becomes," He says to a thing, "Be," and it becomes.

The fa in both cases indicates sequence and immediacy; that is, the thing comes into being instantly without delay. Allah, Exalted, has explained the swiftness of this immediacy in His saying: "And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye" (54:50). The glance of the eye: there is nothing faster than it, and the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is one, like the glance of the eye.

Allah the Exalted said: "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is." This is the seventh proof.

And if this is Allah's command and affair, would it be impossible for Him, if He said to decayed bones, "Become a complete human being," for Him to do so? No. For this reason Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Nāziʿāt: "It is but a single shout, and at once they are on the surface" (79:13–14), and He said in this surah: "It will be but a single shout, and at once they will all be brought before Us" (36:53).

He said: "So exalted is He in whose hand is the dominion of all things" (36:83). "Exalted is He" (fa-subḥāna): in the sense of declaring Him far above (tanzīhan). It is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), and the verbal noun is tasbīh. It is always in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), and always in construct as well, so that even if it is detached from the construct in wording, it is still construct in meaning.

The meaning of "fa-subḥāna" is tanzīh (declaring Him free of imperfection). Free of what? We mentioned shortly before that Allah is declared free of deficiency in His attributes and of resemblance to created beings. For example, He is declared free of having a face like the face of a created being, and free of any deficiency affecting His attributes in any way. For example, the knowledge of human beings is deficient at beginning, at end, and in comprehensiveness, is it not so?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: At the beginning, because it is preceded by ignorance; at the end, because it is followed by forgetting; in comprehensiveness: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little" (17:85). But the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is complete in all these respects, at beginning, end, and comprehensiveness. He, Glorified and Exalted, knows by His eternal knowledge, which He is described with from eternity and to eternity, and He does not forget, as Moses, peace be upon him, said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets" (20:52). And His knowledge encompasses everything: "Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven" (3:5); "That you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge" (65:12).

Thus Allah, Exalted, is free of deficiency in His established attributes. Second, He is free of resemblance to created beings. Is "resemblance" (mumāthala) what we say, or "similarity" (mushābaha)? "Likeness" (mumāthala), not "similarity" (mushābaha); the difference is clear. First: likeness is the term whose negation came in the Qur'an: "There is nothing like unto Him" (42:11), and it did not say "nothing similar to His similitude," and He said: "So do not strike forth comparisons for Allah" (16:74).

Second: there are no two existing things without some kind of resemblance between them; were it not so, we would not understand anything of the attributes of Allah. For example, existence of the created and existence of the Creator have some resemblance in the basic meaning, though this differs. Knowledge: the knowledge of the Creator and the knowledge of the created have resemblance in terms of the basic meaning, but they differ. So if you negate similarity absolutely, this is a negation of existence in reality.

Third: negating similarity has come to mean, for many people, negating the attributes, because many of the people of ta'ṭīl (denial of attributes) describe those who affirm the attributes as "mushabbiha" (anthropomorphists). So if you say, "without similarity," that is, without affirming, since to them every affirmer is an anthropomorphist, the expression "negation of likeness" (nafy al-tamthīl) is better than the expression "negation of similarity" (nafy al-tashbīh) for three reasons.

We say: He is free of resemblance to created beings. The resemblance of a created being in reality is a deficiency; merely the resemblance of the Creator to the created would be considered a disparagement of the Creator.

This is "malakūt" (36:83), as the author said: "Its root is mulk, but the waw and the ta' were added for intensification." The intensification in Allah's dominion over all things: because Allah's dominion over all things is complete dominion, not preceded by non-existence, nor followed by cessation, whereas the dominion of anyone else is deficient. You did not originally own this thing, then you came to own it; and despite your owning it, this ownership is subject to cessation; moreover, your ownership of it is not absolute, so that you may do whatever you wish with it, but is restricted. As for Allah's dominion, it is complete; therefore the waw and the ta' came for intensification.

"The malakūt of all things" (36:83): that is, the dominion of all things. Can we take this as a proof? Yes, an eighth proof.

First: Allah's freedom from all deficiency. This is a proof, because His incapacity to give life to decayed bones would be a deficiency contrary to this declaration of freedom from imperfection. If it is established that He, Mighty and Majestic, is free of every deficiency, it follows that He is free of incapacity to restore these bones.

Also, "in whose hand is the malakūt of all things" (36:83) may perhaps be taken as a proof. How? Because one who owns all things with absolute ownership, intensified by the waw and the ta', is able to transform what is owned into whatever He wills. For this reason the author, may God have mercy on him, interpreted sovereignty here as power, saying: "power over all things." But his statement needs examination; rather we say: "Owner of all things." If He owns it with absolute ownership, He is able to dispose of it as He wills. How many proofs is this?

* Student: Nine.

* The Shaykh: The tenth: (He said: "And to Him you will be returned," that is, you will be returned in the Hereafter). "To Him" and not to other than Him; "you will be returned": you will be returned in the Hereafter, to be recompensed. The point of proof from this clause is that there is no return to Allah in the Hereafter except after the revival of these decayed bones. If we said He is not capable, the return to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would be negated. If the return to Allah is negated, the existence of the entire world becomes vain and playful, and this is undoubtedly contrary to the perfection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The mere fact of our return to Allah entails the capacity to revive. Is that right? And we cannot say there is no return, because if we said there is no return, the creation of creatures would be in vain; and this is absolutely impossible.

So these are ten proofs in these verses for the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to revive the dead, the revival of bones when they are decayed. And Allah is over all things powerful. That is, if we had nothing but this general sentence, "And Allah is over all things powerful," it would be sufficient to demonstrate His capacity, Glorified and Exalted, to restore, or to revive, bones when they are decayed (...).

Allah the Exalted said: "Has man not considered that We created him from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary?" (36:77), to the end. What is meant by "man"? Brother... Let us begin, I think, from "Has man not considered."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the statement that man was created from weakness, as in His saying: "Has man not considered that We created him from a drop of semen?" And so it is.

* Among its benefits also: that this man, who was created from this weak substance, rises until he becomes one of manifest contention, as in His saying: "Then he is an open adversary."

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the reproach of man for injustice. The reason: how can one who was created from this drop reach the point of being a manifest adversary of Allah, Mighty and Majestic? For man, when he considers his origin, ought to know his own worth, not to be an adversary of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: that contention in falsehood is blameworthy. The reason: the verse is given in the context of reproach, not praise. As for contention to establish truth and refute falsehood, it is praiseworthy, as in Allah's saying: "Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a manner that is best" (16:125). Without argument with the people of falsehood, truth would not be made clear nor falsehood refuted; so man must argue to establish truth and refute falsehood. But if the matter is reversed, it is blameworthy. From here we may divide argument into three categories:

Praiseworthy argument, which is commanded, either obligatorily or recommendedly; blameworthy argument, which is forbidden; and argument that is in between. The praiseworthy argument is that which is intended to establish truth and refute falsehood; this is commanded, and it is like jihad in the path of Allah, just as the mujahid is commanded to bear arms against his enemy and fight him. The student of knowledge is commanded to bear the weapon of knowledge, which is disputation in truth, to refute falsehood with it.

The second: the reverse, which is blameworthy and forbidden. God Most High says: ﴿And those who argue about God after He has been answered, their argument is void with their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment﴾ [Ash-Shura 16].

The third: something in between. That is, it is neither commanded nor forbidden, but there is no doubt that leaving it is better. This is arguing over matters that have no connection to truth or falsehood, as occurs in many gatherings with their disputes. There is no doubt that there is no good in this, and that it is from *al-mira'* (disputation, contentious argument), which a person should avoid. Then, if it leads to harm, it is forbidden, and if it leads to benefit, it is commanded.

How does it lead to harm? When argument, disputation and debate produce enmity between the debaters, or partisanship for one of them among those present, and factionalism arises from that.

It may lead to benefit, such as when the arguer is deluded by himself and thinks no one can overcome him, so you argue with him in order to break the sharpness of this self-conceit. Although nothing beneficial results from it in itself, there is benefit for others in it, namely breaking this person's pride so that he does not remain self-satisfied and haughty over others.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And he presents to Us a parable and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ [Ya-Sin 78].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who argues for falsehood brings the doubts with which he spreads his falsehood. This is shown by His words ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾, for this is a doubt that confuses the common people. He did not say only "Who will give life to bones?" but added ﴿when they are decayed﴾. How can they be brought to life after they have decayed? So the people of falsehood bring doubts in order to confuse people.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this man belittled his Lord, since he set forth parables to show Him incapable. His words ﴿And he presents to Us a parable﴾ mean that he said: "I present to you a parable with this thing that is beyond Him ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾."

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: one who opposes the truth may openly state denial without evasion. This is shown by His words ﴿Who will give life to bones?﴾. Sometimes he evades. Which of the two is easier?
* A student: The one who states openly.
* The Shaykh: The one who states openly and clearly, because his evil can be guarded against. As for the evasive one, he is in reality a danger. That is why the danger of the hypocrites to Islam is greater than the danger of the disbelievers who openly declare enmity, because the hypocrites deceive people and cannot be guarded against.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of all creation."﴾ [Ya-Sin 79].

* Among the benefits of these verses: ﴿Say, "He will give them life"﴾ means the answer to this objector. It shows the strength of persuasion in establishing proof from the speech of God, the Mighty and Majestic. That is, the strongest in presenting and clarifying proofs is the speech of God, and so it is, because the speech of God is the most eloquent and the best speech. God Most High says: ﴿And who is more truthful than God in statement?﴾ [An-Nisa' 87]. So the statement of God, the Mighty and Majestic, is without doubt the most truthful, the most complete, and the best in persuasion and establishing proof.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: inference from the greater to the lesser (*al-istidlal bil-ashadd 'ala imkan al-akhaff*). His words ﴿He who produced them the first time﴾ [Ya-Sin 79] show that He inferred the greater on the possibility of the lesser. What is the greater in our present matter? The greater is bringing them into existence the first time, and the lesser is the restoration.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the one who argues as a debater should bring up something that his opponent acknowledges, so that the proof may be established against him. How? Because He said: ﴿He who produced them the first time﴾. Does the opponent here deny that God produced them the first time? No, he does not deny it. So you should bring up what your opponent acknowledges, in order to establish the proof against him by his own acknowledgment. This is one of the etiquettes of debate, because it is closer to persuasion, and it has parallels. Among them: when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, debated the one who argued with him about his Lord, Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ He said: "I give life and cause death" [Al-Baqarah 258]. Ibrahim then turned away from that and said: "Indeed, God brings the sun from the east," which the opponent acknowledges. "So bring it from the west," and the opponent could not do that. The sum is that a person should confront his opponent from the direction that he acknowledges, in order to establish the proof against him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the complete power of God, glorified and exalted, in producing these bones the first time, because no one can create these bones ﴿O mankind, a parable has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [Al-Hajj 73]. Even though the fly does not contain strong, hard bones, if they cannot do that, they are even more incapable of what is greater.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the knowledge of God, glorified and exalted, of every creation. Is that right? Has it previously been mentioned in the tafsir whether *khalq* here means the thing created or the act of creating? We mentioned that it allows both meanings, but the meaning of the act is more likely. That is, of every creation, God has knowledge of it. It is known that one who knows the creation knows the created, as He said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [Al-Mulk 14].

* So it follows from this: the generality of God's knowledge, glorified and exalted, of every creation, that is, of every work that He makes, whether we can imagine it or not, and of every created thing, because one who knows the creation knows the created.

Then God Most High said: ﴿He who has made for you from the green tree fire, and then from it you ignite.﴾ [Ya-Sin 80].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of God, the Mighty and Majestic. From this moist, cold thing there comes forth something hot and dry. The generation of a thing from its opposite is evidence of perfect power, because it is the custom that opposites repel and never meet, and here one of them comes from the other.

* Among its benefits also: inference from the greater to the lesser, because the contrast between moist and dry, and hot and cold, is greater than the re-creation of creation, or the restoration of bones after they have decayed. So the one capable of this is capable of giving life to the dead.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of God's blessing upon us by this making, that is, by making fire from this green tree. The indication: ﴿He who has made for you﴾ [Ya-Sin 80]. Otherwise, it would suffice to say: "He who made fire from the green tree." But this is for our benefit, so there is in it a blessing from God, the Mighty and Majestic, upon His servants through this fire. God affirmed this blessing in His words: ﴿Have you considered the fire that you ignite? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producers?﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah 71-72]. No one denies the great benefits of thermal energy for creation. Its kinds, indeed its types, cannot be counted, let alone its individual instances.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: establishing a thing by reality. That is, instead of merely conveying it as a concept in the mind, we mention its actual reality. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿Then from it you ignite﴾ [Ya-Sin 80]. He explained that He made for us fire from the green tree, and this gives us a conception that God, glorified and exalted, made for us fire from the green tree that we benefit from. Then He clarified that by mentioning the actual matter, or confirmed it by mentioning the actual reality: ﴿then from it you ignite﴾ [Ya-Sin 80], which you perceive with your reality and touch with your hands.

Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes.﴾ [Ya-Sin 81].

* The benefits of this verse include: inference from the greater to the lesser, because God Most High inferred from the creation of the heavens and the earth, or from His power to create the heavens and the earth, His power to give life to bones when they are decayed.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the power and greatness of God, glorified and exalted, since He created these heavens and earth with what they contain of benefits, interests, stable and unstable celestial bodies. This is evidence of His perfect power, glorified and exalted. And in how many days did He create the heavens and the earth? In six days. Despite their greatness, vastness and immensity, God Most High said: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38], meaning, no weariness or exhaustion.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the philosophers who say that the spheres are eternal.
